en: The consecration of the sacrificial ground preceded by the expulsion of obstacles (81);
the method for the upward ascent of Śakti (328); now.
{The Tantra of the Gandharvas | Proclaimed by Śiva} | [First Chapter]

Oṃ, salutations to the Supreme Deity! I bow to the God who removes obstacles (Vināyaka), whom those of stainless soul describe as the Person beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), whose form is consciousness and supreme bliss. (Note: There is a variant reading for "vināyakam" as "vighnanāśakam," meaning "the destroyer of obstacles.")

Having approached her husband—who is immovable and devoid of the increase of virtues—she sports according to the manner of a tryst; being virtuous, she spreads joy by following the path of noble lineage.
Having gone to the base of Mount Meru, she lies there, coiled like a young serpent sleeping.
May he, who brought forth hundreds of sons, chief among whom was Murajit, protect us. || 2 ||
A king renowned as Viśvāmitra, who was supremely righteous,
having witnessed the spiritual perfection of Vasiṣṭha, performed a most difficult penance.
Without attaining perfection through austerity, he entered the northern direction;
[there he saw] the sage seated at Gaṅgādvāra, devoted to yoga.
Having saluted the illustrious Dattātreya with palms joined in reverence,
he spoke these words to him with his neck bowed in humility.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O best of sages, even after performing sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees, or even after giving all kinds of gifts to worthy recipients, I did not see [this] clearly."
Then, having performed the recitation of the Great Vidyā preceded by preparatory rites,
and having practiced extremely difficult austerities, [he sought] the means for crossing the ocean of existence.
"O knower of the single truth of all scriptures, O one established in Brahman, O ascetic rich in penance!
What shall I do, O Lord, and where shall I go? Tell me that."
Dattātreya said:
"Do not despair, O best of kings; remain steadfast in every way. That which was previously heard by us from Nandikeśvara—" (9)
Then I shall proclaim in its entirety that which is more secret than the secret, the supreme essence extracted by the Blessed One from the entire Yāmala and elsewhere. (10)
He taught to Pārvatī the twelve-thousand-verse Tantra, the sole means for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation; he also taught the Tantra known as Gandharva.
Since it is proclaimed here as the first of all tantras in its entirety,
therefore, O tiger among kings, this tantra is called Gandharva.
Nandikeśvara said:
[He saw] the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa—
five-faced, of massive body, and adorned with a mass of matted hair.
Adorned on his head with a beautiful crescent moon, decorated by a multitude of serpents, endowed with ten arms, wearing a tiger skin, and auspicious; || 14 ||
The god who bears the *kālakūṭa* poison upon his neck, adorned with a necklace of serpents,
and decorated with sacred ashes, has three eyes in each of his faces.
Endowed with fifteen eyes, resembling crystal in appearance, he also holds a spear, a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. 16.
Holding a rosary, a citron, a serpent, a hand-drum, and a bow in his right hands, and adorned with a crown of matted locks in his left [hands]. 17.
Seated upon a bull, draped in an elephant hide,
his entire mind was absorbed in the lotus-face of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Having bowed with supreme devotion, the virtuous goddess Pārvatī, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the Lord, the Supreme Ishvara.
Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, destroyer of the afflictions of devotees!
O Lord, if you are pleased with me, what indeed is that which is called Brahman? || 20 ||
"O Supreme Lord, tell me what yoga is and what the body is.
To him, the all-pervading Mahādeva, who consists of perfect bliss, spoke with a smile.
With the face known as Vāmadeva (the mantra reading "kha"), the All-pervading Lord (the Master, according to the "ka" reading) replied to his beloved. The Lord said:
"There is no gain higher than that gain; there is no happiness higher than that happiness. (22)
Ascertain that Brahman is that knowledge beyond which there is no other knowledge;
it is that visible reality beyond which there is no other visible reality, and having seen which, there is no further rebirth. (23)
That which is full in the horizontal, upward, and downward directions, which is existence-consciousness-bliss, immutable, infinite, one, and eternal—know that to be Brahman. 24.
Pārvatī said:
O Maheśvara, how can one who is bound by the noose of karma, an enjoyer devoted solely to worldly pleasures, become liberated from that very enjoyment, O God? (25)
"O Īśāna, if I am dear to you, tell me all of that.
Īśvara said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is a secret and most wonderful. (26)
"You must not say to people anything that has been told by me;
because our bodies are non-different, O lady of good vows, I shall speak to you. (27)
Regarding that which was stated by me to you—the Tantra being threefold and consisting of the three qualities—wherein is the *tāmasa* declared, and wherein is the *rājasa* as well? (28)
Therefore, the wise man should extract the *sāttvika* element from it wherever it may be found;
the *tāmasa* leads only to hell, while the *rājasa* leads to heaven, O beloved. (29)
O Śivā, they say that the fourth [state] is sattvic, bestowing liberation and being fruitless;
O Girijā, understand from me that the scriptures are indeed tāmasa.
O beloved, those Purāṇas and Tantras which are characterized by tamas lack both heaven and liberation; one should avoid them with great effort. (31)
O Goddess, it was this very matter that the son of Devakī previously asked me—
having propitiated me and performed austerities— concerning the means to liberation through worldly enjoyment.
To him, I also spoke that which cuts through doubt;
then he, in turn, spoke it to Brahmā in the form of a swan.
O Nandikeśvara, this has indeed been told by me once again;
he too became himself a creator, equal to me, O high-minded one.
Then, O fair-faced one, this tantra was proclaimed by Puṣpadanta;
he gave this most wonderful secret to the Gandharvas. (35)
And it was likewise obtained by Brahmā; therefore, O beloved, those sages [attained it].
From Aṅgiras it was obtained by Purandara, and from Bhārgava by the lord, the king of the Daityas.
In this manner, the descendants of Pulastya and Paulastya [ruled] on the surface of the earth in succession;
likewise, Namuci and other great Daityas [reigned] in the past during the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara.
They possess great retinues of strength, great heroism, and great majesty;
they delight in all dharmas, are pure, and are entirely free from all evil. || 38 ||
O Maheśānī, having heard that all those devoted to the dharma of the three Vedas, led by Indra, had been defeated, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [acted]. 39.
Having approached me and propitiated me with hymns of praise, he spoke these words in a gentle and sweet voice: || 40 ||
Brahmā said: O Omniscient One, Lord of all worlds, Destroyer of all suffering! O Lord, since this Tantra that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation has been revealed by you, || 41 ||
O Mahādeva, having obtained that [state], how could men, rākṣasas, and dānavas—who would then become bestowers of siddhi—perform the practice of the Lord’s name? (42)

O God, Śaṅkara, tell me: if all beings were to go [to liberation] through knowledge by means of the Brahman-self, what indeed would creation be? What purpose would there be even here? Tell me. (Note: *ka* is the reading in manuscript *pā*; *na* is the reading in manuscript *ā*. 43.
Having thus informed me, Brahmā departed for the assembly of the gods (the reading *brahmasadaḥ* is found in manuscript *da*).
Then, O Supreme Goddess, I went to Mount Mandara.
Then, having called those brahmins to mind and consulted with them,
he quickly summoned Nandikeśvara and stationed him at the gate.
"O auspicious one, you must protect [him] if a slayer of demons (Vighna) should arrive here.
Having thus instructed me, he entered that great, utterly solitary place. (46)
For the purpose of deluding those beings, especially the Daityas and others, various scriptures were proclaimed here by him together with the twice-born. (47)
O Great Goddess, by the mere hearing of which even the wise fall from their state, and by the contemplation of which Gotama, the bull among sages [fell]. (48)
Known as Akṣapāda, he was once intoxicated with pride and censured me;
yet, having experienced the taste of that [censure], he then sought refuge in me alone. (49)
Therefore, O Goddess, being compassionate, I myself have commanded this:
"O Sage, always recite the Vaiṣṇava Tantra and praise Viṣṇu. (50)
When Viṣṇu is propitiated, you will then attain perfection;
that which was taught by me to you is the Tantra of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. (51)
Having studied everything from Nārada, the sage then attained perfection;
for it was by me alone that the Śaiva, Pāśupata, and other systems were first proclaimed. (In the Kha manuscript, "proclaimed by me" [mayā proktam] is the reading.)

Thereafter, the great Vaiśeṣika scripture was proclaimed by Kaṇāda, following that which had been proclaimed by hundreds of Brahmins possessed by the power of Mātsya. (Note: There is a variant reading *āveśitaiḥ*.)
The Nyāya system was taught by Gotama, while Sāṃkhya was taught by Kapila;
likewise, the highly censurable Cārvāka doctrine was proclaimed by Dhiṣaṇa (an alternative reading is Dhīṣaṇa).
For the sake of destroying the Daityas, Viṣṇu, in the form of a Buddha, proclaimed the false Buddhist scriptures, such as those concerning the naked ones and the blue-robed ones. (55)

Demonstrating that the Vedic injunctions lead to what is censured by the world, it is indeed established here that the very nature of ritual action must be abandoned. (Note: *āpātya* is a variant reading for *āpātataḥ*; *karmasvarūpatyājyatādātmya* is a variant reading for *karmasvarūpatyājyatva*).

That which has fallen away from all ritual actions is called *vikarman* (or *asatkarma*, according to the reading in manuscript Kha); for indeed, all those who are devoted solely to the meaning of the scriptures proclaimed by Gautama [are so described]. 57.
O Śivā, in the past they entered the womb of jackals, rendered incompetent in all actions for the purpose of deluding the entire world. (58)
O Goddess, this great śāstra of Māyāvāda, which is non-Vedic though appearing to possess the meaning of the Vedas, was spoken by me alone for the sake of destroying the worlds. (59)
Formerly, the twice-born Jaimini composed a very extensive treatise through a doctrine devoid of God, asserting that the Veda was meaningless. (Sarvaveda Kha-pāṭha) 60.
In that very place, having corrupted the great mantras with extensive faults, I composed an expansion of the tantra filled with ambiguous passages. (61)
Then, when the body of the mantra was defiled, all the gods and goddesses became defiled, their vigor and prowess diminished. || 62 ||
Then all the inhabitants of heaven, being weak and deprived of their limbs, reached the world of Viṣṇu and reported that calamity to him. || 63 ||
Having understood the various calamities of those gods,
Viṣṇu mounted Vainateya in the presence of Nandikeśvara.
Eager to see me, he arrived but was turned away by him;
O Maheśānī, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of the World, remained there. (65)
And in order to increase his body, he commanded Vainateya;
then, standing upon the head of that fully grown lord of birds, [he increased himself].
Seeing him seated, the Blessed One, with a smiling face, spoke these words:
"Why is a dissolution being brought about by you now at an improper time? (Note: *pralaya* is the reading in the Ka manuscript).
"O Mahādeva, it is not proper; this is not right.
Īśvara said:
"The mantras of Brahmā, as well as those of the Sun and those originating from Agni, have been defiled. (68)
Likewise, some here have been corrupted by their youth, as well as some of the glories; so too, some of the great Vaiṣṇava mantras of Sarasvatī have been defiled.
The great mantras of Vaināyaka have for the most part been corrupted by me; likewise, whatever [mantras] there are in the Śakti-tantras that are accompanied by doubtful passages. (70)
The Blessed Lord said:
O Lord of the arts, adored by the world, benefactor of all beings,
O Mahādeva, desist from my command and instructions.
Ishvara said: At that time, I desisted from him by the word of Viṣṇu, the Lord of immeasurable splendor, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.

Having studied those very [works], they will all be deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu; and due to their state of being fools (or "babies," as per the *kha* reading), they will become full of doubt through a lack of conviction.
Deluded and devoted to the doctrine of causal reasoning, they will engage in disputes;
and because of their statements such as "the cause is to be proven," they will turn away [from the truth]. (74)
[Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Introduction to the Tantra," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 1 ||
[The Second Chapter] Pārvatī said:
O Mahādeva, make the Śaktitantra free from doubt.
O Lord of Gods, speak likewise of the means to liberation through worldly enjoyment.
The Lord said:
Listen now, O lady with a face like the full moon, to this great tantra which is free from doubt; it must be kept secret from those who are uninitiated (paśus).
In this work, the identity of the Supreme Self and the individual soul is established by me;
furthermore, I shall describe the supreme, attributeless form of Brahman. (3)
Listen, O pure and auspicious one; once again, I bow down with my own self to the Great Goddess, the fourth state, whose nature is Brahman.
By the mere remembrance of her, one does not sink into the ocean of existence;
having performed her worship, one should not perform the worship of another.

From remembering another [mantra], O Goddess, one incurs the curse of the Yoginīs; premature death shall befall him, and upon death, he shall go to hell. (Variant reading in manuscript Kha: "O Goddess") || 6 ||
O Goddess of the gods, what on this earth cannot be accomplished by worshipping her?
By worshipping her even once, one shall never again be a suckling at a mother’s breast.
Therefore, O auspicious and blessed Goddess, one should take refuge in the fourth [state].
Kāmeśvarī is to be known as the first, and Bhagamālinī as the second.
Vajreśvarī is the third, and Tripurasundarī is the fourth;
she is the impeller of these three deities and is established upon three feet.
She is celebrated as Tripurā; she is Kāmeśvarī, the bestower of desires. Because she grants the three cities [of the body], that Durgā is the Supreme Goddess. 10.
She is celebrated as Tripurā because of her supreme beauty;
she is meditated upon by me as well, and through her grace, I am the Lord.
And through his compassion, the lordship over the worlds was obtained;
likewise, Brahmahood was attained by Brahmā and Viṣṇuhood by Viṣṇu.
The greatness of the lords of the gods, asuras, and sages is due to his grace;
therefore, this great lore is difficult to attain within the three worlds. (13)
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, all the mantras have been revealed to me by you—those mantras of Mahātripurasundarī which were previously indicated. (14)
"Now, O Lord, make them free from doubt regarding those very matters. The Lord said: "In all undertakings, everywhere—whether Tantric or Vedic—" (15)
Lack of faith is a great defect; one should avoid it with effort.
O Goddess, faith is declared to be the cause of complete accomplishment.

Having understood that which is protective, endowed with qualities, and increases vigor—just as a pin is among jewels, or a knot is in sandalwood from the Malaya mountains. (Variant reading: *vardhaka*) || 17 ||
He was a believer, pure, self-controlled, capable (or, according to the Kha-pāṭha reading, "dexterous"), free from duality, and one who had conquered his senses;
he was most devoted to Brahman, a proponent of Brahman, identified with Brahman, and dedicated to Brahman.

One who is completely free from all violence and devoted to the welfare of all living beings is qualified for this scripture; anyone other than such a person is merely a seeker of delusion. (In the Ka-pāṭha reading: "He is qualified for this scripture"; in the Kha-pāṭha reading: "Anyone other than that is not a seeker [of truth] elsewhere. || 19 ||
It should never be spoken to an atheist, one of evil conduct, a hypocrite, nor before a beast, nor to one who is crooked or a kisser [of women]. 20.
Listen, O Goddess of beautiful countenance, to this great secret, the extraction of the mantra;
first, O you who are worshipped by heroes, the fifteenth Vidyā is described.

(“Kāma Ka Yoni E Turyyasvara Ī Purandara La Bhuvaneśī Hrīṃ” is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa. Then there is Kāmadeva, followed by Yoni, Turyyasvara (the reading is "Tu"), Purandara, and Bhuvaneśī; thereafter, it is adorned with five syllables (the reading is "Pañcavarṇa"). || 22 ||
O Goddess, this is that Vāgbhava, which bestows the state of mastery over speech;
having recited this great seed-syllable, what on earth cannot be accomplished? (23)
Within three days, however, one should place [the mark] upon the tongue of the child with honey and white dūrvā grass using a golden probe.
One should indeed write this Vāgbhava-kūṭa in another birth;
he alone shall become a scholar, and certainly not a fool. (The reading "bhūtvā" is found in manuscript *kha*.)

O Dear One, having placed his hand upon the head of even a fool, one should recite this *vāgbhavakūṭa*—which is proven effective—one hundred and eight times. (Note: *etad* is the reading in the Kha manuscript. 26.
O Maheśānī, he too indeed composes verses; of this there is no doubt.
He is one who discerns the essence of words, meanings, and poetic figures, possessing keen insight into the meaning of words and sentences.
O Goddess, by placing [the mantra] upon the tongue, even a mute becomes a skilled poet;
O beautiful one, what is the use of saying more here, or even of speaking at length? (28)
One who rivals Vāgīśa with his words becomes omniscient on earth;
yet Vāgīśa himself becomes mute, like another Vācaspati. || 29 ||

(Śiva, Ha, Candra, Sa, Kāma, Ka, Vyoma, Ha, Purandara, La, Lajjā, Hrī—this is the *kūṭa* of Kāmarāja. O Supreme Goddess, having extracted Śiva and Candra, one should extract Kāma, Vyoma, and Purandara;
then, O Beloved, one should extract the seed-syllable of Lajjā. (30)
O auspicious lady, this six-syllabled Kāmarāja is adorned with all [beauty].
[The Śaktikūṭa is: Candra, Kāma, Indra, Mahāmāyā, and Hrīḥ. Thus, Candra, Kāma, and Indra, followed by Mahāmāyā. (31)
O lady of excellent hips, this seed-syllable of Śakti is endowed with the letters of the Vedas;
she is this Trikūṭā Mahāvidyā, the Great Tripurasundarī. (32)
The Goddess is the essence of all sacred fords, possessing the form of all the gods;
she consists of all the scriptures, is pure, and is entirely free from all defects. || 33 ||
This Vidyā, known as Kāmarāja, is the personification of the four Vedas, the bestower of all prosperity, and the granter of the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (34)
A science equal to this is difficult to find in the three worlds;
O Pārvatī, such is the power and the fourth state of this very science. (35)

In the case of the very same *vidyā* mentioned above, if one omits *e* and *ī* from the beginning of the *vāgbhava* [kūṭa] and places the pair "Śiva" (*ha*) and "Indu" (*sa*) at the start, it becomes the *vidyā* worshipped by Lopāmudrā. Having abandoned [the previous vowels] at the beginning and placed Śiva (*ha*) and Indu (*sa*) at the front, Lopāmudrā is revealed.

[The sequence is: *māra*, *ka*, *yoni*, *kāma*, *śakra*, *īśvarī*, *hrīḥ*. By placing these in the position of the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* and joining them with the *kāmarāja-śakti* as before, it is the *śāmbhavī-vidyā*. *Māra-bīja*, then *yoni*, *kāma*, *śakra*, and likewise *īśvarī*. (36)
As before, there is Kāmarāja and likewise Śaktikūṭa;
this Vidyā, possessing vitality, bestows success and brings the three worlds under control. (37)

Out of affection for you, O Great Goddess, this has been revealed by me; this is declared to be the Śāmbhava [system]. Listen now to the Śākta [system] hereafter. (Reading from manuscript *ra*) || 38 ||

By joining "Śakti," "Maheśa," "Ha," "Kāma," "Indra-bīja," and "Mahāmāyā" with "Hrīṃ" to the "Vāgbhava" portion of the previously mentioned Vidyā, the Śākta Vidyā is produced. "Śakti," "Maheśa," and "Kāma," followed by the "Indra-bīja," then "Mahāmāyā," and thereafter the other [portion] as before. (39)
"O blessed lady, these three sciences are difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
The Goddess said: "The great science of sixteen syllables, which brings the three worlds under one's control... (40)
"Now tell me, O Īśāna, if I am dear to you.
Īśvara said:
"Listen, O Goddess, to the Great Vidyā which consists of sixteen syllables. (41)
O Supreme Goddess, that which is Bhuvaneśvarī in the first world of this very Vidyā is she herself in the form of sixteen syllables.

Having placed the seed-syllable *ramā* in the place of *māyā*, the previously mentioned sixteen-syllable *vidyā* becomes [the mantra] joined with *hrīṃ* at its beginning; or else, when preceded by the seed-syllable *ramā*, it likewise becomes the sixteen-syllable [mantra].
This *vidyā* is the bestower of boons, the giver of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), and the bestower of the abode of Kubera. (The reading *dyāt ka* is an alternative. || 43 ||
This knowledge is a wish-fulfilling gem, difficult to obtain even in the three worlds;
it is adorned by the Vedas and other branches, and is the bestower of liberation. || 44 ||
In the same way, one should likewise extract the seed-syllable of Mahāmāyā (or *kha*, according to the Kha recension), the seed-syllable of Ramā, and likewise the fifteen-syllable vidyā-mantra. (45)

This very [fifteen-syllable mantra] just mentioned becomes a seventeen-syllable vidyā when joined with the syllables *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ* at the beginning by means of *māyā* and *ramā*. This seventeenth vidyā is the manifest embodiment of the waking state.
Then the Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, tell me next of the supreme Rājarājeśvarī. (46)
The sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā, which brings the three worlds under control, the mother of all mantras, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman. (47)
Īśvara said: O beloved, he who knows the Vidyā of the Queen of the Lords of Kings, as well as her armor (kavaca), on the surface of the earth— he is a god, not a mere human.
O Pārvatī, listen as the Vidyā of the Queen of Queens is described:
having extracted the seed-syllable of Ramā, one should apply the seed-syllable of Māyā. (49)
Having written the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), immediately thereafter the seed-syllable of speech (VĀG),
endowed with the fourteenth vowel (AU) and joined with the moon (the letter I) and the pair of dots (the visarga).
O Maheśvarī, O Parameśvarī, one should first extract the Praṇava, then Bhavānī, Īśānī, and Ramā; thereafter, one should extract the fifteen-syllable mantra.

O Supreme Goddess, having written the previously mentioned five seed-syllables (*bīja*) in reverse order, one should enclose [the mantra] within them; this is the Vidyā consisting of sixteen peaks (*kūṭa*). [The mantra is as follows: *Ramā* (*śrīṃ*), *Māyā* (*hrīṃ*), *Kāmabīja* (*klīṃ*), *Vāgbīja* (*aiṃ*) endowed with the fourteenth vowel (*auṃ*) and the *visarga* (*sauḥ*), the *Praṇava* (*oṃ*), *Bhuvaneśānī* (*hrīṃ*), *Ramā* (*śrīṃ*), and then the fifteen-syllable [mantra]. Enclosed by the five seed-syllables in reverse order, it becomes the fourth Vidyā of sixteen peaks. || 52 ||
This fourth [state] is the Great Vidyā, whose nature is solely the Self;
this sixteen-syllabled Great Vidyā is declared to be the supreme Śrīvidyā. (53)

Even with thousands of millions of mouths and hundreds of millions of tongues, this sixteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā could never be fully described. (Variant reading: "I am able to [describe] the sixteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā.")
This sixteen-syllable great vidyā, hidden in all tantras, has been revealed by me out of affection for you, O Great Goddess, to the Gandharva. (55)
[Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Extraction of the Varieties of Vidyās," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 2 ||
[The Third Chapter] The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Lord of the world, destroyer of the afflictions of devotees!
The fifth Vidyā, consisting of five times five syllables, which grants all desires. || 1 ||
"Now, O Īśāna, tell me the complete [mantra] that destroys all sins.
Īśvara said:
"The auspicious five-peak (pañcakūṭa) knowledge consisting of five parts is difficult to attain."
Bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, pure, granting happiness, and destroying suffering—listen, O Goddess, I shall explain how that Supreme One is to be meditated upon. (3)
By the pure practitioner, devoted to the Guru and possessed of keen intellect,
the Goddess [is realized as] this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings, consisting of fivefold nature.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well;
Earth is the power Brāhmaṇī, and Water is likewise Nārāyaṇī. (5)
Tejas is the Śakti of Rudra, Rudrāṇī is that of Vāyu, Īśvarī is that of Īśa,
and Māheśvarī is the Śakti of Maheśvara, who is likewise Ākāśa.
Consisting of the five deities, there are five pentads of the fifth power;
that power which belongs to all beings and has the form of universal consciousness.

She alone is the fifth Vidyā, whose form is the support of the universe; she indeed is the entire world, she alone is the supreme *kalā*. (It should be understood that "she" [sā] refers to the state of the probandum, as it does hereafter.)
O Goddess, there exists nothing higher than that which is outside of it;
within the peak-syllable consisting of the twenty-five principles, there are five deities.
First, Kāmeśvarī is to be known; then the auspicious Vajreśvarī;
the third is Bhagamālā, and the fourth is Tripurasundarī.
The supreme power (kalā) to be meditated upon belongs to the illustrious Tripurasundarī;
she alone is the fifth energy (śakti), whose nature is that of the Supreme Brahman.
That which is the Great Cause of the worlds, whose nature is supreme bliss—
that is the form of that Goddess, which is devoid of rising and setting.
In her gross state she possesses a gross form, and in her subtle state she possesses a subtle form;
through the distinction between the gross and the subtle, she is the form of the cause of the universe.
That Lord who is the Sovereign of the Universe, who stands pervading the entire universe—
he himself is the Goddess Viśveśvarī, established as the all-pervasive one.
She is eternal and of the nature of bliss, bestowing great bliss and purity;
she consists of the joy of her own essential nature and is the embodiment of supreme bliss. (15)
How much more so when she exists in the form of power, having the nature of the Supreme Brahman;
from her, creation arises again and again, and she is always being dissolved.
Therefore, Śakti is primary, and this entire world is pervaded by Śakti;
[he who knows this] always has a heart full of bliss and has reached the further shore of non-dual bliss. || 17 ||
Endowed with the conduct of the observance, a possessor of enjoyments devoted to enjoyment, his soul always purified by knowledge, devoted to the guru, and having conquered his senses; || 18 ||
Having assumed the form of a Gandharva, one should worship the fifth [note];
for he who knows the fifth is the most excellent being upon the earth. (19)
Falling from his status due to a curse, he became a Gandharva rather than a human by the turn of fate—
he who knows the supreme Great Vidyā consisting of five peaks.
O Goddess, he shall become a sky-walker within six months; of this there is no doubt.
With his soul eternally purified by knowledge, that man shall partake in liberation.
If he knows the fifth [syllable], he attains liberation through enjoyment;
that practitioner who knows this five-times-five syllabled lore [attains it]. || 22 ||
He is to be worshipped in all the worlds; he is a god and not a human being (the variant *mānava* is found in the Kha manuscript).
Among the peaks, Trikūṭa alone is the one peak, consisting of fifteen [parts]. || 23 ||
The five-times-five-syllabled Vidyā, consisting of three peaks and five peaks,
is established in the form of letters as the twenty-five principles (tattvas).
In the Trikūṭa of one color, there are five deities; in the Trikūṭa [of other colors], fifteen deities are proclaimed. || 25 ||
By means of the twenty-five principles (tattvas) and the fivefold [arrangement] within the three peaks (trikūṭa), there are seventy-five prior [sections]; by that, their total is three hundred.
The supreme Vidyā Saubhāgyasundarī is endowed with five peaks;
in the form of letters, that Goddess is the very foundation of the universe.
From the Imperishable (akṣara) this entire world, both moving and unmoving, has arisen;
the Imperishable is the eternal, single-syllabled Brahman, the supreme state. (Having recited the imperishable mantra even once, one becomes fit for union with Brahman. || 28 ||
The single-syllable Brahman, situated between the beginning and the end of the *kūṭas*, should be recited;
having recited it, one accomplishes everything. What fruit is there in extensive recitation? (Variant reading in manuscript *kha*: "by means of the recitation"). 29.
That alone is the supreme secret, the bestower of great good fortune;
that alone is the five-peaked [mantra], the fifth [vowel] by means of the five principles.

Kāma joined with Viṣṇu (ka), endowed with A (a), Śakti (e), Māyā (ī), Śakra (la), and Mahāmāyā (hrī)—this is the first Vāgbhava-kūṭa of the fifth Vidyā. O Pārvatī, Kāma joined with Viṣṇu, Śakti, Māyā, and Śakra;
thereafter, O Goddess, one should apply the seed-syllable of Mahāmāyā at the end. (31)

(The three middle peaks of Kāmarāja: Taking *śiva* (*ha*), then *śakti* (*sa*), then *kāma* (*ka*), and adding *bhū* (*la*), *vyoma* (*i*), and *anala* (*ra*), etc., one obtains *hrīṃ*; this is the first peak of Kāmarāja. Having extracted the seed-syllable of Śiva, then the seed-syllable of Śakti after it, and beneath that the seed-syllable of Kāma, joined with Earth (*bhū*), Sky (*vyoma*), and Fire (*anala*). (32)
The first peak-syllable of Kāmarāja, conjoined with the fourth vowel and adorned with the half-moon and the bindu, is worshipped by the three worlds. (33)
I shall proclaim the central peak situated in the middle of Kāmarāja;
O Goddess, it is most secret, yet out of affection I shall speak of it alone. (34)

(Viyat joined with Viṣṇu and preceded by the letter A; then Mādana, Ka, Ha, Sa, Ha, Indra, La, Viṣṇu, Pada, and so forth, ending with Hrīḥ—this is the middle peak-syllable of Kāmarāja. Viyat joined with Viṣṇu, followed by Devī and Mādana;
below that, one should extract the seed-syllable of Haṃsa and the seed-syllable of Indra. (35)
One should extract the seed-syllable of Māyā conjoined with fire (Ra) at the station of Viṣṇu (the letter Sa);
this is declared to be the middle peak-syllable, which bestows great good fortune. || 36 ||
I shall now proclaim the fourth [kūṭa], O Goddess, which is very difficult to obtain; listen!

(By means of *kāma*, *ka*, *śiva*, *ha*, *vāyu*, *ya*, *indra*, *la*, *viyat*, and so forth, one arrives at *hrīṃ*; this is the third *kūṭa* of Kāmarāja. O Great Goddess, the seed-syllable of Kāma follows, and after that, the seed-syllable of Śiva. (37)
Below that, one should apply the seed-syllable of Vāyu (ya), joined with the seed-syllable of Indra (ra), conjoined with Viyat (ha) and Vahni (ra), and adorned with the fourth vowel (ī). (38)
The fourth peak-syllable, joined with the half-moon and the bindu, is supreme.
O Goddess, listen as I proclaim the Peak of Śakti, which is very difficult to obtain. (39)

Having heard which, all practitioners obtain the highest liberation. (By means of the sequence beginning with *prāṇo ha kāma ka indra la devī sa sāntam*, one obtains the *hrīṃ* syllable, the peak of Śakti. Having extracted the seed-syllable of Prāṇa, one should extract the seed-syllable of Kāma. (40)
Likewise, O Goddess, one should apply the seed-syllable of Indra (I) in sequence;
it is joined with the letter 'sa' (the end), conjoined with fire (the letter 'ra'), and united with the fourth vowel (the letter 'ī'). (41)
One should extract the Śakti-kūṭa joined with the Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā;
O fair-faced one, its fruit and the specific means of its accomplishment [shall now be told]. (42)
"It must be told by me, O Great Queen (what is the reading?). O Queen, it is now told in brief:
this knowledge is a great knowledge, more secret than the secret, O Beloved. (43)
She is the giver of enjoyments, the giver of liberation, and the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires and aims;
the first peak-syllable is Vāgbhava, while the fifth is the Śakti peak-syllable.
O Goddess, the three middle peaks are the enchanting Kāmarāja;
I shall explain that Kāmarāja according to its various peak-variants—listen to that. 45.
O Goddess, having known this, one should accomplish it, even that which is impossible on earth;
the first peak-syllable (kūṭa) bestows good fortune and great prosperity. (46)
By merging the three peaks with a single peak, [one attains] the great and supreme Kāmarāja (or Dampāṭha according to the reading);
thus, by means of these very three peaks, she is Nityā Saubhāgyasundarī. 47.
In one place she is with five peaks, and in another she is eternally endowed with three peaks; she is difficult to find in all the worlds, a woman beautiful with great good fortune.
Having recited the middle [syllable] of the middle peak of this very Vidyā, one becomes filled with bliss and shall obtain all desires. (49)
This knowledge-mantra named Svapnavatī is renowned throughout the three worlds; it is a mantra that effects attraction and brings delight to the entire world. (50)
And I shall proclaim the means of accomplishment by which the attraction of women and men in heaven, on earth, and in the underworld may be achieved. (51)
Women are especially submissive, and [by them] the three worlds are brought under control;
this lore, served by the Gandharvas, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 52.
This vidyā brings great wealth and bestows great sovereignty;
likewise, by its grace, the accomplishment known as Madhumatī arises.
He can become large and small, as well as visible and invisible; he can enter the bodies of others and certainly assume any form at will. (54)
The form of men, the form of women, and whatever other supreme forms there may be—all that is the supreme form of her alone; of this there is no doubt. (55)
Beauty, contentment, as well as nourishment, faith, modesty, compassion, pity, fortitude, peace, as well as prosperity, accomplishment, intellect, understanding, and forgiveness; || 56 ||
She is Mahāmāyā, the great intellect, the great knowledge, and the source of great prosperity;
she is the Vidyā who effects the greatest greatness, the absolute Brahmavidyā alone.
If a practitioner performs the rite at night in a cremation ground on a day of the great elements, what on earth cannot be accomplished by means of a thousand repetitions? || 58 ||
The man who recites this fifth supreme vidyā, the Mother of the Three Worlds, is a lord of the gods, like another Mahādeva. (59)
The one whose nature is enjoyment attains experience solely through various enjoyments;
he partakes of manifold pleasures and even diverse kinds of flavors.
That which they call the "Imperishable" (akṣara) in the world brings abundant happiness;
one should meditate upon it in an empty house or a monastery, or otherwise recite the Supreme [Mantra]. 61.
There shall be attraction for him, and from that he shall obtain every desire;
his heart possessing the first bliss, he becomes an enjoyer of the second.
One should desire the third through enjoyment, and the fourth as well;
the fifth is the first merit, which brings about supreme accomplishment of the mantra.
But one should always especially enjoy and desire the fifth;
through the practice of the fifth, the hero obtains the fruit of worship. (54)
One should smear the rosary with substances produced from a *kuṇḍa* and a *golaka*, with *svayaṃbhū* flowers, and with *rocanā* and saffron.
Having adorned the rosary with camphor, agallochum, musk, yellow pigment, and saffron, one should perform the consecration according to the prescribed rite.
Having repeatedly soaked clean, unbroken grains with those liquids,
and having purified them with water, one should then place them into the vermilion.
The man who worships at night upon a pure cloth-painting,
having recited the mantra over a rosary, shall obtain all his desires.
Having brought forth a divine maiden, a woman in the full bloom of youth, nourished by the root-mantra, virtuous, and possessing a beautiful smile; (69)
One whose heart is always full of bliss, devoid of pity and shame, devoted to the guru, well-attired, and intent upon the worship of the deity. (70)
The practitioner of mantra should place the five arrows of desire upon her body;
the practitioner of mantra should place the five peaks and should place the fifty mātṛkās.
Having taken up a divine garland, the practitioner who has conquered his senses should then recite the Svapnāvatī mantra one thousand times.
By this very procedure, there shall be a great attraction;
one should worship the Supreme Goddess in her temple of passion (Madanāgāra). 73.

(The definition of that [mudrā] is as follows: "Having placed the middle fingers in the center, with the little fingers and thumbs pressed together, and having made the index fingers like staffs, with the ring fingers upon the middle fingers—this mudrā, called Kṣobhā, causes the agitation of all. Having bound this Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā, the excellent practitioner should cause the *yoni* to vibrate and contemplate her as being the very form of Kāmeśvarī. || 74 ||
Meditating upon himself as being of the very nature of Kāmeśvara,
the practitioner, remaining himself unshaken, performs the fifth [rite].
Its flower must be guarded with great effort by oneself [as previously stated];
and one should worship it every day with betel, incense, and flowers. (76)
Having diligently provided satisfaction with various kinds of flavorful foods and drinks, one should bring her contentment with garments, ornaments, jewelry, and other such things.
Just as at the proper time, that flower itself, having assumed the form of a cowherd girl,
took hold of that very *svayambhū* flower with great effort.
The supreme practitioner obtains the divine self-arisen flower, which is difficult to find even throughout the three worlds; he shall accomplish on earth that which is hard to achieve.
One should always worship with *svayambhū* flowers together with unbroken grains (*akṣata*);
by reciting the *Svapnāvatī* mantra, swift attraction will occur. (80)
The deities, the planets, the nāgas, the dānavas, and those who are rākṣasas—
as well as all kings and women— indeed become eternally submissive.
Whoever performs worship daily with self-arisen flowers and recites [the mantra] over a divine garland shall obtain all their desires.
Pārvatī said:
"In the past, you also taught me the knowledge of Ekādaśī;
yet because it was not practiced by me, I have consequently fallen under the power of death. (83)
"I now wish to hear the knowledge that is the most essential of the essential.
The Lord said: "The eleven-syllable mantra of Bhairavī was proclaimed in ancient times. (84)
Now, for the sake of your pleasure, I shall describe another supreme [vidyā]:

*Hrīḥ*—beginning with *mādana* (ka), *gotrabhit* (la), and *sānta* (sa)—is the *vāgbhava*. *Hrīḥ*—beginning with *brahmā* (ka), *gagana* (ha), *śakra* (la), and *nakulīśa* (kṣa)—is the *kāmarāja*. *Hrīḥ*—beginning with *śakti* (sa), *mādana* (ka), *śakra* (la), and *hara* (ha)—is the *śaktikūṭa*. This is the eleven-syllable *bhairavī* vidyā. *Mādana* (ka), *gotrabhit* (la), *sānta* (sa), possessing the letter *ra*, *māyā* (ī), and the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). (85)
O Supreme Goddess, the Vāgbhava [Bīja] is joined with Nāda and Bindu;
it consists of Brahmā, Gaganas (the letter Ha), Śakra (the letter La), Nakulīśa (the letter Ra), Anala (the letter Ra), and Śaśin (the letter Sa). 86.
One should extract Māyā and Bindu together with Sanāda as Kāmarāja;
[then] Śakti, Mādana, Śakra, Hara, Vahni, and Indu, along with Māyā. (87)
Pervaded by the resonance of the *kalā*, this mantra is said to be the granter of desires;
it must not be given to just anyone, nor even to a kinsman, O Pārvatī.
Having reflected, Manu said that it should be given to a wise eldest son. || 88 ||
[Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Application for Extracting the Fifth Vidyā," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 3 ||
[The Fourth Chapter] Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, benefactor of the worlds!
O Lord, why has that which was previously indicated not been revealed? || 1 ||
O Bull-bannered Lord, if you are pleased with me, please tell me the auspicious armor (kavaca) of the Goddess Tripura, the Queen of the Queens of Kings.
Īśvara said:
"O Great Goddess, though you have been restrained again and again for hundreds of thousands of lakhs of times, you ask once more due to the nature of women."
This armor, which grants all desires, is extremely difficult to obtain and is a profound secret;
nevertheless, O fair-faced one, I shall speak of it today out of affection for you.
Named Trailekyamohana, it is difficult to find in the three worlds;
it generates all prosperity and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O beloved, it is by holding this that Viṣṇu slew the most terrible Dānavas,
Brahmā expands the worlds, and I am the destroyer.
Even Kubera, the lord of wealth, is one of the guardians of the quarters;
O Pārvatī, I declare that there is no secret more profound than this—indeed, you should know it.
O fair-faced one, this is the essence found within the Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas:
that one's head, along with one's sons, wife, and so forth, should never be given away under any circumstances. (Note: "head" [śiraḥ] is the reading in the Vopadeva manuscript.)
This secret armor must not be given away, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat.
Listen, O lady beautiful in every limb, to this divine and supreme armor.
Śiva is the seer (ṛṣi) of the armor (kavaca) of the Goddess Rājarājeśvarī; the meter (chandas) is Virāṭ, and the deity (devatā) is Mahātripurasundarī. || 10 ||
The *haṃsa* is the power (*śakti*), the supreme seed-syllable (*parā-bīja*) is the seed, and the *ramā*-seed is the pin (*kīlaka*);
their application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. || 11 ||
May Tripurā, who is threefold, protect me for the accomplishment of all goals; may Bālā, the bestower of the attainment of all goals, protect my face with the syllables Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ. 12.

May the Great Goddess Śrīmat Tripurabhairavī, [with the mantra] *hasraiṃ* (or *haisra hesrau*, according to another reading), *(-)hasakalarī(-)*, and *hasrauḥ*, protect my throat; may Maheśānī Mahātripurasundarī protect my heart. 13.
May the Goddess Kamalā, the supreme sovereign, who is the sixteen-syllable mantra of the Queen of Queens of Kings and the source of great prosperity, protect me always in the aperture of Brahmā.
May the Goddess, daughter of the King of Mountains, protect my head eternally;
may the seed-syllable of Kāma protect my forehead, and the seed-syllable of Vāc protect the region of my throat.
May *sauḥ* protect my [heart] (or, according to the Kha-pāṭha, my head), and likewise may the *praṇava* protect my sides;
may the beloved of Śambhu always protect my right and left arms (or, according to the Kha-pāṭha, my forearms).
May Viṣṇupriyā always protect [me] at both wrists;
may Pārvatīśa protect the hands, and Nakṣatravallabha protect the eyes. (17)
May Ratipriya protect the ears; may Śakra always protect the nose;
and may the supreme goddess Pārvatī always protect the region of the back. 18.

Hsauḥ (or *heso* according to another reading): May [the Lord] protect both the inhalation and the exhalation, bestowing supreme accomplishment; may Kāma always protect [her] in the sphere of desire, and Pinākin in the sphere of the Liṅga. 19.
May Sarvasa protect the entire earth; may Hṛllekhā protect the heart;
may Viṣṇupriyā protect the breasts; and may that Destroyer of Cities (Sa-purāntaka) protect the belly. || 20 ||
May Vajradhara protect the eyes; may Māyā indeed protect the belly;
may Sauḥ protect the pair of feet; and may Aiṃ protect the seat of the tongue. || 21 ||
O fair-faced one, may the syllable *klīṃ* always protect [the area] between the teeth and the lips;
may Bhuvaneśvarī protect every limb from the head down to the feet.
O Supreme Goddess, may the beloved of Hari protect all those places that are devoid of protection and lacking in armor. (The reading "pātu" is found in manuscript Kha. 23.
May Vāgbhava protect the base, O beloved, and may Kāmarāja protect the heart;
likewise, may Śaktikūṭa protect the middle of the eyebrows, O Pārvatī. (24)
May the three peaks protect the head; may the one consisting of all mantras protect the forehead. May this [mantra] of twenty-eight syllables always protect the circumference of the face.
This sixteenth [digit] is the Great Vidyā, indeed the exclusive knowledge of Brahman;
she is the Goddess who bestows both enjoyment and liberation, whose nature is solely the Self. (26)
May Kāmeśvarī protect [me] on the forehead, and Bhagamālinī on the face;
may the ever-great Klinnā (or Dīptā) eternally protect the right eye.
May Bhīruṇḍā protect the left eye, and Vahnivāsinī indeed the ear;
may Mahāvajreśvarī protect the region of the left ear. (28)
May Maheśvarī Śivadūtī protect [me] in the right nostril;
may Tvaritā, the bestower of all siddhis, protect [me] in the left nostril. (29)
May Kulasundarī always protect me on the right cheek;
may Trailokyavimalā protect the region of the left cheek. (30)
May she who has a blue banner on her upper lip protect me; may Vijayā protect my lower lip;
and may the goddess Sarvamaṅgalā always protect my upper teeth.
May she who possesses a garland of flames always abide in the region of the lower teeth;
O Pārvatī, may the multiform one protect me eternally upon my head.
May that Mahātripurasundarī, who is the foremost among these [energies] and is the sixteenfold Śoḍaśī, the Supreme Goddess, always protect my mouth. (33)
May those three kinds of gurus always protect the region of the back;
may the supreme goddess Tripurā always protect the two feet. (34)
May the Goddess Tripureśvarī always protect me at the region of the knees;
may the Goddess Tripurasundarī always protect me at the two thighs. 35.
May the Goddess Tripuravāsinī always protect me at the region of the hips;
and may Tripurāśrī always protect me eternally at the secret place. || 36 ||
May the goddess Tripuramālinī always protect [me] at the mūlādhāra;
may Tripurasiddhā protect [me] at the navel, and Tripurāmbā always [protect me] at the heart.
May Mahātripurasundarī always protect [the practitioner] at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
One should place the seed-mantras of these [deities] in the aforementioned locations. || 38 ||
May Buddha protect me in the midst of the assemblies of heretics;
may Brahmā [protect me] in the assembly of Brahmās; and may Śiva [protect me] for the sake of attaining yoga-siddhi. (39)
May Bhāskara protect me in knowledge, and may the Lord Nārāyaṇa protect me in liberation;
that power of all beings which is celebrated as both Vidyā and Avidyā. (40)
May that Śakti always protect [me] in the abundance of wife, sons, and wealth;
may Aṇimā protect in the west, and may Laghimā protect in the north. || 41 ||
May Mahimā protect you from the east; may Īśitā protect you from the south. May Vaśitā, the bestower of the perfection of *prākāmya*, protect you in the abode of Vāyu, the northeast. || 42 ||
May the Siddhi of Enjoyment protect [me] in the southeast; may the Siddhi of Desire protect in the southwest;
may the Siddhi of Attainment protect below; and may the Siddhi of Liberation protect above. (43)
May Brahmāṇī protect me during the two twilights; may Māheśvarī protect me by day;
may Kaumārī protect me at midday; and may Śakravallabhā protect me at night. (44)
May Vaiṣṇavī, the bestower of all perfections, protect [me] during the Brāhma-muhūrta;
may Vārāhī protect [me] at midnight; and may Cāmuṇḍā protect [me] during the battle with enemies.
May Mahālakṣmī, the Great Sovereign, protect me always with great zeal;
may Saṃkṣobhiṇī protect my head, and may Drāviṇī protect my heart.
Ākarṣiṇī is at the crest-lock (śikhā), while [the mantra] in the armor (kavaca) grants subjugation;
likewise, Unmādinī is at the eyes, and Mahāṅkuśā is on all limbs.
May Trikhaṇḍā protect my two arms; may she who is the nature of the seed-syllables protect my seeds; may Khecarī protect my feet, and Yonimudrā protect me from all sides.
May she who has the form of attracting desire always protect [us] in the rite of attraction;
may she who has the form of attracting the intellect protect [us] in the drawing away of the intellects of others. || 49 ||
May she who draws forth the ego always protect me within the ego;
may she whose form is the attraction of sound protect me in the act of attracting sound.
May she whose form is the attraction of touch protect me in the act of touching;
may she whose form is the attraction of form protect me in the drawing away of another's form.

May the Supreme Goddess, who takes the form of the attraction of taste, protect me always in the realm of taste; and she who takes the form of the attraction of smell, may she protect me always in the realm of smell.
May she, whose form is the attraction of the mind, protect me in the rite of summoning;
may she, whose form is the attraction of fortitude, always protect me in the practice of steadfastness. 53.
One should employ the form of summoning mindfulness in the rite of summoning knowledge,
and one should always employ the form of summoning the name in the utterance of the name.
May she who takes the form of drawing forth seeds protect me in the planting of all seeds;
may she who takes the form of drawing forth the supreme life-force protect me in the drawing forth of the self.
May Amṛtākarṣaṇī protect [me] always in the act of making things nectar;
may Śarīrākarṣaṇī protect [me] always in the guarding of the body. || 56 ||
May Anaṅgakusumā protect me in every rite from the front;
may the Supreme Goddess Anaṅgamekhalā protect me from behind. (57)
May Maheśvarī, Anaṅgamadanā, protect me from the left;
may she who is afflicted by the passion of Anaṅgamadana always protect me from the right. (58)
O beloved, may Anaṅgarekhā always protect me from above, and may the supreme goddess Anaṅgaveginī protect me from below. (59)
Likewise, may Anaṅgāṅkuśā always protect me in the cardinal directions at all times;
may Anaṅgamālinī protect me in the intermediate directions at all times.
May the Sovereign of the World, Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, protect me from above;
may Sarvavidrāviṇī protect me from below, and Sarvavikarṣaṇī in all directions.
May the Power that brings delight to all protect me in the intermediate directions;
may the Supreme Goddess, who deludes all beings, protect me on every side. 62.
May she who causes the paralysis of all things protect me within and without;
likewise, may she who causes the expansion of all things protect me eternally in the ether.
May she who brings all under control protect me in Pātāla,
and may she who causes delight to all protect me always in the world of the gods.
May the power that intoxicates all protect me upon the surface of the earth; may the power that accomplishes all aims protect me in the abode of the hosts of spirits. (65)
May she who fulfills all prosperity protect [us] in the abode of the Siddhas,
and may she who consists of all mantras protect [us] in the home of the Rākṣasas and Yakṣas.
May the Goddess, who brings an end to all dualities and bestows all perfections, protect the city of Rājagṛha forever, even in the abode of the Asuras. 67.
May she who bestows all prosperity protect me in my own home amidst every abundance;
may she who makes everything dear protect me at all times throughout all worlds. (68)
May the Goddess, the performer of all auspiciousness, who grants all desires, protect me at all times in every auspicious rite and in all undertakings. (69)

May she who bestows all sovereignty protect me always in prosperity; may she who liberates from all suffering and quiets all death protect my abode eternally. (Note: *sarvaduḥkhavimocinī* is an alternative reading for *sarvaiśvaryapradāyinī*.)
May she who destroys all obstacles always protect me at the commencement of every undertaking;
and may she who is beautiful in every limb protect me during the time of physical adornment.
May she who bestows all good fortune protect [me] at the time of all auspiciousness; may she who is all-knowing protect [me] in the home, and she who consists of all power protect [me] in battle. 72.
On the path, she bestows all sovereignty; in the water, she consists of omniscience;
and everywhere among all diseases, she is the destroyer of all ailments.
May Prabalā, whose nature is the support of all, protect me on the mountain;
may she who removes all sins protect me at all times in all actions. 74.
May the Goddess, who brings joy to all, protect [us] amidst the sphere of various evils; she whose very nature is universal protection, may she protect us from the fear of all enemies. (75)
May Vaśinī, who bestows all desired fruits in all ritual acts involving volition, protect [us] in rites of subjugation; may Kāmeśī protect us in the act of paralyzing.
May Modinī protect me in enchantment; may she protect me in the rite of purification and expulsion. May Aruṇā protect me in debate, and Jayinī in the act of disputation. || 77 ||
May Sarveśvarī protect in matters of desire, Kaulinī in the rite of piercing, and [the goddesses] in causing yawning; O Maheśvarī, may the five arrows always protect [me]. 78.
May the bow protect me in the rite of delusion, while the noose protects me in the act of subjugation;
may that which consists of great splendor protect me in paralyzing, as well as the goad.
May Sarvajñā protect the heart, and she who is eternally insatiable protect the head;
may Anādibodhikā eternally protect the region of the crest-lock.
May Svatantrā protect me in the armor; may Nityāmaluptikā protect my eyes; and may she who grants supreme accomplishment protect me in the inconceivable powers of the weapons. 81.
May Kāmeśvarī protect me in lovemaking, and likewise Vajreśvarī in battle;
may Maheśānī protect me constantly, and Bhagamālinī in the pursuit of fortune and desire. 82.
May the Goddess Mahātripurasundarī, who consists of all bliss, protect me in taste, form, smell, sound, and touch. 83.
May Vaṭuka protect us in the northeast, and may the hosts of Yoginīs protect us in the southeast;
may they protect our skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen. 84.
May Kṣetreśa protect [her] in the southwest; may Gaṇeśa protect her in the northwest;
may Mātaṅgavanitā protect her; and may Śeṣikā Kulasundarī protect her. 85.
"May Śakti, who dwells in the Mūlādhāra, protect me at all times.
O Goddess, this armor (kavaca) is difficult to find in the three worlds. (86)
That which was not stated in the Ḍāmara Tantra, that which was not stated in the Rudrayāmala, and that which was not stated in all the Tantras has been made manifest in the Gandharva. || 87 ||
Out of affection for you, O Great Goddess, this must be guarded with great effort.
O Goddess, when your name is remembered, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. (88)
Victory is attained everywhere; every desire is fulfilled.
A hymn of praise is a hundred times more meritorious than the name, and an exposition is a hundred times more meritorious than that hymn. (89)

Therefore, meditation is a hundred times superior to that; the mantra is a hundred times superior to meditation; and, O Goddess, the armor (kavaca) has been declared by me to be a hundred times superior to the mantra.
It must not be given to just anyone; it is to be well-guarded and is extremely difficult to obtain.
O Goddess of the Gods, it should not be given to the disciple of another nor to one who is miserly.
To a disciple who is devoid of devotion, likewise to a flatterer, to one lacking devotion to the guru, and to one who delights in harming others; || 92 ||
O Maheśvarī, having given [this] to a reviler, one of evil conduct, a hypocrite, to those who are not devotees, or to unworthy sons, one shall meet with death.
O Goddess of gods, he who gives away the armor that has issued from my mouth to those for whom it is forbidden, his accumulation of knowledge, longevity, and fame shall perish. (94)
O Dear One, the yoginīs indeed harm him by my command;
he attains the highest hell for hundreds of millions of births.
To one endowed with all the auspicious marks, devoted to the yantras and mantras, a disciple of peaceful mind, and dedicated to devotion toward the guru. || 96 ||
Just as salt dissolved in water becomes one, O Parvati, so indeed does the mind become absorbed at the feet of the venerable Guru, my beloved. (97)
Then, out of compassion, one should impart the great secret that is exceedingly difficult to obtain;
for if Śrīvidyā is obtained through the grace of the Guru’s feet. (98)
In the same way, O Goddess, that armor is difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
and that god is Hara himself, while his wife is the Supreme Goddess. 99.
O Queen of the Gods, one should not utter the name of the Śrī Guru even through negligence;
O Beloved, he whose devotion to the Guru is constant, like that toward a deity—(this is the reading in the Ta-ka manuscript)—[should do so]. 100.
The accomplishment of that mantra and that yantra occurs, and not otherwise;
likewise, O beautiful one, there is the accomplishment of the armor and of the pill. 101.
If one recites the supreme Sundarī without knowing this armor-mantra, even after reciting it nine hundred thousand times, her vidyā will not be accomplished. (Aiśa reading).
Having become pure and composed, endowed with devotion and faith, [one should worship] at midnight—the time when all beings sleep—in that abode of all beings. (Variant reading: *ardharātrake*) 103.
O Great Goddess, joined with the causal [mantra], seated upon a red seat in a solitary place devoid of common people, and adorned with red ornaments; || 104 ||
With his mouth filled with betel and fragrant with the scent of incense,
he should station on his left side his Śakti, who is devoted to her lord.
Clad in red garments, auspicious, and bearing the Śiva-mantra—she who is Śakti is the Great Goddess (Mahādevī), while the practitioner (sādhaka) is the form of Hara. 106.
O Goddess, divinity arises from mutual contemplation;
endowed with power, one should worship the Goddess within the Śrīcakra, which possesses all auspicious characteristics. 107.

One should cause three handfuls of flowers to be offered to the Goddess with the root mantra, along with enjoyments such as the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and well-scented betel leaves and other offerings. || 108 ||
Having worshipped the Great Goddess, one obtains the fruit of ten million [offerings].
One should place [the deities] at this time in the same manner as previously described. 109.
One should meditate upon oneself as supreme, adorned by celestial women, with a great divine parasol made of a thousand petals held over one's head. (110)
His lotus-face rains down nectar, accompanied by a smile; he possesses divine luster, is the mass of supreme bliss, and is the exultant, supreme, and immutable one. || 111 ||
Richly adorned with divine ornaments and garments, anointed with divine perfumes and garlands,
seated upon a divine throne, and enjoying divine pleasures.
The all-pervading Lord of all beings, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction;
the untainted, stainless, peaceful, and omnipresent Sovereign. || 113 ||
Then, with his mind fixed upon her, he should meditate on the Goddess within the lotus of his heart—resembling a hibiscus flower and as ruddy as the rays of the rising sun. (114)
Seated upon a red lotus, adorned with red ornaments, clothed in red garments, her face resembling the full moon. (Note: "na" is not in manuscript *ka*). || 115 ||
The practitioner should contemplate, through the non-dual realization that "I am she," the Supreme Self as devoid of duality, by means of the state of non-dual bliss. (116)
This entire world, including all things moving and stationary, is pervaded by a crimson radiance;
one who is devoted to contemplation and has attained mastery over it should contemplate [the world] as such. (Note: *bhāvanā* is the reading in the *Taka-pāṭha* manuscript. 117.
For one who is thus intent on such contemplation, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) indeed arise swiftly;
having attained vast enjoyments and the status of sovereignty upon the earth. (118)
Having attained the station of Indra, he then sported in the Nandana grove,
enjoying divine pleasures at his own will with Urvashi and the other celestial nymphs.
Then he attains that supreme station, difficult even for the gods to reach;
thereafter, O beloved, one should recite the divine armor-mantra with a single-minded focus.
For him, there shall be the accomplishment of all aims; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
This is the supreme secret, the great and ultimate means of securing well-being.
O Maheśvarī, it is indeed the warding off and the destruction of all violent beings, ḍākinīs, and the hosts of night-stalkers.
It constantly bestows longevity and strength, brings about contentment, nourishment, and auspiciousness, and grants virtuous sons to women whose children have died. (123)
It wards off infantile seizures from the birth-chamber and the newborn, and it always increases peace for those afflicted by fierce poisons and malevolent spirits. (124)
It is a protection against poison, weapons, fire, and Rudra; it grants victory in battle, and at all times, whether in water, on land, or in the sky, it wards off all calamities. (125)
O Goddess, whoever should recite even once this armor, which bestows all auspiciousness upon the inhabitants of the three worlds and is difficult even for the gods to obtain; 126.
O Goddess, for one who constantly recites or listens with a concentrated mind, there is indeed the fruit of a horse-sacrifice; of this there is no doubt. (127)
He obtains all his desires and shall go to the supreme city of the Goddess;
and in battle, he shall conquer his enemies like a lion conquers elephants.
Just as fire consumes grass, so should one always conquer enemies;
neither missiles nor weapons have power over his body. 129.
Indeed, whatever weapons or even Brahma-missiles reach his body become as pleasant as garlands of flowers. (130)
O Pārvatī, those who turn their backs and depart without fighting never suffer from disease, nor do they ever experience suffering. (131)
His movement shall always be equal to that of the wind everywhere;
he shall be long-lived, an enjoyer of desires, and possessed of an abundance of wealth and grain. (This is the reading. 132.
Having conquered diseases, he shall become handsome and be born endowed with virtues;
the fourfold aims of life shall indeed come into his hand—of this there is no doubt. (133)
He who is beloved by another—this reading is archaic (aiśa)—along with his sons, wife, and family, shall enjoy happiness in this world and become liberated in the next. || 134 ||
O Goddess, for such a person, an evil rebirth never occurs;
even those difficult to subdue become easy to grasp, and men come under one's control. 135.
For him there is no obstacle, nor does grief arise on this earth; even the terrifying vetālas, piśācas, and rākṣasas [cannot harm him]. (136)
O Goddess, by the recitation of this armor-mantra, all those [obstacles] go to destruction;
indeed, his enemies are overcome merely through the application of thought.
They perish without a doubt, for the yoginīs devour them;
[this applies to] rites such as pacification, as well as killing and expulsion. (138)
O Goddess of the gods, by mere speech his [aims] are accomplished on the surface of the earth;
O Goddess, he is not tainted by sins, even those that are most fierce and terrible. (139)
In that land, one does not fall under the power of time, nor is there old age or suffering; neither famine nor pestilence prevails there. (140)
No diseases arise there, nor do portents manifest;
and various yoginīs remain in the presence of that practitioner (the case ending is elided by Vedic usage). 141.
They bestow peace and always protect one like a son;
there is the attainment of happiness at all times, and one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 142 ||
No practitioner like him is born upon this earth;
he is the embodiment of reality for gods, asuras, and humans, bringing them happiness. (143)
O beautiful one, by merely knowing or even just remembering this, one obtains inexhaustible desires and goes to the place of liberation. 144.
Even one devoid of all auspicious marks becomes a remover of impurity through recollection; oh, the greatness of this armor for one who recites it constantly! 145.
Even without the practice of yoga, one shall attain the state of equality with yogins by drawing the wheel fashioned from reality upon the bark of the birch tree. 146.
Having drawn a central triangle and written the syllables of the practitioner and the object of practice,
one should surround the root mantra above that with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
O Great Goddess, this yantra, which is very difficult for even gods and asuras to obtain, [is smeared] with fragrant sandalwood mixed with liquid aloe-wood. 148.
One should draw the armor (kavaca) on the outside of that very [mandala] using yellow pigment and saffron;
having wrapped it with a white thread, one should encircle it with lac.

On an auspicious day, having bathed [the image] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship that pill, which has the form of the Goddess and grants all desires. (150)
One should establish the vital breaths therein with the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra, [visualizing her] adorned with a beautiful golden yoni-mudrā. 151.
Then, having meditated upon the inner womb (antaryoni), the wise one should establish [the mantra] there.
O Goddess, this pill, when worn around the neck, bestows wealth. 152.
On the head, O Goddess, she is the bringer of subjection; on the waist, she is the cause of paralysis.
When bound upon the left arm, she is the destroyer of the faction of enemies. (153)
Situated in the stomach, she pacifies diseases; established in the heart, she bestows sons;
located on the forehead, she brings about knowledge; and in the crest-lock, she grants fame. (154)
If it always remains at the base of the right arm, then there shall be the accomplishment of all aims, whatever resides in the mind. (155)
Truth, truth, again truth; truth, truth, again and again! Indeed, I am unable to describe the power of this armor.
O beloved, this recitation of the armor-mantra alone is the means of accomplishment;
it has been told to you by me out of affection, O dear one, and must always be kept secret. (157)
[Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Armor (Kavaca) called Mahātripurasundarī Trailokyamohana," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 4 ||
[The Fifth Chapter] Pārvatī said:
"If worship is performed without a yantra, the deity does not become pleased."
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, tell me of her enchanting yantra.
By the mere sight of whom poverty is surely destroyed.
Īśvara said:
Having thus reflected, she, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, [appeared] at the beginning of the ocean (or: in her own abode). 2.
Through the conjunction of all the principles (tattvas), she whose form is the substratum of memory manifests the eternal primordial nature (prakṛti) as the Supreme Person (parama-pumān).

That ideation of reality (tattvasaṃjñā), being pure consciousness (cinmātra), through the proximity of light, desiring to manifest, becomes the womb [of creation] and in some cases approaches the bindu.
The supreme power (parā-śakti) is exceedingly manifest, characterized by inseparable existence;
she is the undivided power of pure consciousness, all-pervading, of the nature of consciousness, and omnipresent. || 5 ||
Endowed with the manifestation (*vivarta*) of all principles (*tattva*),
she attains the state of the *bindu*, characterized by the predominance of action (*kriyā*).
The state of having three forms of the Mātṛcakra occurs again as the Baindava;
therein, the Bindu is of the nature of Śiva, and the Bīja is remembered as being of the nature of Śakti.
From the union of those two arises the Nāda, from which I contemplate;
therefore, those wheels and their specific nature are now described.
Then, seated facing the east, he should begin the process of drawing the wheel upon a highly beautiful plate made of gold, silver, copper, or other metals.
O Goddess, in this case, the cloth is described as being square, even, pure, adorned with a raised center,
and joined at its paired parts.
Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess, one should draw a wheel upon the ground in a pure area measuring one cubit, smeared with cow dung.
O beloved, one should draw the King of Mandalas there with vermilion powder or saffron,
using a pen made of gold.
Alternatively, with the roots of kuśa grass in hand and composed in mind, the wise man should fashion a wheel as pleasing to the eye as possible. (13)
One should draw a single triangle with its apex pointing west;
then, above that, one should draw another triangle whose central apex points toward the middle of the eastern triangle.
Then, having pierced the two junctions, one should draw another line with its tip pointing eastward;
thus there shall be an eight-pointed wheel situated within a triangle.
Thereafter, O Pārvatī, hear about the construction of the ten-spoked wheel;
regarding those three lines there that run from south to north—‖ 16 ‖
Leaving aside the central line, one should extend two lines;
by doing so, having formed a hexagon, there is a fourfold division at the junctions.
Having drawn two lines so that a ten-cornered figure is formed, the construction of another ten-cornered figure is thus described. (18)
In this manner, there are five lines running from south to north;
among them, one should omit three lines in the middle, while that [remaining] pair runs from east to west.
O Goddess, one should extend the two outer lines as before;
by that, having formed a hexagon, there are four divisions of the junctions.
Having drawn two lines so that a ten-cornered figure is formed, the construction of the fourteen-spoked wheel is now described. (21)
In this manner, there are seven lines running from south to north;
having omitted three of those lines, one should then [draw] east-west lines on the outside.

The practitioner of mantra should extend two long lines as before; by doing so, having formed a hexagon, there arise four junctional divisions. (Note: *parivarddhayet* is an alternative reading for *parivardhayet*).

Having made it ten-spoked by that very same means through the fourfold breaking of the joints, one should draw two lines on the outside; thus there shall indeed be nine lines. (The reading "vai" is found in manuscript Ka.)
Then, one should fashion the other four corners with its tips;
thus there shall be fourteen spokes, enchanting to the eye. (25)
Listen now to what occurs when the wheel has been thus produced:
there shall be a triangle in the center, and in the middle of that, a bindu is prescribed. (26)
Outside all four wheels, there are forty-three triangular points (trikoṇakas),
and eight beautiful yonis multiplied by three.
There should be twelve matsya-marks, adorned at the four corners;
there should also be eighteen knots, as well as other knots at the six junctions.
Those beautiful crossroads are numbered twenty-four;
likewise, there are three quadrangles with an eight-cornered interior. (29)
In the southern, northern, and eastern directions, they arise in succession;
for there, nine lines run from south to north. (30)

Likewise, there are nine other lines extending toward the directions of fire (southeast) and wind (northwest); and similarly, there are nine other lines extending toward the directions of the Nairṛta (southwest) and Īśa (northeast). || 31 ||
Therein, O Goddess of the gods, those five who are foremost and facing the practitioner are the triangles; they are the five Śaktis from whom auspiciousness arises.
Those four fires which have their tips directed toward the east are thus proclaimed. Having thus fashioned the wheel and drawn a circle on the outside, || 33 ||
By that [measure], one should construct an eight-petaled lotus, and likewise outside of it,
one should draw a beautiful sixteen-petaled lotus with a circular [mandala].
Know that outside of those [circles] are three squares, and outside of those is a square enclosure (bhūpura) with three lines, adorned with four gateways.
In this manner, O Maheśānī, there are nine wheels with bindus in sequence; however, the triple circle is not mentioned for the purpose of worship.
In this way, O Great Goddess, the power of this wheel has been described by me; it cannot be fully told even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Thus, this great wheel, consisting of the Great Śrī Tripurā, is called the body; it is the yantra, the mantra, and the indivisible knowledge. 38.
They say the body is of three kinds: the elemental, the mental, and the supreme, which consists of knowledge, is eternal, indestructible, and continuous. (39)
They say that the *mudrā* is elemental; know the *yantra* to be composed of mind (*manomaya*). Know the *mantra* to be composed of knowledge (*jñānamaya*); thus the body becomes threefold. (40)
Know my body to be the mudrā, as well as its supreme constituent parts; Mahāmudrā, being the source, is proclaimed as the "body. (41)
From its essence are born Kāmeśvarī and the others;
O beloved, O lady of excellent hips, the wheel of the drop (binducakra) consists of all-bliss.
The Great Wheel, which is consciousness and the object of knowledge, should be known as having the nature of Brahman.
Beyond that is Mahātripurasundarī, seated upon the lap of Śiva. (43)
Having invoked the Goddess, one should then worship her with supreme adoration,
O Pārvatī, in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center, as well as in the cardinal points.

Having subsequently worshipped the six-limbed young maidens (the powers such as Sarvajñā and the rest) according to the prescribed rule, one who desires good fortune should then worship the Nityās, who are identical with that [deity]. 45.
There, one should visualize a great triangle consisting of fifteen parts;
the fifteen parts [should be arranged] in sequence by way of counter-clockwise rotation. (46)
One should visualize [the letters] beginning with *a* and ending with *u* on the southern [line].
Then, on the eastern line, there is the pentad beginning with *ū*, such as *dīrghakarṇa*. 47.
Having reflected upon it, one should contemplate [the letters] beginning with *śa* (or *sī*) and *e* on the northern line.

In the same manner, one should worship the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī: (1) Kāmeśvarī, (2) Bhagamālinī, (3) Nityaklinnā, (4) Bheruṇḍā, (5) Vahnivāsinī, (6) Vajreśvarī, (7) Śivādūtī, (8) Tvaritā, (9) Kulasundarī, (10) Nityā, (11) Nīlapatākā, (12) Vijayā, (13) Sarvamaṅgalā, (14) Jvālāmālinī, and (15) Citrā. One should worship them by circling counter-clockwise, using the mantra: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ A Kāmeśvarīnityā-śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi tarpayāmi namaḥ*. || 48 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) and ending with the full moon (paurṇamāsī),
one should worship each Nityā in the sequence of their respective lunar days.
At the beginning, the best of practitioners should worship with an increase of one [offering] at each stage;
O Maheśānī, during the dark fortnight, he should worship the three mandalas. (Note: *pūjayet* is the reading in manuscript *kha*.)
O Varārohā, beginning with Vicitrā and continuing until Kāmeśvarī, they are to be worshipped in reverse order, or the others likewise, O Pārvatī. (51)

At the conclusion of both sessions, through the practice of meditation as described, one should worship the eternal Mahātripurasundarī, the sixteenth [Kalā] residing in the [divine] creation. (The word "should worship" is to be supplied. || 52 ||
Likewise, O fair-faced one, the various vidyās, meditations, yantras, modes of worship, fire-offerings, and all other rites intended for specific desires [are likewise taught]. (53)
O Śivā, I shall later explain [the ritual] in five chapters;
O fair-faced one, listen now to the worship of those who have become the limbs and the enclosures here.
The Lord said:

O Maheśānī, having invoked [the deities] in each respective place according to the prescribed rule, the practitioner should worship them with devotion, following the path of the sequence as it has been taught. 55.

There, one should place the first [syllable] with the root-mantra alone; the second with the Haṃsa-mantra enclosed [by it]; the second [syllable] with the second [mantra]; and the third with the third [mantra].
By the fourth [day] one attains the fourth, by the fifth alone the fifth;
likewise, by the sixth the sixth, and by the seventh the seventh.
With the eighth [day] he should [conquer] the eighth, with the ninth the ninth,
with the tenth the tenth, and likewise the eleventh.
One should perform the twelfth [recitation] with an eleven-syllable mantra, the thirteenth with a twelve-syllable mantra, and the fourteenth with a thirteen-syllable mantra. || 59 ||
One should worship the fourteenth [tithi] there with a fourteen-syllable mantra;
then one should worship the fifteenth with a fifteen-syllable mantra.
O Goddess, one should worship the Ṣoḍaśī with all [the mantras] together; indeed, O Pārvatī, the worship should be performed at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.
She is proclaimed as the Great Goddess (Mahādevī), eternally established in the revealed scriptures;
one should worship her alone, the Great Tripurasundarī. || 62 ||
Since such an eternal maṇḍala has arisen from her, I shall now explain another [maṇḍala], which is for the fulfillment of desired objects and purposes. 63.

One should [approach] a woman born of a noble family as previously described, praised, endowed with beautiful marks, who has reached her season by her own will, and whose childhood has been concealed by full youth. (64)
There, having worshipped the Goddess according to the prescribed rite on the first day, one should worship the primordial Kāmeśvarī; likewise, one should worship the second [form] on the second day.
