Then on the third day, the third [fever]; on the fourth day, the fourth;
on the fifth day, the fifth; and likewise on the sixth day, the sixth.
On the seventh day, one should worship the seventh goddess, and on the eighth day, the eighth;
likewise, one should worship the ninth goddess on the ninth day and the tenth on the tenth.
Likewise, one should worship Rudra on the eleventh day, Dvādaśī on the twelfth day,
and the Goddess Trayodaśī on the thirteenth day, in due order.
Likewise, one should worship on the fourteenth day for Śakra, then on the fifteenth;
when the sixteenth is complete, one should worship on the sixteenth according to the sequence of increase.
One should also worship others afterwards, as another [set] has been proclaimed;
one should worship during the sixteen nights of women's seasons, both in direct and reverse order. (70)
One should proceed according to the rules and in due order, not allowing even a single day to pass by;
nor indeed should one dismiss her as long as she remains desirous of the fruit.
Having recognized her as one who desires the fruit, he should release her and resort to another;
for there are sixteen nights joined together, and likewise sixteen powers.
On a certain day, O Goddess, they may be obtained through the power of fortune;
one should worship them with diligence and according to the rules previously indicated. (73)
By increasing at night and decreasing during the day, remaining powerful in the middle of the *rasa*,
he shall in due course become a celestial wish-fulfilling tree (*surapādapa*) for one season.

In the center of Vimalājayinī, the gurus [are to be worshipped]—it is indicated that the service of the lineage of gurus (*gurukrama*) on the eight-spoked wheel (*aṣṭāracakra*) is to be understood. They have been described to you.
Furthermore, one should worship the Buddha in the Trailokyamohana-cakra. (75)
Those three lines, resembling them [in color], are known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.

Among them, O Dear One, at the beginning, on the line of Brahmā reside Aṇimā and the others—namely, the siddhis of aṇimā, laghimā, mahimā, īśitva, prākāmya, bhukti, icchā, rasa, and mokṣa; these are to be worshipped on the line of Brahmā. (76)
The red goddesses grant boons and fearlessness, bestowing the fruits of one's desires;
Kaumārī is yellow in color and holds a spear and a javelin.
The Supreme Goddess should be meditated upon with her hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
holding in her [other] hands a goad, a javelin, lightning, and a thunderbolt.
Indrāṇī, of golden complexion, should be meditated upon as the bestower of all prosperity;
Vaiṣṇavī is dark-complexioned and holds the conch, the discus, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Bearing [the mudrās] with her lotus-like hands, adorned with divine ornaments,
Vārāhī is dark-complexioned and endowed with the face of a boar.
Holding a plough, a mace (or according to another reading,
a sword), and a shield in her hands, Cāmuṇḍā is black in color and likewise holds a trident and a hand-drum.
He holds a sword and a vetāla with his right hands,
and a shield, a *caṣaka*, a serpent, and a bell with his left hands.

Led by Brahmāṇī—namely Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī—these are to be worshipped on the middle Viṣṇu-line. All [of them] are supported by the Viṣṇu-line.
Brahmāṇī is red in color and adorned with four faces. (83)

Māheśvarī is white in color, three-eyed, and holds a trident; her hands grant boons and fearlessness, and she has a water-pot (or, according to another reading, a *kuṇḍikā*) hanging from her side. || 84 ||
O beloved, she holds a sword and an axe in her hands;
now I shall briefly tell you its supreme secret. (The Kha manuscript reads: "is told now. 85.
Mahālakṣmī, however, is yellow-hued; the Supreme Goddess holds a lotus, a mirror, and a citron fruit. (86)

Relying upon the *śivarekhā* (the auspicious line), the goddesses who are the *mudrās*, beginning with Saṃkṣobhaṇī—the manifest *yoginīs*—are situated within the *trailokyamohana* (*deluding the three worlds*) wheel, which consists of square lines; they are to be worshipped along with the *śivarekhā*.
Red in color, headed by Saṃkṣobhaṇī, they are each endowed with their respective *mudrās* in their hands. (87)
These manifest yoginīs are to be meditated upon for the sake of all prosperity;
O Goddess, Tripurā, the mistress of the wheels, is before Aṇimā.
Resembling pure crystal, adorned with pearl-jewels, [they hold] a book, a rosary, and two excellent lotuses. 89.
Bearing [the three circles], she should be meditated upon for the sake of accomplishment; she is the destroyer of great sins.

O Maheśānī, by the statement "The triple circle (trivṛtta) is not prescribed for worship" (5|36), it is understood that it is not employed in the ritual worship. Know, O Pārvatī, that it has the nature of the moon, the sun, and fire. 90.
In the wheel that fulfills all desires, which possesses twelve petals, one should meditate upon Brahmā there, raining down a shower of nectar. || 91 ||
The goddesses beginning with Kāmākarṣaṇikā, joined with the sixteen vowels, all hold nooses and goads; they are equal to her here in form as well. (Note: *śṛ* is the reading for *sṛ*). 92.

These are the Guptayoginīs—[namely] Kāmākarṣaṇī, Buddhyākarṣaṇī, Ahaṃkārākarṣaṇī, Śabdākarṣaṇī, Sparśākarṣaṇī, Rūpākarṣaṇī, Rasākarṣaṇī, Gandhākarṣaṇī, Cittākarṣaṇī, Dhairyākarṣaṇī, Smṛtyākarṣaṇī, Nāmākarṣaṇī, Bījākarṣaṇī, Ātmākarṣaṇī, Amṛtākarṣaṇī, and Śarīrākarṣaṇī—who, as the Guptayoginīs who fulfill all desires, are to be worshipped in the sixteen-petaled wheel (*ṣoḍaśadala-cakra*). They are to be meditated upon as the bestowers of all prosperity.
At the forefront of Kāmākarṣaṇī, however, Tripureśī is established. (93)
O fair-faced one, Tripureśī, who is similar to Tripurā, should be meditated upon;
O lady of excellent hips, [she is seated] upon an eight-petaled lotus resembling the Japā flower.
Having meditated there upon Śiva, who is named Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa and bestows the fruits of all desires, [the practitioners] should be endowed with the eight groups (vargas).

Anaṅgakusumā and the others are remembered as the most secret [Yoginīs]. (As follows: Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgamadanā, Anaṅgamadanāturā, Anaṅgarekhā, Anaṅgaveginī, Anaṅgāṅkuśā, and Anaṅgamālinī—these most secret Yoginīs are to be worshipped in the eight-petalled wheel that causes universal agitation.
They are all like Sundarī and bestow the fruits of all desires. || 96 ||
At the tip of Anaṅgakusumā, Tripurasundarī should be meditated upon,
endowed with all ornaments, holding a book and a rosary.

Holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and possessing the luster of the Bandhūka flower, she is the bestower of all good fortune; [the two] discs have the luster of the pomegranate flower.
O Goddess, one should contemplate Bhāskara upon the fourteen-spoked wheel.

The Saṃpradāya Yoginīs—namely Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, Sarvavidrāviṇī, Sarvākarṣiṇī, Sarvāhlādinī, Sarvamohinī, Sarvastambhinī, Sarvajṛmbhiṇī, Sarvavaśaṅkarī, Sarvarañjanī, Sarvonmādinī, Sarvārthasādhanī, Sarvasaṃpatpūraṇī, Sarvamantramayī, and Sarvadvandvakṣayakarī—are to be worshipped on the fourteen-spoked wheel of the Bestower of All Good Fortune (*Sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka*). These are remembered as the Saṃpradāyas. (99)
The resident of Tripura, who dwells in the three cities, should be meditated upon as resembling Sundarī; she is the power that agitates all and bestows the fruits of all desires. 100.
In the wheel that accomplishes all aims and likewise protects all, which has ten outer spokes and resembles the hibiscus flower; 101.

Then, having worshipped Nārāyaṇa, one should thereafter worship the Kulakaula Yoginīs—namely Sarvasiddhipradā, Mukhyā, Saṃpatpradā, Priyakarī, Maṅgalakāriṇī, Kāmapradā, Duḥkhavimocinī, Mṛtyupraśamanī, Vighnavināśinī, Aṅgasundarī, and Saubhāgyadāyinī—who are the principal bestowers of all accomplishments (*siddhi*)—upon the outer ten-spoked wheel in the *Sarvārthasādhaka* [maṇḍala]. These are thus remembered. 102.
At the forefront of the bestower of all accomplishments, the illustrious Tripurā is established, possessing the luster of a thousand rising suns and adorned with divine ornaments. 103.
Holding a book and a rosary, and granting boons and fearlessness, they should be worshipped within the inner ten-spoked wheel as bestowers of all prosperity. (104)

Likewise, the Nigarbha-yoginīs—headed by Sarvajñā [this is the reading], Sarvaśakti, Sarvaiśvaryapradā, Sarvajñānamayī, Sarvavyādhivināśinī, Sarvādhārasvarūpā, Sarvapāpaharā, Sarvānandamayī, Sarvarakṣāsvarūpiṇī, and Sarvepsitaphalapradā—these Nigarbha-yoginīs are to be worshipped in the inner ten-spoked wheel of the Sarvarakṣākara. O Dear One!
O Goddess! Tripuramālinī stands in front of Sarvajñā. (105)
The goddess Indragopaprabhā, holding a noose, a goad, and a skull-cup, instantly bestows great fearlessness upon the practitioners. 106.

In the wheel that removes all diseases, which is as red as the rays of the rising sun, one should worship the secret yoginīs there, headed by Vaśinī. (Note: *bālārka* is an alternative reading for *bālārka-lakapāṭha*).

Vaśinī and the others—namely Vaśinī, Kāmeśvarī, Modinī, Vimalā, Aruṇā, Jayinī, Sarveśvarī, Kaulinī, and Vāgdevatā—these secret Yoginīs are to be worshipped in the eight-spoked wheel (vasukoṇacakra) which removes all diseases. O Supreme Goddess, they are red in color, endowed with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and hold a book and a rosary. 108.
O Goddess, one should meditate upon Vaśinī, who bestows all accomplishments, as well as Tripurasiddhā, the destroyer of poisons, standing before her. 109.
O Dear One, on the right and left of the division at the apex of the triangle,
where it meets the fourfold path, one should worship the arrow and the bow.
O Goddess, on the left and right sides of the upper portion of the triangle, which consists of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), the noose and the goad are situated. 111.
O Supreme Goddess, in the triangle of the wheel that bestows all accomplishments,
which possesses the luster of a thousand rising suns and the radiance of the bandhūka flower.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the most secret Yoginīs are established in the front corner, in the fire-wheel at Kāmarūpa, O fair-faced one. 113.
Kāmeśvarī has three eyes and a body as youthful and ruddy as the morning sun;
she holds a rosary, the gesture of granting boons, a noose, and a goad. (Note: *caṣaka* is an alternative reading for *caṣaka*. || 114 ||
O Maheśvarī, she who bestows supreme sovereignty, the power whose essence is Rudra, is to be meditated upon in the left corner of the triangle within the solar wheel (sūryacakra). 115.
In the great sacred seat (pīṭha) of Jālandhara, Vajreśvarī is proclaimed;
she has three eyes, a face like the full moon, and the luster of the Bandhūka flower. 116.
Holding a noose, a goad, arrows, a bow, a rosary, and a citron, she of beautiful form, whose essence is the power of Viṣṇu, should be meditated upon. (117)
O fair-faced one, in the right corner of the triangle, within the wheel of Soma at the abode of Pūrṇagiri, O Goddess, Bhagamālinī has been described. 118.
She has three eyes, her crest bears the young moon, and her body is as red as vermilion;
she holds a book, a rosary, and likewise a noose and a goad.
The supreme sovereign, the power of Brahman and the Self, who is to be meditated upon, Kāmeśvarī is established in the front portion as Tripurāmbā. 120.
She should be meditated upon as resembling Mālinī, bestowing the fruits of all desires;
or else, one should contemplate all the rays in the form of goddesses. 121.
Since the meditation on the nine obscuring powers (navāvaraṇa-śakti) is identical to that of the Goddess,
they constantly issue forth from her just as rays of light emanate from the orb of the sun.
Likewise, O Goddess of beautiful countenance, the goddesses were born from the body of Mahādevī at the sacred seat of Uḍyāṇa, in the Wheel of Brahmā.
The Goddess known as the Secret of the Higher and the Lower, whose nature is Brahman—the best of practitioners should worship her alone as the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśī). || 124 ||
O Supreme Goddess, this worship follows the order of maintenance (sthitikrama), whereas the creation-order (sṛṣṭikrama) worship, which involves the extraction of the yantra, is a great secret.
Pārvatī said:
"The wheel-maṇḍala has been described, but no worship was mentioned for that maṇḍala. Now, O Īśāna, tell me the unsurpassed sequence of worship. (126)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed sequence of worship, by the mere awakening to which one who is liberated while living rejoices. (127)
The worship of the Goddess, ever-arisen, is established in three divisions:
O Goddess, it is the supreme (parā), the lower (aparā), and the third is the intermediate (parāparā).
Having invoked [the deity] into the center of the wheel, she is worshipped with an abundance of ritual substances;
that is declared to be the first [form], as held by Purandara and others. (129)
Seated comfortably on a soft seat, intent on the restraint of the breath, with body, head, and neck held straight, he should be devoted to gazing at the tip of his nose. (130)
Averse to the discursive chatter of conceptual forms and intent upon the true nature of existence,
[he beholds her] who dwells within the interior of the great lotus grove and whose form is supreme bliss.
She whose form nourishes the entire world, who showers the supreme nectar,
and who is the very nature of the Supreme Self within the wheel consisting of various forms of knowledge.
One should worship her, whose form is the source of the [half-]measure (ardhamātrā), consisting of the drop (bindu) and three circles, whose nature is the self, with the flower of supreme bliss. 133.
This second [form of] worship, which is the highest and consists of the self-worship performed with substances that gratify the senses, is always being accomplished by me. (134)
She is declared to be both supreme and non-supreme, wherein both [states] are found;
and she is always brought forth by the Son of Devakī, O beloved. (135)

[Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Yantra, the Enclosures, and the Worship of the Śaktis," in the Gandharva Tantra, from the dialogue between the illustrious Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 5 ||
[The Sixth Chapter] Pārvatī said:
O Maheśvara, the worship of the Goddess that was described as the third has been fully explained.
Speak, O Lord, best of gods, speak now in detail about her who has been spread abroad. (Variant readings: *kathaya*, *vistareṇa*) 1.
In this world, purification of the body occurs in two ways: through knowledge and through action.
You have explained purification by knowledge, but purification by action has not been shown. (2)
How can a body, slippery with excrement and urine, become divine?
Tell me that, O Mahādeva, O Lord whose face is gracious through favor. (3)
Īśvara said:
"Success is attained either through knowledge or through action, and not otherwise.
The yoga of knowledge must be explained; now hear, O beloved, about the yoga of action."
Having risen during the *brāhma* hour, the practitioner, with a steady mind,
sits in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

One should contemplate the Guru within the stainless lotus situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), which is adorned with a thousand petals and possesses a mandala like that of the full moon.
Resembling pure crystal, adorned with white ornaments, and likewise his body decorated with such flower garlands and the like—(this is the reading in the Ta manuscript). || 7 ||
Seated in the lotus posture, served by all the yoginīs, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, peaceful, two-eyed, and composed of compassion. (8)
With her left hand, which is red and possesses the power of reaching her left thigh,
she holds a blue lotus while embracing the Lord with her right hand.
One should meditate upon the Lord, whose mind is dense with the mass of supreme bliss,
whose eyes are red and thick with joy, and whose lotus-face is smiling.

The Bālā-mantra begins with *ai*, followed by Bhuvaneśānī (*hrīṃ*), Ramā (*śrīṃ*), and Khecarī (*hasakhaphre*). Then come Śiva (*ha*) and Candra (*sa*). Following these are the end of the Mātṛkā (*kṣa*), Kāla (*ma*), Śakra (*la*), Ambu (*va*), Vahni (*ra*), Vāyu (*ya*), and Vāmakarṇa (*ū*). Thus, it is *sahakhaphre sahakṣamalavarayīṃ*. Then Śiva and Candra are *hsauḥ*, and Candra and Śiva are *sahauḥ*. The Bālā-mantra begins with *ai*, followed by Bhuvaneśānī, Ramā, and Khecarī;
then Śiva and Candra, the end of the Mātṛkā, and Kāla, Śakra, Ambu, and Vahni. (11)
And the wind, joined with the left ear, is conjoined with the Bindu and Nāda;
having formed the first face among them, one should join the left eye to the ear.
Śiva and Candra are endowed with tridents and adorned with the Bindu;
Candra and Śiva are endowed with tridents and possess the Sarga, O Maheśvarī. 13.
Therefore, one should write "Ānandanātha" at the end of one's own guru’s name;
likewise, one should write the word "Ambā" at the end of the word "Śakti. (Note: there is an alternative reading here for "ambā"). 14.
One should perform the worship according to the prescribed rite, saying: "I worship the sandals.
*Laṃ*: "By means of Brahmā, whose essence is the earth, I prepare the fragrance; O you whose essence is the subtle element of smell, for the sense of smell, accept this fragrance, svāhā!"
Then, with the thumb and the little finger, one should apply the supreme fragrance.
"Oṃ! I offer this flower to Sadāśiva, whose nature is space; O Śabda-tanmātra, accept this sound for the sense of hearing, svāhā!
Thus indeed is the offering of the flower performed with the union of the thumb and forefinger.
Or: "O Lord, who consists of the nature of air, I offer incense; O you whose self is the subtle element of touch, for the sense-organ of the skin, accept the touch! Svāhā!
Indeed, the offering of incense is performed with the union of the thumb and the middle finger. || 16 ||
"Vaṃ-raṃ: With Rudra, whose nature is fire, I prepare the lamp; for the sense of sight, whose essence is the subtle element of form, receive the form, svāhā!
O Maheśānī, with focused mind, one should offer the lamp with both thumbs."
Vaṃ: With Viṣṇu, whose nature is nectar, I prepare this food offering. To the sense of taste, whose essence is the subtle element of flavor: accept the flavor, svāhā!
The union of the thumb and ring finger establishes that food offering. || 17 ||
Having thus worshipped the family preceptor according to the prescribed rite, O Goddess,
one should then display the yoni-mudrā and prostrate for the sake of attaining spiritual perfection.
Salutations to you, O Blessed Lord, the Protector, the Auspicious One in the form of the Guru;
you who have assumed manifold forms for the sake of perfectly accomplishing the descent of knowledge. 19.
Salutations to You, the mass of consciousness, who are ever-new and of ever-new form, whose singular nature is the Supreme Self, and who are the sun that shatters the darkness of all ignorance.
To the independent one whose form is fashioned out of compassion, whose essence is Śiva;
to the one who is dependent upon his devotees, appearing in auspicious forms for those who are worthy of liberation.
Salutations to the one who is the discernment for the discerning, the investigation for the investigators,
the illumination for the illuminators, and the embodiment of knowledge for the wise.
In front, on both sides, behind, above, and below, may you always make your seat by means of your form as the True Mind; I shall pay homage [to you] there. (23)
Salutations to that glorious Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the collyrium-stick of knowledge. (24)
Salutations be unto you, O Guru, whose self is Brahman, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
the cause for crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra seized by ignorance. || 25 ||
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru alone is supreme knowledge, and the Guru alone is supreme austerity.
Therefore, O Goddess of the Gods, in every respect the worship of the Guru is most weighty;
whether it be the service of another deity or the chanting of the name of another deity. (27)
O Goddess, if it is performed before him without the presence of the Guru-deva, then one attains hell; I tell you this as the truth. || 28 ||
When the feet of the Guru are indeed worshipped, one shall become happy among all the gods;
for that Sadāśiva is the father of all mantras and tantras. (29)
O Pārvatī, for one who always maintains devotion toward the Guru as if toward a beloved deity, there shall be the accomplishment of all goals; it is certainly not otherwise.
Having meditated on the dust of the Guru’s feet upon one’s head, one should commence the ritual action;
the Guru, white as camphor, resides in the Sahasrāra at the aperture of Brahmā.
Bestowing boons and fearlessness, eternal, possessing the form of Brahman, and forever sinless, O Supreme Goddess, he remains awake, illuminating his own abode. (32)
Those Śāktas who, having abandoned the Lord of the Family (Kulanātha), serve others—for them, initiation and sacrifice lead only to malevolent magic (abhicāra). || 33 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in a guru of noble lineage;
for it is said that one of noble lineage is qualified for all branches of knowledge. (34)
He alone is the master of initiation here in all the tantras, and no other;
he should perform the worship of the circle of gurus on the seven sacred festival days.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, the movement of Kuṇḍalinī cannot be accomplished without yoga. O Lord, as long as Kuṇḍalinī remains asleep in the root-lotus," (one reading: "will not succeed").

As long as that Goddess does not awaken through the accumulation of many merits, nothing whatsoever—be it mantra, yantra, worship, or the like—will succeed. (The alternative reading is *siddhyet*. 37.
Then, mantras, yantras, worship, and other rites attain their efficacy;
endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers, one may roam the world like Śiva himself. || 38 ||

Through the application of yoga, liberation arises and the perfection of mantra becomes unimpeded; once the mantra is perfected, the supreme state is attained—such is the definitive conclusion of the scriptural meaning. (39)
By means of this, one whose self is disciplined may dwell in heaven, the mortal world, or the netherworld;
and being liberated while living, he shall attain supreme nirvāṇa at the end of the body.
"Therefore, O Lord, tell me in its entirety that supreme yoga, that yoga.
The Lord said: "I shall speak out of affection for you, O Pārvatī, for you are worthy of yoga."
Liberation, which is the crossing over from saṃsāra, is expressed by the word yoga;
for Yoga is indeed the goddess Lalitā—know this for certain, O Pārvatī. (42)

There is no yoga on the back of the sky, nor on the earth, nor in the subterranean realm (rasātala); those expert in yoga declare that the union of the individual soul (jīva) and the Self (ātman) is yoga. 43.
Desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy—these groups, known as the six, are declared to be the obstructors of yoga. (This is the reading in the Ka-Ka manuscript.)
Having conquered these limbs of yoga, yogis shall attain yoga:
namely, restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), and breath control (prāṇāyāma), followed by that which comes after. (45)
Withdrawal, that which is called concentration, meditation, together with absorption—these they call the eight limbs for the yogi in the practice of yoga. (46)

Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, straightforwardness, forgiveness, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the ten restraints (yamas). (Note: Some readings include *dhṛti* instead of *mitāhāraḥ*. 47.
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the deity, listening to the established doctrines, modesty, intelligence, recitation of mantras, and burnt offerings; 48.
These ten observances (niyamas) have been proclaimed by those proficient in the Yoga scriptures:
Padmāsana, that called Svastika, Bhadra, and likewise Vajrāsana; || 49 ||
This is declared to be the vīrāsana; thus, in order, the fivefold group of postures [is completed]. Having properly placed both soles of the feet upon the thighs— (50)
Then, one should bind the two thumbs with the hands in reverse order;
this is called the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is dear to the hearts of yogins.
Having placed both soles of the feet properly between the thighs and knees, the yogi should sit with an upright body; that they call the Svastika posture. (Verse 52)
One should place the other two ankles very firmly on the sides;
below the scrotum, one should bind the heels of the feet with both hands. (Note: *sīva* is an alternative reading for *sema*.)
The Bhadrāsana has been thus described and proclaimed by the yogis:

having placed the feet successively upon the thighs with the knees [downward] (variant reading: *ūrvor upari*), and with the fingers facing backward (*pratyaṅmukha*) (variant reading: *pratyaṅmukhāṅguli*).

One should assume the unsurpassed vajrāsana posture, which is described as follows: placing one foot below and resting the other upon the thigh. (The reading *nidadhyāt* or *nidadhīta* is also found. 55.
The yogi should dwell with the body straight; this is called the heroic posture (vīrāsana).
One should draw in the external air through the *iḍā* [nāḍī] for sixteen measures (mātrā).

The yogi should hold [the breath] when it is full for sixty-four measures (*mātrā*). As for the definition of a measure, Nārada says: "The time required for one's own hand to circle the circle of one's knee should be equal to a measure, according to the duration of a single inhalation. Likewise, in the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*: "Circumambulating the knee, neither too quickly nor too slowly, the snapping of the fingers that is performed is proclaimed as a measure.
[He should hold it] properly within the center of the *suṣumnā* for thirty-two measures, slowly. (57)
In this manner, the best among those who know yoga should exhale through the piṅgalā nāḍī;
those expert in the yoga scriptures call this prāṇāyāma.

One should practice this for him again and again in sequence, alternating [the breaths], according to the gradual increase of the measures (mātrā), properly [reaching] twelve and sixteen [counts]. 59.
The wise know that prāṇāyāma joined with recitation, meditation, and so forth, to be "with essence" (sagarbha); they know that which is devoid of these to be "without essence" (vigarbha). || 60 ||
For a person practicing in due order, the emergence of sweat in the body is considered the lowest [stage];
that accompanied by trembling is the middling; and the abandonment of the ground is regarded as the highest.
The attainment of the highest qualities is what is intended by the practice of discipline, which keeps the wandering senses undisturbed amidst their objects. (62)
The forceful withdrawal from those [objects] is called *pratyāhāra*.
[It is practiced] at the thumbs, ankles, knees, the perineum, the penis, and the navel. (63)
In the heart, the neck, the throat region, then in the uvula, in the nose,
between the eyebrows, on the breast, on the head, and at the dvādaśānta, according to the prescribed rule.
The retention of the vital breaths is called *dhāraṇā*, performed with a concentrated mind abiding within consciousness. (65)

(1 maṇa ka pāṭha | 2 se kha pāṭha |) Meditation here is said to be the contemplation of one's chosen deities within oneself, and the constant cultivation of equanimity between the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*). 66.
The sages have declared that samādhi is characterized by eight limbs;
thus, O Goddess, I have described to you the destruction of the sixfold group beginning with desire.

Samādhi—the arising of consciousness regarding the unity of the supreme Self and the individual soul—is difficult to attain for those attached to sense-objects, but easy for those whose minds are self-controlled. (68)
O lady of excellent vows, O Supreme Goddess, if the individual soul were distinct from the Supreme and were to become an effect, it would follow that it possesses non-consciousness, just like a jar.
"Perishability and fear are indeed the second [state]," so you have heard in the sacred tradition;
for the Self is eternal, omnipresent, immutable, and free from defects. (70)
Being one, it appears divided through delusion and illusion, but not by its own nature;
therefore, for me there is no duality, nor the phenomenal world, nor transmigration.
Just as space is described as being twofold—as the space within a jar and the great space—so too is delusion said to be twofold, in the form of the individual self (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). (72)
I am neither the body, nor the vital breath, nor likewise the senses; I am not the mind, nor the intellect, nor the thought-organ, nor the ego-sense.
I am neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor likewise air;
I am neither space, nor sound, nor touch, nor likewise taste.
There is neither smell nor form, neither am I illusion nor the cycle of worldly existence;
because I am eternally of the nature of the witness, I am indeed Brahman alone. (Note: *pādvā* is a variant reading for *pādvāka*.)
"I am that Brahman, not a transmigrating being; never is there anything other than Me"—one should know one's own Self thus; this is proclaimed as Samādhi. (76)
In samādhi, this very nature of one's own is indeed the sound of the Fourth (turīya-svara);
it is the portion of the Fourth, the Supreme Power (parā-śakti), the essence of the Bindu, and absolute Brahman alone.
Some say that the Self is wisdom (prajñā), while others say it is the absolute Brahman;
one should know the individual soul (jīva) as being identical with the Lord (īśvara), thinking "I am He" with certainty.

Just as foam, waves, and the like that have arisen from the ocean dissolve back into the ocean, O beloved, so too does the world dissolve into the Self. (The reading "priye" is found in manuscript *kha*. 79.
He for whom the Supreme Self is thus revealed as non-different from himself attains the supreme state; he himself directly becomes the highest nectar.
When consciousness, which is the self of all, shines eternally within the mind,
then it is spontaneously attained by the yogi without any interval.
When one perceives all beings within one's own self,
and the self within all beings, then one attains Brahman.
When one established in samādhi perceives no beings at all,
having become one with the Supreme, then he becomes absolute.

When that supreme knowledge of Brahman alone—which is the sole remedy for birth, old age, suffering, and disease—arises, then one becomes Śiva. (Note: *tadā* is the reading; *yadā* is an alternative.)
Therefore, liberation comes from knowledge and not otherwise, even through millions of births;
just as poison that has been consumed is digested by the power of mantras and medicinal herbs. // 85 //
In the same way, all actions of the knower are digested in an instant when the identification with the body has dissolved and the Supreme Self is realized. (86)
Wherever the mind goes, there are meditative absorptions;
one should contemplate: "I am Brahman (O Goddess, according to the Kha manuscript), I am not another, I am liberated. (87)
"I am of the nature of Truth-Consciousness-Bliss, eternally possessed of a liberated essence.
He who is thus engaged in samādhi is fit for samādhi. (The variant reading "kalpyate" is also acceptable.)
Having declared, "I am Sadāśiva," the ascetic may wander according to his own will;
he is not smeared by sin, nor is he bound by karma. (89)
Just as gold melted by fire burns away its impurity in an instant,
so too does one who has surrendered the self to Brahman burn away all karmas.
Abandoning the deity residing within oneself, one searches for deities outside;
like one who, having abandoned the Kaustubha gem held in his own hand, wanders about in thirst for glass. 91.
Indeed, without yoga, without a machine, and without mantra, that [Brahman] is not attained;
rather, through the practice of both together, Brahman is the cause of perfect realization. 92.
Just as a jar in a house enveloped by darkness is seen by means of a lamp, so too the Self, though veiled by Māyā, is made an object of perception through the Mantra. || 93 ||
This great knowledge of Brahman has been told to you, O Goddess;
having learned it from a guru and having chanted it, one may cross the ocean of worldly existence.
Wherever this knower of Brahman dies—whether in the Ganges or in the dwelling of a dog-cooker—he is fit for becoming one with Brahman; it is not otherwise, my dear.
O beloved, the universe is said to be the body, consisting of the five elements;
through the splendors of the moon, the sun, and fire, it takes on the singular form of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman.
It is held that there are thirty million channels in the body; among them, ten are declared to be principal, and among those, three are established as primary. (97)
Here, within the spinal column (merudaṇḍa), the principal channel takes the form of the moon, sun, and fire;
that channel is of the nature of Śakti and is the very embodiment of nectar.
The channel named iḍā is situated on the left, white and having the form of the moon;
and that which is called piṅgalā is on the right, having the form of a man and the nature of the sun. (99)
Another is considered to be called Viṣā, resembling the flower of the pomegranate;
it is situated in the center of Meru and extends from the base up to the aperture of Brahmā.

That Suṣumnā (the reading *suṣumnā* is found in manuscript *ka*) consists entirely of splendor and has the form of fire; in its center is the auspicious one called Vicitrā, which flows with nectar. 101.
She consists of all the gods and is dear to the hearts of yogins;
she truly abides pervading everything from the visarga to the bindu.
In the Mūlādhāra, known as Tripura, which consists of will, knowledge, and action,
there is in the center the self-arisen Liṅga (Svayaṃbhūliṅga), possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Above that, one should meditate on its fourth [aspect], which resembles the bandhūka flower.
Above that is Kuṇḍalinī, whose form is like a crest and whose body is red.
For she alone is the supreme, subtle Mahātripurasundarī;
she is the consciousness of all beings, that which is called the Śabdabrahman.
Having attained that form of Kuṇḍalinī situated within the bodies of living beings,
it is composed of all splendor, and is indeed the imperishable Saccidānanda (Existence-Consciousness-Bliss).
Outside of that is a four-petaled lotus, possessing the luster of gold (meaning it is endowed with the letters from *va* to *sa*, i.e., the semivowels and sibilants);
one should visualize there a lotus resembling molten gold. || 107 ||

Above that is the center known as Svādhiṣṭhāna, resembling fire in appearance, possessing the luster of a diamond, having six petals, and joined with the six syllables beginning with *ba* and ending with *la*. (Note: *ṣaḍvarṇena* according to the *kha* manuscript; *ṣaḍarṇena* according to the *ka* manuscript.)
Among the six root-supports (mūlādhāras), they know the first to be the Root Support (mūlādhāra);
by the word "self" (sva), they know the supreme linga to be the Self-Established (svādhiṣṭhāna). || 109 ||
Above that, in the region of the navel, is the great city of Maṇipūra;
it has the luster of gold and the brilliance of lightning, and is likewise composed of manifold splendor.
Because that city is pierced by the jewel (maṇi), they know it as Maṇipūra;
it is endowed with ten petals and is filled with the letters beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *pha*. || 111 ||
The lotus presided over by Viṣṇu is the cause of the manifestation of the universe;
above that is the Unstruck (Anāhata) lotus, resembling the rising sun.
It is beautifully adorned with the letters from *ka* to *ṭha* and with *arka* leaves;
in its center is a *bāṇaliṅga*, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns. (Note: *akṣāntadalaiḥ* is an alternative reading.)
The sound consisting of Brahman, the unstruck (*anāhata*) sound, is perceived there;
that lotus is celebrated by yogis as being named *anāhata*. || 114 ||
That is the supreme abode of bliss, presided over by the Puruṣa;
above that is the one called Viśuddha, endowed with sixteen petals.
Endowed with sixteen vowels, smoke-colored and of great luster,
it bestows purity upon the living being because of its perception as the world of the *haṃsa*.
The pure lotus is called "Space," most wonderful;
above that is the wheel of command (ājñācakra), supreme and presided over by the Self.
The lotus with two petals beginning with *ha* and *kṣa* is presided over by the Moon;
the transmission of the command (*ājñā-saṃkramaṇa*) therein is celebrated as the "Command of the Guru. (118)
Above that is the one called Kailāsa, and above that is Bodhinī;
O Goddess, there is the thousand-petaled lotus, and above that is the station of the Bindu.
First, by means of the practice of inhalation (pūraka), one should fix the mind in the foundational center (svādhiṣṭhāna).
Having contracted that Śakti located between the anus and the genitals, one should awaken her. (Note: "gude" is an alternative reading for "de").
One should lead the drop (bindu) through the sequence of the differentiation of the signs (liṅga) and contemplate that supreme Śakti as having become one with Śambhu. 121.
Having caused that power—which is beyond perception and bestows the perfection of yoga—to drink the nectar arising from that [union], which flows from the mouth and resembles liquid lac; 122.
Having satiated the deities of the six chakras there with a stream of nectar,
the wise one should bring [the nectar] back again to the mūlādhāra by that same path.
One should effect the dissolution of the mind there by means of the very process of going and returning;
thus it should be practiced day after day, O Pārvatī. (124)
"One is liberated from the bonds of existence, such as the sufferings of old age and death"—thus has been taught the supreme yoga, which is the binding of the *yonimudrā*. (125)
Now I shall further explain the samādhi that destroys worldly existence;
or else, O Supreme Goddess, through the yoga of meditation as previously described. (126)

With undivided mind, one should meditate upon the Goddess in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus; having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the body, one should contemplate the Self as being of the nature of Tripurā. 127.
One should constantly contemplate the identity of oneself, one’s guru, and the deity;
"I am the Divine, I am not another; I am indeed Brahman, not subject to sorrow. (128)
I am of the nature of Truth-Consciousness-Bliss, possessing a pure and awakened self-nature.
Having first extracted the syllable *praṇava* (Om), one should then place the word *tat* after it. (129)
Having reflected thus, "It is so," the wise man should perform his duty;
by remembering his duties from the very beginning, he is fit for becoming Brahman. (130)
Endowed with all auspiciousness, the practitioner, having gone outside and voided urine and feces, should thoroughly cleanse his hands and feet. (131)
O Goddess of the gods, having washed one's face and then both nostrils,
and having applied collyrium to the eyes, one should resort to a pure place.
If one should look upon the solar orb without having applied collyrium to the eyes, the merit acquired throughout his life would perish; what then can be said of that evil-minded person? (133)
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times with the three principles (tritattva), one should practice the cleansing of the teeth.
He who, having chewed the tooth-stick, worships the deity [attains success]. (134)
O Goddess, that worship is fruitless, and upon death one goes to hell.

One should write Kāmadeva, whose essence is *klīm*, at the end of all [the syllables], followed by the word "people" (*jana*)—or according to another reading (*khapāṭha*), "all people" (*sarvajana*). 135.

This mantra, ending with *hṛdayāntaḥ* [or *dantadeha* according to the Kha-pāṭha], is for the purification of the beloved heart; one should wash the mouth with the fourteen vowels for the sake of attaining purity. 136.

[Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sequence of Karmayoga and Other Practices," in the Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between the illustrious Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 6 ||
[The Seventh Chapter] Śaṅkara said:
Then, one should perform the morning bath while applying the Traipura sequence.
Or again, with pure, fragrant waters at a sacred bathing-place (tīrtha) belonging to one's own lineage. || 1 ||
One should bathe according to the rules in a river or similar body of water, arranging the *kula-darbha* grass;
the silver [ring] on the right index finger and the gold [ring] on the ring finger.
The little finger of the left hand with gold [threads] is declared to be this "family-darbha";
this alone is the true darbha, not the darbha produced in the forest.
One should make the hand non-empty by establishing the fire, moon, and sun;
through this most beautiful mudrā, one shall become a subduer of all beings.

Having sipped water three times with the *tritattva* mantra and having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the removal of sins, one should then [place] a vessel of the lineage (*kulapātra*) containing gems, sesame seeds, and water.
Having taken it, one should perform a bath for the pleasure of the family deity; for one who has not bathed, there is no fruit, nor for one who does not likewise offer libations to the ancestors.
This Viṣṇubhairava mantra, uttered as "vicakrame," should always be recited during the ritual act of touching the clay.
Having placed the *kulacakra* in the water and having formed the *kulamudrā*, [he says]: "Come, O Gaṅgā, salutations to you who are endowed with all sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*). (8)
"O Goddess, O beautiful one, I invoke you here for the purpose of bathing;
having invoked you, I unite you with the mandalas of the Moon, Sun, and Fire within the water."
Having reflected thus, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon Tripurasundarī in the center of that [space].
And with the Gāyatrī of the Great Goddess, he should invoke Śivā as Sundarī. (Note: "ca" is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
One should consecrate the water three times with the root mantra;
then, while recollecting the root mantra in one's heart, one should sprinkle it upon the head. (Note: *mūrdhni* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
One should perform an immersion three times by means of the three *tripurā* seed-syllables;
then, O Goddess of the Gods, having arisen from that, one is freed from the entire physical body.
Having uttered the three-syllabled mantra, one should cause [the disciple] to put on a garment that is unwashed, torn, covered with hair, and infested by mice. (13)

One should avoid that which is dirty, belonging to another, or stale; and having applied the sectarian mark (tilaka) according to one's family tradition and having sipped water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule.

Then the practitioner should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) for the destruction of sin. Bathing is declared to be of three kinds, and the twilight worship is likewise remembered as being of three kinds. (Note: *sādhaka* is the reading; *sādhana* is an alternative reading. 15.
O Goddess, there may be an internal [bath] and likewise an external one, as well as a mental one;
indeed, he whose mind is always pure performs the mental bath.
O Goddess, one who touches the sandals (or, according to the *kha* manuscript, "the ointments and so forth") is indeed always free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).
The external [practice] has been declared by means of mantras; now hear the internal [practice]. (According to the *kha* manuscript, "by means of food alone. 17.

The wise one, devoted to *prāṇāyāma* according to the sequence previously described, should unite the Śakti with Paraśiva in accordance with the prescribed rule. (This is the reading from the Mārdhaka manuscript. 18.
Having repeatedly immersed oneself in the nectar arising from that,
one should indeed bathe once more in the pure sacred ford (tīrtha) residing within the heart, at Puṣkara.
Or, having bathed at Bindu-tīrtha, there is no rebirth;
one devoted to meditation should always properly meditate upon the Self. (20)
O Dear One, this mental twilight (mānasī saṃdhyā) is supreme due to the distinction of its deities;
it is that time in which the union of Śiva and Śakti arises.
That twilight is perceived by those established in samādhi who are devoted to the Kula;
now I shall describe another [twilight] here, which destroys all sins.
Having sat down in a pure place, one should sip water three times with the three *tattvas*.
Having performed three *prāṇāyāmas*, one should [perform] the threefold purification (*adhividhi*) by means of the three seed-syllables (*bījas*). (23)

Taking water in the left hand, one should perform a sevenfold sprinkling over the head with the falling drops of water while recollecting the mantra. (Note: *mūrdhni* is the reading in manuscript *ka*).
Having taken the remaining water in his right hand,
the practitioner should touch his nose with that water and then perform the Aghamarṣaṇa rite.

Having drawn [the water] in through the *iḍā* [left nostril], the mass of sins within the body is washed away; that water, now black in color, is expelled through the *dakṣa* (or *vāma*, according to another reading) channel.
The mantra-practitioner, having visualized that [impurity] in the form of sin in his right hand, should cast it away before him onto a vajra-stone by means of the Astra-mantra. || 27 ||

Having thus performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* and likewise sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), the best of practitioners should then sprinkle [the water] upon his head according to the prescribed rite. (28)
Oṃ, we purify ourselves with the divine waters, the essence, the nectar, the pure Brahman.
[One should offer] three handfuls of water upon the ground to Mārtaṇḍabhairava. (29)
Then, with arms raised, the practitioner of mantra should take refuge in the Sun.
Oṃ. His rays bear aloft that god, Jātavedas. || 30 ||

For the vision of all, one should utter Bhairava upon the remnant of Mārtaṇḍa. (O Goddess, one should utter the word Bhairava upon the remnant of the Sun-Mārtaṇḍa; this is the reading in manuscript Kha.
One should contemplate the Kula-cakra within the solar orb. || 31 ||
Desiring that which is appropriate for childhood, [he beheld] the young girl from the midst of the wheel—
shining with the luster of the orb of the rising sun, and having eyes like the sun, fire, and the moon.
One should meditate upon the auspicious Goddess holding a noose, a goad, arrows, and a bow;
at midday, one should contemplate the Goddess adorned with the beauty of fresh youth.
In the evening, one should meditate upon the Goddess, who is the singular radiance of the three worlds,
endowed with all youthfulness, resplendent, and the supreme digit.
At night, the wise enjoyer, devoted to enjoyment, should contemplate her alone and recite the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.
Having prostrated before the Goddess who resides within the solar orb, one should conclude [the rite].
Having thus completed the twilight worship (saṃdhyā), one should then contemplate the supreme Vidyā within the heart. (36)
Or else, O Supreme Goddess, one should always contemplate her.
The Goddess said:
"Now I wish to hear how one attains the qualification for this. (37)
O Śiva, [this may be performed] for those who have committed offenses, such as those devoid of Vedic vows and those under religious observances,
as well as for the uninitiated, women, and Śūdras.
O Mahādeva, how do these people attain unsurpassed liberation?
For the Veda declares: "One cannot be released from the bondage of the body without a Brāhmaṇa. (39)
Īśvara said:

Formerly, in the Devadāru forest, having observed some brahmins of exceedingly wicked speech, the Blessed Viṣṇu approached me and offered his salutations. (Note: *atidurdhiyaḥ* is an alternative reading for *atidurhṛdaḥ*).
Then, O Great Goddess, the God, his heart melted with compassion, sat down and asked me the cause of their liberation.
The Blessed One said:
"All these are of evil intellect, excluded from the conduct prescribed by the Vedas;
they are addicted to unrighteous sexual intercourse and devoted to the drinking of liquor. (42)
O Lord, tell us the means by which liberation may be attained for those who are devoid of self-knowledge and who have abandoned the practice of yoga. (43)
"How, O Lord, can Śūdras and others have the qualification for initiation?
Īśvara said: "Even one who has committed wicked deeds, fallen, and is excluded from the Vedas [is qualified]. (44)
Whether it be a woman, a Śūdra, or even an outcaste (vrātya), by knowing her a Brāhmaṇa becomes one;
she through whom Brahman—the imperishable, being-consciousness-bliss—is realized. || 45 ||
I shall now relate that very [teaching] which resides within your own heart,
fashioned from the twenty-four principles and having their very nature as its form.

One should meditate upon him who has three forms, yellow like a campaka flower, whose nature consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, seated upon a hundred-petaled lotus throne while himself remaining in the lotus posture (padmāsana).
One should thus meditate upon the syllable *Pukāra*, which resembles an *atasī* flower, situated in the center of a lotus, gentle, and the destroyer of minor offenses (*upapātaka*). (48)
O best of gods, one should constantly meditate upon the syllable *ra*, which is tawny, seated upon a lotus throne, peaceful, and the destroyer of great sins. (49)
One should thus contemplate the syllable SU, possessing a luster equal to sapphire;
it shall burn away all sufferings arising from planetary influences and diseases. (50)
O bull among men, one should contemplate the syllable *nda*, radiant with the brilliance of fire;
the sin committed through the killing of a fetus perishes at that very moment. (51)
One should meditate on the pure syllable *Riṃ*, which destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin;
the wise one should contemplate the syllable *Rīṃ* as resembling pure crystal.
The sin arising from approaching those who should not be approached perishes quickly;
the yogi should contemplate [the deity] as beautiful, resembling pure crystal. 53.
The sin of consuming what is unfit for consumption perishes at that very moment through the syllable *he*, which has the color of a star and is adorned by the moon upon its crest. (54)
The yogi should meditate upon the bestower of boons who destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin;
he has the form of the letter 'Ka', is black in color, and possesses a luster like a dark blue cloud. (55)
O tiger among men, by meditating upon it, one certainly destroys sin—[meditating] on the syllable "Me," which is red in color and seated upon a lotus throne. (56)
It destroys at that very moment the sin committed through the killing of a cow and other such acts.
One should meditate upon the supreme Śvaka (or Yakā, according to another reading), which resembles molten gold. (57)

The practitioner should visualize the one seated upon a lotus throne who grants liberation from the sin of killing—a syllable *Ri* (or *Ryai*) which is white in color and possesses a radiance equal to a jasmine flower. (58)
By meditating upon it, one burns away the sin committed by killing a guru at that very moment.
One should contemplate the syllable *dhī* as white, with a luster equal to the *kunda* flower. (59)
One is liberated from the sin of killing one's father or mother; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should contemplate the letter *ma*, which has the luster of a ruby and is blazing with splendor. (60)
The sin accumulated in previous births perishes at that very moment.
One should contemplate the syllable *Hīṃ*, which is conch-white in color and possesses a luster equal to the full moon. (61)
One should constantly meditate here upon Acyuta, the burner of all sins without exception;
one should meditate on him as white, seated upon a lotus, and possessing that [syllable] *kāra*.
The sin committed through receiving gifts perishes by mere remembrance [of this].
One should visualize the syllable *naḥ* as red in color, with a luster like that of the indragopa insect.
Having meditated thus, O Lord of the World, one should burn away the sin of killing living beings;
one should then recollect the syllable *klim*, which is red in color and possesses a brilliance equal to a vajra. (64)
It burns away all sins and is not defiled by other evils;
first, one should visualize the letter *Na*, which has a face with a radiance like the rising sun. 65.
O best of gods, by meditating on him even once—he who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus and has a face turned toward the south—one shall go to the abode of Brahmā. (66)
O best of gods, by meditating on it even once, he shall go to the station of Viṣṇu;
[he should visualize] the syllable OṂ, which is gentle, yellow like gorocana, and facing north.
O best of gods, by meditating on it even once, he shall again attain the state of Rudra—
the syllable *da*, which resembles the autumnal moon, is peaceful, and faces the west.
O best of gods, by meditating on this even once, one shall go to the state of Īśvara.
"Yāt" is said to be the head, and "ūrdhvānana" (or "ūrdhvā," according to another reading) is declared to be [the face]. (69)
O best of gods, by meditating on this even once, one shall go to the city of Sadāśiva.
Now, the deities of all the syllables will be described in their proper order.
Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Vidyut, Yama, and Varuṇa;
Bṛhaspati (or Ka according to another reading), Parjanya, Indra, and Gandharva. || 71 ||
Pūṣan, Śiva, Tuṣṭa, Savitṛ, and Marut; Soma, Aṅgiras, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, and Prajāpati. || 72 ||
Having meditated upon all the gods—Rudra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other deities—at the time of recitation, one shall attain union (sāyujya) with them. || 73 ||

This three-footed [mantra] of Lalitā, consisting of the three Vedas, is composed of her three seed-syllables. The wise person who, having understood this, performs recitation and fire-offerings, [attains success]. (Note: The variant reading *strīpade* is found in manuscript Kha.)
For one who, having first performed the six-limbed rite, meditates upon that Supreme Deity, there shall be no birth-impurity (sūtaka), nor does death-impurity (mṛtaka) exist for him. 75.
O sinless one, for him who does not know the Gāyatrī in this manner according to the prescribed rule, I have described both birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka).
When such impurity (sūtaka) exists, one shall obtain neither the fruit of giving, nor the fruit of sacrifice, nor is the fruit of visiting sacred fords said to accrue to him. (77)
This is declared to be the Gāyatrī, the Traipurī, which bestows all perfections;
because it protects one who sings [it], it is therefore called Gāyatrī. (78)
Even one who is burdened with great sins, O Great Goddess, if he should mutter [the mantra] ten times, truly, truly, he becomes liberated at that very moment. (79)

One should indeed recite this one thousand and eight times with undistracted mind; [if one recites the Gāyatrī one hundred times, as in the Kha manuscript reading], being liberated from all sins, one becomes entitled to perform worship. || 80 ||
The son of Jamadagni, my disciple, was liberated while yet alive from terrible sins such as the murder of his mother; likewise was the other, Mīnanātha.
Jageṣavya, Candra, and Vāsava were liberated;
likewise, Agastya was released from [the sin of] approaching the teacher’s bed and other such [transgressions]. || 82 ||
By this very [means], he was liberated from the sin of eating what is unfit to be eaten;
and Vasiṣṭha also was liberated from such acts as approaching a Cāṇḍāla woman.
Dattātreya [fell] from drinking liquor, and Jvalana from eating all things;
yet they were all Brahmās, created by the powerful Viṣṇu.
"By this very [means], O Great Goddess, all have been liberated.
The Goddess said: "I am blessed and favored by you, my Lord Śaṅkara. (85)
"I am free from doubt, O Lord of Gods; my delusion and duality have been destroyed. How many times does that [delusion] arise, O God? Tell me that now, O Lord. (86)
Īśvara said:
She is indeed one alone, O Great Goddess, yet she has attained manifold divisions:
as Saurī, Vaiṣṇavī, Śāktī, Brāhmī, and Śāmbhavī. (87)
Those [mantras] are to be employed in that tantra; the Traipurīya [system] has been revealed.
Now listen to this, which is declared to be the threefold libation (tarpaṇa). (88)
From the friction of the moon, the sun, and fire, that supreme nectar which flows forth—by means of that divine nectar, one should satisfy the Supreme Deity. (89)
Now hear this internal libation, which is mental:
by constantly remembering the Self as being composed of that [divinity], one whose soul is ever-satisfied attains fulfillment. (90)
Always content in all undertakings and with a steady mind,
one should sit in a clean place and then begin the libation (tarpaṇa).
Having first gratified the gurus, one should then gratify the Root Goddess;
thereafter, the Vidyā consisting of two seed-syllables joined with the beloved of the Fire-god [should be recited]. 92.
Then, at the end of the Goddess’s own name, one should append the words "tarpayāmi" and "namaḥ";
likewise, one should satisfy the gods, the ancestors, and the sages with water from the family vessel.
One should employ [this mantra] at the beginning of the libation (tarpaṇa) and other rites, saying: "May Vṛddhabhairava be satisfied;
likewise, O Supreme Goddess, may Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Prajāpati be satisfied. (94)
Having thus gratified the sages and the Bhairava ancestors as well, [he says]:
"May the mother Sundarī be satisfied; may the father Bhairava be satisfied. (95)
At the beginning, one should employ the mantra preceded by "Tripura" for libations (tarpaṇa),
as well as for ancestral rites (śrāddha), marriage, giving gifts, bathing, and the worship of Anaṅga.
At all times and in all undertakings, whether pertaining to the Tantras or the Vedas, one should likewise remember Tripurabhairava and Tripurasundarī. 97.
Recalling his own sacred knowledge (svavidyā), he should perform every rite prescribed for him;
the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) for the twice-born are declared to be those spoken in the Vedas. || 98 ||
For them, however, one should perform the ritual procedure with the Vidyā even in those various instances;
for other castes as well, one should bring the rite to completion by means of the Vidyā alone.
He alone who is refined by knowledge is considered a Brāhmaṇa; by the absence of knowledge there is burning, while by knowledge one may perform other [virtuous] acts. 100.

By that very [means], O Goddess, success is certain everywhere for one who is absorbed in that, provided that the water-offering (arghya) is not given to the Sun according to the prescribed rite. (101)
By whom can the worship performed according to the prescribed rite be surpassed?
[One should offer] arghya to Mārtaṇḍabhairava with dūrvā grass and white rice grains. (Note: *śitaiḥ* is an alternative reading for *sitaiḥ*.)
One should offer red flowers and sandalwood to the Lord together with his retinue.
(By the words "Śiva" and so forth, the extraction of the *hrīṃ* seed-syllable is performed: The seed-syllable of Śiva, situated in fire (*ra*) and adorned with the left eye (*ī*). 103.
Then one should write the word *haṃsa* joined with the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*;
then one should write "to Mārtaṇḍabhairava" and the Power of Radiance (*prakāśaśakti*).
Having said "sahitāya" (together with), and after this [the word] "idam arghyam" (this water of honor),
having joined it with the wife of Vahni (svāhā), one should offer the *arghya* to Sūrya.
O Maheśvarī, one should not offer arghya to the Sun with water from a conch;
for Sūrya embodies all the gods and is saluted by all the gods.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite and circumambulating him, one who bows down to the Blessed One is indeed liberated from all sins. (107)
Whoever should always worship the Lord, or having seen Him, bow down to the Master—who is worshipped as the deity pervading within the entire universe—[attains the highest state]. (108)
O Goddess, by performing a single circumambulation, one immediately obtains the fruit that is proclaimed to come from visiting thirty-five million sacred sites (tīrthas).
Whatever merit is gained from visiting various sacred fords (*tīrtha*s), all that is obtained simply by beholding the Sun;
he who is always bathed by the rays of the Sun is as if bathed in the nectar of all sacred fords. (Note: *sa* is the reading in manuscript *kha*.)
Then, one should offer the *arghya* to the Goddess with the *Tripuragāyatrī*. (This is to be understood here as pertaining to the secret initiation.
[One offers it] to her who resides within the solar orb, by means of the previously described yoga of meditation. (111)
Having meditated on the Wheel-King (cakrarāja) in the heart, one should bring the Goddess there, reciting the Vidyā one hundred and eight times with undistracted mind. (122)
[Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bathing, Twilight Devotions, and Other Rites," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 7 ||
[The Eighth Chapter] Ishvara said:
Then the silent one, whose self was purified, touched the supreme Vidyā within his heart.
Then the yogi, with his mind not directed outward, should enter the sacrificial ground.

It should not be infested with hair or insects; it should not be oily nor excessively slippery; it should indeed not be rough (according to the *ru* reading), nor too low, nor too high (nor too hot, according to the *kha* reading), nor covered by forest growth.
It was not shrouded by winds, nor crowded with other living beings; it was free from dust and mud, and was not gazed upon by domestic animals. || 3 ||
Unobstructed by trees and the like, crowded with flowing water,
and open on all four sides, it brings delight to the mind.
One should not perform worship even in a sacred place that is saline or subject to cultivation;
this is declared to be a prohibited sacrificial ground. Now, the prescribed [grounds] are being described.
Situated near ponds and wells, located in the midst of a garden of *sumana* flowers,
endowed with various pavilions, and adorned with a pure sacrificial altar.
It was crowded with banners and flags, its coverings reddened with lac;
it was strewn with heaps of flowers and adorned with bells and chowries.
Equipped with lamps and mirrors, adorned above with a canopy, provided with drinks and foods, and perfumed with camphor and agallochum incense. || 8 ||
Resplendent like the rising sun, beautiful, and bringing delight to the mind,
her interior was filled with various weapons and she was adorned and worshipped.
Thus, O Great Goddess, this sacrificial ground has been described;
it stands outside the altar of worship, at a distance of four cubits, according to one's understanding.
If he is at home, standing at the doorway, having sipped water (ācamana), he should mentally bow to his gurus,
his chosen deity, and also to the guardians of the directions.
I salute Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and Varuṇa; likewise Pavana, Dhanada, Īśa, Prajāpati, and Ananta. || 12 ||
I bow to Gaṇeśa and Kṣetreśa, as well as Dvāraśrī;
to Gaṇanātha and Vaṭuka, Durgā, Kṣetra, Rati, and Smara.

I bow to Prīti and Vasantaka, as well as the treasure-vases Śaṅkha and Padma; likewise, I bow to Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, Māyā, and Durgā. (Note: "Śaṅkhapadmanidhī" is the reading found in manuscript Pāṭha.)
I bow down to Bhadrakālī, Svasti, Svāhā, and Śubhaṅkarī; likewise, I bow to Gaurī, Lokadhātrī, and Vāgīśvarī. || 15 ||
I bow in due order to Brahmā and the Vāstupuruṣa;
then, with supreme devotion, one should offer a handful of flowers to them.

Having drawn a square mandala to the left, O Maheśvarī, one should worship the support there, as well as the vessel provided with food and water. (The variant reading *kha* has "a square [mandala] with water.")
O Supreme Goddess, having performed the consecration, one should offer the bali-oblation to all beings;
first the Tāra (Om), then Bhuvaneśānī, and then the word "sarvavighna" (all obstacles).
Uttering "Hṛdante sarvabhūtebhyo huṃkāraṃ vahnivallabhām," one should offer the bali-oblation with the mudrā known as Tattva.
The joining of the thumb and the ring finger is declared to be this *tattvamudrā*.
Having written the weapon-mantra (*astra*) at the end of the *bālā* mantra, ending with the letter *ṅ* and joined with the syllable *phaṭ*.
This is declared to be the weapon-mantra (astramantra), which destroys the entire multitude of obstacles.
Then, having consecrated unbroken grains (akṣata) seven times properly with this very mantra, || 21 ||
May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth, those who move in the intermediate space, and those who have gone to the divine worlds; may they perish by the command of Śiva. 22.
O Maheśvarī, with this very mantra—*aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*—one should scatter unbroken grains (*akṣata*) there upon the sacrificial altar (*yajñamaṇḍapa*) for the worship of the Goddess. (23)
Contracting his left limb, he should enter with his right foot;
then, he should dispel the obstacles that have come to the sacrificial hall.

Having performed these three claps of the hands while striking the heels and opening the mouth wide, one should dispel all obstacles. (Note: *vaktrakaiḥ* is an alternative reading for *vaktrakaḥ*). 25.
Then again, having gazed at the sides, above, and below with the "krodha-dṛṣṭi" (wrathful gaze) while uttering "huṃ phaṭ," one should become well-disposed. || 26 ||
The gazing [at the sacrificial ground] is said to be performed with the seed-syllable of the armor;
it consists of the fourth [vowel] joined with the nasal drop (bindu), and endowed with the digit (kalā) and the sound (nāda). || 27 ||
This is declared to be the seed-syllable of Dharma, the means for accomplishing virtue, desire, and wealth.
One should perform the sprinkling of the sacrificial ground with the Astra-mantra. (Note: *baddha* is an alternative reading for *badhna*.)
Contact with impure birds, the sprinkling of bird droppings, and contact with mice, frogs, worms, insects, and the like. (29)

O Dear One, whatever place has been defiled by those whose faults are unknown, or what occurs during cleansing and other such acts—all these perishes through seeing and touching [the deity]. (Note: *tadūṣita* is the reading in manuscript *kha*.)
The earth, having attained solidity through the masses of fat from Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
is forever pure for all the worship of the gods everywhere.

For the sake of liberation from that defect, one should write the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) upon the ground; having personally offered the food oblation and other items, one should burn away impurity with fire and gaze upon all of that with the Śrīvatsa mudrā. || 33 ||
Whatever flaw in the flowers and so forth has not been correctly perceived by oneself, or even the absence of contact and so on, or whatever may have been acquired through improper means; || 34 ||

Likewise, contact with floral remains (nirmālya), the climbing of insects and the like—whatever such [impurities] there may be—all that goes to destruction by the mere sight of the food offering (naivedya) and so forth. (35)
Whatever food offerings and the like, as well as flowers, scents, and so forth, all should be prepared for covering until one has invoked the Supreme Goddess.
Having invoked and established [the deity], one should display it uncovered;
for, O beloved, the Rākṣasas accept that which is uncovered. (37)
Then one should prepare a seat that is neither too low nor too high;
furthermore, one should not use a seat or an arghya vessel that is broken.
Success in liberation is achieved on a black antelope skin; both prosperity and liberation on a tiger skin;
for the sake of desired objects on a woolen blanket; and likewise, one's specific wish is fulfilled on a red woolen blanket.
Success in all [aims] is achieved on a seat of kuśa grass; for the rite of killing, a black woolen blanket;
and for the worship of Tripurā, a red woolen blanket is recommended as a seat.
One should not collect for the rite of worship an image that is longer than two cubits, wider than one and a half cubits, or higher than three finger-breadths. 41.
One may prepare the leather seat as desired; that which was mentioned previously bestows success.
A householder who has been initiated should never sit upon the skin of a black antelope.
The arising of suffering on the ground leads to misfortune; a seat made of wood causes destruction.
A seat made of mango, neem, or kadamba wood brings about the ruin of one's lineage. (Note: "sarva" is the reading found in all manuscripts.)

The Bakula, Kiṃśuka, and Panasa trees have had their beauty destroyed; [the city] is constructed of bamboo, bricks, stone, earth, grass, and sprouts (or Bilva leaves, according to the Kha manuscript).
The practitioner of mantra should avoid a seat that bestows poverty, disease, and suffering—one that is pierced by iron arrows, split by water, shattered, or broken. (45)
One should avoid that which has been kept overnight by others and that which has not been washed; however, a vessel made of clay or one made of various auspicious woods is recommended. (46)
The practitioner should not use a seat at will during the rite of worship; O Dear One, he should always use a seat made of wood or similar materials, and it should be of moderate size.

O Śivā, a wooden seat should be twenty-four finger-breadths long, sixteen finger-breadths wide, and four finger-breadths high. [O Goddess of excellent complexion, this is declared to be the praiseworthy seat for the worship of Kambala, Armaṇa, Śaila, and Mahāmāyā. (This is the additional reading from manuscript *kha*. || 48 ||
One may make it half an aṅgula [in thickness], but one should not make it higher than that;
[this applies] due to the contact with cloth on the ground, and for wood, due to the contact with a woolen blanket.
The contact of silk and deerskin destroys previously acquired merit;
therefore, the practitioner of mantras should sit upon an auspicious seat according to his ability. 50.

Holding the seat with both hands, one should spread it upon the ground; having uttered the seed-syllable of Parā (here, the *hrīṃ* seed-syllable is to be understood), followed by the *ādhāra* [mantra]. (51)
Having written the word "śakti," one should write "kamalāsana" (the lotus-seat).
One should employ the word "namaḥ" ending in the letter "ṅ"; with this very [formula], one should worship the seat.
One should contemplate the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) and the Tortoise (kūrma) in that very place;
having also worshipped Ananta, one should present the water offering (arghya) for the Earth.
Having first uttered the Praṇava and also saying "Salutation to the Earth," one should hold the seat with both hands and meditate upon the Lord according to the prescribed rule.
Merupṛṣṭha is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), Sutala is said to be the meter (chanda), and Kūrma is indeed the deity for sitting upon the seat. 55.
The application (viniyoga) has thus been declared; one should sit down with the recitation of the mantra:
"O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu. (56)
And you must always support me; make this seat pure, so that any defect of other seats—such as being poorly crafted by an unskilled artisan—is not present here. (57)
O beloved, that which is of unknown form goes to dissolution according to the rule;
it consists of two equal parts properly situated upon the two thighs. (58)
Having taken up the left foot, one should place it upon the right;
having pressed the two heels against the hips, one should fix the gaze upon the tip of the nose. (59)
This lotus posture (padmāsana) is recommended for the worship of Tripurā;
likewise, the swastika, the cow-mouthed (gomukha), or the upward swastika postures may also be used.
The paryanka posture is indeed praised as a seat; thus seated with legs bound, O beloved, while gazing upon one's chosen deity, one does not perceive any defect in the feet.
Otherwise, it would not be proper to show one's feet during worship of the gods;
among the directions, the northern quarter is the one that bestows the pleasure of Śiva.
Therefore, one should always worship Tripurā while seated facing that direction;
when one worships the Goddess, one should be oriented facing north.
Then, O Goddess, the northern direction becomes the eastern direction; of this there is no doubt.
The northeast corner becomes the southeast, and likewise, the northwest becomes the northeast. (64)

Then the southern direction is to be known [as such], O Maheśvarī, and the western direction likewise; the south-eastern corner (āgneya) would be Rākṣasa, and the south-western corner (nairṛta) would also be Rākṣasa. (Note: *vāyukoṇam* is the reading in the Kha manuscript, while *āgneyam* is the reading in the Kha variant for the second half.)
In worship facing east or west, the western direction is considered worldly;
in worship facing south or north, the western direction is considered to be directly in front.
In the worship of the circle of Yoginīs, this direction must not be otherwise.
[The deity] has a body reddish with saffron and is adorned with red ornaments. (67)
Seated upon a red seat, situated in a house as crimson as lac,
his face colored by betel, he is made fragrant by the scent of incense.
His limbs were smeared with camphor powder and adorned with red sandalwood;
richly arrayed in all the finery of amorous attire, his body was fashioned into three cities.
Or the practitioner, whose mind is fixed and who is devoted through the mental resolve, having joined his palms in reverence, with the lotus of his face bearing a gentle smile; || 70 ||
Then, on the upper part of the left ear, one should bow to the Guru;
and on the upper part of the right ear, the wise man should bow to Gaṇeśa. (Note: *ūrdhva* is the reading for *arddha*.)
One should bow to Durgā in front and to the Kṣetranāyaka behind;
then, one should place the lamp to the right or left of the Goddess.
Then, O Goddess of gods, having touched the crest of the lamp with the mantra "Ram" and according to the prescribed rite using the *devatīrtha*, one should touch it.
May this lamp, a great light that is brilliantly radiant and dispels all darkness, be a bestower of auspiciousness—a light that shines both within and without. (74)

That lamp, bestowing auspiciousness, would become [beneficial] to him by its mere touch, even when it comes into contact with moths, insects, hair, and the like, or with flesh-eating creatures. (Note: An alternative reading includes "saha"). 75.
Since the production of fat, marrow, and bone is initially useless, everything whose nature is unknown should destroy any defect through contact. (76)
The King of Wheels (cakrarāja) is colored with rocanā and saffron, along with musk, sandalwood, and camphor, and is joined with self-arisen flowers (svayaṃbhūkusuma). || 77 ||
Then, O Goddess, having suddenly established her upon a lion-throne before them, covered with vermilion powder, together with the Yoginīs; || 78 ||
Then, having meditated upon the form of the Goddess, one should offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).

One should ensure that [the vessel] is not empty of flowers; for if it were empty, obstacles and other hindrances would arise manifold. (Note: *aśūnyam* is the reading in manuscript *ka*, while *aśūnyaku* is the reading in manuscript *kha*. Similarly, *vighnādyanekaśaḥ* is the reading in manuscript *ka*, while *vighnādyane kaśaḥ* is the reading in manuscript *kha*.)
One should place the perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth on the right side;
thereafter, one should place a vessel for the washing of the hands.
One should place the water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other items in front, and the water-pot on the left;
having prepared a square mandala with water to the left [of the pot].
Then, O Goddess of Gods, one should place there a beautiful support made of gold, silver, copper, or other materials, holding it with both hands. 82.
One should worship that [deity] in the form of a circle of fire together with its constituent parts (kalās).
The auspicious jar should be made of gold, without cracks, and beautiful. (Note: "dhanya" is the reading in the Dhāka manuscript.)
The practitioner, having observed the secret [mandala], should [offer] water contained within a jar that is filled with cloth-strained water, scented, and free from defects. (84)
O Goddess, one should place it there upon the support with the left hand;
O Supreme Lady, one should worship that [support], which has the form of the sun, with its constituent parts (kalās). 85.
Having worshipped that ritual vessel (kalasa) with special care, O fair-faced one, one should contemplate the nectar residing therein as being manifest in the form of the moon. (86)
Having worshipped the lunar disc with its digits, O Goddess honored by the gods,
one should there worship Ānandabhairava and Ānandabhairavī.
If any other defect should occur in the vessel or the water through ignorance, all of that shall perish, and the jar shall become worthy of worship. 88.

Having sprinkled the vessel with weapon-mantra water, one should then place it upon the fire-mandala to the right (O Goddess, one should then place it on its support according to the rite and worship it). || 89 ||
Having honored [the vessel] filled with pure water, one should then recite the root mantra and the vidyā. One should sprinkle the flask with the water contained in the *prokṣiṇī* vessel.
Likewise, having installed the conch on the left according to the prescribed rite,
one should place the water for washing the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) to its north.
Having bowed to Śivā upon the wheel, one should then perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi);
for the body, though composed of the five elements, is eternally pure by its very nature.
The mind is always joined with putrefaction, being slippery with phlegm, feces, and urine;
indeed, for the sake of its purification alone, [it is cleansed] by the syllables of wind, fire, water, and earth. 93.
Drying, burning, as well as the scattering of ashes and the raining of nectar, and the flooding—these should be performed by means of pūraka, kumbhaka, and recaka [breathing techniques]. || 94 ||
Whatever is performed by one devoid of the five purities is like a malevolent rite (*abhicāra*);
likewise, worship performed without devotion yields a contrary result. (95)
O Dear One, this purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) consists of the cleansing of the elements that constitute the form of the body, through contact with the imperishable Brahman. 96.
The light of the Self functions within the internal organ;
