those yogins who know the reality call that the subtle body (liṅgadeha). || 97 ||
Indeed, through its purification, every form of purity arises;
that very [principle] is the cause of the birth of the universe and the cause of individual birth. || 98 ||
Liberation occurs upon the realization of that [reality], and not otherwise even through ten million births.

Having performed three *prāṇāyāmas*, one should likewise meditate while employing the *yonimudrā* (the characteristics of which are as follows: "Having bound the two little fingers together, with the two index fingers [holding] the ring fingers; the two thumbs should be placed below the long middle fingers which are joined above the ring fingers—this is declared to be the *yonimudrā*"). || 99 ||
O Goddess, having meditated with the intellect upon the three peaks of the Vidyā— composed of Fire, Sun, and Moon— within the three cities, one should then contemplate their unity.
In that luminous orb, the abode of being, consciousness, and bliss,
in the eternal Supreme Brahman which consists solely of the bliss of self-experience— || 101 ||
Having immersed oneself in the abode of the Bindu and remained there for a moment, one should contemplate;
one should remember that very [Bindu] as consisting of light, reddened by the rays of the rising sun.
In the midst of a most enchanting ocean of pure lac and nectar, upon an island composed of the nine gems, within a pavilion of wish-fulfilling jewels (cintāmaṇi). || 103 ||
Upon a lotus on a jeweled lion-throne, she who is the embodiment of fire, sun, and moon, resembling ten million rising suns—the supreme fourth digit (kalā). 104.
In the lower right hand he holds arrows, and in the lower left hand a bow;
in the upper right hand a mace, and in the left hand a noose. (The reading *dhṛtam* is found in manuscript *kha*.)
Having meditated upon her as non-different from oneself— possessing three eyes, clad in garments as red as the dawn, and whose nature is pure knowledge— 106.
One should contemplate the Self as consisting of pure experience and bliss;
O Śivā, by means of the mantra "Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, therefore I am He (so'haṃ), svāhā," [one attains it]. 107.

At the end of the three seed-syllables of the Child, O Mahātripurasundarī, one should perform protection by touching the heart while reciting, "Protect, protect, my self! (This is the reading in the Dra manuscript).
Thus, one should perform the binding of the directions with one's own fingers and with snapping sounds on all sides.

[Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Sacrificial Abode, Worship, Purification of the Elements, and so forth," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 8 ||
[The Ninth Chapter] Īśvara said:
Only a god should worship the God; one who is not a god should not worship the God.
O Śivā, they say that recitation performed without the ritual placement (nyāsa) is demonic and fruitless.
Having become identical with that through ritual placement (nyāsa), and having thus become the deity, one should worship him;
for through breath control (prāṇāyāma), meditations, and ritual placements, one attains the state of being the body of the deity.
O wise one, listen to the procedure for nyāsa, preceded by the purification of the hands:
having extracted the first [syllable] of the Mātṛkā and the second [syllable] along with the bindu.

Joined with the end of *śānta* [the letter *sa*], conjoined with the end of that which ends in *e* [the letter *au*], this great vidyā is thus considered to be the purifier of the hands. (With the bindu, beginning from the first letter of the alphabet *a*, and ending with *sau*—that is, *a-au-ḥ*—this is the vidyā that purifies the hands. 4.

Then the practitioner, having taken a red flower together with its fragrance, [places] that flower upon the palm of his hand with this very mantra. (This is the reading from the Kottama-kha manuscript.)
Having wiped it with the left hand after cleaning it with the right hand,
one should then wipe it with the Kāmabīja and smell it with the Vāgbhava.
O Pārvatī, one should cast this [water] toward the northeast with the *śeṣa* (or *śava*, as in the Kha manuscript) seed-syllable;
by grasping the flower, the tips of the fingers become purified.
Purity of the hands comes from rubbing them, while that of the backs [of the hands] comes from wiping;
the gods are pleased by the scent, and there is the gathering of sacred fords (tīrthas).
By this casting away, all obstacles are indeed placed at a great distance;
furthermore, whatever defilement there was in the two hands from contact with foul odors, vomit, or excrement is thereby removed.
One should destroy all that which is of unknown form by means of this following procedure:
first, having performed the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi), one should then perform the nyāsa on the ṛṣis and so forth.
When it is recited without the placement of the seers, meters, and deities,
even if it has been mastered, one shall not obtain its fruit therein.
O Maheśānī, the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
likewise, Paṅkti is declared to be its meter (chandas). Now listen, O Pārvatī, to the Vidyā. (Note: *paṅkti* is the reading in the Ka-pāṭha.)
The deity is the Supreme Sovereign, Mahātripurasundarī;
her application is declared to be for the accomplishment of enjoyment and liberation. 13.
One should place [the letters] upon the head, around the face, and in the heart;
listen, O Goddess of gods, to the Mātṛkā which destroys all sins.
All the mantras of those goddesses who are proclaimed as mothers, headed by Brāhmī, as well as their respective consonants (or vowels, according to the reading *sva*); || 15 ||
Joined with the lunar bindu, they bestow the fruits of all desires;
the seer is declared to be Sammohana, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī. (The reading "chanda" is preferred over "cha"). 16.
This goddess is proclaimed as the supreme mother of all beings;
O Goddess, the vowels are her powers (śaktis), while the collection of consonants is her seed (bīja).
The application (viniyoga) has been fully described for the purpose of deluding all people;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the vowel joined with the long [vowel]. 18.
O Goddess, one should then assign the Heart, the Head, the Crest, and the Armor; thereafter, one should assign the Eye and the Weapon, accompanied by their respective mudrās and the word "namaḥ."

O Dear One, one should append *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* at the end; O Śivā, this is the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) mantra of the Mātṛkā, following every word. (Note: There is a variant reading: *svāhā vaṣaṭ vauṣaṭ astrāya phaṭ*).

I bow to her who holds in her lotus-like hands a rosary of crystal, a bow made of sugarcane, the five arrows of the God of Love, and the Vidyā-mantra; she who has three eyes and is as radiant as ten million rising suns.
One should meditate upon the Mother of all beings, who has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
One should contemplate the sixteen vowels upon the eight-petaled lotus at the throat;
one should place the twelve consonants beginning with *ka* upon the twelve-petaled heart-lotus.
One should place the ten letters beginning with *ḍa* in the ten-petaled lotus at the navel;
and one should place the six letters beginning with *ba* in the six-petaled lotus situated in the middle of the *liṅga*.
One should place the four vowels, beginning with *a*, upon the support in the four-petalled [lotus];
one should contemplate *ha* and *kṣa* in the two-petalled lotus situated between the eyebrows. (24)

Having thus recollected the internal *mātṛkās*, one should then perform the external placement (*nyāsa*). (The reading "in Śiva" [ka-pāṭha] is found. [He describes the external *mātṛkā-nyāsa* with the words beginning with "akāra": It should be understood that "klīṃ namo on the forehead" and so forth. The *mātṛkās* are proclaimed to be those beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'. (25)
One should install each [mantra] beginning with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) and so forth, which bestow all desired fruits;
these should be joined with the lunar drop (candrabindu) and end with "namaḥ. (26)
On the forehead, the face, the eyes, and the ears, O Pārvatī;
on the nose, the cheeks, the lips, and the teeth, as well as on the head and the mouth, O Śāṅkarī. (27)
O Śivā, one should sequentially place [the syllables] at the inner joints and tips of the pair of hands and feet,
and then sequentially on the two sides, the back, the navel, and the abdomen.
O Goddess, one should then place the elements along with their corresponding constituents (dhātus) in due order:
skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituents. (Note: *majjā* is the reading; some manuscripts read *majjaka*.)
The vital self (prāṇātman), the individual self (jīvātman), and likewise the supreme self (paramātman) [are located] in the heart, at the base of the arms, and in the region of the throat. || 30 ||
O Goddess, one should place [the mantras] in sequence upon the shoulders, the region of the heart, the pair of hands and feet, as well as the belly and the face, and indeed upon all the limbs.

(He indicates the *mātṛkā-nyāsa-mudrā* with the verse beginning "on the forehead, the ring finger," etc.): One should place the ring and middle fingers on the forehead; the index, middle, ring, and thumb [fingers] on the lotus-face;
and indeed the index, middle, and ring fingers on the two eyes. (32)
O Goddess, [place] the thumb on the two ears; O Beloved, the little finger and thumb on the two nostrils; the three middle fingers on the two cheeks; and the middle finger on the two lips. (33)

O Goddess, one should place the ring finger on the two teeth, the middle finger on the head, the ring and middle fingers on the mouth, and likewise the ring and middle fingers on the hands, feet, and sides. (34)
Then, O Pārvatī, one should place those [fingers]—the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger—on the back;
then all of them, including the thumb, on the navel; and [finally] on the belly.
And the entire palm [is placed] on the heart, the two arms, the region of the throat, the two shoulders, the edge of the chest, and likewise on the pair of hands and feet. (36)
O Goddess, the palms alone are proclaimed for the pair of stomach and mouth;
these mudrās of the Mātṛkās have thus been described in their proper order. (37)
If one performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) without knowing [the procedure], that nyāsa shall be fruitless;
however, one may perform it with the fingers, or with flowers, or even mentally.
O Supreme Goddess, he who performs the Mātṛkā-nyāsa in this manner becomes purified and fit for all sacrifices and worship. (39)
Indeed, there exists no mantra anywhere superior to this.
Whatever mantras belong to the deities, the sages, or even the rākṣasas— || 40 ||
All of them are eternally established within the Mātṛkā-mantra;
this [mantra] consists of all mantras and likewise consists of all deities. (41)
This Mātṛkā-nyāsa bestows the fourfold aims of life, grants contentment and nourishment, and is said to consist of all sacred seats (pīṭhas). || 42 ||

Whoever should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa without first worshipping the deity, from him the fourfold host of spirits will constantly stand in fear. (Note: "yaḥ" is the reading according to the Ka-pāṭha.)
Even the gods long to behold that one of great majesty;
he shall bring all under his control and shall never suffer defeat.
One should recite one hundred and eight times the supreme fifty-lettered Vidyā, the Mother of all, which is encapsulated by the seed-syllable *sarva*.

Having meditated on the Goddess of Speech in the heart and all the letters upon the head, one should [worship] with the Mātṛkā mantras in two ways: both in their regular order and in reverse order. (46)
O Great Goddess, having performed the mantra-ritual, he who drinks the water at dawn becomes eloquent, learned, wise, and an eminent poet. (47)
O Dear One, the wise man should first recite the vowels joined with the lunar bindu;
however, he should recite all the consonants alone.
Having taken water in the palm of his hand and recited the collection of syllables,
he should consecrate that water with mantras and drink it first with the *pūraka* breaths.
The second [time] by means of retention (kumbhaka), and the third by means of exhalation (recaka);
thus, having drunk the water three times in this manner, the wise one— || 50 ||
Having thus drunk [the water] at the three junctions of the day, consecrated with the Mātṛkā-mantra, one shall become firm-limbed, wise, and endowed with sons and grandsons. (51)
He who constantly recites [the mantra] consecrated with the Mātṛkā-mantra attains poetic skill as well as all his desires. (52)

O Great Goddess, by means of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka), one who drinks the water [of breath] attains all desires and becomes prosperous with sons and grandsons. (53)
Having become a great poet in the world, powerful and of truthful valor,
and having become rare to find everywhere, he shall attain liberation in the end.
Whether it be a king, a prince, or a beloved wife, one who observes the mātṛkā-mantra brings them under control before long. (55)

[Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Internal and External Mātṛkā Nyāsa for the Purification of the Hands," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 9 ||
[Tenth Chapter] The Śrī Devī said:
O God, O Bull-bannered One, please explain the Mātṛkā known as the Sixfold (Ṣoḍhā).
Īśvara said:
The first assignment is with the Gaṇeśas, while the second is considered to be with the planets.
The third [placement] is with the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), the fourth with the yoginīs;
the fifth placement is with the zodiac signs (rāśis), and the sixth is said to be with the sacred seats (pīṭhas). || 2 ||
This sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhā-nyāsa) has been proclaimed as the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
The Goddess said:
"Explain its fruit and its practical application clearly according to the truth."
Īśvara said: Nārāyaṇa is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi); Triṣṭubh is cited as the meter; and Sadāśiva is the deity, consisting of the collection of syllables whose essence is Śiva-Śakti. || 4 ||
The *haṃsa* is the power (*śakti*), the supreme seed-syllable (*parā-bīja*), and the glorious seed-syllable (*śrībīja*) is the pin (*kīlaka*);
its application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the accomplishment of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). || 5 ||
O Goddess, one should contemplate the venerable Guru, whose form is Śiva, upon the crown of the head;
thereafter, the supreme seed-syllable *Ramā* is said to be preceded by the vowel from the *Haṃsa*. (1–6)

Having indeed addressed Vighneśvara, one should then say "Salutation to Śrī. (The ritual placement [nyāsa] should be understood as follows: "Salutation to Avighneśvara and Śrī" on the forehead, and so forth.
In this same manner, one should likewise [place] Vighnarāja and the others, together with their Śaktis.
O Śivā, one should place [the mantra] in the location of the Mātṛkās, accompanied by a single Mātṛkā;
thereafter, O Queen of Devas, [one should add] "Vighnarājāya hriyai namaḥ."
One should assign [the mantra] with "Obeisance" to Vināyaka, to Tuṣṭi, to Śivottama, and likewise to Vighnakartṛ for nourishment (puṣṭi). || 9 ||
One should install [the mantra] "Salutation to Sarasvatī, the remover of obstacles";
then, as before, one should install [the mantra] "To Vināyaka" and "To Medhā. (10)
Salutation to Ekadanta and Kānti, to Dvidanta and Yāminī;
to Gajavaktra and Mohinī, and likewise to Nirañjanajaṭa (the application should be understood as *namaḥ* to Nirañjana and *jaṭāyai*). || 11 ||
To Kapardin and Tīvrā; Jvālinī and Dīrghavaktraka; to Śaṅkukarṇa and Nandā; Svarasā and Vṛṣadhvaja. || 12 ||
Gaṇanātha with Kāminī, Gajendra with Śubhā, Jayin with Śūrpakarṇa, and Trilocana with Satyā. || 13 ||
To Lambodara, the Lord of Obstacles; [Mahānanda] is her own essential form (svarūpiṇī).
She is the embodiment of desire and compassion, possessing four forms; beyond that is Sadāśiva. 14.
Āmoda is joined with Madavihvalā, and Vikaṭa with Āyutā;
Durmukha is joined with Ghūrṇā, and Sumukha with Bhūti. || 15 ||
Pramadā, likewise Bhūmi, Ekapāda, and Mati; Dvijihva joined with Ramā, and Surasena with Mānuṣī. (16)
O Supreme Goddess, the Hero is joined with Makaradhvaja;
he is six-faced, possesses distorted ears, is the bestower of boons, and is endowed with a frown.
Then, O Dear One, [the mantra] for Vāmadeva is joined with Lajjā and Dīrghaghoṇā; [the mantra] for Aghora is Vajratuṇḍa and Dviraṇḍa, joined with Dhanurdharā.
To Senānī belongs Yāminī; to Grāmaṇī, Rātri;
to Matta, Candrikā; and to Vimatta, Śaśiprabhā. (Note: *vimattāya* is the reading in manuscript *kha*.)
In the same way, O Supreme Goddess, [there are] Lolaya, Mattavāhana, Jaṭila, Capalākṣī (one reading is *Capalākṣiṇya*), Muṇḍī, and likewise Ṛddhiyuta. || 20 ||

O Supreme Goddess, the one who bears the sword, when joined with the unfortunate, should be replaced by the excellent one joined with the fortunate; so too the bull-bannered Lord should be established by Śivā. 21.
To Bhaktapriyā, Durgā, and Meghanāda, Kālikā is [the consort];
Gaṇeśvara is proclaimed as being joined with Kālakubjā (or Jihvā, according to the Kha-pāṭha). || 22 ||
Ganesha should be installed by the best of practitioners together with Vighnahāriṇī;
then, O Great Goddess, one should install the wish-fulfilling [deities] beginning with Sūryamukha. (23)
Having first extracted the vowels, provided with the moon-bindu (anusvāra),
and having uttered "Sūryāya namaḥ," one should place [the mantra] upon the heart.
Likewise, one should place Soma in the middle of the eyebrows with the *ṣa*-group,
and similarly, Bhūputra in the pair of eyes with the *ka*-group.
O Goddess, one should place Budha in the heart with the *ca*-group of consonants;
likewise, one should place Bṛhaspati in the throat with the *ṭa*-group of consonants.
O beloved, one should place Bhārgava at the region of the throat with the *tavarga*;
Śani at the navel with the *pavarga*; and Rāhu at the anus with the *śavarga*.
One should thus install the banner on the two feet according to the prescribed rule: first the letter preceded by a vowel, then the second [letter], and also "Aśvinyai namaḥ. (28)
Having placed [the syllable] upon the forehead, one should likewise place the others;
O Goddess, one should place Bharaṇī, joined with the syllable *iṃ*, in the right eye.
One should place *īṃ*, *uṃ*, and *ūṃ* upon the left eye as Kṛttikā;
and, O Goddess, one should place *ṛṃ*, *ṝṃ*, *ḷṃ*, and *ḹṃ* upon the right ear as Rohiṇī.
One should place Eṃyutā and Mṛgaśīrṣā on the left ear;
likewise, one should place Ādrā with the syllable Aiṃ on the right nostril.
Oṃ auṃ; one should place Punarvasu in the left nostril.
And one should place Puṣya, joined with *ka* (or *tā ka*, according to another reading), in the region of the throat, O Pārvatī. (32)
Likewise, O Goddess, one should place Āśleṣā on the right shoulder with the two letters Kha and Ga,
and one should place Maghā on the left shoulder with the two letters Gha and Ṅa.
O Goddess, one should place *caṃ* and *phalgunī* on the right elbow,
and *chaṃ* and *jaṃ*, along with *uttaraphalgunī*, on the left elbow.
One should place *jhaṃ* and *ñaṃ* on the right wrist; likewise, one should place *ṭaṃ* and *ṭhaṃ* on the left wrist, and then place *citrā*. (Note: There is a variant reading *hastaṃ* for *hastāṃ*.)

One should likewise place Svātī on the palm of the right hand with the syllable *ḍaṃ*; and Viśākhā on the palm of the left hand with the two syllables *ḍha* and *ṇa*. (Note: *tī* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
Likewise, being composed, one should place Anurādhā at the navel;
Dhanisthā and Jyeṣṭhā on the right hip, and Mūla with the three [stars] on the left.
Then one should assign Pūrvāṣāḍhā to the right thigh with the syllable *va*,
and immediately thereafter, Uttarāṣāḍhā to the left thigh with the syllable *bha*.

One should place Maṃ and Śravaṇa on the region of the right knee; and one should place Dhaniṣṭhā, conjoined with Yaṃ and Raṃ, on the left knee. (Note: The reading "Śravaṇā" is found in manuscript Ka.)
One should place Śatabhiṣā with the syllable *la* in the region of the right calf,
and Pūrvabhādrapadā, situated in the color of the bamboo, on the left.

In the same manner, one should place Uttarabhādrapadā with the six letters from the right foot; then, one should assign Revatī with the two lakṣas (the letters *la* and *kṣa*) and the two dots (*bindu*) on the head.
(4) And [one should visualize] Raktākṣī, who is white in color, auspicious, and causes fear to the beasts;
she holds a sword, a cup, a trident, and a khaṭvāṅga staff. || 42 ||
And [he should worship] Anugrāma with fierce fangs, who has a single face and destroys enemies;
she is offered milk-rice (pāyasa) and her form is fashioned by the vowels. (43)
One should meditate upon the goddess Ḍākinī, who fulfills all desires.

(Aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aṃ ḍāṃ ḍīṃ ḍamalavarayūṃ ḍākinyai namaḥ | O Ḍākinī, you who reside in the skin-element, sovereign of sixty-four million and four hundred thousand yoginīs, you who bring all beings under your power, grant me your command, Vicce! Thus it is clearly stated. Having first extracted the vowels, they are endowed with the moon-bindu (anusvāra). (44)
Following that, the two syllables ending in *ṭha*, pierced by the fourth *pāśa* and joined with *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, are declared to be the two seed-syllables (*bīja*). (45)
The letter ending in *ṭha* (ṭha), *bha*, the seed-syllable of the Earth (*la*), the one belonging to Varuṇa (*va*), Fire (*ra*), and Wind (*ya*);
then, O Goddess, the left ear (*śa*) joined with Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā. (46)
Having addressed the Ḍākinī with "Obeisance to the Ḍākinī" at the end, one should then say,
"Residing in the skin-element [of milk-rice]," and thereafter recite the sixty-four words.
At the end of the word *lakṣakoṭi*, one should say *yoginīsvāminī*, and then the word consisting of the syllable *kari* (or *kavi*), which brings all sentient beings under control. (48)
"Then give me your command; thereafter, O Goddess, one should place my two feet upon the purification and then meditate upon Rākinī."
She is situated in the center of the heart-lotus, with a face formidable with fangs,
dark as a fresh rain-cloud, and possessing full, elevated breasts.

Holding a trident and a hand-drum upon a vajra-lotus (or, according to another reading, holding [them] upon a vajra-lotus), she has a white face, is seated upon a funeral pyre, and her physical form is of a dark-brown complexion. || 51 ||
Then, [place] the letters of the Kaṭha school followed by the letter *ra*, differentiated by vowels as before;
having omitted the final letter of the group ending in *ṭha*, place the seed-syllable of fire (*agnibīja*) immediately thereafter, as before. (52)
Having addressed and awakened her with "Obeisance to the Rākī," it should likewise be so when she has entered the blood-element; thereafter, there are thirty-two lakṣa and koṭi [of repetitions].
At the end, in the Yoginīsvāmin [mandala], immediately following that as before, one should visualize her as red in color, three-eyed, and united with the Lord of the Gods of gods. (54)

One should meditate upon the supreme goddess, who has fangs, a fierce appearance, and holds a vajra, a spear, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she is intensely eager for molasses and rice. 55.
Having thus meditated upon Maheśānī, whose body consists of the syllables *ḍa* and *pha*,
one should then [place] the syllables *ḍa* and *pha*, O Goddess, as well as the pair of earth-seeds (*bhū-bīja*).

Leaving aside the fire-syllable (*vahni*), [one should take] the earth-seed (*mahī-bīja*) as before, and likewise the other; having uttered "Salākinyai namaḥ" and having thus awakened [the deity], one should proceed. (This is the reading in manuscript *kha*. || 57 ||
Afterwards, when the flesh-element has been reached, one should place everything else as before, starting from sixteen lakṣas and koṭis, within the navel-lotus.
And in the lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna, one should contemplate Kākinī, who is yellow in color, greatly intoxicated, and whose breasts resemble the frontal globes of an elephant. (59)
And [he saw her] with a mind intent on curd-rice, worshipped by the most excellent of gods,
holding a trident, a hand-drum, a noose, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness.
[One should worship] Parameśānī, who carries [the mantra] whose form consists of the letters from ba to la;
likewise, [one should worship] Kāṃkī, [with the mantra] ka-kamala-vara-yūṃ. || 61 ||
Having addressed Kākinī at the end with "Obeisance to Kākinī," one should likewise [recite] eight hundred million [times] after [the mantra] has entered the fat constituent (medas-dhātu). || 62 ||
The Mistress, having spoken as before, [described] the other [form] likewise:
five-faced, three-eyed, and having the nature of fire and the sun. (63)
The Supreme Goddess is depicted holding in her lotus-like hands a bow, an arrow, a noose, a sword (or a staff, according to another reading), a book, and the gesture of wisdom (jñānamudrā). 64.
One should contemplate [the goddess] joined with the joy of mung-bean rice in the *mūlādhāra*;
likewise [the syllables] from *va* to *sa*, as well as *sāṃsīṃsa* (or *śāśīṃśa* according to another reading) and *malavarayūṃ*. 65.

Having addressed Śākinī with "Obeisance to Śākinī" at the end, one should then [recite] four hundred thousand or ten million times for the attainment of the bone-element. (Note: *sākinīm* is the reading in the Śākapaṭha. 66.
The Yoginī is at the end of the word *svāmin*, likewise in the state of the feet of the Bestower of Excellent Boons;
she resides in the *bindu*, is white in color, and has the nature of the syllables *ha* and *kṣa*.
She always holds with her arms a hand-drum, a rosary, a skull-bowl, a sword, a book, and the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā).
She is endowed with three eyes and six faces, enchanting all beings;
she is devoted to food seasoned with turmeric and filled with the joy of the intoxication of honey.
One should meditate upon the supreme goddess Ḍākinī, who is worshipped by the lords of gods;
O Queen of Gods, [her seed-syllables are] Haṃ Kṣaṃ Hāṃ Hīṃ, and likewise Hamala Varayūṃ. (70)
Having uttered "Hākinyai namaḥ" and thus addressed Hākinī, one should then [recite] the word "dvilakṣakoṭi" while [the consciousness] has entered the marrow constituent (majjā-dhātu). || 71 ||
Having extracted the remainder as before, one should place it between the eyebrows;
one should utter the entire Mātṛkā, from the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa'. (72)
O Supreme Goddess, having addressed Yākinī at the end with "Yāmalavarayūṃ" and likewise "Yākyai namaḥ," [one should worship her]. (Note: *yāṃyīṃ* is an alternative reading for *yāṃ*). 73.
Then, having placed the ten million words within the semen-element as before, one should thereafter perform the placement of the zodiac signs (rāśi).

"Aṃ Āṃ Iṃ Īṃ, salutation to Aries on the right ankle," and so forth should be understood. [The phrase] "with the four syllables of the Vedas" means with four letters. O Pārvatī, having then placed Aries on the right ankle with the four syllables of the Vedas, one should place Taurus on the right knee with three syllables, and Gemini on the testicles with three. || 75 ||
With two [syllables] comes a crab on the belly, with two a lion on the shoulder;
with the anusvāra and visarga, and with the ka-group of consonants, one obtains a maiden.
O you who are worshipped by heroes, one should place [the letter] on the right side of the head;
likewise, one should place the scale on the left side of the head with the *ka*-group.
Then one should place Scorpio upon the shoulder with the *ca*-group;
then one should place Sagittarius upon the belly with the *ṭa*-group.
One should place the Makara with the *tavarga* on the testicle (either the right or the left);
likewise, one should assign the Jar with the *pavarga* to the left knee. (79)
With the *ya*-group and the letter *kṣa*, one should place [the seed-syllable] for Pisces at the left ankle;
joined with the dative case-ending (*caturthī*), one should thus deposit [these syllables] in these locations in sequence.
(6) Then, one should arrange the seats (*pīṭhas*) according to their proper places, preceded by *Parā* for all of them, and the *Mātṛkā* separately for each. 81.
One should place the fourth [syllable], joined with the prostrations (namas), in sequence according to the Mātṛkā;
then Kāmarūpa, the great seat (mahāpīṭha), and after that Vārāṇasī.
Nepāla (the reading "Medāna" also exists), Mahāpīṭha, and Pauṇḍravardhana (the reading "Paugaṇḍavardhana" also exists), O Great Goddess; after that, Purasthira, Carasthira, and beyond that—83.
The great seat (pīṭha) of Pūrṇaśaila and Arbuda after that;
likewise the seat of Kāśmīra, and then there is Kānyakubja. (84)

O Śivā, thereafter are the sacred seats (pīṭhas) Āmrātakeśvara (also read as Dārukeśa in manuscript Kha), Ekāmra (also read as Agra in manuscript Kha), and then the seat of Trisrotas; after that is Kāmakoṭṭa (also read as Koṭṭi in manuscript Kha). 85.
Kailāsa, Bhūtanagara, Kedāra, the supreme Pīṭha, Śrīpīṭha, likewise Oṃkāra, and thereafter Jālandhara. (86)
And Mālava (the reading "nava" is in the manuscript), Kulānta, and Devamātṛka;
then, O Goddess, Gokarṇa and Māruteśvara. || 87 ||
Then Aṭṭahāsa and Viraja, and beyond that Rājagṛha;
O Dear One, Kollagiri is a pīṭha, and after that Elāpura.
The great seat Kāleśvara, Praṇava, Jayantikā, the seat Ujjayinī, and also the seat Kṣīrikā. || 89 ||
The seat of Hastināpura, the seat of Uḍḍīśa, Prayāga, Ṣaṣṭhīśa, Māyāpura, and Jaleśvara; || 90 ||
And one should likewise place Malaya as a great seat (mahāpīṭha), or else Śrīśaila, O beloved;
and one should also place Mount Meru, Mahendra, and Vāmana. 91.
The seat of Hiraṇyapura, Mahālakṣmīpura, and the great seat of Uḍḍīyāna; after that is considered Chāyāpura. (Note: "Chāyāpīṭha" is an alternative reading found in manuscript *kha*).
This sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) has been declared to always remove all sins.
O Goddess, he who is devoid of the sixfold placement yet bows down to Sundarī [is like one who bows to a corpse]. 93.
He attains death before long and falls into hell;
yet, one who has thus cast off the body shall become Gaṅgādhara himself.
There is no doubt that such a minister is capable of both punishment and favor;
in this world, no man—neither father nor mother—is worthy of his worship.
And that best of practitioners who does not pay homage to anyone whatsoever—he shall meet with death; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. 96.
One should never perform a salutation even to one’s elder brother;
nor should one prostrate before one’s teacher [the reading "vandeta" is also found]. One dies [for doing so], there is no doubt about this. || 97 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid salutation, as well as desire, anger, greed, deceit, and egoism. 98.
One should not form intentions or engage in conversation with anyone; one should eat only that which has been prepared together with a woman. (Note: *yatkiṃcit* is the reading in manuscript *ta*. 99.
O Goddess, one whose mind is disciplined should perform this placement three times a day, by day and by night;
I shall now describe the proficiency that arises through such practice.
O Goddess, wherever this practitioner who performs the sixfold installation (ṣoḍhānyāsa) may dwell,
that place shall become a divine field extending for a hundred yojanas in every direction.
All the gods pay homage to him; I too bow to him without doubt, O Goddess, wherever the practitioner goes after performing this ritual placement (nyāsa).

In that regard, whatever object and whatever measure [is involved], together with the men, those dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, on earth, in the mountains, in the waters, and in the forests— 103.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, yakṣas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and rākṣasas,
as well as other violent beings, behold him mounted upon the fire.
In battle crowded with hosts of enemies, or even in calamities, no fear exists for him; he shall attain auspiciousness in the next world. (105)
Whatever multitudes of sins have arisen throughout the interval of seven births,
they perish by the mere act of ritual placement (nyāsa), just as darkness is destroyed by the sun.

Through the yoga of constant practice for six months, a human being burns away all sins, including even the killing of a Brahmin. Furthermore, what need is there to say more? He shall certainly become equal to me. (107)
[Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sequence of the Sixfold Deposition," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 10 ||
[The Eleventh Chapter] Īśvara said:

Next is the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*), the placement of the Ṛṣis (*ṛṣinyāsa*)— [according to the Kha manuscript, "the elements" (*bhūta*)— ], and thereafter the seat (*āsana*) as well as the placement of the throne (*pīṭhanyāsa*).
Then, one should perform the six limbs on the hands and limbs, followed by Vaśinī and the others, and then the Mātṛkā-nyāsa (according to the reading in manuscript K). || 1 ||
Likewise, there is the placement of the reality of the fourfold manifestation of the human womb,
as well as the arrangement of the root syllables and so forth, which is indeed called Sammohana.
For this alone is declared to be the obligatory [rite], while another is proclaimed as optional;
beginning with the Karaśuddhikarī [the Vidyā "a ā sau" which effects the purification of the hands], one should then utter the word "Tripurā."
After the word *amṛtārṇava*, [one should say] *śabdo-paryāsana-āya namaḥ*; this is the mantra.
One should then place [the seed-syllable] at the feet; finally, at the end of the *Bālā* [mantra], [one places] *Tripureśvarī*.
At the end, one should place "namo" at the knees for her who sits upon a lotus-throne;
then, having uttered "hrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ tripurā," one should then say the word "sundarī. (Note: *drī* is an alternative reading for *klīṃ*). || 5 ||
At the end of the seat of the Self, having uttered "Namaḥ," one should place [the seed-syllables] upon the thighs:
the first, the middle, and likewise the last of the Kumārī, conjoined with Śiva (in the case of Bālā, this means the letter *ha* joined with the word "Śiva" in the triad of seed-syllables). || 6 ||
Having uttered "Tripuravāsinī," [place it] on the seat of the wheel (cakrāsana);
then, having placed [it] in the two hips (or, according to another reading, in the region of the waist), make Śiva joined with Soma.
Within the three seed-syllables of this very vidyā (the vidyā just mentioned), Śiva—the letter *ha*—is joined with the letter *sa*. Then follows the word *stripuraśrī*.
At the end of the seat for all mantras, one should duly place "namo guhye. 8.

(Parā hrīṃ, the seed-syllable of desire klī, Vāruṇa va, Indra la, Yoni e, with the bindu—therefore ble. Then follows Tripuramālinī: Parā, the seed-syllable of desire, Vāruṇa joined with Indra, joined with Yoni, and with the bindu. || 9 ||
One should install [the mantra] with "Namaḥ" at the root for the sake of the seat;
[namely,] Māyā (hrīṃ), Ramā (śrīṃ), and the third [syllable] of Bālā (sau). [Thus: the Māyā-bīja, the Ramā-bīja, and the third [syllable] of Kumārī. (10)

Likewise, in the Tripurasiddhānta, one should then place the Sādhyasiddhāsana; having placed it in the region of the navel, one should then place it in the heart. (The reading "sā" is found in the manuscript of the Tripura.)

Śiva and Candra are the letters *ha* and *sa*; "Fire" (*vahni*) refers to the letter *ra*. Mounted upon these is Vāgbhava, *aiṃ*; thus, [the first seed-syllable is] *hasaraiṃ*. By joining the aforementioned letters, the other two seed-syllables—Kāmarāja and Śakti—are also to be understood. However, in the final *kūṭa*, one should place a *bindu* in the position of the *visarga*. Thus, [it becomes] *hasakalarīṃ* (or *hasarau*). [The verse states: "Śiva and Candra situated in Fire constitute Vāgbhava;
immediately after that, make Kāmarāja endowed with Śiva and Candra for Kumārī. (12)
Then, from the seed-syllable of Earth (la), one should place Fire; thereafter, in the seed-syllable of Śakti (ha), one should likewise join Śiva and Fire, having abandoned the emission of the Bindu.
O Supreme Goddess, having then joined the word "Tripurāmbā," one should place [the mantra] "namo paryaṅkaśaktipīṭhāya" upon the heart. 14.

"Vadanyā" is the Bhairavī-vidyā that bestows prosperity; it is as follows: *haṃsraiṃ ha-sa-kal-arīṃ haṃsraḥ*. At the end of all the seeds of Vadanyā, one should write "Mahātripurabhairavī" and "to the lotus-seat of the great corpse Sadāśiva. (15)
The best of practitioners should place the syllable *namaḥ* in the unbound aperture (*brahmarandhra*).

[The mantra is: Vahni (ra), Varuṇa (va), Śakra (la), the sixth vowel (ū), joined with Nāda and so forth, and the letter Ū; thus indeed is the Vidyā of Vaśinī, the Goddess of Speech: *ū*. Vahni, Varuṇa, and Śakra, adorned with the sixth vowel. (16)

Then, one should duly install the word "Vaśinī," joined with the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā* [syllables], followed by the goddess of speech (*vāgdevatā*) in the dative case, ending with "namaḥ," along with the vowels. (17)
*Mādana* (M), *Śakra* (Ś), mounted upon the letter *La* (L), and *Mahāmāyā* (Hrīṃ)—this is *Kāmeśvarī*. *Mādana* (M) mounted upon *Śakra* (Ś), followed by *Mahāmāyā* (Hrīṃ):
this should be known as *Kāmeśvarī*, [formed] with the *Ka*-group on the forehead. (18)

(The letter ending in *dh* [i.e., *ḍha*], Varuṇa [the letter *va*], and Indra [the letter *ra*], with the fourth vowel and the bindu—this is indeed the goddess Modinī in the middle of the eyebrows within the *ca*-group. The letter ending in *dh* (i.e., *ḍha*), Varuṇa (*va*), and Indra (*ra*), combined with the fourth vowel and the bindu—this very goddess Modinī resides in the *ca*-group between the eyebrows. (19)
(Vāyuḥ ya purandara la tena blūṃ. O Goddess, Vāyu and Purandara, adorned with the sixth vowel, joined with Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā—this is proclaimed as Vimale. (20)
O Pārvatī, it should be placed upon the region of the throat with the *ṭa*-group itself. [The mantra is:
*cha-anta*, *bha-anta*, *jvalana*, and the fourth vowel (*ī*) with the bindu; thus, *jmrīṃ*. [It is said: *cha-anta*, *bha-anta*, and *jvalana*, with the fourth vowel and the bindu. (21)
The goddess of speech, Aruṇeyī, is remembered in the heart with the *tavarga* [the dental consonants].
Then, O Goddess, Jayinī [is remembered]—[namely] Nakuli and Ha, Soma and Śakra; thus the letters *sa* and *la*. [This results in] Nakuliḥ and Somaśakrakam. (22)

(The Vāruṇa [syllable] and the Vāyu [seed-syllable], likewise with the sixth vowel, are *ha sa la va yūṃ*. O fair-faced one, the Vāruṇa and the Vāyu seed-syllable, adorned with the sixth vowel and the labial class (*pavarga*), are declared to be in the region of the navel. (23)

The letter ending in *ja* (ja), the letter ending in *bha* (bha), then the letter *ra*, combined with the seed-syllable of Vāyu (*ya*), and joined with the sixth vowel (*ū*), [forming] *te ta jha ma ra yū*. [It is said: "The letter ending in *ja*, the letter ending in *bha*, then the letter *ra*, endowed with the seed-syllable of Vāyu, joined with the sixth vowel, and possessed of the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*. (24)
O Maheśānī, [the mantra] of Sarveśvarī consists of the group of vowels (*svaravarga*); it is situated upon the lotus known as Svādhiṣṭhāna.

[The seed-syllable is formed as follows: *saṃvartaka* (kṣa), *kāla* (ma), *vahni* (ra), *māyā* (ī)—therefore, it is *kṣamrī*. O Maheśānī, *saṃvartaka* (kṣa) is situated above the seed-syllable of *kāla* (ma). (25)
Then follows the seed-syllable of fire (RA), endowed with Māyā (I) and the digits of Nāda and Bindu;
in the Mūlādhāra, Kaulinī is proclaimed together with the group of consonants beginning with ŚA.
O Goddess, one should duly install these deities of speech, beginning with Vaśinī, by repeating the root mantra twice upon all the surfaces of the fingers.
O Supreme Goddess, one should place the six limbs upon the limbs [of the body] in sequence:
*namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ* constitute the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*). || 28 ||
Then, having placed [the mantras] on the two hands, one should likewise place them upon the six limbs:
the heart ending with *namaḥ*, the head ending with *ṅe* (as per the reading in manuscript *ka*), and likewise the head ending with *svāhā*.
O Īśvarī, [the mantra] ending in the dative case is followed by *vaṣaṭ*; then the armor (*kavaca*) ending in *huṃ* and *ṅe*;
then the three eyes (*netratraya*) with *vauṣaṭ*, and the weapon (*astra*) ending in *phaṭ*.

(With the words beginning "the heart," etc., he indicates the mudrās for the six-limbed placement. The heart is said to be formed by the middle, ring, and index fingers; the head (*śiras*)—[this is the reading of *ta* and *śiva*]—is formed by the middle and index fingers, while the crest-lock (*śikhā*), O Dear One, is formed by the thumb. (31)
The armor is said to consist of ten [syllables], the eye is declared to consist of three;
likewise, the weapon is declared with sound by means of two fingers.
Even worship, austerity, adoration, and fire-offerings performed with perfected mantras will not yield their fruits if they are devoid of the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa). // 33 //
O Goddess, immediately thereafter, one should install Vaśinī and the others;
thus, by means of the three root-syllables (kūṭas), one should install them in these locations in sequence.

(He states the *navayoninyāsa*: "In the two ears," etc. This should be performed with the three root-syllables alone. Having placed [the syllables] in the two ears, the chin, the two temples, and again in the mouth; then having placed them in the two eyes, the nose, the shoulders (*aṃśau*—this is the reading), and the belly. 35.
Again, [one should place them] on the two elbows, the belly, the two knees, the top of the penis,
the feet, the private parts, the two sides, and the lotus of the heart.
One should thus place [the mantras] on the two breasts and the region of the throat according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, O Goddess, one should place the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) together with the pedestal (pīṭha).

(To be clearly understood as follows: *namaḥ ādhāre ai agnicakre kāmagiryālaye mitreśanāthātmake kāmeśvarī-rudrātmaśakti-śrīpādukāyai*). Having uttered the root *vāgbhava* [syllable], then the word *agnicakre*, and after that the word *kāmagiryālaye*, one should extract the word *mitreśa* [or *mitrīśa*, according to the reading in manuscript K]. (38)

After that, one should place the word *nāthātmake*, then the word *kāmeśvarī*, and then, from the word *rudrātmaśakti*, one should assign [the mantra] "Obeisance to the Śrīpādukā" (*śrīpādukāyai namaḥ*). (39)
O Supreme Goddess, [place it] in the support (ādhāra) and then in the heart;
having uttered the second root [syllable], then the word *sūryacakra*.
From the word *jālandhara*, [one should utter] the word *pīṭha*; then, having pronounced the word *ṣaṣṭhīśanātha*, one should then utter the word *ātmake* followed by the word *vajreśvarī*. (41)
At the end of the words "Viṣṇu-ātma-śakti," that which was previously uttered is recited;
then, having pronounced the Śakti-kūṭa, the word "somacakre" follows.
After "Pūrṇagiri," one should place the word "pada";
after that, O Goddess, the word "Uḍḍīśa," and then the word "nāthātmake. (43)
At the end of that, O Goddess, one should join Mālinī preceded by Bhaga;
at the end of the words Brahma, Ātman, and Śakti, one should place [the mantra] as before upon the two petals.
Then, having uttered the seed-syllable of the Fourth (Turya), one should [place] the word "Brahmacakra" therefrom;
likewise, in the seat of Oḍḍiyāna, the word consisting of Caryānātha.
At the end of that, O Supreme Goddess, is Mahātripurasundarī;
at the end of Para-Brahmātma-Śakti, as before, she resides in the Brahmarandhra.
O Great Goddess, having performed the placement [of the mantra] in this manner, one should perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa);
from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and again from the base to the end. (47)

Having uttered the root Vāgbhava [syllable], then the word for the principle of the self (ātmatattva), followed by "Mahātripurasundarī" in the dative case ending in the fourth case, [ending with] "Vyāpikāyai. (48)
Having first assigned "namaḥ," then the Kāmarāja mantra, and before the word *vidyātattva*, one should proceed as previously described up to the heart.
One should place [the goddess], whose nature is the Śiva-tattva, at the end of the third seed-syllable;
[extending] from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and from that point down to the creeper-like eyebrows.
Then, O Great Goddess, one should separately place the three Vidyā-kūṭas on the roots, middles, and tips of the hands, and on the root, the heart, and the space between the two breasts.
One should place [the mantras] in these locations in sequence by means of the repetition of the three root-vidyās;
and one should place the fourth [vidyā] in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) as the all-pervading [mantra] by that very same [method].
Likewise, [one should place them] at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the foundation (ādhāra), the heart, the three eyes,
as well as on the two ears, the circumference of the face, the two arms, and the region of the back.
Likewise, one should place the root-syllables on both knees and at the navel;
having oneself become the body of the mantra, one should worship the Goddess who consists of mantra.
Meditating on the three worlds as crimson, one should remember the Śrīvidyā in the mind;
O Great Goddess, one should place the Yonimudrā at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head).

Having placed it on the forehead and between the eyebrows, one should place it in turn upon the face, the region of the throat, and the heart. (Note: *vinyaset* is the reading according to the Prakāśa commentary.)
This ritual placement (nyāsa), known as Saṃmohana, is capable of enchanting the three worlds.
The Goddess said: "Tell me the procedure for the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) as well as the procedure for the external sacrifice (bahiryāga). (57)
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the great internal sacrifice;
the purification of the mind and the individual soul (*jīvātman*) arises through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). (58)
And whatever impurity is internal, that too becomes purified;
O Goddess, without breath-control (prāṇāyāma), performed action is useless. (59)
The reality higher than breath control; the austerity higher than breath control;
the knowledge higher than breath control; the supreme state higher than breath control. (60)
There is no yoga superior to breath control; there is no wealth superior to breath control.
There is nothing, nothing, and once again, nothing superior to it—this has been told to you, O lady of excellent vows. (61)
Through the practice of this for two years, Brahman will certainly become manifest;
just as the veil over consciousness is destroyed, there is no doubt in this matter.
I have declared that without *prāṇāyāma*, there is no path to liberation;
by means of *prāṇāyāma*, O sages, [the wise] attain perfection, and not otherwise. (63)
The yogi who is devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma) is not truly a yogi; he is Śiva himself.
Such is the retention of the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa), as well as its coming and going.
This is declared as *prāṇāyāma* by those expert in the Yoga scriptures:
*prāṇa* is known as the vital air (*vāyu*), and *āyāma* is its restraint. (65)
What is called *prāṇāyāma* is declared to be the means for accomplishing yoga for practitioners of yoga. The filling of the air from the outside into the abdomen constitutes *pūraka*. (66)
The retention of breath like a full pitcher is *kumbhaka*; the expulsion of breath from the abdomen is *recaka*. (Verse 67)

Inhalation (pūraka) should be performed according to one's capacity, retention (kumbhaka) four times that duration, and exhalation (recaka) should be half of the retention; this is declared to be prāṇāyāma.

(He indicates the *prāṇāyāma-mudrā* with the words beginning "kaniṣṭhā..."): The holding of the nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb—excluding the index finger and the middle finger—is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*. (Note: "prāṇāyāma" is the reading in manuscript *ka*. 69.
One should slowly fill the breath through the middle channel (the suṣumnā),
retain it through the right [or left, according to the variant reading], and release it through the other in forward and reverse order.
Restraining the vital breaths as much as possible and recollecting the Supreme with the mind alone, O Dear One, one should mutter either the "face-seed" of the mantra or the entire mantra. (71)

In the Mūlādhāra, known as the triangle and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, one should constantly meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī, who resembles the crest of the fire of time (or the bliss of desire, according to another reading). 72.

One should meditate upon her as red and subtle, whose nature is the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe; she transcends the universe, is of the nature of knowledge, and flows upwards. (73)
By the mere utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*, having raised [the consciousness] to the supreme Śiva, and having pierced the six cakras, one causes it to reach the supreme Śiva. (74)
Having united her, who is of the nature of supreme bliss, with Parānanda, one should, with an undisturbed mind, meditate upon her as having attained non-difference from him. (75)
Having caused [the breath] to flow, one should bring it to the power-circle at the *mūlādhāra*;
by that very division of the wheel, one should lead it back to the *mūlādhāra*.

One should meditate upon the deity who is the essence of the mantra, having the nature of a lotus fiber, extending from the base (mūlādhāra) to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and possessing the luster of a thousand rising suns. (77)
Therein, one should contemplate the threefold Kuṇḍalinī as well as the three seed-syllables in their triple form;
and the fourth Kuṇḍalinī, Mahātripurasundarī, at the crown of the head.
One should meditate upon the Vāgbhava [bīja] at the base of the navel, resembling molten gold;
likewise, one should meditate upon the Vahni-kuṇḍalinī from the base up to the heart.
In the heart is Kāmarāja, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
there also is Sūryakuṇḍalinī, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
O Śivā, one should meditate undisturbed from the heart up to the throat;
then, between the eyebrows, the seed-syllable of Śakti, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
O Śivā, [visualize] the Moon-kuṇḍalinī from the midpoint of the eyebrows up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
resembling ten million moons and having a form that flows with nectar.

One should meditate upon her who consists of the three seeds, who is the fourth state within the *bindu*, who is composed of the three *bindus*, who is unconditioned by space and time, and who is composed of all splendor. (83)
In the same way, having meditated upon the Fourth Kuṇḍalinī, who is pure and whose form is knowledge alone,
one should then mentally recollect the complete Vidyā.
O beloved, with a single-minded focus, one should satisfy the Supreme Deity—who consists of consciousness and bliss and is perfectly pure—with a downpour of nectar. 85.
Having meditated again and again upon her whose form is innate bliss, one should repeatedly satisfy her with the nectars flowing from the *bindu*. (Variant reading: *bindusruta-sudhābhiḥ*). 86.
This is declared to be the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), which bestows liberation upon the living;
the eligibility for this belongs solely to sages and those seeking liberation.
One should regularly perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) every morning and evening;
[thus] one destroys all sins, just as fire consumes a heap of straw. (88)
This is remembered as the expiation for all sins;
just as a snake, having cast off its skin from its own body, becomes free from disease. (89)
Likewise, through breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should cast off ignorance, desire, and action,
as well as the sin born from the misdeeds of others and the sin arising from the theft of another's property.
A hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) shall burn away the sin produced by sexual intercourse with another's wife,
as well as the various great sins (mahāpātakas) such as the killing of a Brahmin.
All these are burned away by four hundred *prāṇāyāmas*.

The power of the mind (*manaḥ-śakti*) is fully described as being fivefold; these five reside within the body. (Note: The reading *pañcāsyāḥ* is preferred over *pañcasyāḥ*; the manuscript *ka* reads *pañca ge*.)
Having made [the self] of one form as Śiva, one should place her upon his lap;
having established both in the supreme state of emptiness, they remain equally situated.
Having bowed, the practitioner should contemplate the form of sound belonging to those two in succession;
within that, he should mentally perceive himself as the eternal, luminous form.
Having attained samādhi, one should abandon the bonds of saṃsāra. || 94 ||

[Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Rule for Daily Deposition and Internal Sacrifice," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 11 ||
[The Twelfth Chapter] Īśvara said:
Or else, [one should worship] the Supreme Sovereign Goddess, whose form is assumed through divine play (līlā).
Restraining the senses and the mind, one should fix [the consciousness] upon her who dwells in the center of the heart-lotus.
With his mind fixed on that, the best of practitioners should mentally worship Śivā with the index finger of the left hand and the little finger of the right. (2)
Likewise, one should join the right index finger with the left thumb;
the right thumb should be raised, while the middle and other fingers of the left [hand] [are bent]. (3)

One should join the fingers on the back of the right hand; likewise, with the *pitṛtīrtha* of the left hand, one joins the middle and ring fingers. (Note: *vāmasya* is the reading in manuscript *ka*).
Having taken a red flower and formed the "tortoise" hand-gesture (*pāṇikacchapa*) in this manner, one should place it with the face downward upon the right hand.
Having assumed a firm posture, with body, head, and neck held straight, one should close both eyes and bring [the mind] near to the heart.
Then, as if seeing the Goddess with a one-pointed mind,
he beheld her within his heart through mental offerings.
One should worship Śivā, who resides in the heart, with sixteen types of offerings;
first, one should offer a seat—a beautiful throne of jewels.
One should offer water for the feet at the [deity's] feet and present the arghya offering upon the head,
consisting of the supreme nectar-water, well-scented with the flowers of devotion.
Having placed water in a golden vessel, he should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with it in his mouth;
then he should offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and after that, the ritual sipping again.
Having drawn a mandala to his left, he should visualize himself in the cross-legged posture;
having offered the glorious jeweled sandals, he should lead her to the bathing chamber.
One should perform the ritual rubbing (udvartana) for her as she sits upon an auspicious seat;
having performed the rubbing with ghee, one should contemplate [the deity] in the mind. 12.
With camphor, agallochum, musk, and likewise with deer-musk, mixed with yellow pigment and saffron, and endowed with various fragrances. (13)
One should bathe the Supreme Goddess with fragrant divine oils,
using thousands of golden jars by means of thousands of celestial maidens.
One should contemplate the Supreme Deity as being bathed with water sprinkled by rivers, the lords of rivers, hosts of celestial nymphs, and serpents. 15.
Having wiped the body with *dukūla* cloths and having likewise dressed it in *dukūla*, the hair was groomed with a comb and bound according to the prescribed rite. (16)
One should apply a string of pearls to the mass of hair, vermilion in the midst of the hair, a tilaka mark on the forehead, and red lac upon the lips. (Sūtrāvalī, verse 17)
Having applied collyrium to the eyes and anointed the limbs with fragrant unguents,
one should place a beautiful golden necklace upon the chest.

Then one should offer ornaments made of gold, silver, and so forth, as well as radiant jewelry for the head, ears, neck, and arms. (Note: The reading *ujjvalābharaṇāni* is preferred over *ujjvadīpāni*.)
Then one should give two anklets and a brilliantly shining pearl necklace (the reading "ānandahāra" appears in some versions);
as well as other ornaments, wherever and by whatever means they may shine.

Having offered the two precious jeweled sandals, one should bring [the deity] into the center of the wheel, as well as perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings. (Note: *Śrī* is repeated; *ka-pāṭhaḥ* indicates the reading from manuscript *ka*.)
Divine, well-prepared *paramānna* served in golden vessels, combined with the ghee of a tawny cow and accompanied by various side dishes. || 22 ||
Food to be chewed, as well as food to be swallowed, licked, drunk, and sucked, combined with milk and water, and accompanied by curd and honey. (23)
One should mentally offer betel-leaf with camphor;
even if the food offering is presented to the Great Goddess only in thought, [it is accepted]. (24)
That person who is endowed with devotion shall become long-lived and happy;
he who mentally offers a garland of a thousand lotuses [attains the same]. (25)
Having remained in your city for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of eons, he shall become a glorious universal monarch upon the earth.
But he who performs a circumambulation of the Great Goddess even mentally shall not see the southern house of Yama, nor the hells. (Note: *naraka* is omitted in some readings. 27.
The man who, with devotion, performs mental salutation to the Goddess, having conquered the worlds, is glorified in the world of men. (28)
"I worship the great goddess Mahāmāyā with various kinds of food offerings according to my ability"—thus is he who is overwhelmed by such thoughts. (29)
He who repeatedly says, "Give me the food offering (naivedya) by all means," even he, having pierced through the worlds, is glorified in the world of the Goddess.
One should perform the external worship of the wheels (cakras) by means of the mind alone;
indeed, the worship of the powers (śaktis) of the nine enclosures is performed by the mind alone.
Having thus propitiated [the deity] within by means of the mind alone, one should mutter the mantra;
then, becoming a lord of supernatural powers (siddhi), one may move about upon the earth like a god.
In this very way, O Great Goddess, I worship the Great Sovereign;
and yogins and sages likewise always worship her, my dear. (33)
A householder cannot achieve perfection through the mind alone; rather, O bull among sages, it is by means of that very [mind] together with the external that one becomes a true householder-muni.
Pārvatī said:
"O Mahādeva, O Lord, I desire to hear about the yoga of meditation;
O Īśāna, tell it in its entirety, by which one may become a supreme perfected being. (The reading "nara" is found in manuscript *ka*.)
Īśvara said:

"O Pārvatī, without the ritual placements (nyāsa), without worship, and without the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa)—even without recitation—one may become perfected through the yoga of meditation; indeed, it cannot be otherwise."
Through the yoga of meditation, I attained perfection, as did Viṣṇu and the Grandfather (Brahmā);
even sinful human beings have attained supreme perfection through the yoga of meditation. (Note: *siddhāḥ* is an alternative reading for *siddhaḥ*.)
That which is secret in all tantras and bestows all accomplishments—without which one does not succeed even in hundreds of millions of years. (38)
I shall now proclaim the yoga of meditation, which bestows all essential truths;
having taken up one's seat in a solitary, secluded, and pleasant place. (39)
With all mental fluctuations ceased, his form was sealed with the [mudrā of] restraint;
he was filled within and without by the abundance of causal bliss.

Having bowed to the gurus according to the prescribed rite, the wise one should contemplate the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, based on the realization that "I am That" (so'ham). 41.
One should also contemplate the principles (tattvas) of all beings within the Cause,
merged in the state of seeds within the Supreme Self in reverse order.

Having reflected thus, O Goddess of the Gods, one should contemplate the earthly element as having gone into the water, the water as dissolved into fire, and the fire as [dissolved] into air. (Regarding the phrase "jalaṃ ca tejaso rūpaṃ tejorūpaṃ vicintayet," the reading in manuscript *ka* is: "nirvāṇavāyunā vahnir vāyunātra vicintayet" [one should contemplate the fire here by means of the extinguishing wind]). || 43 ||
The wind is withdrawn into space, and space dissolves into the mind;
the mind, which is under the sway of the ego, likewise abides within the Great Principle (mahat). (Note: There is a variant reading "tathā vai manasi" for "tathāhaṃ").
O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate the Great One as dissolved within Prakṛti;
the seeker of liberation should contemplate Prakṛti as dissolved within the Supreme Self. (45)
There was neither day nor night, neither twilight nor sun, nor even moon;
all this was composed of darkness and devoid of worlds.
O Great Goddess, having contemplated that which is unperceived, unobservable, and as if entirely asleep, one should not conceptualize anything at all. 47.
There was one Supreme Brahman—eternal, subtle, beyond the senses, consisting of perpetual bliss, a primordial abode whose nature is light. (48)
That very [nature] is Prakṛti; she is eternal, consisting of the form of light, the goddess whose body is perpetual bliss, having that as her form and illuminating it. 49.
From the union of those two, there arose a rain consisting of supreme nectar;
O Goddess, it likewise inundated this entire universe in its fullness.
There, in that water, the supreme practitioner should contemplate his own self;
he should contemplate a bubble therein, and he should contemplate the Supreme Nature.
For from Prakṛti indeed arises Mahat, and from Mahat likewise arises Ahaṃkāra;
from Ahaṃkāra arises Manas, and from Manas the ether (kha) has arisen.
Having drawn forth wind from space, one should contemplate fire arising from that wind; having reached water from fire, and then earth from water. (53)
Then, having set it aside and established it in its proper place according to the ritual rule,
one should meditate upon the golden cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) as being firmly fixed by means of these [syllables] with the seed-syllable of the earth (bhū-bīja).
Having divided [the vessel] into two parts with the syllable *praṇava*, one should fill it completely with floods of water;
within the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is the water, and beneath that is the imperishable frog (*bheka*).
O Great Goddess, upon his back is the form of Kālāgnirudra;
and right there is the Support Power (Ādhāraśakti), whose nature is that of Mūlaprakṛti.

The Goddess, seated upon the Brahma-stone, having the form of a tortoise and the luster of the moon, holds two lotuses and bears a tortoise upon her head. (In some readings, "karma" appears instead of "kūrma" in the phrase "bearing [the tortoise] upon her head. || 57 ||
One should contemplate the tortoise Ananta as having a blue luster, resembling a jasmine flower;
upon its head, O Goddess, stands the white form of Varāha.
One should meditate there upon him who holds the earth— dark as the tamāla tree— in his teeth,
and one should contemplate her there as well, bearing a blue lotus.
One should contemplate [the earth] filled with waters, girdled by the four oceans;
in its center, O Goddess, one should contemplate the wonderful ocean of nectar.
There, one should contemplate nectar with a reddish luster, resembling pure lac juice; in the center of that, O Goddess, one should visualize an island resembling coral.
A vast sugarcane forest surrounded it, strewn with hundreds of mountain kings;
and upon the mountain was the Golden Mountain, and on the slope of that mountain was the Kalpa-grove.
With *campaka*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, and *pāṭala* trees, as well as *kuṭaja*, *lavaṅga*, *mādhavī*, *bilva*, *devadāru*, and *nameru*. (63)
It was adorned on all sides by divine celestial trees, such as the Mandāra and Pārijāta, which were beautifully in bloom and bore fruit and flowers perpetually.
With sandalwood trees, karṇikāras, mātuluṅgas, karañjakas, grapes, sugarcane, lotuses, rose-apples, madhukas, and mangoes as well; || 65 ||
It was adorned with pomegranates, mangoes, breadfruit, betel nuts, camphor, plantains, jasmine, dates, and coconuts.

With kadamba, karavīra, tagara, and nāgakesara flowers; with yāvantī (or pāvantī according to the reading in manuscript Kha), svarṇayūthī (or yūthikā according to the reading in manuscript Ka), vajra, and damanaka as well. || 67 ||
It was beautified by *mālatī*, *mallikā*, *jātī*, *ketakī*, and *śatapatraka* flowers, as well as other fragrant blossoms such as *yūthikā* and the like. || 68 ||
It was adorned with groves of trees entwined by mutually clinging creepers, and graced by trees bending under the weight of blossoms from every season. (69)
The quarters of the sky were filled with the fragrance of flowers scattered by a gentle breeze,
and it was crowded with bees delighted by the scent of blossoming flowers.
The quarters of the sky were made resonant by flocks of warbling cuckoos, and groups of peacocks danced at the sight of the dark clouds. (71)
It was filled with the sweet warbling of numerous śārikā birds and parrots,
as well as various kinds of deer moving about in pairs.
Adorned with rivers, lakes, and ponds, and beautified by white and blue lotuses,
in those lakes there was an abundance of the great nectar of exquisite flavor.
It was divinely adorned on all sides with shimmering golden lotuses, frequented by intoxicated bees and by birds of melodious song. || 74 ||
On the banks of that great lake, which was strewn with swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, cakravāka birds, and cranes, and adorned with jeweled stairways, [he saw her].
It was cooled by the surging waves of the agitation of great flavors,
divine, yielding all desires, and endowed with every kind of jewel.
One should visualize there a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) adorned with pearls, flowers, garlands, silken garments, and golden archways; and beneath it, a ground made of jewels.

It was vast and pervaded by beautiful flowers (the reading *mahadvyā* is found in manuscript *ka*). In its center was a pavilion of jewels, surrounded by *pārijāta* trees, radiant and cool as the moon.
Resembling the rising sun, adorned with jeweled stairways, extending for a hundred yojanas, and provided with four gates. (79)
At the doors, there were diamond door-panels shining with coral thresholds,
joined by eight highly resplendent door-panels fashioned from jewels.
It was richly adorned with the splendor of various jewels, decorated with jeweled walls,
and featured lofty ramparts and gateways fashioned from the nine precious gems.
Adorned here and there with various jewels strewn about, it was graced by a great expanse of emeralds and coral altars.
Its peaks were made of sapphire and adorned with golden pitchers,
while its diamond walls were graced by the tips of radiant rubies protruding from them.
It was graced with various sacrificial pavilions and costly golden archways; it shone with all manner of increasing prosperity and with pillars made of sun-crystals.
It was adorned with rows of banners hanging from crests of golden staffs, and presided over by the world-protectors stationed in their respective places. (85)
Its quarters were inhabited by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas,
Mahoragas, Kinnaras, and Apsarases who were sporting there.
It was filled with throngs of celestial women devoted to dance and music,
and it shone with rows of pillars set with the nine precious gems.
It was enchanting with windows fashioned from molten gold,
and adorned with hundreds of millions of golden ornaments set with various gems and silken cloths.
It was adorned with banners bound with *kiṅkiṇī* jewels,
and embellished with great rubies, beryl, gems, and yak-tail whisks.
Adorned with vast, variegated jewels made of gold, and graced with garlands of rubies, gems, lapis lazuli, and gold; || 90 ||
It was adorned with canopies of various colors, variegated and enchanting to the sight, interspersed here and there with jewels that were beautifully joined together.
It was adorned with large, lustrous pearls hanging down profusely,
arranged in separate chambers one above the other.
It was beautiful with well-arranged couches, fans, and seats made of *kaśipu* (cushions),
endowed with divine furnishings, and bringing happiness at all times.
It was resplendent with various colors of *dukūla*, *kṣauma*, and *kauśeya* fabrics, and with garlands of variegated flowers and bees making sweet humming sounds. (94)
Smeared with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and musk, and perfumed with the incense of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, it was most enchanting. 95.
It was filled with breezes carrying the fragrance of various flowers,
situated in the midst of the Nandana grove, even beneath a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
Having thus reflected with the mind upon a most beautiful pavilion,
one should meditate on a radiant pavilion of great rubies shimmering in its center.
An umbrella resembling the autumnal moon, adorned with pearls and rubies, with its golden handle reaching down to the top, and decorated with white chowries; || 98 ||
One should meditate upon a great ruby altar situated below that, red in color, adorned with the rays of the rising sun and moon, and beautified by its four corners. (99)
There should be a railing in the place of the railing, and upon that, a lion-throne (this is the Aiśa reading).
One should then visualize Dharma and the other [Bodhisattvas] in its corners, beginning with the southeast. 100.
There, one should contemplate Adharma and the others in the cardinal directions, embodied in the form of limbs;
they have the luster of red, dark-blue, yellow, and sapphire, and are embodied as the feet.
One should visualize the deities of Dharma and the others in the forms of a bull, a peacock, an elephant, and a lion;
there, in the center of the lion-throne, is a cushion of flowers.
In the center of that, one should meditate upon the supreme lotus, which consists of all principles (tattvas); its root is bliss, and its stalk is consciousness.
It has thirty-two petals and filaments in the form of primordial nature and its transformations,
and it is adorned with a pericarp enriched by the seed-syllables of the fifty letters.
One should visualize the sun in the pericarp, and in its center, the lunar maṇḍala;
(and within the lunar maṇḍala, one should visualize the fire maṇḍala). || 105 ||
One should contemplate the sattva situated in the middle of the circle of fire; having contemplated rajas there as well, one should likewise contemplate tamas in its center.

O Goddess, one should worship the self of the principle of knowledge (jñāna-tattva), likewise the self of the principle of illusion (māyā-tattva), the self of the principle of wisdom (vidyā-tattva), and the self of the principle of limited agency (kalā-tattva).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these five great spirits (mahāpreta) are stationed in the four directions and the center. || 108 ||
Above Sadāśiva is the imperishable light of the three peaks;
in its center is a great lotus filled with nectar.
There, one should meditate upon Tripurā, the manifest Goddess, seated upon a throne of the ocean of nectar;
likewise, one should meditate upon Tripureśvarī, seated upon a lotus-throne of wine.
The practitioner should meditate with devotion upon the sovereign mistress of the secret Yoginīs;
there, he should remember Tripurasundarī as seated upon his own seat. 111.
One should meditate upon the goddess Guptatareśvarī seated upon the wheel-throne,
the goddess Tripuravāsinī, the sovereign of the assembly of traditions.

O Goddess, one should then contemplate Tripurāśrī (as the reading *Tripurāśri* appears), the Mistress of Kula and Kaula, seated upon the throne of the deities to be accomplished, upon the seat of all mantras. || 113 ||
O wise one, [worship] Tripuramālinī, the sovereign mistress of the Nigarbha Yoginīs;
thereafter, upon the Siddhāsana, [worship] the Siddhā preceded by Tripura.
One should meditate upon Tripurāmbā on the seat of the Śakti-paryaṅka, the supreme digit (kalā) seated upon the lap of Kāmeśvara. 115.
The Goddess resembles a red lotus, as crimson as the rays of the rising sun;
she is like the hibiscus flower and possesses the luster of the pomegranate blossom. (Note: *mopamām* is a variant reading for *ka*.)
Resembling a ruby and appearing like saffron water,
she was adorned with a network of tinkling bells and a glittering crest-jewel upon her crown.
Her sprout-like, curling locks of hair resembled a swarm of black bees, and the orb of her lotus-face appeared like a freshly blossomed, deep red dawn.

[I salute] the Supreme Goddess, whose forehead is slightly curved like a crescent moon and adorned with a soft fillet, and whose beautiful eyebrows have the form of the Pināka bow. (The reading "bhrūlatā" [creepers of eyebrows] is also found. 119.
Her eyes were playfully swinging with waves of bliss and joy;
her golden earrings shone with a mass of flickering rays.

(Lalita’s reading: Her expansive, well-rounded cheeks surpassed the orb of the nectar-filled moon; her eyes were like those of the son of the Moon (the deer); and her nose was clearly defined by the measuring line of Viśvakarman’s craftsmanship. (121) (Ka’s reading: [Her eyes were] like those of the son of the Moon. (Kha’s reading: [Her nose was] clearly defined by the measuring line of Viśvakarman’s craftsmanship. (121)
Her lips are red like copper or coral, resembling the bimba fruit; she is like nectar itself, and her row of teeth shines with the brilliance of pomegranate seeds and diamonds. || 122 ||

Her tongue shines like an island of jewels, speaking with sweetness; it is adorned by the root of her tongue as she utters radiant speech, surpassing the ocean of the essence of sweetness with the sweetness of her smile. (Note: This half-verse is absent from the Ka manuscript; the Kha reading is provided here.)
She was adorned with a chin-region endowed with incomparable qualities,
possessed a neck like a conch shell, and had arms as graceful as lotus stalks— such was the Great Goddess.
She was adorned with ornaments that were heavy with the weight of jewels, bracelets, and armlets;
her lotus-like hands, delicate like the petals of a red lotus, graced her. (Note: *pariśobhitām* is an alternative reading for *praśobhitām*. || 125 ||

The expanse of the sky was illuminated by the moonlight of the nails on her lotus-like hands; she possessed full and elevated breasts adorned with strings of pearl necklaces, and she was graced by a slender waist, while her middle region was beautifully adorned with the curvature of the three folds [of skin]. || 126 ||

Adorned with a navel shaped like a whirlpool in a river of loveliness, she possessed hips encircled by a girdle fashioned from priceless jewels. (The variant reading *suśobhitām* [well-adorned] is found in manuscript *ka*; the variant reading *anarghya* [priceless] is found in manuscript *ka*. || 127 ||
The mistress possesses hips like a pair of elephant-ivory globes, with a line of hair like a choice goad;
her thighs are as delicate as the graceful pillars of a plantain tree.
Her pair of shanks was adorned as if they were two stalks of the plantain tree (the reading *kadalī* is found in manuscript *kha*),
and her pair of feet with concealed ankles and foreparts surpassed the beauty of tortoises.
She was most enchanting with her lotus-feet shining with anklets,
and her lotus-feet were rubbed by the crest-jewels on the heads of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
It was adorned with slender, long fingers and shining moon-like nails,
and it laughed with a continuous stream of splendor resembling a hundred moons.
She possesses the luster of the Japā flower and the pomegranate, which surpasses the redness of the Lauhitya river and vermilion;
she is clothed in red garments and adorned with red ornaments.
She is the Supreme Goddess, holding in her hands the noose consisting of the power of will (icchā-śakti) and the goad in the form of knowledge (jñāna-rūpin),
as well as the bow and arrow consisting of the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
Her mouth was filled with betel leaf mixed with pieces of camphor,
and her body was crimsoned with the intense saffron and great musk.
Abounding in all the splendor of amorous attire, adorned with every ornament, she is the one who generates delight for the world and brings enchantment to the world. || 135 ||

She who attracts the world, whose form is the cause of the universe, the Goddess consisting of all deities and mantras, the supreme one consisting of all mantras, the beautiful lady of auspicious fortune. || 136 ||
[She who is] composed of all prosperity, manifest as the form of supreme bliss, [the beautiful one];
the stainless, quality-less, pure Self, which consists of Tripura. (137)
By contemplating [the deity] as non-different from one's own self, a person attains identity with that;
by constantly reflecting "I am she," one becomes absorbed in her. (This is the reading in manuscript Kha. 138.
O Goddess, one should contemplate only her and nothing else apart from her;
one should perceive this entire universe as completely filled with her splendors. || 139 ||
Thus permeated by meditation, he may move upon the earth like a god;
for him who is devoted to the yoga of dhyāna, there is no one in this world worthy of his worship. (140)
He alone is the one of meritorious deeds in the world; he is the one worthy of worship, not the worshiper.
He whose self is yoga and who knows the science of yoga is a god, not a mere mortal. (141)
He is a true renunciant and a master of placement; he is considered a sage whose self is disciplined.
For him, nothing remains unattainable; he is a perfected one, the foremost among yogis.
One should always satisfy and adorn oneself with substances that please the senses;
one should constantly worship one's very self with the thought that it is the deity. 143.
One who is devoted to yoga should always dwell like a god; whatever one sees, whatever one hears, and whatever [one perceives] such as song and dance—[all these should be regarded as the Lord]. (144)
