Whatever the practitioner himself puts on, whatever he anoints, and whatever he mounts—be it elephants, horses, chariots, couches, or the like. (145)

Whatever he does and whatever he eats, all that he experiences as objects of the senses with the thought that they are deities—just as a sovereign enjoys those very things which are the objects of his own desires. (146)

Having approached each and every one of those [states] as a whole with the thought that they are deities—everything from the waking state up to deep sleep—with the thought that all of it is that deity. || 147 ||
In that regard, it must be divine and never otherwise;
therefore, one who is devoted to the divine [should worship] the Goddess whose form is bliss. (148)
One should constantly worship Mahātripurasundarī with devotion;
one who seeks liberation and is devoted to the yoga of meditation attains liberation. || 149 ||
But he who, being a seeker of enjoyment and devoted to meditation, should contemplate her at night—the supreme digit seated upon the lap of Kāmeśvara—[attains success]. (150)

One should meditate upon her who is beautiful in all her limbs, charming, with a face and eyes radiant with grace, while fixing the mind on all her limbs and [contemplating] her compassion (the reading *sakāruṇām* is found in manuscript *kha*). 151.
The fourfold aims of life are in his hand; he alone is indeed liberated while living.
[Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the Description of Dhyāna-yoga, in the Śrī Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 12 ||
[The Thirteenth Chapter] Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Supreme Lord, explain the procedure for the external sacrifice (bāhyayāga) together with its ancillaries.
The arrangement of the special arghya offering and the daily worship itself. || 1 ||
The Lord said: Having meditated upon Ambikā in that manner and having made oneself threefold and identical with her,
one should indeed place that very [form] upon the head by means of that same root mantra.
One should offer a flower to one's own [deity] and likewise perform the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
"I am that Lord, who is the consciousness of all beings; I am Brahman" (the reading *brahmā* is found in manuscript *ka*). || 3 ||
Through the constant contemplation of "I am He," the divine nature of the self arises perfectly from such right meditation; of this there is no doubt.
In this context, even the articles of worship attain the status of a deity;
furthermore, through the vision of all things as deities, purity itself arises.
"I am the God; whatever is offered as food (naivedya), flowers, perfumes, and so forth, I am indeed the support of the gods, for I am the God; there is no god anywhere who is superior to me. (6)
I worship only the God, for I myself am the God of gods;
even if the abundance of external materials for worship should exist. (Note: "bāhyārcanadravya" is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
Then, O Goddess, one should unweariedly perform the special offerings of arghya and so forth;
[one should prepare] the vessel for worship and arghya, as well as the vessels for the food offerings (naivedya) and for drinking.
One should make everything used here in worship out of copper;
the gods delight in copper, and the gods always abide in copper.
Copper is pleasing to the Goddess; therefore, one should employ copper.
A vessel made of conch, mother-of-pearl, silver, or gold is desired for the divine [deities]. (Note: "silver" is the reading in some manuscripts.)
For heroes, [the conch] should be made of mahāśaṅkha; for forest-dwellers, it should be made of fruit-wood.
It should not be less than eight finger-breadths, nor more than half a cubit.
The measurement for all the vessels is prescribed as follows:
one should have five vessels made for the Great Goddess using the five jewels.
For the sake of prosperity, one should diligently prepare the general and specific water for the feet, the water for sipping, and the ritual pitcher, all adorned with jewels.
The jewel known as Gaganaratna, and likewise Svargaratna;
the jewels of mortals and Pātāla, and likewise Nāgaratna. || 14 ||
One should know that the five jewels— namely, emerald, ruby, diamond, lapis lazuli, and sapphire— should be applied in their respective order.

I shall now describe their five seed-syllables, which are very difficult to obtain, in due order, O Dear One: *ga*, *sa*, *pa*, *ma*, and *na*; thereafter, those situated in Indra (meaning situated in *la*, thus: *glūṃ*, *slūṃ*, *plūṃ*, *mlūṃ*, *nlūṃ*). 16.
Endowed with the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, and adorned with the left ear, they are especially for the purpose of libation during the offering of the worship of the *cakra*. (17)
The wise and excellent practitioner should prepare the Śrīpātra according to the prescribed rite;
having first assumed the Yonimudrā, he should perform the preparation of the Arghya offering.
One should cause a square to be made between the self and the śrīcakra;
in its center, a hexagon, and in the center of that, an excellent circle.
O fair-faced one, having drawn a triangle there with sandalwood paste,
and having worshipped that mandala, one should then prepare the seat.
O Goddess, thereafter one should accomplish the three seed-syllables of Bālā, as well as Tripurasundarī, the vessel for the arghya offering, and the seat, thinking, "I shall accomplish them. (21)

In the same manner, O Supreme Goddess, having washed [the image] with water from the general *arghya* vessel accompanied by the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), one should then place it upon the mandala.
One should worship that [disc], which has the form of a circle of fire, together with its constituent parts (kalās).
O Supreme Goddess, the practitioner, as before, should wash the vessel.
Immediately after the word "viśeṣārghya" and the word "pātram," one should place [the vessel] with the mantra "I establish," and immediately thereafter— || 24 ||
One should worship that [deity] in the form of a solar disc together with its digits;
one should worship it according to the ritual procedure with streams of nectar flowing from the *bindu*.

One should fill the *mātṛkā* with nectar consecrated by the root mantra in reverse order (*pratiloma*), or likewise with the first [mantras] and with flower-liquor (*puṣpāsava*). (Note: The reading *pra(kāprati ka pāṭhaḥ)* indicates a variant reading *prakāśa-pratiloma*.)
Likewise, with the milk of a tawny cow, or even with the nectar of coconuts, with fragrant sugarcane juices, or with the three sweets; || 27 ||
One should at times fill that great vessel with various substances; for indeed, the varieties of substances arise according to the distinctions among those qualified [to perform the rite]. (28)
There, one should offer *svayambhū* flowers mixed with camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and saffron, and perfumed with musk. (29)
O Supreme Goddess, the best of practitioners, having visualized there the previously described mandala, should place sugar mixed with honey. (30)
Thereafter, one should indeed request the holy ford (tīrtha) with the goad mudrā;
in this mudrā, the middle finger is straight, its middle joint is pressed down, and the index finger is turned downwards.
This is the Vijñeya-aṅkuśa-mudrā, with the middle joint bent;
thereafter, one should likewise invoke the Tīrtha from the solar maṇḍala.
By means of the Gaṅgāvatāra mantra, even the Gaṅgā, together with all the hosts of sacred fords (tīrthas),
comes toward the water in the vessel of worship, as does the Yamunā.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, having formed the fish-seal (mīnamudrā) with both hands and covered the excellent vessel, the sacred water consisting of pure consciousness arrived.
Both hands are placed face down, resting one upon the other, with the thumbs extending toward both sides; this is declared to be the fish mudrā (mīnamudrā).
O Goddess, ruby, pearl, coral, emerald, topaz, diamond, sapphire, and auspicious hessonite; || 36 ||
One should place beryl and the nine gems there in the water;
one should worship Ratneśī there, the destroyer of all sins.

The seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Parā, and likewise the five seed-syllables—one should subsequently apply them in reverse order to the preceding seed-syllables. (Note: "tu" is the reading in manuscript Kha.)
This nine-syllabled mantra of Ratneśī is the goddess who removes defects in substances;
one should worship the previously mentioned six limbs within the hexagon. (39)
And in the center of that, O Supreme Goddess (the variant *pareśāni* is found in manuscript *kha*), one should contemplate that nectar in the form of a lunar orb, like a full moon. || 40 ||

Having worshipped him with the *kalās*, one should then contemplate the central mandala, which is enriched by three lines beginning with 'a', 'ka', and 'tha', and situated within the interior of the syllable 'Ha'. (Note: 'Ha' is the reading according to the manuscript of Jñāna. 41.
In front of that is Kāmarūpa, Jālandhara to the left,
Pūrṇagiri to the right, and Uḍḍiyānaka in the center.
In each of those places, one should worship the Goddess, who embodies the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha),
resembling ten million suns and possessing the splendor of ten million times ten thousand moons.
Likewise, one should visualize the ten-armed deity with five faces and three eyes,
holding a sword, a khaṭvāṅga (or shield, according to another reading), a paṭṭiśa, a mallet, a trident, and a spear (or tusk, according to another reading).
He bears a shield and a spear, with hands granting boons and fearlessness;
in his lap is the goddess Surā, possessing the splendor of ten million moons.
White as snow, jasmine, and the moon, with her primary weapon raised in her hand, she was smiling, large-eyed, and facing the God of gods. (Note: "khe" is an alternative reading for "mukhe").
Having meditated thus and having invoked the omnipresent one who consists of both Kula and Akula,
the master should perform the rite of nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa) with the mudrā known as the Cow (dhenu).
Then, having veiled her, O you with large lotus-like eyes, the practitioner of mantra should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the six limbs as before.
Then one should perform the act of making supreme by means of the Mahāmudrā;
one should display the Musala-mudrā, the Yoni-mudrā, and the Gālinī-mudrā. || 49 ||
Within the left fist, with the thumb [extended], one should touch the tips of the fingers of the right hand;
the joined right [hand] should be placed below.
Having formed fists with both hands, placing the right hand over the left—this is the *musalamudrā*, which destroys all obstacles. || 51 ||
The little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are bent toward each other;
the index, middle, and ring fingers are joined together and free from curvature.
This mudrā is called Gālinī, which bestows the supreme nectar.

(Śiva-candrau, ha-sau; the end of Mātṛkā, kṣa; Kāla, ma; Śakra, la; Ambu, va; Vahni, ra; Vāyu, ya; the left ear, ū; by that: *hasakṣamalavarayū ānandabhairavāya vauṣaṭ*. Thus. Śiva and Candra, the end of Mātṛkā, Kāla, Śakra, [Āditya], Ambu, and Vahni. || 53 ||
And having joined the wind with the left ear, one should utter this seed-syllable of Bindu and Nāda,
as well as Ānandabhairava.

Then, one should again write the seed-syllables joined with the *śikhā-mantra*. (Having omitted the letter *sa* from the beginning of the stated mantra, the letter *ī*—representing the left eye—should be placed in the position of the left ear. Thus: *sahakṣamalavarayī surādevyai vauṣaṭ*. In reality, however, instead of the reading *hitvā* ("having omitted"), the clear reading *kṛtvā* ("having made") should be understood according to the oral tradition of the Guru. Therefore, it should be known that the letter *sa* is placed at the beginning; thus the mantra begins with *sahakṣama* etc. Having omitted the moon (*ca*), one should place the left eye in the ear. (Note: The reading *candram hitvā* is found in manuscript *kha*; the reading *dinataḥ* is found in manuscript *na*. 55.
Then, with "Svadhā" for the goddess and "Vauṣaṭ," she is Ānandabhairavī;
having united those two by means of this, they are delighted by supreme bliss. 56.
Then, through the union of those two, nectar flows forth immediately;
one should employ five *ṛc* verses during their fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*).
First is *Prakṛteḥ haṃsaḥ*, then *Tad viṣṇoḥ* immediately after;
the third should be *Traiyambakaḥ*, and the fourth begins with *Tat padam*. (58)
O Daughter of the Mountain, having touched the nectar, one should recite the vidyā ten times, beginning with "Viṣṇur yonim"; this is proclaimed as the fifth [method].
One should utter the Vāgbhava (AIM), the Kāmabīja (KLĪM), and the syllables "Manu-yuk" (YU) and "Bhṛgu" (M);
likewise, one should speak the word "Amṛta" (AMṚTE), followed by "Amṛtodbhave" (AMṚTODBHAVE). || 60 ||
Having said "So be it," O Amṛteśvarī, thereafter, O showerer of nectar, [the mantra] ending with the wife of fire (svāhā) causes nectar to flow:
*ai klīṃ sau amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛteśvari amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaṃ srāvaya 2 svāhā*. || 61 ||
The Vāgbhava [syllable], the pair of words "vāgvādini," and again the Vāgbhava; having uttered the Kāmabīja, then "klinne" (or "klīnne" according to the Ka-pāṭha), and "kledini kledaya. || 62 ||
Then follow the two syllables of Mahākṣobhya and the seed-syllable of Kāma;
having uttered the third as "Liberation," one should then speak the pair of syllables of Kuru.

Furthermore, at the end is the seed-syllable of Śakti, followed by the mantra of illumination: (Ai vadavada vāgvādini aiṃ klī klenne kledini kledaya mahākṣobhaṃ kuru 2 klī sauḥ mokṣaṃ kuru 2 sauḥ—this is the Saṃdīpinī-vidyā). O Dear One!
Having performed the illumination and other rites, one should then awaken [the disciple] with the Bodhinī-mantra. 64.

Having joined the palms in *añjali*, one should remember the mantra—beginning with "Born from the fragment of the cosmic egg [as previously written]" and ending with "O fair-faced one, cause the radiance of consciousness to arise within me" (an additional reading is seen here in the form of a variant).
In this manner, there shall again be a set of four vessels for Vaṭuka and the others. 65.
Of the gurus, there are three, and for oneself there is one;
thus, there are exactly nine vessels that are indeed most excellent.
There should be five vessels in the center, while the middle one consists of a single vessel;
he should offer that to the Guru, the Guru’s son, and his wife.
Having offered the vessel of the hero (vīrapātra) to the power of the hero (vīraśakti), one should unite it with oneself;
O Goddess, by worshipping in this very manner, the supreme nectar (amṛta) arises. 68.
Having taken up the nectar that purifies all with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass,
one should satisfy the three gurus and then fully satisfy Vaṭuka and the others.

Then, one should offer [the oblation] into the fire of consciousness, which resembles the fire of universal dissolution. Herein is the mantra: "The moist [fire] blazes; I am indeed light, I am Brahman, I am She; I alone offer myself to myself—svāhā!
Having thus offered [the oblation] into the Brahma-randhra of one's own Kuṇḍalinī, one should indeed perform the sacrifice.
Having consumed [the substance] three times with the three seed-syllables and the mudrā known as Tattva,
one whose inner mind is purified and cleansed shall become fit for the ritual of sacrifice.
By drinking the nectar, a person attains immortality and poetic inspiration;
however, by the falling of even a single drop from this vessel onto the ground through its breaking, [he loses these]. (72)
If that [oblation] should be impure, then there is no pacification for him through that fire-sacrifice nor by any other means;
he should instead sprinkle himself with that [liquid], using either the root-mantra or the Varuṇa-mantra.
Likewise, having sprinkled the ritual implements for worship three times with the nectars (amṛtas), everything thus consecrated becomes identical with Brahman.
Whatever other substance is given, such as ornaments and the like,
one should perform their sprinkling with the seed-mantra of Varuṇa alone.
Having uttered "Devam" for all [the deities] and having uttered the root mantra, one should first offer [the water] from the arghya vessel with each individual name.
However, that which has been mixed with other substances from elsewhere— other than those contained within the vessel for the *arghya* offering—
the beloved Goddess does not accept it, even if it is offered according to hundreds of ritual injunctions.

[Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sequence for Preparing the Special Arghya Vessel and Other Implements," in the Ritual of the External Sacrifice within the *Śrīgandharvatantra*, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 13 ||
[The Fourteenth Chapter] Īśvara said:
O Daughter of the Mountain, beginning from Ādhāraśakti and ending with Kāmeśvara—
The practitioner should worship with devotion the seat consisting of mantra before him.

The first syllable of the name of the deities, situated between the syllable *oṃ* and the nasal bindu, is their own seed-syllable; it bestows prosperity and supernatural powers during their worship. (2)
Then, having meditated upon the seat of Kāma, the practitioner should likewise worship the god Kāmeśvara there, who has one face and four arms.
In the middle of the heart, he is smeared with ashes and reddened with saffron;
in his two left hands, he holds a trident and a Pināka bow.
Likewise, having meditated upon an utpala and a bījapūra in the two right [hands],
and [the deity] seated upon a white lotus, one should worship in the center.
O Goddess, when the practitioner, endowed with power, contemplates at night the true form of the weapons as being identical with the Root Goddess.
The practitioner should worship the God with the Śāmbhava [mudrā] (the variant reading is "vākya") and with that which was previously mentioned;
having uttered the root mantra on the seventh day, [he worships] Mahātripurasundarī.
Having first uttered the word "Amṛta" (Nectar), one should likewise contemplate the form with the mantra: "I fashion the embodiment of consciousness. (8)
The Goddess, seated upon the lap of Kāmeśvara, delighted by supreme bliss,
bestowing the four aims of human existence upon the practitioner.
One should perform protection with the mantra from behind for her who gazes with a compassionate, moist glance, languid with bliss, by means of the nārāca-mudrā. || 100 ||
Then, having veiled himself, the practitioner of mantra should perform the binding of the directions;
then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), he should take up a handful of flowers.
One should never invoke the Goddess without an offering of flowers;
thereafter, one should meditate upon the Great Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, as she has been described.
Then, having realized this within his heart, the practitioner who has mastered his vital breaths should contemplate the unity between the two forms—the external and the internal—of the Goddess. (13)
Then, by means of the seed-syllable of Vāyu, flowing through the nostril,
one should draw out that consciousness and place it within a handful of flowers.
From the emission of the breath through the nose, the deity resides within the flower; one should not separate one's hand from it as long as one continues to stabilize the goddess. 15.
O Maheśvarī, when the flower has been separated from the hand,
the Goddess is worshipped by the Gandharvas, yet the fruit is not obtained even by those who perform the worship.
Then, by means of the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā and the vidyā of invocation, one should cause her,
who possesses an exceedingly radiant luster, to emerge and place her within the *śrīpīṭha*.
Having properly joined both hands together in an even manner through the application of rotation, one should then hold the ring fingers with the two index fingers.
One should join the two middle fingers in the center, and then the two little fingers below them; likewise, the two thumbs should also be joined in three ways according to the sequence of pairs.
This great mudrā consists of three parts for the rite of summoning Tripurā;
it is mounted upon the seed-syllable *hasa* (or *hasa ka*, according to another reading), and Bālā is situated upon a seat of fire.
(Anayā hasraiṃ hasakalarī hassrau—this is the *trikhaṇḍā-vidyā*. Having recited the root mantra and with the *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā*:
"O Thou who dwellest within the forest of great lotuses, whose form is the bliss of the primal cause! (21)
O Mother, who acts for the welfare of all beings, come, come, O Supreme Goddess!
O Queen of the Gods, who are easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by your retinue.
Come to abide within this form; by my grace, take up your residence here.
Come, O Goddess, auspicious one, destroyer of fear, through your own power! 23.
"Remain perfectly steady for as long as I shall worship you.
O Mistress of Desire, come here together with all your retinue. (24)
O passionate one, manifest your presence here for the rite of worship;
O Kāmeśvarī, come and sit upon the lap of Kāmeśa.
"Grant me an uninterrupted, pure intellect and a voice from my throat;
O Great Goddess, when this is done, her stability shall arise. (26)
The hands are completely filled with flowers and joined in the añjali gesture;
this is declared to be the Āvāhanī mudrā, which accomplishes all purposes. (27)
When that same [mudrā] is turned face downwards, it becomes the Sthāpanī;
when the two fists are joined together, it takes the form of the Saṃnidhāpanī.
When this very mudrā, which consists of the form of closing the fist with the thumbs inside, has its two index fingers extended; || 29 ||
This is the Avaguṇṭhana-mudrā, considered to provide all forms of protection;
the practitioner should perform the rite of nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa) with the Dhenu-mudrā.
After turning the two hands over, join the two index fingers and the two middle fingers;
then, let the pair of little fingers and the pair of ring fingers be joined to one another.
O Dear One, this is declared to be the Dhenumudrā for the purpose of making [the ritual substances] nectar-like;
O Goddess, the best of practitioners should place the limb-mantras upon the limbs of the Goddess. (32)
This mudrā, characterized by pervasion, is called sakalīkaraṇa;
it consists of the thumbs interlaced with one another and the other fingers extended.
This is declared to be the Mahāmudrā for the sake of attaining the supreme auspiciousness;
thereafter, one should veil the Goddess with the Avaguṇṭhana-mudrā.
O Goddess, *āvāhana* is indeed the invocation from afar;
O Goddess, *saṃsthāpana* is that which effects immobility. (35)
Proximity is said to be the state of standing near;
the restraint of the mind through the desire for nothing else is called *saṃnirodhana*. (36)

O Dear One, the making whole through the complete establishment of the *yāma* (postures), the bestowing of that which is not the object of unworthy vision, and the veiling [are the functions of the *kalās*]. (37)
O Śivā, [this] abiding in the state of being filled with bliss is the act of immortalization;
it manifests the capacity for endurance toward all varieties of transgressions.
"Making supreme" (paramīkaraṇa) here refers to earnest prayer;
one should then pray to the Goddess face-to-face with the *saṃmukha* mudrā. (39)
With the two thumbs held in a fist, facing each other and joined together, one should raise them; this is the Saṃmukha-mudrā. 40.
Having recited the root-vidyā of Mahātripurasundarī, one should then, with devotion, worship the Śrī-pādukā, saying: "I worship. (41)
One should offer three handfuls of flowers to the pair of lotus-feet of the Goddess;
likewise, at the end of the mantra "I satisfy," one should perform the libation three times with the appropriate mudrā.
Then, with the *prārthanā-mudrā*, one should entreat [the deity] with this [verse]:
"O Goddess, O beautiful one, being well-disposed toward me through your grace, be gracious. (43)
"O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, accept this portion of my worship;
for although I am weak and possess few means, O Goddess of gods. (44)
"I perform worship to you with devotion; please favor me with your grace.
[With this prayer,] the two hands, with fingers extended and joined together, are held facing each other. (45)
And this very mudrā, known as *prārthanā* (supplication), should be placed upon the heart; one should display it preceded by its respective seed-syllable (*bīja*). Thus, there are nine mudrās.
Then, in sequence, follow the nine mudrās known as Saṃkṣobhaṇī, Drāvaṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, Vaśyā, Unmādinī, Mahāṅkuśā, Khecarī, Bījā, and Yonī.

O Maheśānī, one should visualize all these mudrās, which have the luster of bandhūka flowers and saffron, with their respective hands [held] facing toward Śrīvidyā. (Note: *mudrā* is the reading for *mudrāka*). 48.
Then, one should thus present these offerings to the Supreme Goddess:
"O Goddess, these have been made with devotion; may they bring the presence of the God to the practitioner. (49)
Because they cause [the breath] to circulate, they are therefore called *upacārakas*; or because they circulate in proximity, they are likewise said to be at the end of the *bālikā*. (50)
One should offer a seat ending with "namaḥ," and there should be a welcome and a greeting.
Water for the feet and the water of honor (*arghya*) for the feet should likewise end with "namaḥ. (51)

The sipping of water (*ācamana*) and likewise the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) are prescribed with the word *svadhā*; with that same mantra, ending in *namaḥ*, one should perform the sipping of water and the ritual bath.
The two garments are said to end with "namaḥ," and likewise the ornaments for the limbs;
one should offer perfume and flowers ending with "namaḥ," while [the oblation] ends with "vauṣaṭ. (Note: There is no reading for "kunda" in manuscript K.)
One should offer a flower to the Goddess with the mudrā known as Jñāna;
this Jñānamudrā is said to be formed by the joining of the thumb and the index finger. (54)
Likewise, one should offer incense ending with the word "namaḥ," as well as a lamp, a garland, and then the fourfold food offering as prescribed. (Note: "pamā" is an alternative reading for "dīpaṃ").
One should offer sweet water for drinking and then again water for sipping;
one should also present betel-leaf mixed with camphor to the Goddess.
Furthermore, one should offer libations with the Tripurātattva-mudrā;
this mudrā is said to be formed by the joining of the thumb and the ring finger. (This is the reading in manuscript Ga Ka. 57.
They say the thumb is Śiva, and the ring finger is called Śakti;
the libation (tarpaṇa) is performed by the union of these two with nectars using the left hand.
Having displayed the *yonimudrā*, one should then display the other mudrās in their proper sequence;
having praised and prostrated according to the rules, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind. (59)
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer oblations into the fire; at the conclusion of the oblations, one should present the bali offering;
and at the conclusion of the bali offering, one should present the various articles of food.
Then, one should again fumigate the Goddess with incenses such as the ten-ingredient blend (daśāṅga);
thereafter, rows of lamps should be displayed from her feet up to her forehead.
Then one should cause vermilion to be offered with "Vīreśvarāya vauṣaṭ" (the reading "vauṣaṭ ca ṣaṭ" is found in manuscript K).
Likewise, one should provide vermilion for the body ointments and wine for the drinks.
Among garments, red silk (the reading *kauśeya* is preferred) bestows pleasure upon Tripurā;
having offered collyrium for the eyes, one should likewise show her a mirror. 63.
Then, having placed a parasol over her head, one should fan the Supreme Goddess with red or white yak-tail whisks, but never with black ones.
Furthermore, one should repeatedly sound the conch and the bell and thoroughly fumigate [the area].
Then, one should gratify the Goddess with the sounds of song and instrumental music. (65)
O Goddess, with various kinds of musical instruments, with playful and auspicious festivities, and with troupes of actors and dancers as well as courtesans, O Pārvatī,
one should offer oneself with one's whole being and become absorbed in that.
[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the description of the procedure for the external sacrifice, in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 14 ||
[The Fifteenth Chapter] The Illustrious Goddess said: O Lord, how are the ritual services (upacāra) performed, and what is their fruit?
O Śaṅkara, tell me everything that is most dear to the Goddess.
Īśvara said:

O Pārvatī, listen as I describe the sixteen services (*upacāra*) by which the Goddess is directly pleased when performed according to the prescribed rites. (Variant reading *sākṣāt* for *syāt*; variant reading *vihitaiḥ* for *vidhānaiḥ*).
One should first offer a seat made of gold or silver, or likewise fashioned from cloth or gems; or else one made of flowers or even of wood.
One should never offer a leaf or a seat here during the worship;
rather, one should offer a red woolen blanket to the Goddess according to the prescribed rule.

(Reading according to manuscript *sva*: Upon a seat fashioned from a lotus at the footstool of Mount Sumeru, O Supreme Goddess, O Mother who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, please remain here. (Reading *kha* for "that seat": ...upon that seat... 5.
O Śivā, for him who offers a prescribed seat to the Goddess with this very [mantra],
enjoyment and liberation are in the palm of his hand, and he shall become established everywhere.

O Goddess, this water for the feet—mixed with sandalwood and agallochum, and offered very cool—is presented by me for the comfort of your feet. (The word "niveditam" [offered] is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. 7.
Then, one should cause [the guest] to receive [the water] with a lustrous vessel or a conch shell;
it is considered the abode of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—[this is the reading for "pādya"]. || 8 ||
The mantra for the water for the feet has been proclaimed by me; with this very [mantra] one should present it.
Through the *arghya* one obtains desires, and through the *arghya* one obtains wealth.

By means of a conch shell established previously, one shall indeed obtain sons, long life, happiness, and liberation through the gift of that which is worthy of honor, according to the prescribed ritual itself. 10.
O Maheśvarī, [one should offer] white mustard seeds, mung beans, sesame seeds with milk, as well as barley and red sandalwood flowers to Tripurā.
Having placed it before [the deity], the practitioner should offer the *arghya* with the *arghya-mantra*:
"O Goddess, this *arghya*, this *arghya*, is offered by me with devotion. (12)
Taking water together with fragrant substances from a conch-shell vessel, place it upon his head; for water that is free from bubbles should be offered. (13)
That sipping of water for the sake of the deity is called *ācamana*;
it may be performed with water scented with camphor or perfumed with black agallochum (*kālāguru*). || 14 ||
In whatever manner, one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) using fragrant waters that are clear and free from froth, with auspicious liquids containing perfumes. || 15 ||
O beloved, having offered the water for sipping (ācamanīya) which bestows an increase in longevity, strength, and fame, using either a golden vessel or even a conch shell; || 16 ||
The practitioner always obtains his desires exactly as he wishes, O Goddess;
this perfumed water for rinsing the mouth has been offered by me with devotion. (17)
For the increase of longevity, strength, and fame, let this be accepted:
curd, clarified butter, water, honey, and sugar, along with sugarcane juice. (18)

The Madhuparka is proclaimed as that which bestows pleasure upon the Goddess; it consists of water from a coconut, sugar, curd, and ghee, all in equal measure. (Note: *madhuparkas tu* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
One should employ honey in greater quantity than all other ingredients in the *madhuparka*;
furthermore, one should offer it using either a bronze vessel or a silver vessel.
O Supreme Goddess, whatever merit a man obtains from the Jyotiṣṭoma, Aśvamedha, and other such sacrifices—all that is established in the Madhuparka offering. || 21 ||

"O beautiful one, take this madhuparka—clarified butter mixed with curd and honey, as well as water with sugar—and eat it from this silver vessel. (The reading "raupyapātre" is supported by the Rauṣmaka recension.)
Worship without the madhuparka causes the ruin of the practitioner;
indeed, the Supreme Goddess will devour the practitioner if she does not see the madhuparka. (23)
Camphor, agallochum, musk, yellow pigment, and saffron, as well as coconut water, honey, and excellent sugarcane juice; || 24 ||

Sita (or "Tā" according to another reading), the five products of the cow, and likewise the collection of all medicinal herbs; at the end, water is prescribed—this is the bathing substance dear to Tripurā. (25)
Alternatively, the practitioner should offer [the water] to Tripurā using a golden pitcher or conch shells;
by means of this bathing and giving, he shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
One who desires long life and the enjoyment of sensual pleasures shall be freed from great sins, provided that for each of all the items, the measure is one thousand palas. (27)
O Goddess, the great ablution (mahāsnāna) shall consist of one hundred palas;
the middling [ablution] shall consist of [one hundred palas], while the lowest ablution is said to consist of ten palas.
When all [the substances] are mixed together, no separate bathing [of each] is prescribed. One should bathe the Goddess first with the verse beginning "tripād" (Ṛgveda 10.90.3). || 29 ||
Thereafter, one should also offer with the root mantra and with this [mantra]:
"You are the waters and you are the earth; you are indeed light and you are the wind. (Note: *pṛthivī* is the reading in manuscript *ka*. 30.
O Goddess, I bathe you with a heart of pure devotion alone;
yet, having bathed the Great Goddess, if one does not offer her a garment, [the rite is incomplete]. (Note: "sna" is an alternative reading for "snā").
That shameless and supreme sinner falls into the ocean of sin;
in the absence of a garment, one should then offer a red lotus, or likewise a hibiscus flower.
Having caused the Great Queen to bathe, one should cause a pair of garments to be given;
for by means of clothing shame is concealed, and by means of clothing sin is removed. (33)
Among all varieties of ornaments, clothing is said to be the most excellent;
auspicious clothing brings delight to the Goddess and bestows the fourfold aims of human life.
One that is ten days old, soiled, worn out, torn, or clung to the body;
one belonging to another, bitten by insects, pierced by a needle, or likewise left overnight—[such a rosary is unfit]. (35)
One should employ the "needle-pierced" (sūcividdha) technique on objects such as banners, canopies, and the like;
however, one should not use it on hair, unwashed items, or things defiled by phlegm, urine, and so forth.
One should not offer to Mahādevī clothing scorched by fire or that which is worn out; however, variegated cloth and fine silk (dukūla) are supremely pleasing to the Goddess.
This garment bestows all accomplishments and yields the fruit of the Vajapeya sacrifice;
it is endowed with the threads of knowledge and permeated by the syllables of the mantra.
O beautiful one, knowledge and ignorance are your two garments, red and dark;
your pair of garments is exceedingly pure, resembling the rising sun. (39)
O Queen of the Gods, put on this new [garment] which gives comfort to the body, as well as the crown, the crest-jewel, the earrings, and the forehead ornament. (40)
A palm-leaf ornament, a necklace, a necklet, and then a finger-ring; a string of beads upon her mass of hair, earrings, bracelets, and armlets. (41)
The toe-ring, the thread-ornament, the anklet, and the small bells—
these are declared to be the sixteen ornaments among ornaments.

One should offer to the Goddess, according to one's ability, that which constantly bestows the four aims of life, which is an ornament granting all happiness, and which produces contentment and nourishment. (The reading "nityam" is found in manuscript *ka*. 43.
O beautiful one, may these ornaments, fashioned from molten gold and set with the nine precious gems, adorn your limbs. (44)
O Mistress of Desire, O You who can assume any form at will, O Bestower of the fruits of all desires!
Accept this ornament, O Lady of beautiful limbs, which has been offered by me with devotion. (45)
Whether it be powdered, rubbed, or even drawn out by heat; whether it be produced by friction or even derived from a limb of a living being. (46)
Fragrance is said to be of five kinds, which bestows pleasure upon the Goddess; indeed, by means of the application of excellent fragrances and various aromatic powders, [one attains this]. (47)

These should be called "fragrances" (gandha), and that is remembered as the first type of fragrance; it is the sandalwood (malayaja) scent ground together with the *nameru* tree, which is variegated (*śabala*). 48.

Furthermore, for that [substance] to which a paste of aguru and other such materials is applied, the essence is extracted after burning it with aguru, devadāru, and other woods. (Note: *devadāru* is the reading in place of *agurude*. 49.
That fragrance drawn forth by burning is proclaimed as the third;
it consists of the fragrant *bilva* and *tilaka*, and the *śatapatrikā*. (50)
That which is extracted by pressing is called *saṃmardaja* (produced by friction);
or it is that which arises from the musk-deer (*mṛganābhi*), or indeed from its pouch (*tatkośodbhava*). (Note: *ṣodbhava* is an alternative reading.)
Fragrance produced from the limbs of living beings is declared to be the fifth;
thus the detailed classification of fragrance has been illustrated merely by way of direction.
Among all varieties of fragrant substances, that which originates from Malaya is most highly praised;
therefore, one should always offer sandalwood with every possible effort.
The fragrance produced by equal parts of saffron, agallochum, musk, camphor,
and sandalwood is that which bestows pleasure upon Tripurā.
Fine sandalwood paste, cooled and mixed with *kālīyaka*, is the foremost of ointments and supremely pleasing to the Goddess. 55.
Likewise, lac-dye on the tips of the nails brings delight to the Goddess;
through its fragrance one obtains all desires, for fragrance always bestows righteousness.
The fragrance of your limbs is a means of accomplishment and is established even in liberation;
O Maheśvarī, I do not know your body nor your movements. 57.
"Accepting the perfumes offered by me, let her be anointed;
when the Goddess is well-pleased with these perfumes, she shall become the bestower of the fourfold aims of life. (58)
O Great Goddess, with this very [mantra], one should offer scents to the Goddess,
using a lamp-fire fueled by ghee, oil, and so forth, in a vessel such as gold.
When collyrium is produced, having prepared it mixed with camphor,
one should offer it to Tripurā for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
O Daughter of the Mountain, a widow should not apply collyrium for the sake of Mahāmāyā;
nor should the practitioner apply eye-salve using an earthen vessel. (61)

One does not obtain the fruit of worship through water-offerings placed in an earthen vessel, nor through those belonging to another, nor those that have been smelled, nor those that have been stolen or crushed. (62)
O Goddess of the Gods, by offering flowers, incense, perfumes, and other such articles that have been smelled, a man shall obtain the fruit of a name-syllable (namaka).
O Supreme Goddess, one should never worship Maheśvarī, the Great Tripurasundarī, with flowers or leaves that have become stale. (64)
All stale leaves, flowers, and fruits,
as well as white and red lotuses, lilies, and blue water-lilies, are to be avoided.
Regarding these, one should suspect that they have become stale after five days;
for other flowers, this applies until there is a change in their fragrance.
O Maheśānī, in the case of the bilva leaf, there is no such thing as it becoming stale;
likewise for the bakula, kesara, vajra, mālya, kunda, and śālmalī flowers. (Note: "mālya" is an alternative reading for "lākha").
Karavīra, arka flower, bandhūka, and likewise lotus;
mālatī, mallikā, jātī, yūthikā, and likewise mādhavī. (68)
Tagara, karṇikāra, droṇa, utpala, and campaka; aśoka, kumuda, śephālikā, and kadambhaka—69.
The ketakī, the forest garland (vanamālā), as well as the kusumbha and kiṃśuka, the kahlāra and bakula, and likewise the lavaṅga and nāgakesara. (70)
Among all varieties of flowers, these alone are always dear to Tripurā; one should not worship Śivā with leaves.
Among leaves, the bilva leaf, as well as the sprout of the madana tree and the shoot of dūrvā grass are prescribed; one should not employ any other leaf.
O Great Goddess, one should offer Mallikā, Mālatī, Kunda, Droṇa, and the white lotus to Tripurā during the bright fortnight. (73)
Among all varieties of flowers, O wise one, the red lotus (raktapadma) as well as the hibiscus (javā) brings delight to the Goddess and bestows the fruit of all desires. (74)
O Goddess of gods, even a jewel-flower made of gold and other precious materials can never equal the red lotus with the thunderbolt (vajra) in any respect. (75)
Whatever fruit a man obtains by making a garland from any one of these species of flowers and offering it to Mahādevī— 76.
Even with a thousand mouths, the Lord would not be able to describe it;
therefore, Brahmā dwells at the root of the flower, while Keśava dwells within its center.
I am eternally situated at the tip of the flower; all the gods are situated upon the petals;
and all beings, both moving and unmoving, are traditionally held to always reside within the fragrance of the flower.
The supreme light, residing within the flower, is propitiated by the flower alone;
the flower bestows both enjoyment and liberation, and grants contentment, prosperity, nourishment, and joy. (79)
With flowers, the Goddess becomes pleased, bestowing dharma, kāma, and artha;
therefore, a man endowed with devotion should always worship the Goddess with flowers. (80)
Flowers alone are always dear to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others; O Mother, I offer this pure flower to you—please accept it. (81)
[Food] that has a pungent odor or is foul-smelling, defiled by worms, hair, and the like, or placed in an impure vessel or held in unworthy hands, [is unfit]. (82)
If one does not offer what has been brought to the Goddess even through negligence, it causes fault;
likewise with water brought after bathing, stale offerings, those obtained by begging, or those that are black in color. (83)
One should not worship with buds that have opened by themselves, been released, or fallen to the ground on their own, nor with buds other than those of the *campaka* and the lotus.
Whether it be a flower, a leaf, or a fruit, it is not desired if held face down;
that is declared to bring suffering, for it should be offered exactly as it was produced.
In all forms of variegated worship, there is neither contradiction nor fault;
however, offering flowers face-down is not desired, except in the ritual of the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
Moreover, what is the use of saying too much? This is stated in general terms: [one may worship] with flowers, whether already offered or not yet offered, both aquatic and terrestrial. (87)
With all available leaves, one who is devoted should constantly perform sacrifice;
in the absence of flowers, one should sacrifice with leaves, and when leaves are unavailable, with their fruits.
One should not neglect the worship, whether with unbroken grains or even with water;
but if these too are unavailable, one should resort to mental devotion.
When wood or other materials are being burned, that from which a fragrance arises—one that brings pleasure to the nostrils and other senses and is exceedingly captivating—is called *niḥtāpa*. (90)
This is to be known as the incense that bestows delight upon the Goddess:
*patra* (the reading "putra" is also found), *musta*, *nakha*, *kuṣṭha*, *jaṭā*, *māṃsī*, and *śailaja*. (91)
Sarala wood, devakāṣṭha, lac, and true sandalwood, mixed with the ghee of a tawny cow, camphor, sugar, and agaru; 92.
The great incense of sixteen ingredients bestows delight upon the Sixteenth [Tattva].
One should not let the incense fall upon the ground, nor upon the seat, nor indeed upon the water-pot.
Having prepared it in whatever manner is appropriate and placed it upon the support, one should present it, saying:
"This is an excellent fragrance, rich in scent, produced from the essence of the forest tree. (94)
"May this incense, which is to be smelled by all the gods, be accepted.
Now I shall describe the lamp, which bestows the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. (95)

The first lamp is one with ghee; then that produced from sesame oil; the mustard oil lamp is declared the lowest; any other than these is considered censurable. (Note: The reading *ghṛtadīpaḥ* is supported by the Kaśmīr manuscript.)
The first wick is said to be made from lotus fibers, another from cotton, and yet another from the core of *darbha* grass. || 97 ||
A practitioner desiring prosperity should not take cloth made of silk or wool, nor cotton that is soiled or stale, for the purpose of making wicks. 98.
A lamp-vessel made of metal, earth, or iron is recommended;
and lamp-stands made of metal and other materials should also be fashioned individually.
A lamp should be offered upon a tree, but never on the ground;
for that man who offers a lamp while causing distress to the earth [is at fault]. (100)
He certainly reaches the terrible Tāmisra hell; of this there is no doubt.
[But he who is] pleasing to the eyes with his own radiance and free from causing distress even from afar— || 101 ||
With its flame intact, soundless, smokeless, and not too short,
[the lamp] stands upon a vessel placed on a lamp-stand, filled with pure oil.
A lamp that burns with a beautiful, bright flame spiraling to the right is declared here to be the best; it brings about the delight of Tripurā. || 103 ||
A lamp devoid of a wick is proclaimed as mediocre;
one lacking both a vessel and oil is proclaimed as inferior. (104)
A garland of lamps should be prepared; a single lamp should never be used.
O Supreme Goddess, three or five lamps should be offered.
One should never give less than this to Tripurā;
nor should a flickering lamp be offered for the sake of increasing prosperity.
One should not offer lamp oils such as ghee and the like by mixing them together;
having mixed the oils, one shall go to the Raurava hell.
One must never extinguish a lamp, even one prepared for the sake of the gods;
the stealer of a lamp shall become blind, and the one who extinguishes it shall become lame. (108)
The best of practitioners should not even engage in worldly discourse regarding the light of the sun, the moon, lightning, or fire. (109)
"You alone are the light of lights; let this lamp be accepted.
The lamp should be placed to the right of the Goddess, in front of her, but certainly not to the left. (110)
The incense should likewise be offered to the left or in front, but never to the right;
one should present the perfume, flowers, and ornaments in the space directly before [the deity].
The food offering (naivedya) should be placed to the right, the left, or in front, but never behind;
and whatever is suitable to be offered upon the body, one should present that specifically upon the yantras.
One should offer unfit food, such as sacrificial offerings (naivedya) and meals, in front;
one should offer liquor behind, and other drinks to the left. (113)
O Goddess of the gods, whatever knowledge regarding Śrīvidyā is here devoid of liquor (or, according to another reading, "devoid of the aspirant"),
it is declared to be fruitless and serves only for malevolent magic.

[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual Offerings for Worship and Their Fruits," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. It is complete. 15.
[The Sixteenth Chapter] Īśvara said:
Having taken sugarcane juice that has been kept overnight and well-prepared, [one should proceed].
One should pour mango juice mixed with honey into it. || 1 ||
There was the juice of the jujube and the rose-apple, as well as that of the date-palm, and the juice produced from the coconut, and the unsurpassed juice of the grape. || 2 ||
Powder derived from the fruit of the *mohinī*, as well as the pollen of the *jātī* bud, powder of the seeds of *kanaka*, and that produced from the *jātī* fruit. (3)
O Śivā, [one should prepare] the powder of trijāta, trisugandhi, trikaṭu, and triphalā,
as well as other fragrant substances.
Having added small amounts of various substances, one should perfume it with camphor;
O beloved, this should be done in a vessel of gold or silver, or else in a leaf-cup.
O Supreme Goddess, having placed the white [substance] there, one should cast it in;
O Goddess, having cast it, one should carefully cover it with red cloths.
Having been kept for seven nights, it indeed becomes like nectar;
one should offer it after fumigating it with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
This is declared to be the most excellent of all, always the most beloved of the Goddess;
she is known as Madirā, the bestower of supreme bliss. (8)
Having offered this to Sundarī, one should obtain all supernatural powers (siddhis).
After remaining for a long time in the world of the Goddess, one shall thereafter become a king upon the earth.

And there too, O Mistress of the Gods, by worshipping with this [mantra], one shall attain liberation as absolute isolation (kaivalya); this has been prescribed for one who possesses conceptual thought (savikalpa), and not otherwise.
O Goddess of the gods, in the scripture established by the Suras, that which is free from conceptual construction is indeed nectar, and it is also the primordial matter (mādyam). 11.
Even in times of distress, a twice-born man should never offer liquor to the Goddess;
if he should offer liquor out of delusion, he falls away from his very Brahminhood.
He alone would be a slayer of a Brahmin; therefore, one should avoid liquor.
O lotus-eyed one, in ancient times, liquor was indeed consumed.
In the past, having drunk liquor, Śukra even forgot his own self;
and having drunk and become intoxicated, the Lord of the Night seized that wife of his preceptor.
Therefore, that sage also pronounced a most terrible curse;
and Brahmā, together with the sages, sang this very same thing in the past.
The twice-born who, overwhelmed by ignorance, gives liquor to Mahādevī, and he who remains in the state of a beast (paśu), shall be a perpetrator of a great sin (mahāpātakin). || 16 ||
Furthermore, liquor is prescribed for the remaining two who are free from conceptual construction;
it is not prescribed for the first [type], and therefore he would become a slayer of Brahman.
Therefore, O Sulocanā, this earth-field was to be avoided;
yet it is the bestower of perfection upon the wise and the granter of immortality. (18)
And this [knowledge], when refined by wisdom, destroys great sins—such as the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and the theft of gold. (19)
If one becomes free from conceptual construction, O Goddess, he may destroy [the karmic bonds] through the power of worship;
when he is free from conceptual construction, he should offer the wine to Mahādevī.
One undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Agniṣṭomas (or Vahniṣṭomas), and even a hundred Rājasūyas. || 21 ||
One becomes the master of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, before long;
however, O Goddess, when one possesses conceptual thought (*savikalpa*), one becomes a partaker of sin—of this there is no doubt. (22)
You are indeed the abode of the sinless, and you are the *svāhā* of the celestial dwellers;
you are the *svadhā* of the foremost ancestors, and the bestower of success upon human beings.

Formerly, during the churning of the Ocean of Milk, she was brought forth in the assembly of the gods together with Ānandabhairava as Ānandabhairavī. (Note: "kṣīrābdhimathanakāle" is an alternative reading.)
If she shows favor toward you, success will surely follow—of this there is no doubt;
but if she is averse, then she will destroy his lineage and knowledge.
Indeed, you are well-disposed toward the gods and likewise toward the gandharvas;
you have repeatedly turned your face away from the daityas, bringing about their total destruction.
"O Goddess, speak to me today; grant the vibration of consciousness within me.
Having thus praised the Goddess Surā, she was consecrated with the previously mentioned [mantra]. (Note: *surādavyai* is an alternative reading for *surādevyai*. 27.
Having offered it to Tripurā, he becomes capable of both restraint and grace;
[the offering] consists of four kinds: that which is to be chewed, sucked, licked, and drunk.
This perpetual offering, consisting of all sacrifices, bestows satisfaction upon all;
it grants knowledge, fulfills desires, and is meritorious, as well as providing strength and health. (29)
Through the offering of food (naivedya), one attains heaven; through the offering of food, one becomes immortal.
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are all established within the offerings of food.
Therefore, with every effort, one should indeed cause an offering to be presented;
for even if an offering is given to the Great Goddess merely in thought, [it yields great fruit]. (31)
The man who is endowed with devotion shall become long-lived and happy;
[he should offer] sacrificial oblation well-prepared, divine, mixed with clarified butter and sugar.
O Goddess, it resembles pure crystal, possesses a luster equal to the orb of the moon, is produced from shining rice grains, is endowed with a lovely fragrance, and is soft. (33)
Fragrant śāli rice, accompanied by honey and meat, along with cakes, milk-rice, milk, and other food, is recommended for the Goddess. (34)
Whatever beasts and birds are prescribed for the offerings of sacrifice,
their flesh and various kinds of fish should be presented.

Every side-dish should be rich with fragrant scents and most enchanting; whatever food may be prepared, effort (or "carefully," according to the *ka* manuscript reading) should be exerted to provide it accordingly.

Having prepared it with spices such as *veśavāra* and other ingredients, one should offer it to Mahādevī; that which is endowed with a foul odor, burnt (or, according to another reading, milked), and excluded from enjoyment.
It has been said: "One should never offer black pot-herb (kālaśāka), peas (kalāya), palanka (pālaka), or potherb (potikā) to Tripurā. (38)
Whoever, endowed with devotion, should offer these vegetables—mustard, radish, vāstūka, and kalambikā—to Mahādevī; || 39 ||
He attains incomparable prosperity and is honored in the world of the goddesses;
[he who offers] a side-dish of black gram, mung beans, lentils, and so forth, seasoned with salt. (40)
Having prepared it with asafoetida, cumin, black pepper, and other spices, as well as fresh ginger, and having combined it with pieces of tamarind, one should offer it with devotion. (41)
Having obtained the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, one shall attain the world of the gods;
there are various kinds of drinks and many varieties of side dishes as well. (42)
Then, all products of the cow such as milk and those of the buffalo, as well as *āmikṣā*, curd with sugar, [should be offered] to the Supreme Goddess. (43)
Milk-rice with sugar-cakes mixed with the ghee of a tawny cow, and very delicious cooked food prepared with sugar and camphor. || 44 ||
Having made the *vaṭaka* cakes reddish with saffron and coated them with sugar, [he should offer] boiled milk with sugar, accompanied by plantains and other fruits. 45.
One should offer wine with white side-dishes in a golden vessel, or alternatively, in a silver vessel, or again, in a copper vessel. (46)
Due to its absence, or if it is otherwise, one would go to hell;
one should never give raw food to Mahādevī. (47)
One who is intent on his own welfare should never offer to the deities (or to the Guru, either to the left or in front) food offerings that have not been purified by mantras and time. 48.
Having offered liquor mixed with sugar and combined with honey, one shall dwell for a long time in the world of the Goddess and attain the liberation of absolute isolation (kaivalya). || 49 ||
Having offered water from a coconut along with curd (āmikṣā),
it should be accompanied by milk, ghee, honey, camphor, sugar, and yogurt.
O Śivā, one should prepare a fragrant powder with the three spices (trijātaka), the three pungents (trikaṭu), cloves (lavaṅga) for both [the tooth-stick and the powder], as well as other substances.
Having prepared it by this method and perfumed it with fragrant powders,
one should offer the drink to the Goddess in a vessel made of precious metal.
Listen to the fruit of his merit with a mind inclined toward devotion:
for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas. (53)
Having resided in Devīpura, the illustrious one becomes a sovereign ruler on earth;
thereafter, he attains liberation (kaivalya) according to his desire.

O Maheśvarī, by offering merely coconut water to the Goddess, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and is glorified in the world of men. (Note: *avahni* is an alternative reading for *agni*.)
One should worship the Goddess with all kinds of fruits, both cultivated and wild;
and the food offering (naivedya) should consist of items dear to Bali, such as kaśeruka, viṣa, and so forth.
Except for the śleṣmātaka, the bilva, and especially the śaunaka, one may eat fruits that have ripened without effort and are naturally sweet. (57)
Those which are well-cooked, fragrant, and captivating—
these alone are praised as auspicious givers of merit, and no others.
One should offer the food-oblation dear to Tripurā upon a plate made of gold, silver, or copper, or even on a stone slab or a lotus leaf. (59)
Having perceived it as being without covering, one endowed with devotion and faith should dry it with the seed-syllable of air (Yam) and likewise burn it with fire (Ram).
One should flood [the vessel] with the Varuṇa-mantra by means of the Sudhā-ṛṣṭi and the Dhenu-mudrā;
having protected it with the Astra-mantra, one should then consecrate it with the Mūla-mantra alone.
At the end of the root deity's own name, one should utter "naivedyam" (the food offering).
The mantra for the food offering is said to end with "gṛhāṇa" and the wife of Vahni (svāhā). || 62 ||
O Goddess, this fourfold food, endowed with the six flavors, has been offered by me with devotion; please accept it. (63)
O Goddess, please partake with compassion of these foods—lickables, suckables, drinks, and so forth—which I have brought here with great effort. (64)
O beautiful one, take these holy water-offerings (ācamana) which perfume the mouth, consisting of the waters of the celestial river scented with nutmeg, cloves, and kakkola berries.
O Goddess of Gods, one should offer five oblations in sequence with the root mantra:
to Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna.
One should know this to be the essential nature of the five oblations;
O Dear One, the five oblations should be performed in sequence using the five fingers themselves. (67)
Having again offered water for sipping (ācamana), one should present mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa)—
betel leaf combined with fragrance and well-scented with camphor and other ingredients.
Having consecrated it with various fragrant substances, he should present it while praising [the deity] with diverse hymns, endowed with a spirit of devotion. (69)
The best of practitioners should prostrate to the Supreme Sovereign according to the prescribed rite;
[for she is] the gods, humans, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas.
The great-souled ones are satisfied on all sides by a prostration;
through prostration, one obtains the fourfold aim of great prosperity. (71)
For the sake of attaining all accomplishments everywhere, bowing alone is praised.
Having bowed, one conquers the worlds; having bowed, the Dharma proceeds. (The variant reading *natirekā* occurs in manuscript *kha*.)
Through this salutation, one obtains long life and uninterrupted progeny;
the devoted practitioner shall attain the fourfold aims of human existence before long.
Salutation is a great sacrifice that always bestows delight in every respect;
therefore, prostrate before the Great Goddess and circumambulate her with devotion.
Even he who performs a prostration with devotion to the Great Goddess even in his mind, having conquered the worlds, is glorified in the world of the Goddess. || 75 ||
Salutations are known to be of three kinds—physical, vocal, and mental—and they should be understood as being superior, inferior, or middling. (76)
The gods are pleased in every way by physical prostrations; among all forms of salutation, the physical is considered the foremost. (The variant reading in manuscript *kha* is "always. || 77 ||

Having gone to the ground on one's knees and touched the earth with the head, that salutation which is performed is declared to be physical (kāyika). (Note: "procyate kāyikastu sa" is the reading in manuscript *kha*. || 78 ||
Having joined the palms over the head, a salutation is offered;
yet he who does not touch the ground with both knees and the head is called the lowest. (79)
That physical prostration which is performed without touching the ground with the knees and without touching the earth with the head is the middling [type]. (80)
Whether by means of the Purāṇic or Tantric rites, or again with the root mantra,
one should perform circumambulation and prostration as a means for accomplishing dharma and worldly prosperity.
Extending his right hand while bowing his head himself once more, he showed his right side, filled with devotion and faith. (82)

Having performed a single circumambulation in a circular form, the practitioner should know that this circumambulation grants satisfaction to the entire multitude of gods. (The reading "sarvadevaugha" is found in manuscript *kha*. 83.
He who performs one hundred and eight circumambulations of the Goddess shall attain all his desires and subsequently obtain liberation.
The triangle, the hexagon, the half-moon, the circumambulation, the staff, the eight-limbed, and the fierce [prostration]—these are the seven characteristics of bowing. (85)
Having gone from the south to the northwest direction, and from there to the northeast;
then, having gone again to the south, the salutation is performed like a triangle.
The salutation known as the triangle bestows pleasure upon Tripurā;
having gone from the south to the northwest, and likewise from the northwest to the northeast.

Having gone from there to the south, having abandoned that [direction], and having entered the fire, one should go from the fire to the direction of the Rākṣasas (south-west), and from there enter the direction of Kubera (north-west). || 88 ||
Then, having gone to the south-eastern direction, the salutation is proclaimed;
this salutation known as the "six-cornered" (ṣaṭkoṇa) bestows pleasure upon Durgā. (89)
Having gone from the south to the northwest, and turning back from there toward the south,
that salutation which is performed is the "Half-moon," which is dear to me.
O Adrijā, one should know their Prakrit form in the salutations:
having left one's own seat and position, one goes behind them and is then saluted. (91)
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground and having touched it with the heart, likewise falling like a staff upon the ground—this is called "daṇḍa" by the wise. || 92 ||
Indeed, [it may be perceived] by the chin, the mouth, the nose, and the jaw;
or by the eyes, the two ears, and even the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 93 ||
That [prostration] by which the ground is touched sequentially with the eight limbs is called the "eight-limbed" (aṣṭāṅga);
it is that salutation in which there is contact with the earth through the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head). 94.
That [prayer] is to be known as "Ugra," which bestows satisfaction upon Viṣṇu;
it is a salutation composed by oneself in both prose and verse. (95)
The vocal [worship] performed by one endowed with devotion is considered the highest;
it is performed as a salutation through Puranic, Vedic, or Tantric [mantras]. (96)
That middle salutation would always be verbal; whenever there is a salutation to others by means of both prose and verse. (The reading "dācārata" is found in manuscript Kha. 97.
That verbal [salutation] is to be known as the lowest among all forms of salutation;
it becomes threefold according to whether the minds [of those offering it] are directed toward the desirable, the intermediate, or the undesirable. (98)
Bowing with the mind is said to be superior, middling, or inferior;
and among these three types of salutation, that which is performed with the body is considered the best.

[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for the Fruits of the Ritual Services," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 16 ||
[Seventeenth Chapter] The Holy Goddess said:
O God, O Supreme Lord, how are Prakaṭā and the others worshipped?
O Īśāna, tell me all of that, as well as the arrangement of the mudrās.
Īśvara said:
One should worship those [energies] with devotion according to the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
one should worship the Mohana and Kṣobhaṇa wheels in the order of clockwise rotation.
One should worship the remaining wheels in a counter-clockwise sequence;
O Goddess, beginning from the west, one should conclude at the northwest (vāyavya) direction.
O Goddess, I worship your multitudes of rays according to the prescribed rite;
O Mother of the World, command me, for you alone are both [the source] and they [the rays]. (4)

O Great Goddess, having received the command of the Goddess with palms joined in reverence, the best of practitioners, being satisfied, should perform worship according to the previously mentioned sequence. (The reading *tuṣṭo* is found in manuscript *ka*. || 5 ||
O Goddess, the propitiation of the powers of the supreme worship is performed with perfumes, flowers, water, and unbroken grains,
accompanied by the knowledge-mudrās and the reality-mudrā.

(1) Having first extracted the letter of Varuṇa (va), which is the Lord who is the Great Master of Yogins, the Yogin composed of compassion, and adorned by the moon on the right ear (the bindu). || 7 ||
Having said "Homage to the Buddha," one should worship the Lord of the World;
then, in the four directions starting from the west, one should worship the [deities] beginning with Aṇimā.
One should worship those beginning with *vaśitva* in the corners starting from the northwest;
*prāpti-siddhi* in the lower part, and likewise all desires (*sarvakāmān*) in the upper part. (Note: *kāmān* is the reading in the Kāpāṭha manuscript.)
O Maheśvarī, having first performed the conjunction with Māyā and Lakṣmī,
one should likewise utter the word "Siddhi" at the end, and then say "Śrīpādukām."
One should worship with the mantra "I worship" according to the prescribed method;
likewise, one should worship Brahmāṇī and the others on the second line.
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, and likewise Krodha;
and also Unmatta, O Goddess, Bhairava, and Kapālī. (12)
One should worship Bhīṣaṇa and Saṃhāra together with those [deities]; likewise, the goddesses headed by Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī reside in the third line.
One should worship the Mistress of the Wheel in the east, who purifies the hands;
in the south, one should worship the Goddess’s Mudrā, the Stirrer of Agitation.
One should worship Animā on the left; furthermore, having placed Buddha in front of her, one should place [the other deities] in the middle, with the little finger and the thumb joined together. (15)
Having formed the two index fingers like staffs, with the ring fingers above the middle fingers—this is the first mudrā, which causes universal agitation. (16)

(The extraction of the seed-syllable *drāṃ* is performed by [the phrase] "the end of *khā*" [i.e., *tha*], etc. Mounted upon fire (*ra*), adorned with the second vowel (*ā*), and joined with the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, that is proclaimed as her seed-syllable. (17)
Then, taking the special *arghya* water with his right hand,
he should utter the two seed-syllables and likewise [invoke] these manifest [deities].
The yoginīs, along with the mudrās, together with the siddhis and their weapons, as well as with their retinues and all the ritual offerings. || 19 ||
"In the wheel that deludes the three worlds, likewise presided over by Tripura, may [the deities] be worshipped and gratified; one should offer [the oblation] into the hand of the Goddess. (20)
In this manner, according to the words as they have been spoken, one should offer the worship of the wheel to the yoginīs of great splendor who reside in the entire wheel.
(1) One should worship those eternal digits with the digits of the goddess Māyālakṣmī.
Brahmā holds a water-pot, has four faces, and four arms. || 22 ||
Seated upon a royal swan, he is tall and lofty-shouldered (the variant reading is *tuṅgāṃsa*).
Sāvitrī stands on his left side, and Sarasvatī on the right.
All the gods stood before him, and all the Vedas stood at his front;
he was red and fair-limbed in complexion, with his hands occupied in the act of reciting prayers.
The God who bestows boons and fearlessness, the grandfather of all the worlds, [is to be worshipped];
having first extracted the Praṇava, one should write "Salutation to Brahmā. (25)
O Goddess, one should worship Brahmā with this mantra;
having joined it with the Bālā [vidyā], one should worship the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakranāyikā). || 26 ||

One should display the Drāviṇī mudrā preceded by its respective seed-syllable (*bīja*). [The extraction of the seed-syllable *drī* for the Drāviṇī mudrā is as follows: ending with *tha* (i.e., *thā*), and so forth, followed by *drī*. It is mounted upon fire (*ra*) and adorned with the fourth vowel (*ī*). (27)
When the middle [finger] is relaxed in the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇīmudrā, it possesses the supreme seed-syllable of Drāviṇī, joined with Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā. (28)
O Supreme Goddess, they are then made into the All-Enchanting [Mudrā];
[it is] like pure crystal, with five faces and three eyes. (29)
Always seated in the lotus posture upon a lotus placed on a tiger skin,
he is ever embracing the goddess Umā, who holds a chowrie and a blue lotus.
She has two arms and a body as fair as gold; her form is gentle and exceedingly beautiful, and she always holds a playful lotus in her left hand.
Then, having taken up a white chowrie and placing her right hand upon the right side of Śiva’s body, one should visualize her standing there. (The reading "tiṣṭhantī" is found in manuscript *ka*. 32.
Having meditated upon the Goddess, the mother of the three worlds, and Śiva, the father of the three worlds— the two Umā and Maheśvara— one may delude this entire world.
One should indeed [place] Śakra and likewise Ākāśa (the reading "śatu" is found in manuscript *ka*), adorned with the fourth vowel;
these two, joined respectively with Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā, are their seed-syllables (*bīja*). || 34 ||

Likewise, Maheśvara, accompanied by Umā, is known as the King of Mantras, who bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. (Note: *Umā-ṅentā* is the reading; *ṅentota* is an alternative reading. || 35 ||
Having worshipped those two with this [mantra] in the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaka [cakra],
one should then worship Anaṅgakusumā in the east with the *ka*-group itself.
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship Anaṅgamekhalā with the *ca*-group in the south;
and O Goddess, one should worship Anaṅgamadanā with the *ṭa*-group in the west.
One should worship Madanāturā in the northern part with the *tavarga* [consonants],
and likewise Anaṅgarakhā in the southeast with the *pavarga* [consonants].
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship Anaṅgaveginī in the southwest with the *ya*-group, and Anaṅgāṅkuśā in the northwest with the *śa*-group. || 39 ||
O Supreme Goddess, having invoked Anaṅgamālinī at the Lord (Īśa) by means of the two lakṣas,
one should worship the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakranāyikā) in the prescribed place.
Then, having placed the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) at the forefront, one should display the mudrā;
with the middle and ring fingers, the little fingers and the [other] ring fingers should be level. 41.
O Supreme Goddess, when the two middle fingers are shaped like hooks,
this is the Ākarṣiṇī mudrā, which effects the attraction of the three worlds.
(4) One should contemplate Bhāskara within the wheel that bestows all good fortune, resembling a ruby and adorned with a crown and armlets. 43.
The all-pervading Lord is seated in the lotus posture, embraced by His own Śakti;
with His arms, the God holds a red lotus, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness. (Note: *padmava* is an alternative reading. 44.
One should worship the Sun with the mantra previously mentioned;
having worshipped the [lineage] traditions, one should then worship the Mistress of the Wheel (cakranāyikā).

The seed-syllable of Varuṇa (the reading in the Vārakha manuscript is *vāruṇam*; he extracts the seed of the Vaśyamudrā as "Varuṇa," namely *vrūṃ*) is situated within the seed of Indra (*i*), adorned by the right or left ear [the letter *u*], and joined with the digits of Nāda and Bindu; this is the great seed-syllable that brings about subjugation. (46)
Having formed the hands into the shape of a casket, the two index fingers take the form of hooks;
by means of this very sequence of rotation, the two middle fingers are positioned below them.
Gradually, O Goddess, by that same method, the little finger and the ring finger should also be joined and pressed firmly against the region of the thumbs. 48.
O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā is considered to bring everything under control;
it is located on the outer ten-spoked wheel of the Sarvārthasādhaka [maṇḍala]. (49)
Seated upon that most enchanting pedestal of great jewel-lotuses made of mani-gems, he possesses the brilliance of a hundred suns.

O Pārvatī, [one should meditate on] Viṣṇu, who has the color of molten gold, who possesses the splendor of Garuḍa through meditation, and who is seated upon the high shoulder [of the mountain], resembling coral.
Embracing the goddess Padmā seated upon his own left lap, he has reddish-brown eyes,
is clothed in yellow garments, and possesses a smiling countenance and beautiful ornaments.

O Maheśānī, having meditated upon the Lord of the Universe as always holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus in his arms, one should worship him. (The reading "rīm" is found in manuscript Ka. || 53 ||
I shall proclaim the mantra of this [deity], which bestows the four aims of human life:
having extracted the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), one should follow it with Hṛṣīkeśa. (54)
And one should worship that [deity] with this [mantra] joined with the prostration (namaḥ).
Having worshipped the Kulakaulas, one should then worship the Mistress of the Wheel (cakranāyikā). || 55 ||
One should display the mudrā that causes universal intoxication, preceded by its seed-syllable.
Bhṛgu is the seed of this [mudrā]; this is declared to be its seed. (The phrase "sasarga" means accompanied by the visarga; thus is the extraction of the seed-syllable of Sarvotmādinī. 56.

Having placed the two hands face-to-face, one should worship [the deity] in the middle of the two middle fingers, with the little fingers [placed] between them; the two ring fingers should be straight, and the two index fingers outside of them. (Note: There is a variant reading "me madhyame" for "madhyamāmadhyage.")
Then, the two thumbs, shaped like staffs, should be placed at the tips of the nails of the middle fingers;
this mudrā is named Unmādinī, which causes all women to become moist with passion.
(6) Likewise, within the wheel that produces all protection, inside the ten-angled figure,
one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds, resembling the bandhūka flower in color.
Resembling a *javā* flower, with the luster of a pomegranate blossom, and like the rising sun, [he sits] upon a lotus at a jeweled lion-throne. (60)
Seated in the lotus posture, with four long arms,
he holds a noose and a goad, as well as a flower-arrow and a sugarcane bow.
Her pair of long, tremulous eyes were reddish and rolling with intoxication;
she was enriched with every elegant ornament and adorned with a crown and armlets.
Wearing red garlands and garments, and anointed with red perfumes,
he embraces with his right hand the Śakti seated upon his left thigh.
Holding a lotus with her left hand, she possesses a pure smile;
she is enriched with ornaments such as beautiful armlets and resplendent in a clean silken garment.
The supreme sovereign lady, whose heart was scorched by passion, whose womb was moistening, who was endowed with youth and possessed of a sweetness refined by artistic grace. (65)
[He beheld] the Supreme Lord, who was embraced very firmly by [Śiva] whose arm still held the bow, and who was gladdened by the supreme bliss produced thereby.
It was surrounded by the limbs of Nāgas, Gandharvas, and Devas,
whose bodies were playful with passion and adorned with ornaments.
He who meditates upon Viṣṇu, the God of gods and teacher of the world, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds, as non-different from his own self, shall become the Enchanter of the Three Worlds. (68)
I shall declare its seed-syllable (*bīja*), which consists of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa:

Brahmā (*ka*), Purandara (*la*), Māyā (*ī*), and the vowel *svar* (*e*), followed by the primordial sound (*nāda*); thus, it is *klīṃ*. After Brahmā and Purandara, there follows Māyā and the vowel *svar*. (69)

The seed-syllable (bīja), joined with the digits of sound and the point (nāda-bindu-kalā), is worshipped by the three worlds; it is the essence churned from the Vedas, the cause of the [attainment of] deities,
the bringer of welfare to the three realms, and the granter of wealth and other desired objects.
It destroys the fear of death, eliminates all doubt, dries up the ocean of existence, and illuminates the blindness of the mind. (This verse appears to be an interpolation.
Having worshipped him with this [verse], one should worship the *nigarbha-yoginīs*. (70)
Having worshipped the heroine there, one should likewise display the mudrā;
for this [mudrā], one should place the pair of ring fingers below in the shape of a hook.
One should also apply the two index fingers in that same sequence;
this is the Mahāṅkuśā mudrā, which accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings.
