(The letter *ka* mounted upon the letter *ra*, with the thirteenth vowel; thus it is *kro*. Kāmadeva mounted upon fire, endowed with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*, and joined with the thirteenth vowel—this is declared to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the Mudrā. 73.
(7) O Maheśānī, one should worship the secret Yoginīs in the eight corners;
all of them, headed by Vaśinī, are to be worshipped as before, conjoined with their seed-syllables.

"I worship the sandals"—by this very assignment (nyāsa), one especially worships the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī), who is of the nature of knowledge; and to her left, one should worship the Śakti who bestows the perfection of enjoyment (bhukti).
Then, one should display that khecarī-mudrā;
the left [hand] is on the right side, while the right [hand] is on the left side.
O Maheśānī, having formed the *bāhu* [mudrā] and having rotated both hands, O Goddess, one should join the little fingers and the ring fingers in that sequence. (77)
O Maheśānī, one should place both index fingers over both middle fingers from above, and here one should make both thumbs straight.
This is that Khecarī Mudrā, O beloved, which is supreme among all;
this Great Mudrā, when performed, is the snatcher of all vital splendor. (79)

Śiva (ha), Candra (sa), Kānta (kha), Pānta (pha) joined with Vahni (ra), and the eleventh vowel (e)—that is to say, endowed with Nāda and Kalā and so forth—therefore [the mantra] is *hasakhaphre*; this is the *Khecarī-vidyā*. Śiva, Candra, and likewise Kānta, followed by Pānta joined with Vahni, and endowed with the eleventh vowel—this is proclaimed as its seed-syllable (*bīja*). (The reading is *ta ka*. || 80 ||

(8) And in the central triangle-wheel, O Śivā, one should worship those very [deities] in the front, right, and left [corners], according to the procedure stated for the ritual placement (vinyāsa). 81.
"I worship the sandals"—this specific distinction is revealed here;
one should likewise worship Tripurāmbā as the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśī) and Icchāsiddhi to the left.
O Dear One, having turned the hands over so that they are clearly in the shape of a half-moon,
one should then simultaneously join the pair of index fingers with the pair of thumbs.
One should place the two middle fingers pressed down below by the little fingers;
likewise, the two ring fingers should be joined at the very bottom in a curved manner.
This is declared to be the Seed-Mudrā, the supreme Mother of the Three Worlds;
it is enriched with the seed-syllable of Sadāśiva (*hsauṃ*—this being the seed-syllable of Sadāśiva)—having displayed it according to the prescribed rite. (85)
(9) Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite the Goddess Bhairavī, the Mistress of the Wheel, who embodies Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa within the wheel consisting of all bliss; 86.
To the left, one should worship the accomplishment of liberation in the form of knowledge, will, and action,
and in front of the Goddess, the lion who is the support of the universe.
One should constantly worship with devotion him who beholds the face of Ambikā;
having first extracted the seed-syllable of speech (Vāgbīja), one should display the Yoni-mudrā. 88.
O Goddess, by means of the rotation of the pair of ring fingers, one should hold them with the two index fingers in the form of hooks. (89)
Place the two middle fingers together in the center, and likewise the two little fingers;
then place the two thumbs in the form of a staff, positioned above the little fingers.
This is declared to be the supreme Yonimudrā, the mother of the three worlds;
having uttered the word "atra" (here), one then [becomes] composed of all-bliss.
At the end of the word *cakrarāja*, one should draw the form of Brahman;
thereafter, one should utter the word *saṃvid* (or *saṃvinmaya*) within the bindu-cakra.
From the word "parāpara," she is the secret Yoginī;
thereafter she is the nature of Brahman, and finally, she is Mahātripurasundarī.
Likewise, she is accompanied by her ocean [of retinue], her weapons, and her vehicles;
similarly, she is together with her attendants and all the articles of worship. || 94 ||
"Having been worshipped, O Goddess, you have been gratified"—as before [with the word *tamī* in the Kha manuscript].
Then, having honored her with handfuls of flowers, one should gratify her according to the prescribed rite. 95.

[Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sequence for the Worship of the Goddesses, both Manifest and Unmanifest," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 17 ||
[Eighteenth Chapter] The Lord said:
Meditating upon the Goddess whose face is gracious with favor, one should recite the mantra.
Among all sacrifices, everywhere the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña) is praised as supreme. || 1 ||
The gods are pleased by recitation, and practitioners achieve success through recitation;
therefore, with every effort, one should be devoted to the practice of recitation. || 2 ||
Japa is the repetition of syllables, neither too fast nor too slow.
Worship, meditation, recitation, and fire-offering—this is the fourfold path of dharma. (3)
If the practitioner desires success, he should perform this himself every day;
at the end of the recitation, he should meditate on Śiva, and at the end of the meditation, he should recite again.
The knower of mantras, joined with recitation and meditation, attains success quickly;
Śivā is the power whose form is recitation, and Sadāśiva is whose form is meditation. || 5 ||
From the union of these two, O Pārvatī, accomplishment arises; it is certainly not otherwise.
Having joined that which is joined, one should not join that which is not joined. (6)
As is the accomplishment, so is the rosary, which is a limb of the rite of recitation;
for one who recites constantly with a rosary, there is indeed accomplishment—of this there is no doubt. (7)
The garland consisting of letters is proclaimed to bring about swift accomplishment; it is formed by the letters of the Mātṛkā, both in direct and reverse order, together with the bindu.
A garland made of *sūsameru* beads should always be fashioned, as it bestows all prosperity;
one should complete it again with groups of eight or eighteen beads.
Having rendered the weapon-mantra invisible by means of color, the practitioner should recite it;
in the absence of a rosary, the wise one should then recite it upon his own fingers.
One should always perform the recitation (japa) with the hand, but never that which is for the sake of specific desires;
beginning from the middle of the ring finger, one should proceed in order by way of circumambulation (pradakṣiṇya).
One should recite [the mantra] over the nine joints up to the base of the index finger;
likewise, the wise man who recites it at the tip and the middle of the index finger [attains success]. (12)
Four things perish for him: life, knowledge, fame, and strength.
One should not cross over the middle joint of the ring finger, treating it as Mount Meru. (Note: *merum* is the reading in the Kha manuscript. 13.
Circumambulating Mount Meru while reciting the mantra with the joints of the ring finger, one should not touch the lines with the joints of the fingers.
One should not employ the fingers in any way contracted upon the palm;
for when the fingers are separated, the recitation flows away through the gaps. || 15 ||
In this case, a rosary made even of crystal and other materials bestows success in recitation;
having placed the rosary either in front [of oneself] or held in the right hand. (16)
At the beginning of the recitation (japa) and other rites, one should worship the rosary after diligently sprinkling it with water;
this sprinkling of the rosary with the chosen mantra is thus proclaimed.
Aiṃ Māṃ! O Garland, Great Garland, whose very nature is all powers!
The fourfold aims of life are entrusted to you; therefore, be the bestower of success upon me. 18.
Having worshipped [the rosary] with moonstone, sandalwood, musk, gorocana, agallochum, and saffron, one should then take up the rosary with the right hand.
Having first uttered the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati, and immediately thereafter, one should take up the rosary with this [mantra]: "O Mālā, perform thou the removal of obstacles. (20)
One should act in such a way that the rosary does not fall from the hand while reciting;
if it falls from the hand, there will be an obstacle, and if it is broken, death will occur. || 21 ||
One should guard this with effort; one should not cause it to wander nor shake it.
One must never reveal the Guru, the Yantra, or the Mantra.
One should not show the rosary or the mudrā even to one's guru.
[For otherwise] bhūtas, rākṣasas, vetālas, siddhas, gandharvas, and cāraṇas [would seize them]. (23)
Since they carry [the mantra] openly, one should always recite it in secret;
the rosary should be held near one's own heart and the right hand. (24)
In the middle portion of the middle finger, having excluded the index finger, [the thumb] is joined from its bent side with the ring and little fingers. || 25 ||

Having placed the garland there, one should take each individual seed-syllable situated therein with the tip of the thumb; one should perform this with the left hand and not touch it [with the right].
One should recite the mantra slowly at each repetition without moving the lips;
one should not touch the rosary with the index finger—this is the method of counting according to the liberated ones.
One should perform the ritual rotation while staying between the joints of the thumb;
an action performed without the thumb becomes fruitless. (28)
O Goddess, the thumb bestows liberation; the forefinger destroys enemies;
the middle finger serves for the attainment of wealth; and the ring finger is used for rites of pacification. (29)
It should be known that for attracting the youngest [of sisters] and in the rite of recitation, it bestows success;
however, the seed-pearls of the rosary must be recited over while ensuring they do not touch one another.
If one who is reciting the *pūrvabīja* should touch the *parabīja* with the thumb, his recitation of that [mantra] shall be fruitless. (31)
The garland, accompanied by the sound "kiṭi," may even be broken or torn;
O Supreme Goddess, having placed the right foot upon the left thigh... (32)
The mantra-practitioner, having assumed the vīrāsana posture and not looking toward the directions, should contemplate with his intellect the unity of the Guru, the deity, and the mantra. || 33 ||
Alternatively, one should meditate on the Guru at the crown of the head according to the distinctions of color and so forth;
having visualized the mantra at the throat, one should contemplate the deity within the heart.

O beloved, a wise person, intent on the nature of the deity, should begin the recitation either aloud, in a whisper, or even mentally. (Note: "vāpi" is an alternative reading found in manuscript *ka*. 35.

O Supreme Goddess, that which is uttered with clear speech without hesitation is called *vyakta* (articulate); that which is indistinct, with the mouth quivering, is proclaimed as *upāṃśu* (whispered).
When one recites the sequence of syllables, consisting of phonemes, vowels, and words, while recollecting them with the intellect, that is declared to be mental recitation (mānasa-japa). || 37 ||
One should contemplate the mere sound that has arisen on the path of the Suṣumṇā,
while also contemplating the syllables of the mantra as being woven into the power of consciousness (cicchakti).
Sustained by the supreme nectar in that very highest heaven,
he reveals the true nature of the Self even without worship, fire-offerings, and the like.
Having withdrawn the mind from sense objects, with the intellect focused on the goal, one should recite [the mantra] neither too fast nor too slow, like a string of pearls. (40)
O fair-faced one, daughter of the mountain, that which is recited a hundred thousand times in a loud voice (nigada) becomes equal to a single whispered recitation (upāṃśu). 41.
O lotus-eyed one, O lady of excellent complexion, that which is muttered in a whisper for the duration of a single breath is equal to that which is recited mentally. (42)
In the Tripurātantra, mental recitation (mānasa-japa) is especially praised;
one should either contemplate the hymn with the mind or recite the mantra with the voice.
Both of these are fruitless for him, like water in a broken vessel.
The highest [fee] is ten thousand, and a thousand is remembered as the middle.
O Śivā, one should know that the minimum is one hundred and eight;
O Maheśānī, less than this is not recommended for the rite of japa.
One should perform the recitation according to one's capacity with diligent attention to the prescribed number;
for that which is recited without a count shall all be fruitless.
The Rākṣasas seize [the merit] of one who wears many garments; therefore, a wise person should never count [the recitations] while dressed in this way.
One should not recite the mantra wearing only a single garment, nor while distracted by many clothes.
Or with his hands uncovered, or even with his head covered;
or with a mind distracted by anxiety, or even angry, or filled with haste. (48)
One who is dull-witted, displeased in mind, not dejected, nor afflicted by hunger, and likewise being single-minded—without prattling, one should recite the mantra. (49)
Whether sitting, lying down, walking, or even eating,
having performed the recitation according to the rules with the mantra and the water for the guest-offering (arghya), || 50 ||
One should offer that recitation into the left hand of the Great Goddess;
one should then contemplate the fruit of the recitation, in the form of radiant energy, as accepted by Śivā.
Having brought [the deity] down from one's own head with both hands using the Śrī-bīja,
one should then establish [the deity] with both hands using the Sārasvata-bīja.
O Dear One, this is the procedure for the rosary in the rite of recitation;
O Dear One, the practitioner who prepares the rosary and performs the recitation in this manner [attains success]. (53)
O Goddess, he attains his desired goal; for one who is deficient, there is a reversal of lifespan.
Just as water without a dam flows downward in an instant, so does it pass away.
In the same way, a mantra that lacks its bridge (niḥsetu) slips away from practitioners in an instant.
Therefore, among all mantras, all castes, beginning with the twice-born, [are eligible]. 55.
On both sides, the practitioners should establish the bridge during the rite of recitation.
Prajāpati [established] the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*. (This is the reading from manuscript *ka*. 56.
In ancient times, having extracted the *praṇava* from the three Vedas, he fashioned it;
at the beginning and end of the act of recitation, the *praṇava* serves as a bridge.
O Great Goddess, one should employ [the mantra] for the sake of accomplishing all tasks;
at the end of the recitation, one should offer oblations into the fire in a quantity equal to one-tenth of the recitation.
Then, in front of the Goddess, the practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the Supreme Goddess in the consecrated fire, while mentally recollecting the Goddess there. (59)
O beautiful one, having addressed her with this, one should offer oblations with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," using milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in sweet substances.
Then, having offered oblations both individually and collectively, and likewise for other deities when possible, these six oblations performed with the six limbs are declared to be the daily homa.
On one side are all ritual actions, and on the other side is the fire sacrifice (*homa*);
the rite of *homa* is superior to all, for what is there that cannot be accomplished through *homa*? (62)
If a mantra consecrated by this initiation is devoid of fire-offerings (homa), one encounters threefold suffering; therefore, one should be constantly devoted to performing homa.
For those who do not perform the Agnihotra, the Great Goddess, having become the fire itself, swiftly devours their wealth, as well as their houses, fields, and cattle. 64.
The Sovereign Goddess quickly devours those things acquired and accumulated with great hardship—which are dearer than her own life—in no time at all. 65.
One should always perform the Agnihotra, because the Goddess consists of fire;
by means of the ritual of the Agnihotra, one shall become a vessel for all prosperities.
For one devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice in this world, the external fire becomes cool; however, the supreme digestive fire increases with respect to houses, fields, wealth, and other possessions.
Fire alone is the mouth of the Goddess; therefore, one should always offer oblations into the fire, whether fortnightly, monthly, or annually, according to the prescribed rule. (68)
In the event of being unable to perform the fire sacrifice (homa), one should recite the vidyā twice the number of times required for the sacrifice;
while praising her with various hymns, one should prostrate and circumambulate her to the right.

Having thus gratified the Goddess with various offerings, the best of practitioners, with a mind inclined toward devotion, should present the articles to be offered. (The variant reading *bhaktipraṇava* is noted as an alternative. 70.
An ointment, vermilion, and the most excellent collyrium for the eyes;
the fragrance of incense, lamps, as well as a mirror and a fan. (71)
The parasol and the fly-whisk, the unsurpassed sound of bells, instrumental music, song, and likewise dance, for the sake of play, curiosity, and auspiciousness. (72)

And for the sake of accomplishing the purpose, there should be the sprinkling [of water] with rows of lamps, and the gradual offering of *dūrvā* grass along with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) upon the head. (Note: *nirmāñchanam* is one reading; *nirmārjanam* is another. 73.
With a mind inclined toward devotion, and through self-surrender as service,
the wise one should thus offer the articles of worship to the Goddess.
He is the blessed one of all the worlds, and none other on earth is worthy of worship—neither among the gods, the sages, the Daityas, nor the Rākṣasas. (75)
He is worthy of honor by all the Gandharvas without exception, by the high-souled Nāgas and others, and by all of us as well, including the gods and the Asuras.
Having attained the status of a sovereign ruler, he thereafter attains absolute liberation (kaivalya);
having anointed the Great Goddess, he shall cause this world to abide [in peace].
By applying a tilaka with vermilion to the Goddess, all women become submissive;
and by applying the unsurpassed divine ointment, one shall attain divine knowledge. (78)
By the offering of garlands and other such things, Mahālakṣmī becomes firmly established in the home;
likewise, O beautiful one, by the offering of betel-leaf and even water.
May she always be filled with bliss and forever free from suffering;
may the Goddess be thoroughly perfumed by incenses and illuminated by lamps. (80)
It bestows wealth, sons, land, prosperity, and freedom from disease;
it grants grain (or the fortunate, according to the Kha manuscript), all desires, and likewise auspicious wisdom in righteousness.
Only by showing a mirror does one attain similarity with the All-pervading Lord;
or likewise, by fanning Maheśvarī with fans or chowries. || 82 ||
Mahālakṣmī, holding two chowries, shall conquer him;
and for half a moment, she shall hold the parasol over the Great Goddess.

Above him, the Lord of the Thirty-three (the All-Conqueror, the Master of the Gods), having arrived together with the World-Protectors, shall hold a great parasol resembling the full moon. (Note: "Sarvajit" is an alternative reading for "tridaśāpati. || 84 ||
He who pleases Maheśvarī with the sounding of bells and conchs,
and with the music of kettledrums and tabors, shall be followed by Indra.
Or even if he is not [an initiate], he should not himself ring the bell or the conch;
how can that shameless person say, "I worship Maheśvarī"? (86)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and all others play the conch and other instruments;
therefore, one should play such instruments as the conch and the bell in the presence of the deity. (Note: *śaṅkhaghaṇṭādi* is the reading in that manuscript. 87.
He who causes instrumental music, song, and likewise dance to be performed for the Goddess—just as Tumburu, Nārada, Hāhā, and Hūhū do; (88)
The noble Vidyādharas, Apsarases, and others, as well as young women matured by intoxication, constantly please him after having caused him to enter according to the prescribed rite. (89)
If all the courtesans, fully adorned, were to sport sufficiently for her sake before him,
hear now the fruit of that merit:
Urvaśī and the other courtesans would sport with him joyfully and abundantly.
One should cause a festive spectacle to be performed for the Goddess, whatever may bring about laughter and joy.
Rejoicing thereby, he is eternally honored in the world of the goddesses, after having caused auspicious rites to be performed for the Great Goddess according to the prescribed rule. (92)

Having ascended the most excellent celestial chariot, preceded by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, [he enjoys] divine happiness fulfilling all desires, endowed with every kind of jewel. (This is the reading in manuscript *Tā*. || 93 ||
As he was proceeding to the world of the goddesses, followed by Indra and the other gods together with their wives and mounts, the celestial women approached him. (94)
Then Arundhatī, Sāvitrī, Ahalyā, Śacī, Anasūyā, Aditi, and the Mothers, along with their followers, [approached]. (Note: *Māra* is an alternative reading for *Mātaraḥ*. 95.
Having created divine pearl ornaments and offered jewel-lamps,
they, filled with joy, gratify the head [of the deity] with imperishable auspiciousness.
O Beloved, for as long as a mustard seed placed upon a cow's horn remains there, for that long a man, having cultivated devotion toward Mahādevī in his heart, [attains the fruit]. 97.
Even if one is evil-minded or a doer of evil, he is purified from all sins and is glorified in the heavenly world together with the families of his father and mother. (98)
Then, having returned here after a long time, the devoted lord,
having attained the status of a sovereign ruler (sārvabhauma), shall thereafter attain absolute liberation (kaivalya).
Moreover, because of the abundance of devotion toward the state of the Mother of the World, [this truth] is to be inferred by this very fact; what is the use of much speech? (100)
Furthermore, O Great Goddess, devotion (*bhakti*) here consists of single-mindedness;
it is worship with one's entire being, following the path of the served and the server. (101)
He who declares, "I am the servant of the Great Goddess, the Mother of the World"—even for him, the gods, headed by Indra, become his servants. (102)
He who, having slain his father, mother, Brahmins, cows, and numerous dependents, offers himself at the lotus feet of that [Lord], [attains the supreme state]. 103.
The pure one attains a body composed of qualities and reaches the supreme Brahman;
I, however, [shall enter] this entire universe, the cosmic egg, together with Brahmā.
Having pierced and cut through the worlds in that manner, and having gratified the Supreme Goddess and offered myself to her,
I shall go to the eternal Brahman.
Therefore, whatever action is performed, and whenever the thought "this is mine" arises,
one should offer oneself at the lotus feet of that [Lord] with the Great Mantra.
Having again offered the libations (tarpaṇas), one should display the nine mudrās;
because they bestow joy (mudaṃ rānti), they are therefore proclaimed as "mudrās. || 107 ||
Accompanied by her mudrās, that goddess herself, eager to depart, swiftly bestows upon the practitioner desire, liberation, as well as dharma and wealth. (108)
The nine mudrās are traditionally taught in sequence as: Saṃkṣobhaṇī, Drāvaṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, Vaśyā, Unmādinī, Mahāṅkuśā, Khecarī, Bījā, and Yonī. (Note: *Drāviṇyā* is the reading in manuscript *kha*.)
When these mudrās have been displayed, the completion of the worship occurs;
the binding of each mudrā is proclaimed to be performed with its own respective seed-syllable (bīja). || 110 ||
The visualization is performed with the root mantra, and the offering with the Krodhabhava mantra.
If a wise man should wear a mudrā without knowing its ritual application, [he incurs a fault]. (111)
All that [offering] of his becomes fruitless, like a body devoid of life;
yet, when these [mudrās] are displayed during worship and other rites, the presence of the Goddess shall be attained. (112)
In this very [practice], there is abundance of devotion, as well as worship with faith;
solitude, purification of the self, and likewise freedom from defects. (113)
In this world, there is an abundance of ritual implements for worship and their purity;
likewise, they produce wonder through fragrance and its exceeding sweetness. (114)

The physical form [is] through manly prowess alone; the charm of one's own self, the preeminence of the Soma-king, the fine attire of the sacrificer, and indeed the plaintive tone of his speech. (115)

In the rituals of worship, there should likewise be skill (*dākṣya*) and one-pointedness of mind; as well as praise, prostration, recitation (*japa*), the offering (*bali*), and the drink (*peya*). (116)
The cause for bringing about the presence of the Goddess has been fully explained here:
wine is to be drunk, vermilion is to be used, and saffron is to be applied as a body unguent. (117)

Thus, whatever specific detail has been proclaimed regarding the worship of Tripurā in this context—this [work], which falls within the scope of the Tripurā-tantra, is accompanied by these specific details. (118)
[Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the description of the rules for recitation and other rites, in the Śrīgandharvatantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 18 ||
[The Nineteenth Chapter] Īśvara said:
Now I shall speak, O Maheśānī; listen to the ritual procedure for Vaṭuka and the others.
By the mere performance of which the practitioner shall attain accomplishment. || 1 ||
O lady of virtuous vows, for him by whom these have been gratified with offerings and worshipped, all perfections (siddhis) are held in the palm of his hand; of this there is no doubt.
Otherwise, being provoked to anger by those obstacles, he will be overcome by them;
therefore, one should diligently offer an oblation to them for that reason.
Rice prepared with meat, sugar-candy, curd, and cakes, various kinds of meats, excellent milk, and fish as well—[these were offered]. (4)
O Goddess, O Pārvatī, surrounding the Śrīcakra are four mandalas located in the corners of Īśāna, Vahni, Nairṛtya, and Vāyu.
Then Viṣṇu was meditated upon by the Goddess as her son, this boy assuming the form of a *vaṭu*;
he was *Vaṭuka*, lotus-eyed, golden-hued, and four-armed.
Holding a mace, a conch, a lotus, and a discus in his hands, he stands before the Goddess, seated upon the throne of the lord of elephants (or birds). || 7 ||

(The letter of Varuṇa joined with Śakra, endowed with the fourteenth vowel, and accompanied by the moon and the bindu; thus: *klauṃ vaṭukāya namaḥ*. The letter of Varuṇa joined with Śakra, endowed with the fourteenth vowel, and accompanied by the moon and the bindu, followed by "salutation to Vaṭuka" at the end. || 8 ||
Then, O Goddess, one should worship with this mantra using perfumes and other offerings;
before that, O Supreme Sovereign, there should be a vessel provided with food and water.
Having performed the ritual there according to the rules, one should cause the *bali* offering to be given with the mantra:

*(Ehyehi devīputra vaṭukanātha kapilajaṭābhārabhāsvara trinetrājvālāmukha sarvavighnān nāśaya nāśaya sarvopacārasahitaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā)*—this is the *balimantra*. "Ehyehi" [is used], ending with "devīputra," then "vaṭuka," and then "nātha. (Note: "devī" is the reading in manuscript K. 10.
O you who are at the end of Kapila, radiant at the end of the mass of matted hair, three-eyed one!
O you whose mouth is a flame! Destroy, destroy all obstacles at the very end! 11.
The mantra of Vaṭuka is declared to be that which accepts the bali offering accompanied by all ritual services, consists of two words, and is joined with the wife of Agni (svāhā).
One should offer the bali-oblation to him with the left thumb and ring finger;
O lady of excellent vows, by performing the worship of this very one, even a person of meager fortune [attains success]. (13)
Completely liberated from all afflictions, he shall become a vessel for prosperity;
and the worship of this deity, along with its constituent parts, has been described previously.
O Śivā, the mere offering of the bali has been described here incidentally;
thereafter, one should satisfy the ḍākinīs and others with the bali. 15.
In the same way, one should visualize the Yoginīs in the mandala to the left of the Goddess;
or else, one should contemplate these Yoginīs as the bestowers of all spiritual accomplishments.
The Yoginīs, capable of assuming any form at will, shine like molten gold;
they are intoxicated, adorned with garlands of skeletons, and bent forward by the weight of their hips.
Rich with the scent of flowing blood, wearing red garments as upper cloths,
they bear in their hands a linga, a noose, a skull, and a goad.
Bestowing upon their own devotees what they desire, and filled with joy, one should worship them with perfumes and other offerings and cause the bali-oblation to be given with the mantra. || 19 ||
Having uttered the syllable *yām*, then [the word] *yoginībhyaḥ* (with the reading *bhyasaṃtaṃ* at the end of *svāhā* according to manuscript *ka*),
one should write the word *yoginī* at the end of all the syllables.
Having drawn the armor (*kavaca*) and the weapon (*astra*), one should again write the *vahnijāyā* (the consort of fire, *svāhā*).
Or else, with this mantra, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the Yoginīs.
One should join the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger in the shape of a vulva (this reading is found in manuscript Kha).
Then, O Goddess, with palms joined in reverence, one should make this prayer: || 22 ||
Whether above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) or in heaven, in the sky or on the surface of the earth, in the formless realm, in the netherworld (pātāla), in fire, or in water and wind— wherever situated;
or having taken their place in sacred fields (kṣetra), seats (pīṭha), and secondary seats (upapīṭha), [may they be worshipped] with incense, lamps, and other offerings.

May the goddesses, who are always pleased with us through the rite of auspicious offerings and are worthy of worship by the lords of heroes, protect us. (The reading *devendravatyah* appears as an alternative. || 23 ||
One should visualize Kṣetrapāla to the left of the Great Goddess;
he is a great-souled being encircled by Aparājita creepers.
It was constantly adorned with reddish flowers, provided with the cool shade of *tintiḍī* and wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), and embellished with jewels. || 25 ||
Resembling a mass of blue lotuses, he holds in his lotus-like hands a sword, a skull-cup, a trident, and a hand-drum (ḍamaru). || 26 ||
One should meditate intensely and with equanimity upon the Supreme One, whose lower lip is bitten by His fangs;
having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should offer the oblation (*bali*) with the mantra: "To all the Yoginīs, to the Yoginīs of all castes, *ha phaṭ svāhā*.
O Dear One, one should write the letter *kṣa* conjoined with the six long vowels.
Then, O protector, one should write the word for the field (kṣetrapada), or [the words for] incense, lamps, and so forth.
Having drawn the offering (bali) together with its accompaniments, one should then say: "Take, take!

This mantra, joined with the wife of Fire (svāhā), is as follows: (KṢĀṂ KṢĪṂ KṢŪṂ KṢAIṂ KṢAUṂ KṢAḤ KṢETRAPĀLA DHŪPADĪPĀDISAHITAṂ BALIṂ GṚHṆA 2 SVĀHĀ—this is the summary). O Pārvatī, this is for Kṣetrapāla. || 29 ||
Having first formed the left fist, make the index finger straight;
with this mudrā, O Goddess, one should present the bali offering to him.
In the fourth maṇḍala, to the right of the Goddess, [is he] dark as a fresh rain-cloud and adorned with all ornaments. (31)
The Lord has a protruding belly, the face of an elephant, four arms, and is naked;
with his left, right, and upper hands, he holds a noose and a goad.
With her very lower right hand she holds a skull-cup filled with honey;
her form resembles vermilion, and she is overwhelmed by unrestrained intoxication. (33)
With his other hand, he touched her red lotus-like face;
with his left hand, he embraced her temple of love.
Having meditated upon that Supreme Lord as touching [the disciple], one should worship Him;
then, having written the three syllables *gāṃ*, *gīṃ*, and *gūṃ*, followed by Gaṇapati ending in *ṅe*.
At the end of *vara*, at the end of *varada*, and at the end of *sarva*, one should write "jana";
then, having uttered "me vaśam ānaya," one writes the two-word phrase "balim gṛhṇa. (36)
The mantra of Gaṇeśa, joined with the wife of Vahni (the fire-syllable *svāhā*), has been declared: *gā gī gū gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya baliṃ gṛhṇa 2 svāhā*.
O Goddess, place your fingers in the middle of the fist like a staff. (37)
The Elephant-Trunk Mahāmudrā is always dear to Gaṇeśa;
at the end of this, O Maheśānī, one should offer the bali-oblation to all beings.
Gods, humans, ancestors, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas—these are designated as the beings; one should satisfy them with offerings. || 39 ||
When these are gratified with offerings, they provide assistance in the sacrifice;
when they are not gratified, they indeed take on the form of obstacles.
O Pārvatī, one should offer oneself and all actions with the great mantra;
thereafter, one should especially dedicate them to her whose nature is Brahman.

Three times prior to this, and thereafter, following the authority over the body and its functions during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, [the breath and intellect] proceed from here. (42)
Then by mind, then by speech, and thereafter by action;
then by the two hands, then by the two feet, and thereafter by the belly. || 43 ||
Whatever has been remembered, whatever has been spoken, and whatever has been done after [the ritual],
O Goddess— both that which belongs to me and that which is mine, all of that thereafter, and even beyond that.

In the same way, the mantra ending with the word "tvayi" (in you), followed by "brahmaṇyarpitamastu" (let it be offered into Brahman) and ending with "svāhā," is declared to be the mantra [for self-surrender]. (Prior to this: "Whatever has been remembered, spoken, or done by me through mind, speech, action, the two hands, the feet, the belly, and the generative organ—whether in the states of waking, dreaming, or deep sleep, regarding the vital breaths, intellect, body, and duties—all that which is mine, let it be entirely offered into you, O Brahman, svāhā! This is the mantra for the surrender of one's own self. In this mantra, the word "mām" (me) should be understood as an indeclinable used as a substitute for a case-ending. This is for the purpose of surrendering one's own self. (45)
At the conclusion of this, one who is disciplined should utter these great mantras:
"I do not know how to invoke; I do not know how to dismiss. (46)
"I do not know the portion for worship; You are my refuge, O Supreme Goddess!
Truth, truth, and again truth—this is declared with arms uplifted. (47)
In body, mind, or speech, there is no other refuge for me but you;
as the inner mover of all beings, you alone abide within.
Whatever leaf, flower, fruit, or water is offered with mere devotion, and whatever food offering is presented—please accept that out of compassion. (49)
Whatever has been worshipped deficient in ritual, deficient in action, or deficient in devotion;
whatever may be deficient in syllables (or, according to the *ka* reading, "whatever has fallen away from the syllables") or deficient in prosodic measures (*mātrā*).
"O Goddess, you ought to forgive my offenses, such as the intervention of the bodiless god of love and hundreds of other transgressions, for you alone are my refuge. (51)
May my heart be in you, may my consciousness be in you, and may my mind be in you;
O Mahāmāyā, let these faculties, when applied, flourish in your worship.
Furthermore, may those who create obstacles perish by your command;
when these mantras are recited, the Goddess herself becomes propitious. (53)
"O Goddess, you shall grant the fourfold aims of life; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus entreated the Mistress of the Gods and having praised and lauded her with great devotion, [one should proceed]. (Verse 54)
One should offer the retinue into the form of the principal deity;
for within the very body of that Great Goddess, Maheśānī, reside all the deities. (55)
One should contemplate that [the deities] have dissolved into the limbs of the body by means of the root mantra and are merged therein;
then, one should meditate upon oneself in the form of Kāmakalā. || 56 ||
Then, one should dismiss that Supreme Sovereign Lady into the lotus of the heart, [saying]:
"O Śivā, whatever has been performed by me, whether knowingly or unknowingly... (57)
"O Mother, forgive me for all this which was my duty;
having dismissed the Supreme Sovereign, one should unite her with the Sky-farer within the self. (58)
Meditating with this very mantra, one should establish her in the heart:
"Stay, O Goddess, in the supreme place; stay in your own place, O Supreme Sovereign. (59)
Having thus dismissed the Great Goddess, he should then take her in with the breath of inhalation (pūraka) by means of the saṃhāra-mudrā, inhaling according to the instructions of the Guru.
One should cause that consciousness to enter the very root by means of its own root-mantra;
having gratified it with breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas), one should worship the Goddess who bears the remains of the offering (nirmālyadhāriṇī).
Having first led that power of consciousness (citkalā) [within], one should cast the floral remains (nirmālya) upon the ground;
for she alone is the one who consists of the universe, and she alone is the supreme residue (śeṣikā).
Thereafter, indeed, through the knowledge of reality, I am the Lord;
[I perceive her] situated within the interior of the śṛṅgāṭa located in the midst of the great lotus forest.
Having beheld the supreme Goddess, one should contemplate the Self;
having become Śiva at the end of the Unmanī state, one should remain filled with bliss.
Having attained oneness with Śiva until the dissolution of the mind at the end, one whose samādhi has been perfected should offer [the fruit] to the Guru who dwells upon his head. || 65 ||
One should prostrate with the forehead touching the ground and offer the *arghya* according to his command;
having prepared a mandala in the northeast, excluding the gate and the lotus.
There, one should worship Śeṣikā Sundarī with the remains of the offerings (nirmālya).
[One should offer] foods to be licked and sucked, drinks and the like, betel-leaf, garlands, and ointments. (67)
"I offer this remains-of-offering (nirmālya) as food for you by the command of Śrī Śiva.
With this mantra, one should worship the Goddess who wears the remains-of-offering (Nirmālyadhāriṇī).

[Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Bali Offering to Vaṭuka and Others," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 19 ||
[The Twentieth Chapter] The Goddess said: O Śiva, how is that Supreme Sovereign, the Residual One (Śeṣikā), to be worshipped?
O Lord, tell me in its entirety: what was that Great Goddess like?
Īśvara said:
O beloved, I shall describe the goddess Śeṣikā Sundarī, who is most secret;
the goddess Mātaṅgī, preceded by Ucchiṣṭa, who bestows all supernatural powers (siddhis).
This is the lore that carries one across all transgressions and is free from all defects;
O Goddess, by the knowledge of which calamities come to an end.

O Goddess, this knowledge destroys poison—whether it be from immobile sources, mobile sources, artificial, or born of the body—residing in one's own or another's limbs. (Note: "Poison" is the reading in manuscript *kha*).
This is the lore, the great lore that removes all sins;
it bestows heaven, it bestows liberation, and likewise bestows sovereignty and good fortune.
This goddess was previously accomplished by me in a secluded place, O Goddess;
this Vidyā, when recited even once, destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin.

O Goddess, if one should ever remember the Goddess while becoming eight-faced (*ucchiṣṭamukha*), then he becomes as if having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācānta*), even though no sipping has been performed. (This reading belongs to the Īśvara [tradition], meaning "without sipping"; the same should be understood for what follows. || 7 ||
The poor man obtains wealth, and the fool may acquire knowledge;
hear the mantra of the Great Goddess, which I shall relate to you exactly as it is.
Having uttered the word "ucchiṣṭa" as well as "caṇḍālinī," then, O Goddess, [the words] "sumukhī" and "mahāpiśācinī. (9)

After that, the seed-syllable of Māyā, followed by two *ṭha* syllables with the *visarga*, [as follows]: (O Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālinī, O fair-faced Goddess, O Mahāpiśācinī, *hrīṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*). O Great Goddess, this bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhis*). || 10 ||
Now I shall proclaim another mantra, which is extremely difficult to obtain:
the seed-syllables of Speech, Māyā, and Kamalā, followed by "namo bhagavatyai. (11)

"Mātaṅgeśvari" at the end of all [the preceding parts], followed by "janavaśaṃkarī," and joined with the wife of fire (svāhā), is the mantra: (Ai Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, O Mātaṅgeśvarī, who brings all people under control, svāhā). This is another mantra that bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). || 12 ||

O Goddess of gods, there is no fault regarding women here, nor is there any obstacle, nor any restrictive rule; there is neither the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) nor the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), nor is there any presiding deity for this.
He in whom this mantra abides shall become a celestial tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
O Sovereign of All, I shall now describe her meditation exactly as it is.
Seated upon a corpse, clothed in red garments, richly adorned with red ornaments, and resplendent with a necklace of *guñjā* seeds. || 15 ||
Endowed with fresh youth, possessing full and elevated breasts,
holding a skull and a chisel in her hands, she is the embodiment of the supreme light.
And I shall describe the procedure here; listen, O Goddess, to this captivating account.
O Goddess, immediately after eating, even if the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) has not been performed— || 17 ||
Having first performed the bali offering with the root mantra,
the practitioner should then meditate upon the mantra and recite it ten thousand times.
The recitation of this [mantra] must be performed with the remains of food (ucchiṣṭa) by one desiring its accomplishment.
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I shall proclaim another [method] that yields fruit. (19)
For the fulfillment of all purposes and the attainment of one's goals, there should be both the fire sacrifice (homa) and the act of satiation;
having prepared a square mandala with a central dot upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
The practitioner should worship the maṇḍala of the Goddess with the root mantra;
having invoked the Goddess there, she is established in the form of fire.

Having performed worship, one should carry out the fire-oblation with curd, white mustard seeds, and rice grains according to the procedure of one thousand repetitions; thus the king becomes subject to one's will.
By performing a fire-oblation for the Goddess with the flesh of a cat, one attains supreme knowledge that brings mastery over both weapons and scriptures. (23)
One should perform a fire-oblation with the meat of a goat, mixed with honey and clarified butter, in a measure of one thousand; thereby the accomplishments of the fruits come to pass.
One who desires knowledge should perform oblations with honey and clarified butter; by means of this single measure [of practice], the desired accomplishment will certainly be attained. || 25 ||
Immediately, by means of cat-flesh together with ghee and honey,
combined with the hair of a Caṇḍāla, there shall be a great attraction.
By performing a fire sacrifice with the flesh of a hare mixed with honey, one obtains knowledge, wealth, and beautiful women.
By means of an offering of *dhustūra* wood into the funeral pyre fire, the knower of mantras may destroy his enemies through oblations made with the feathers of the *kokila* and the crow. (28)
The knower of mantras should perform a fire sacrifice for the eradication of enemies in a fire made of funeral pyre wood, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
By performing a continuous fire sacrifice with the feathers of an owl and a crow,
one shall cause two enemies to hate each other, becoming agitated and overwhelmed by mutual strife.

By means of an oblation of owl feathers, the miscarriage of a woman's fetus occurs, provided that for one month [one performs it] continuously with bilva leaves smeared with honey. (Note: *su* is the reading; *sa ka* is an alternative reading. 31.
Having performed a fire-oblation with one thousand measures while composed in meditation,
even a barren woman may obtain an excellent son who lives a long life.
Having offered a red bandhūka flower mixed with honey and sugar, even a woman who is unfortunate will undoubtedly become fortunate. || 33 ||
Having arrived through [the power of] *iḍā* or *haṭha*, those afflicted by desire embrace him by force;
she is the Goddess Maheśānī, who bestows the fruit of the left-hand path (*vāmācāra*). 34.
Through the practice of right conduct, she will not fail to grant her fruit;
and after every meal, one should offer her an oblation day by day.
O Śivā, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while using the remnants [of food],
whether in a hut, a cremation ground, an empty house, or at a crossroads.
Through the offering of oblations, the Goddess certainly becomes manifest;
by consecrating medicinal herbs with this very [mantra], they grant all accomplishments. (37)
The wielder of the moon, the wielder of the discus, likewise the wielder of the thunderbolt, the trident-bearer, and the mace-bearer—
residing within the bodies of men in battle, she is the destroyer of all weapons.
The root of the Apāmārga plant, gathered under the Puṣya asterism, serves as a protection against all weapons for the wise through mere application as an ointment. (39)
A man who applies *arjuna*, *nārāja*, *campaka*, *unmattaka*, and *kuhū* merely as an ointment will become a victor in battle and possess a body as hard as adamant. (40)
The date palm is held in the middle of her face, the ketaka flower is bound at her waist, and the palmyra tree rests upon her staff-like arms; she is the warder-off of all weapons.
If the Sun is situated in the right arm, or Rudra is in the left arm or at the heart, and Puṣpa is in the hand during battle, a man shall possess a body as indestructible as a diamond.
Having encased the mercury, which is endowed with the brilliance of a diamond, in three metals, it wards off all weapons from the hand of one standing in battle. (43)
One should collect girikarṇī, śamī, dūrvā, and white guñjā;
when all these are combined with sandalwood and applied as a tilaka, one becomes victorious in battle. (44)
Adhaḥpuṣpā, Śikhī, Śvetā, and Girikarṇikā,
when combined with Gorocanā, form a forehead mark (tilaka) that deludes enemies.
One who applies a tilaka with gold, the moon, fire, the Indra-tree (devadāru), and likewise a fifth [ingredient],
shall see his enemy in five ways.
One should take a liquid as formidable as a black cobra, mixed with earth, and sow white guñjā seeds therein; from that, one should collect its root.
A sectarian mark (tilaka) combined with *harītakī* is a deluder of enemies;
seeing a soldier who has applied this mark, the enemy will perceive himself as being surrounded by dogs. (48)

If it is being devoured by swarms [of insects], it surely falls from there to the ground; that *kāsamardaka* whose shadow enters the water should be gathered. (Note: "śva" is the reading in the manuscript. 49.
By means of this mark, an enemy perceives a well or a pond;
likewise, Brahmadaṇḍī, Kaumārī, Īśvarī, and Vaiṣṇavī [are perceived].
Vārāhī, Vajriṇī, Cāndrī, and likewise Mahālakṣmī—these are the divine medicinal herbs, and they are also known as the Mothers (Mātṛs). || 51 ||
Having bound it upon the hand, it wards off all enemies. What is the use of saying more? It is now described in brief. (52)
The Vidyā that possesses the sixfold ritual action bestows all accomplishments through its application;
however, by the improper application of the Root Vidyā, the loss of accomplishment will certainly occur. (53)
O Goddess, when there is a desire for practice, one should employ this [mantra] at that time;
by means of this, the best of practitioners should accomplish all rites. (54)
O Goddess, this has been spoken incidentally; it must be guarded with great effort.

[Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Application of the Śeṣikā Vidyā," in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara within the venerable Gandharva Tantra. || 20 ||
[The Twenty-first Chapter] | The Lord said:
Then, indeed, while recollecting Maheśānī with the mind through the root mantra,
And having first partaken of the water for the feet, one should consume the remains of the offerings (nirmālya). || 1 ||

He who wears [the Linga] upon his head but lets even a single drop fall to the ground should be known as a slayer of a Brahmin, for he has [only] taken it into himself out of devotion. (Alternative reading: *...or lets a drop fall to the ground*). 2.
Having taken auspicious fragrant substances, the knower of mantras, holding them in his left hand, should look at them in the water of a conch shell using his right hand.
Having consecrated it seven times, one should contemplate it as containing all sacred fords (tīrthas).
With that water, one should sprinkle oneself while recollecting the Root Goddess in the heart.
One should drink the water from the feet with devotion and apply the remainder to the head;
having performed the smearing of all limbs, as well as the application of the yantra and so forth.
One should emanate [the deity] from oneself by means of the seed-syllable of desire and the root mantra;
one should also touch the forehead with the tip of the ring finger.
Wearing the floral remains upon his head and applying the ointment to all his limbs,
he should offer the *arghya* to the Sun with the mantra for the sake of making the rite flawless.
Having gone to the ground on his knees and recited the prescribed mantra,
he should maintain the integrity of the rite with one-pointed mind through his words.
May whatever flaw there may be in my sacrifice, whatever flaw in my austerity, and whatever flaw in my worship of me—
all that become flawless through the grace of Mārtaṇḍa.
Afterwards, having prostrated before Mārtaṇḍabhairava, one should gaze upon him;
for at the beginning and at the end of the rite, there must be salutation and gazing upon the deity.
One should always perform [this] with devotion for the sake of accomplishing dharma, kāma, and artha;

first there is the eligibility for sacrifice, and afterwards the completion of the rite. (Note: *yājñādhikāritā* is the reading in manuscript *ka*, while *yajñādhikāritā* is the reading in manuscript *ā*. 11.
Due to a reversal of fate, the Rākṣasas carry off what has been prepared for him;
therefore, one should sacrifice as soon as he is seen setting out, and then again when he has set.
Having realized the oneness of both, he then rises up from that state once more;
for he alone was at the beginning, he abides within, he is indeed infinite, and he is truly the end itself.
Having understood the beginning and the end, one shall obtain the fruit of all ritual actions;
thereafter, whatever flowers, food offerings, water-vessels, and so forth [are presented], [they too yield their fruit].
One should again behold all of that with the seed-syllable of Māyā—whatever and wherever it was previously performed, whether by hand or by eye. (15)
The placement of the vessel for each [deity] should be performed by him;
having sprinkled that place with water, he should then sweep it clean.
One should discard the floral remains (nirmālya) there in water or at the foot of a tree;
all offerings such as the food-oblation (naivedya) and so forth should be given to the Guru or the Guru’s Śakti.

Having offered the gift with devotion to Śiva in the form of the Guru (or to Śivā, according to the reading in manuscript *ka*), one should go to the ground on both knees and prostrate like a staff, O Beloved (or likewise, according to the reading in manuscript *ka*). || 18 ||
Having received what was given by the preceptor, one should accept it according to the prescribed rule;
in the absence of those two, one should give it to young maidens according to the rite.

The deity should consume the nectar; having consumed it, he attains divinity. One should recognize that as nectar which has been offered by the deity. (Note: *daivatena* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
O beloved, nothing other than the garland belonging to the deity may be taken; nor may anything whatsoever be taken without first being offered to Śiva. (21)
And that animal, O beloved, eats the dead [flesh] while being endowed with both worlds;
whereas formerly all humans and others did not eat this dead [flesh]. (22)

Since one would not otherwise attain the state of a deity, one should never consume it at any time; however, if one whose self is purified by divine nature should consume the nectar [of the senses], [then it is permissible]. 23.
By the constant practice of yoga, a man shall become one who goes to the gods;
indeed, having made the "spreading of the nectar" (the lower lip), he should likewise perform the "covering" (the upper lip).
Taking the remainder of the *bali* offering, one should perform the oblation as before;
having offered it, one should then consume the nectar with devotion and purity of heart. (25)
O Goddess, having then consumed that nectar, one should place the hand upon the head;
having sipped water three times according to the three principles (tritattva), one should then duly assign the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Śiva is the giver and Śiva is the enjoyer; Śiva is this entire universe.
Śiva is victorious everywhere; he who is Śiva, I am indeed that very one.

The attendants (*śaktis*), with faces adorned [and] well-attired, are exceedingly beautiful; one should behold them with the vision of a deity, for they are indeed deities themselves. (Note: In some manuscripts, the reading is *alaṅkṛtavaktrās tu*. 28.
In that same manner, one should look upon the Brahmins, the gods on earth, who are pure in mind;
having bowed with devotion, one should then look at one's own people with great joy.

O Goddess, having worshipped the Supreme Goddess according to this rite, one becomes like me on earth, filled with the higher knowledge obtained through her grace—or, as another reading suggests, "whether devoid of such attainment or endowed with it, I alone [am he]. || 30 ||
One who has attained perfection through the power of cultivation may, however, depart at his own will.

The Goddess said: "How is worship performed so that it may be accepted [O Father; this is the reading in manuscript *kha*]? Or how does the mind gain conviction? Tell me the means for that, O Lord. (31)

The Lord said: "Well asked by you, O blessed lady, is this which bestows liberation through mere remembrance—the form of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, the unsurpassed and great state. (Note: *Śiva* is an alternative reading for *śakra*).
Situated within that is the supreme Brahman, eternal and of the nature of light;
indeed, the Self shines by itself like the sun when the clouds have passed away.
Having practiced there many times by the path shown in the scriptures, one [perceives] the form of the letters of sound, as well as the actions inherent in them. (34)
Having recited [the mantra] and performed [the rite], one shall then attain the perfection consisting of both enjoyment and liberation,
until the mind dissolves into that very Self which consists of consciousness.
Until then, the practitioner of mantra should perform the recitation and fire-offerings of his chosen mantra;
beyond that, there remains no further duty for him.
Once the supreme reality is known, there is no need for all the various observances;
what purpose would a palm-leaf fan serve once the Malaya breeze has been obtained? (37)
The fruit that arises from attaining that [state] is inevitable; he who acts for its attainment should be known as a believer (āstika), for he is gradually established in liberation. || 38 ||
Having attained that [state], one should then place [the self] therein; having made it free from that, one should place it;
and having performed the placement of that which consists of both, he is considered a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and a sage (muni). || 39 ||

O lotus-eyed one, having understood that the body is called a *yantra*, and having established the notion of "I" therein, one should worship with devotion and a concentrated mind. (Note: The reading *kṛtvāvahamara tatra* is found in manuscript *ka*.)

Having worshipped that form of the Supreme Goddess—whether it be partless (niṣkala) or with parts (sakala)—as non-different from oneself, one should worship the Self as the beloved Sovereign Lady. 41.
Then, without a doubt, she goes to the abode consisting of bliss;
thus is the fifth [vow] described, whose manifested form is proclaimed to be fivefold.
Indeed, within the body composed of the five principles (pañcatattva), these are directly perceived by them;
it cannot become manifest elsewhere except through contemplation upon the Self. 43.
Inference belongs to Maheśānī alone within her own self and nowhere else;
having inferred the Supreme, one should conduct oneself as if everything were the Self.

Just as the most excellent deities are satisfied by the mere scent of objects and see their beauty, so too, O Pārvatī, they are to be won over through praise. (Note: *labhyāśca* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas, as well as human beings and other creatures, are satisfied by means of enjoyment. || 46 ||
Abiding within the body of the guru—especially that of virgins, as well as Brahmins and cows—the supreme deities partake of the food. (47)
Therefore, one should always feed them with effort and satisfy them;
for when these are satisfied, the Great Goddess, who pervades the universe, is thoroughly pleased. 48.
The ancestors likewise eat from the bodies of the Brahmins;
there should be no physical separation, for that which is physically deficient [is unfit]. (49)
All that becomes complete with its ancillaries through the feeding of Brahmins with sweet foods.

[Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Method for the Means of Completing the Worship," in the Śrī-Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 21 ||
[The Twenty-second Chapter] Īśvara said:
Having abandoned the Supreme Self residing within the heart, one strives for something else.
"Alas, O beautiful woman, he is a fool, for like a blind man he searches for it outside. (1)

Having realized that which resides within the heart and is the supreme object of primordial nature, one perceives this [Self] in the very Self through action directed toward That; [this is the usage of the root *iḍ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*) in the active voice]. || 2 ||
Upon the realization of that, O Pārvatī, [the goal] is accomplished; indeed, it is not otherwise.
I am Viṣṇu and the Self-born; we are all of us the Self-born.
Having experienced that within this body, we worship that very same [reality];
having summoned that which resides within it, we thus offer sacrifice to that very same [reality]. || 4 ||
Having withdrawn that [internal] self and established it within one's own heart,
one should offer that very same offering to Him alone for His pleasure.
The hosts of deities desire nothing other than nectar;
their worship is performed with nectar alone, so one should indeed offer nectar.
"By accepting what is offered as a self-surrender, the hero shall attain immortality. Thus, O Goddess, has this supreme nectar of Śeṣikā been described to you.
Through the grace of the Guru, they are known according to the distinction between gross and subtle;
namely, as the obligatory (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the optional (kāmya) acts, each separately.
One should perform the threefold ritual of the Triple City (Tripura) in its proper sequence;
having abandoned that which is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), one should diligently practice all else.
Therefore, the daily [rites] performed constantly ward off sin;
likewise, the monthly rites on specific lunar days and the annual rites bestow fruit.
One should recognize that for whom there is constant hell resulting from the destruction of faith through excessive fasting; one should perform such occasional rites with faith.
One should recognize that for which only the fruit is heard of, as enjoined by the Śruti and Smṛti, is a rite performed with a specific desire (kāmya); it is honored in that context. 12.
One should diligently perform that which is honored by the world;
one should even abandon dharma if it is censured by the world. (Note: *sādhu* is the reading found in manuscript *ya*.)

In this context, the daily (nitya) rite is purely sattvic, while the occasional (naimittika) is rajasic; one who understands the fruits of action should perform the optional (kāmya) rite as tamasic, being free from thirst for rewards.
Having abandoned that craving from afar, one should contemplate the mind as full;
when the mind is full, craving ceases, and this entire world becomes full. (15)
For one whose feet are covered by shoes, the earth is indeed as if covered with leather;
likewise, the optional, the obligatory, and the occasional rites [yield no fruit] when devoid of their proper results. 16.
Having performed the offering to her, one should know that which is done for the pleasure of Tripurā to be *sāttvika*, bestowing the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation. (17)
Whatever threefold action has been prescribed for one within its proper sphere,
even that which is declared in the Śruti and Smṛti, one should not neglect it even in thought.
O Dear One, by the omission of ritual duties, the lowest of practitioners is born in a womb;
however, having understood from a true guru that the universe consists of Śiva and Śakti, [he attains liberation]. 19.
Through the distinction between gross and subtle, and by means of the natures of the father and mother,
one should always satisfy those two through ritual actions, while remaining ever absorbed in that state.

One who possesses both natures attains accomplishment, but not one who possesses only one nature and is devoid of knowledge; having understood the unity of those two through the eye of knowledge, following the sequence of the venerable Guru.
Having experienced that bliss, the self should then enter into it,
just as a child gradually acquires proficiency through its mother and father.
Through the unification of the equality of those two, the perfected one should attain knowledge;
for they say that the deities are Śakti, and the ancestors are Śiva.
He should satisfy all those previously mentioned friends with offerings; otherwise, he will be slain by those very friends.
Having presented an offering to them, he should satisfy both of those [deities];
afterwards, having made an announcement to them, he should sport joyfully with his friends.

To the gods, [the offering is made] with "svāhā" at the end; to humans, by means of the "hantakāra"; and to those [beings] beginning with the yakṣas, with "svadhā" at the end; but to the ancestors, it is obtained by ending with "namas. (Note: *tebhyaḥ* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
O Pārvatī, his ancestors will surely depart in despair, as will his friends and kinsmen, for he has not honored them even with a mere word. (27)
Friends devour one's stature, and kinsmen devour the accumulated merit of one's actions;
one's father destroys what is gained in this world, and one's mother destroys what is gained in the next world.
But one who is devoid of both worlds certainly does not attain success (or, according to another reading, "does not bestow it").
Without having sacrificed to the Father, one should sacrifice to the Mother, Ambikā. (29)
The eternal [goddess] does not favor a sacrifice even with hundreds of ritual procedures;
therefore, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for one's father with devotion at both the beginning and the end.
One should not accept what is not given; therefore, one should give to him whatever is beyond that—cows, land, gold, clothing, and so forth, as well as various kinds of food and edibles. (31)
Having set aside his necessary worldly duties, he was intent on devotion [to the Lord] for the sake of the female residents, the twice-born, and the poor, the blind, and the wretched. (32)
Whatever is beneficial for security and well-being, he should perform that by means of instruction;
being capable, he should sustain his own dependents out of affection. (33)
From the wicked, from those of evil intent, from the violent (or "from the harmful," as per another reading), and likewise from the reckless;
from the powerful, from those intoxicated by wealth, and especially from the scribes (kāyasthas). || 34 ||
A virtuous person should guard and protect [them] like his own breast-born sons;
and perceiving the three kinds of worlds, he should always cherish and protect them.
One should execute those who deserve execution and punish those who deserve punishment in accordance with the teachings of the scriptures.

[The sin] incurred by the execution of one who should not be executed is equal to that incurred by the punishment of one who should not be punished. (Note: Regarding the reading "tasya tu kaḥ," the variant "tasya tu saḥ" is more appropriate.)
"The sin incurred by failing to punish one who deserves punishment is equal to that incurred by protecting one who deserves to be executed.
Having realized this, one whose self is absorbed in yoga should attend to the welfare and security [of all beings]. (37)
One should perceive the manifestations of the Self and, through their attainment, offer them up;
he who displays the manifestations of his own Self to Mahādevī [attains success]. || 38 ||
Endowed with those very same powers, such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest,
one should perform the visualization of the body for a duration of exactly three muhūrtas.
When midday has arrived, one should contemplate the Supreme Brahman;
for a period of only three muhūrtas, one should attend to it even while asleep.
Then, having understood [this], at the proper time one should attend to her alone, as well as graceful dances and sweet songs. (41)
One whose soul is absorbed in that state should show [the ritual] to the Goddess and cause her to hear it; she should gaze upon it.
In the dances, the goddesses, adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste, remain fixed in song.
Adorned with beautiful ornaments, he should remove them with those very [hands];
then, in the center, the Lord himself is like another Kāmeśvara. (43)
Having become united with Kāmeśvarī, one should then worship Kāmeśvarī;
rejoicing in the supreme delight of contemplation on Brahman, one becomes a thinker of sovereignty.
One should spend just three muhūrtas in sleep;
during the day one should offer [oblations] to the fathers, and at night, being intent on that, one should offer them to the mothers.
The night is declared to be the mother, and the day indeed is the father;
by realizing the unity of these two, one becomes perfected, and not otherwise.
Soma is Śakti and Śiva is Sūrya; night is Śakti and day is Śiva.
When that Blessed Lord, the Great Tripurabhairava, [manifests], [this is so]. 47.

The infinite one, the supreme refuge of both the higher and the lower, filled with the bliss of the supreme beyond, [worships] the Yoginī named the Secret of the Higher and Lower, whose form is Brahman. 48.
When one draws upward Mahātripurasundarī, who consists of the bliss of Śiva and Ānanda, and remains [there], that day is proclaimed. 49.
From the union of Śakti and Bhairava, arising from the radiance of bliss within bliss,
that supreme creative power (kalā) is the inner play, the foremost essence of Bhairava-bliss.
One should know that to be midday, characterized by three muhūrtas;
at that time, Śakti and Bhairava remain in equal portions.
Then the eastern and western [sides] should be known as marked by twice that [measure];
they desire non-duality with each other, yet they attain duality in the middle.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should know that at that time it is called the constellation Abhijit;
pervaded by their respective splendors, there occurs then a union of those two. (Note: *ākīrṇā* is an alternative reading.)
Then the God appeared with ten arms, five faces, and three eyes, resembling ten million suns and possessing the radiance of ten million times ten thousand moons.
Clad in white garments, white in complexion, and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
the Great Goddess, possessing the radiance of ten million moons, sat upon his lap.
Laughing, the large-eyed one was delighted by supreme bliss;
desiring to attain that very form, she longed for the sight of that form. (56)
O Goddess, at that time there is no other means for pleasing Him than white clothing;
however, when the practitioner is impelled by destiny, he may assume another form there.
The Blessed Lady, becoming enraged, would bestow a most terrible curse upon him;
therefore, one should then worship her with all white materials and in white attire.
In the sky, the goddess should be visualized with a face resembling the autumnal moon;
there, O lady of beautiful countenance, worship should always be performed, especially so. (59)
One should always offer with devotion, as is most beautiful, drinks, things to be sucked, things to be licked, things to be chewed, and foods to be eaten, along with refreshing offerings. (60)
One should worship with ritual services in the morning and at midday with delicious foods and drinks,
accompanied by song, dance, and so forth, preceded by sacrifice at night.
For one should sacrifice facing east in the morning, facing south at midday,
facing west in the evening, and always facing north at night.
There, with one-pointed mind, one should recite the Vidyā according to the Śāmbhava division.
One who desires their own welfare should avoid the piercing of the *śakti*, [which occurs] when that [space] is previously covered by the rays of the dawn before the rising of Bhairava. (63)
One should know Ardhanārīśvara; there, the acts of worship are equal.
Then one should perform the service with ritual offerings according to the prescribed rule. (The reading "saparyā kāryā" is found in manuscript Kha.)
If the householder and his wife remain established in equal shares in their service, desiring the supreme state of bliss and ever increasing that bliss, [they shall attain it]. (55)
When those two, the former and the latter, are both of great merit and equal in form,
one should constantly contemplate them with devotion according to the procedure for that specific time.
One should recite the Vidyā with undistracted mind, according to the divisions of Śakti and Śāmbhava;
in that rite, one should wear white garments and be adorned with white garlands and unguents.
One should see those wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents;
the quarters and intermediate directions should likewise appear red to the wise.
The entire universe becomes as crimson as lac, and one should become that very thing oneself therein.
Resembling a ruby (a variant reading says "resembling the king of the gods"), with a splendor equal to ten million suns, the Lord Kāmeśvara is there, indeed, with one face and four arms. (69)

The goddess, resembling a red lotus (the reading *bhā* is found in manuscript *ka*; the reading *ṇām* is found in manuscript *ka*), is as crimson as the rays of the rising sun; desiring to attain that very form, they enter him (the reading *tā* is found in manuscript *ka*) because they are of that same nature. || 70 ||
Having then experienced that bond, which is filled with the bliss of Bhairava,
she, desiring the opposite and longing for its conquest, [remains].
Then that time became filled with dust; it is celebrated as the evening twilight.
Beholding the western quarter completely overspread with blood, [he... (72)
The practitioner should worship with devotion and ritual offerings according to the prescribed rule, when that Supreme Śakti, assuming the form of the universe by her own will, [manifests]. (73)
When the desire arises to take pleasure with the Puruṣa after having cast him down,
then the Goddess herself, standing above Bhairava, should mount him.
Increasing one's own bliss through the masses of innate bliss, at that time the universe becomes one's own; therein lies the most exalted worship. (75)
By means of various lamps consisting of those respective visions and diverse enjoyments, everything should always become red as lac, and one should likewise become so oneself. (76)

One should contemplate the Vidyā, which consists of the differentiation of powers, encapsulated by the seed-syllable *haṃsa*, interspersed with the *praṇava* (oṃ), pure, the play of sound (*nāda*), and identical with that [reality]. (77)
Extending from the root (mūlādhāra) to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
thinner than a fiber of a lotus stalk, she is like a restless female swan upon a lotus in a distant pool, yet appearing as if perfectly steady.
Having invoked and worshipped the flowing stream of nectar, which resembles pure lac-dye, within the city of his own lotus-marked abode; 79.
Having completely conquered the senses and the mind, one should recite [the mantra] whose nature is bliss;
one should know the middle to be the mouth and the two preceding and following parts to be the pair of breasts. (The reading "mukha" is better than "sukha. 80.
The supreme form is the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*); below those two is the "midnight.
It yields infinite fruit, is meritorious, and bestows the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation. (81)
O auspicious lady, the four junctions (saṃdhyās) have been described, which are difficult to find on earth;
they should be known as the four arms of the Great Goddess and as the four periods of time.
She is the Supreme Sovereign and he is the Supreme Lord; they are the very Self.
If any limb of theirs were to be deprived [of its power], that would be the amputation of a limb for them both.
In that regard, whatever auspicious rite is performed is the supreme blessing:
meditation, worship, recitation, fire-oblation, ritual placement, and libation. (84)
O sinless one, when the Goddess is worshipped here, she fulfills one's heart's desires; whatever merit is gained here, O faultless one, by one endowed with devotion and faith— || 85 ||
In a sacrifice performed according to the prescribed rites, which is filled with supreme bliss, even Ananta is unable to describe it fully, even with thousands of millions of mouths. (86)
Even a single handful of nectar here is comparable to the ocean of ambrosia (or, according to another reading, equal to the ocean of nectar).
O Pārvatī, he who does not worship the Goddess here even with water— || 87 ||
He who does not bow to his gurus with devotion is called a slayer of a Brahmin;
those who are intent on sleep here go to the city of Mahākāla, O beloved.
Deceit, delusion, as well as sleep, laziness, and external thoughts; lust, anger, as well as greed, violence, and envy. (89)

Having abandoned [all else] with great effort, one should practice the Vidyā alone, having cast off the evil latent impressions accumulated over ten million births. (Note: *vān* is the reading in manuscript *kha*.)
One who enjoys worldly pleasures attains liberation in a single birth; of this there is no doubt.
At that time, he shall never behold anything other than the face of Śakti.
Animals and men who worship others should be shunned from afar;
by thinking of anything else here, they enter the womb of a barbarian and fall downward.
And through meditation on the eternal Brahman, they go upward to the supreme abode;
for them, there is no ritual service preceded by physical austerity.
Those who are constantly engaged in honoring [the teacher] are thus celebrated;
even the gods pay homage to such a person—how much more so then humans and monkeys? (94)
Therein, the portion of the Goddess becomes the subduer of all the worlds;
even the immortals desire that mortal who is beloved of the Kula. 95.
Having seen the god, who possesses the luster of the autumnal moon and a face resembling the full moon, all the young women were filled with joy and became mutually enamored. (96)
Even if there were a woman equal to him who speaks with various forms of wit, cleverness, and affectionate nectar-like speech, or even if there were a man equal to her; (97)
Upon seeing the lord of men, that tiger among men, one's mind may become agitated;
yet whatever object was given previously, it becomes four times greater when given to him. (98)
One should present various kinds of offerings to Mahādevī;
having offered royal honors at the end, and having praised and extolled her, one should dismiss her. || 99 ||
O beloved, if one is unable [to practice] even during the three periods of time, then at the fourth period,
one should worship entirely by night while fasting and turning away from fear and sleep.
One should perform the morning oblation or likewise at midday;
now I shall describe the time for sleep for the benefit of practitioners. (101)
O Great Goddess, after that, there are nine muhūrtas during day and night;
the sleep of the Goddess is said to have a duration of three muhūrtas. (The reading *tā* is found in the Kha manuscript.)
In this regard, one should attend upon the Goddess who is intent on sleep with sleep itself;
for he who, being deluded, should mutter prayers or perform worship at the time of sleep [attains no fruit]. (103)
O Goddess, for that ignorant person who engages in [sexual] union elsewhere than during the time of sleep, four things are destroyed: life-span, knowledge, fame, and strength. (104)
Therefore, with every effort, one should awaken [the disciple] at the time of awakening;
[one should avoid] looking at him, gazing at him, conversing with him, or looking toward others. 105.
Having understood the five characteristics of the self-entry into the mantras, one should recite the mantra and obtain all accomplishments. 106.
O lady of virtuous vows, at the junction of the Vedas, or at the three junctions, or even at two junctions,
