one whose self is absorbed in yoga, who possesses the knowledge of yoga, and who is endowed with the yoga-mudrās— || 107 ||
He who, established in the vow of celibacy, recites [the mantra] for one year,
should recite it a thousand times at the beginning and also a thousand times at the end.
One should recite the vidyā during the two middle [periods] (or even within the middle, according to the Kha manuscript); one should perform the remainder with equal distribution.
O Goddess, it should be one hundred thousand [recitations], likewise completed within thirty days. || 109 ||
One should perform it without stiffness or contraction, neither too fast nor too slow;
one should contemplate it as the mere sound that moves through the transition from syllable to syllable.
O beautiful one, even now, established in this vow, I too recite this;
that Brahman is recited at the three junctions of the day for the sake of attaining that supreme state. (111)
In this manner, one shall gradually become a perfected being (siddha), an enjoyer devoted to enjoyment;
thus for a month, a season, a year, and even a yuga.
O Supreme Goddess, one should cause [the disciple] to understand this, or else the [mantra] of the intermediate kalpa and so forth.
This supreme secret must never be disclosed; it is the convention of the conduct of the observance (samaya), which bestows the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation. 113.
[Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Symbols of Conventional Conduct," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 22 ||
[The Twenty-third Chapter] | The Lord said:
Rituals such as the fire oblation (homa) and so forth are fruitless without the worship of the maiden (kumārī).
By whomsoever the maiden is worshipped, by him the three worlds are worshipped. || 1 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as all the sages, the ancestors, the guardians of the quarters, the gandharvas, the apsarases, and the asuras. || 2 ||
Likewise, the wives of the gods, the nāgas, the mothers, the siddhas and cāraṇas, the viśvedevas along with the yakṣas, and the rākṣasa deities [were there]. || 3 ||
All beings, whether stationary or moving, all living creatures—
whosoever they may be— attain satisfaction when young maidens are honored there.
But even if many are not obtained, there should be at least one woman of excellent complexion;
she should be a young woman intoxicated with youth and supremely beautiful.
From the age of five until eight, she should be worshipped according to the prescribed rites;
the water offered to a maiden is equal to the waters of the ocean.
O Beloved, whatever food is offered to her becomes equal to the Kulācala mountains;
O Goddess, the worship of the Kumārīs should be performed with the Kumārī-mantra.
Just as the Goddess is worshipped, so too should they be worshipped;
for that reason, they should be fed with milk-rice mixed with sweet substances. (Note: *bhojitavyāḥ* is an archaic form resulting from the elision of the causative suffix *ṇic*.)
Then, with offerings dear to children, perceiving her as Tripurasundarī,
one should praise, bow down, and satisfy her, and thereafter pray for one's own desired object.
And from the hand of the goddess, who has been worshipped and is pleased,
a devoted man should receive with his head the unbroken grains (akṣata) accompanied by her blessing.
"Whatever she, being well-pleased, speaks, that certainly comes to pass.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this most wonderful secret. (11)
O Great Goddess, without that [initiation], one shall not partake in the fruit of worship, nor in daily rites, initiation, or the preliminary practices (puraścaryā) and so forth. (12)

At the beginning, at the end, and in the middle, and especially when the hundred thousand [recitations] are complete, young maidens must be worshipped; for if one does not worship the maidens, [the rite is fruitless].
If a maiden does not perform its worship, all the fruit of that [worship] is carried away by yakṣas and rākṣasas;
if she does not worship it, then she is beset by obstacles. (Note: *tadvi* is the reading in manuscript *ka*; *pari* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
The fruit of what was previously acquired may perish; what need is there to speak of [the loss] in a future birth?
Therefore, with every effort, one who desires his own welfare [should act accordingly]. 15.
O Supreme Goddess, these highly fortunate maidens should be worshipped after rising in the morning during the ritual worship, or again at the time of bathing.

Whether they be conditioned or unconditioned, or likewise born of low birth, they are to be saluted by the best of practitioners who are of noble lineage during supreme worship. (Note: *te* is the reading in manuscript K; *ye* is the reading in manuscript P. 17.
For those whose minds are dedicated to Brahman, there is no division whatsoever here in this world.
O Goddess, without the worship of the Kula, the Supreme Kuladevī turns her face away.
O auspicious lady, when one’s own wife becomes the preceptor of other women—whether they be Brāhmaṇī, Kṣatriyā, Vaiśyā, or Śūdrā who are ornaments of their families—[then she should be honored]. (19)

A courtesan, the daughter of a barber, a washerwoman (or, according to the reading in manuscript *kha*, an actress), and likewise a female ascetic—these women are skilled in various forms of cleverness and endowed with artistic talents, beauty, and virtuous qualities. || 20 ||

Having observed their forms, dispositions, and wrathful gestures, they were designated by the names of the eight Śaktis, beginning with Brāhmaṇī. (The reading "sajñakā" is found in manuscript *kha*. || 21 ||
First, he offered them a seat and repeatedly welcomed them;
then he presented water for honoring the guests (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), drinking water, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
One should bathe [the image] with perfumes, flowers, and water, and likewise perform the grooming of the hair; having fumigated the hair, one should then offer silk (kauśeya). || 23 ||
Then, having led [the image] to another place and having spread out a seat with devotion,
one should cause it to rest according to the prescribed rite, following the sequence starting from the east.
Having adorned [the deity] with various ornaments, decorations, and the like, as well as with unguents, and likewise offering fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings; || 25 ||
Milk, curd, ghee, buttermilk, fresh butter with sugar, coconut, wood-apple, and the excellent orange. || 26 ||
Having offered flour-cakes and milk-rice accompanied by various flavors,
and having worshipped according to the prescribed rules, one should then gratify [the deity] with hymns of praise.
O Mother Goddess (O Mistress of the Body, according to the Ka-pāṭha reading), salutations to you who bear the form of Brahman, O sinless one!
By your grace, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Maheśī, O boon-granting Goddess, whose form is supreme bliss, please remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra. (The reading "ṇī" is found in manuscript *kha*.)
O Kaumāri, sovereign of all vidyās, supreme in the play of Kumāra, out of compassion remove my obstacles and grant me the accomplishment of the mantra. (30)

O Vaiṣṇavī, you are the form of Viṣṇu, the destroyer of all obstacles. O Goddess who bears the form of Viṣṇu, who carries the son of Vinatā, please remove my obstacle and grant me the perfection of the mantra. || 31 ||
O Vārāhī, O boon-granting Goddess, whose form is supreme bliss, (O You who have bitten and swallowed the earth— variant reading),
by Your grace remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.

O Indrāṇī, O boon-granting goddess, you indeed stand upon the shoulder of an elephant; (O goddess who bears the form of Śakra, worshipped by Śakra and the other gods—this is the reading from manuscript Kha).
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra. || 33 ||
O Cāmuṇḍā, adorned with a garland of severed heads, O destroyer of fear (or, according to the *kha* manuscript, O destroyer of obstacles),
out of compassion remove my obstacle and grant me the perfection of the mantra.

O Mahālakṣmī, O remover of the continuous flow of great delusion (or, according to the Kha manuscript, of great zeal), by your grace remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra. || 35 ||

O Goddess, who consists of the three mothers (or, according to another reading, who is beyond the three mothers), who art present in every single being and in abundance, O Goddess of universal form, homage be to you! 36.

Whoever, being self-controlled, recites this hymn at the commencement of undertakings after having observed those who are clever (or, according to the *kha* manuscript, "those who are wise"), no obstacle shall arise for him.
Having sipped water, one should offer betel-leaf as an oral fragrance;
then one should again present a garland smeared with fragrant sandalwood paste.
If, by the turn of fortune, they become intent on play, then he, devoted to the essence of play, should cause them all to play with various games. (39)
Therefore, O beloved, they must always be protected with every effort, O wise one, so that they may be bowed down by those who are devoted solely to the spirit of devotion. 40.
Having taken the excellent blood from a woman who has reached her season by her own will, and having combined it with yellow pigment (rocanā), camphor, saffron, musk, and aloe-wood; 41.
Having taken divine Svayambhū flowers and likewise divine fruits,
one should worship the Goddess Mahātripurasundarī.
Or else, it may arise from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*; the flower does not exist elsewhere.
Likewise, there is wine, meat, the *mudrā*, the *śakti*, and the self-born flower (*svayaṃbhūkusuma*). (43)
O Great Goddess, by means of these very [substances], the Supreme (Parā) is made manifest through the purification of substances that arises from the purification of Śakti.

Having worshipped the goddess Tripurā, one may accomplish even that which is impossible to achieve; for others do not go [to their goal] as easily as one does through one's own daughter. (Note: *nijakanyā* is the reading in manuscript *ka*, while *anujātmajā* is the variant.)
An elder sister, a maternal aunt, or a mother along with her co-wife—whether inferior in age or by birth—are to be protected like a sister. (46)
They should be worshipped by all the best of the lineage who have abandoned their own egoism;
having himself become unshakable, he should not practice the root-yoga.
Even the accomplishment of longevity achieved through the fundamental yoga perishes certainly;
for in the absence of all [the deities], one or another must be worshipped with diligence. (48)

Whether they be refined or unrefined, or even a wanton woman or a courtesan—the latter is to be understood as superior in the absence of the former, because women are a portion of that [divinity]. (49)

If one woman who knows the family scriptures (*kula-śāstra*) is obtained by those expert in the *kula* tradition, she is worthy of worship; O Goddess, she is the means for accomplishing both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (50)
And when a single young woman is honored and looked upon there, then all the goddesses are honored and all the deities are worshipped. || 51 ||
Thus it has been told to you, O Goddess; it must never be disclosed.
[Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Worship of the Virgin," in the Śrī-Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 23 ||
[The Twenty-fourth Chapter] Īśvara said:
Thus, the wise person who, endowed with devotion, performs this worship daily, [attains the fruit].
Among women he was like Kandarpa, another lord of Gaurī as it were. || 1 ||
He alone is a man of merit in this world; he alone is the ornament of his family.
Blessed indeed is his mother, and blessed truly is his father. (Note: "ornament" is the reading in manuscript *kha*.)
There, a divine portion arises which is equal to mine; a great-minded one becomes the lord of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇiman*—of this there is no doubt.

Like fire, he is the destroyer of enemies; like the moon, he is the bestower of happiness; like the ancestors and the gods, he is the teacher; and indeed, in his purity, he is like the sacred fire itself.
He who is an eloquent speaker equal to Bṛhaspati and as patient as the earth—
Sarasvatī resides in his mouth and Lakṣmī is always in his home.
Indeed, all sacred fords reside within his body, and for him there is no rebirth;
by wealth he becomes a lord of riches, and by splendor he is like the sun.
For by his strength he is indeed like the Wind-god, and by his generosity he is like Vāsava;
and by his singing, he who has constantly worshipped him is Tumburu himself.
O Goddess of gods, if one does not worship Mahātripurasundarī for even a single day, one should therefore perform an expiation.
Having fasted and performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), one should perform worship on the following day;
having duly honored the preceptor, one should then complete the worship according to the rules.
Having given food to the maiden, one should also feed the Brahmins;
thereafter, one should again perform the initiation and carry out one hundred thousand recitations.
He who leaves the worship of Mahātripurasundarī and likewise that of the Yoginīs neglected for two or even three days; || 11 ||
His spiritual accomplishment will perish, and he shall incur the curse of the Yoginīs;
his four—life-span, knowledge, fame, and strength—shall be destroyed.
The hosts of Yoginīs consume his flesh, semen, form, and blood, as well as even his most cherished desires. (13)
He shall have terrible quarrels with his kinsmen, especially with his wives;
the earth shall be devoid of crops, and he shall encounter obstacles at every step.
Truly, truly, he becomes diseased and is born into poverty;
even in this world, he experiences three kinds of hair-raising suffering.
Another, having fallen from heaven, becomes a leader of kings on earth;
then, having attained incomparable devotion, he obtains absolute liberation (kaivalya). || 16 ||
He who, having set out to contemplate Brahman, abandons the deity and proceeds by means of *vinayā* (or *vinaya*),
he indeed is a slayer of Brahman.
If the mantra-practitioner, intent on recitation and meditation and devoted to spiritual security and well-being, should himself be deluded, he should employ a guru in that matter. (18)
He who has a guru devoted to his welfare becomes one intent on knowledge and action, pure, composed of all the gods, and a lord; for him, all perfections are attained.
Whether monthly or annually, one should personally perform a great worship on an auspicious day, adorned with all its constituent parts.
One should always perform the worship of the Goddess, whose beautiful form is adorned with various kinds of offerings. 21.

The practitioner of mantra, devoted to daily rites, should perform the occasional observances; the virtuous one, intent on both daily and occasional rites, may then contemplate the optional rites for specific desires.
The optional rite is superior to the occasional, and the obligatory is superior to the occasional;
he who neglects the obligatory conduct [performs] either the optional or the occasional rite. (Variant reading in manuscript Kha: "or even the occasional rite.")
That person of dull intellect performs [other acts], yet he does not obtain their fruit,
because disregarding the daily obligatory rites (nityācāra), he strives for something else.
That person's action is as fruitless as sexual union with a barren woman;
however, one may worship the deities of the wheel even with flowers and fruits. (25)
A man who is deficient in a limb cannot be a proper performer of sacrifice;
likewise, worship that is deficient in its components does not bestow the full fruit. (26)
Meditation, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings constitute the four hands;
the body is the network of ritual placements (nyāsa), and the self is indeed the knowledge thereof.
Devotion is said to be its head, faith its heart, and skill its eye;
having thus understood the body of sacrifice, the best of practitioners [should proceed]. (28)
O beloved, one should always complete the sacrifice with all its constituent parts;
indeed, there is great fault in a sacrifice deficient in its parts, therefore one should not neglect a constituent part. || 29 ||

The person whose every limb is complete is called the Sacrifice (*yajña*); he is the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). Śakti, who is intent upon various activities, is Accomplishment (*siddhi*); [the state of] those two in conjunction is [the ultimate]. (30)
Just as there is no fault for anyone else when there is an affliction of a limb in the case of the Śrīmat Tripurasundarī, who is the complete sacrificial body, so it shall be here. || 31 ||
Worship should indeed be performed according to one's own means for the sake of prosperity;
however, by neglecting this, one becomes deficient and incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Neither more nor less [than this] should be done, for both extremes bring about evil;
[this applies] on the fourteenth day, the eighth day, and the full moon day within the month.
Or one should perform an extensive sacrifice on a day of the great elements (mahābhūta),
or when a Tuesday coincides with the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
That day of the great elements indeed brings all beings under its control;
if it should coincide with the Puṣya asterism, then it bestows infinite fruit.
If one should recite the mantra over a corpse in a cremation ground according to the prescribed rite, or otherwise recite the goddess Mātṛkā in her blue form; 36.
Having performed [the ritual] and recited [the mantra], one should then subjugate the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas;
having brought them under control, one will go to their world and likewise to this world together with them.
Having brought [the deity] under control, the wise man, endowed with prosperity, rejoices with his sons and grandsons;
likewise, having performed the rite at home or outside, the wise man should perform the recitation (japa). 38.
Having made the Rākṣasas and Kiṃnaras his subjects both in that world and here, he, rejoicing with them and possessing enjoyments, partakes of pleasures according to his desire. (39)
A wise man who, having performed [the rite] and recited [the mantra] in his own home— which is always pure and very beautiful— shall bring all the yakṣas under his control.

Having enjoyed [wealth], he is delighted in the world, a man of riches, skilled in matters of wealth, one whose life is his wealth, and whose very self is wealth; he finds happiness from constant reflection upon it. (41)
Having experienced that bliss there, O beloved, one likewise shines here as well—
either near a river or a stream, or at a sacred seat (pīṭha) of the ancestors.
Having performed and recited that [mantra] in both that world and here, he is gladdened by them;
he becomes one whose soul is desire, who can assume any form at will, full of longing, and captivating to those with desire.
Having enjoyed all desires like another Kāmarāja,
the king shines constantly, surrounded by other kings and horses.

Having performed [rites] and recited [mantras] in a field of merit, at a great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha), near a holy tree, this proud man becomes worthy of honor even by the King of the World of Yama. 45.
One who is always victorious in this world shines upon the planes of accomplishment (siddhibhūmi);
yet, without human birth, such accomplishment is again exceedingly difficult to obtain. (Note: *siddhi* is the reading in the manuscript; *siddha* is the emendation. 46.
Because it bestows the direct experience of enjoyment for all the worlds in a most enchanting garden strewn with blossoming flowers. (47)

When the quarters of the sky are filled with the fragrance of blossoming kunda flowers, one should perform the recitation at the foot of a tree, or else, having placed one's hand upon one's own head. (48)
Having assumed the form of a Gandharva and becoming skilled in song and dance,
he made the Gandharvas and Kinnaras his followers, both in that world and likewise here on earth.
Having attained supreme bliss consisting of the sphere of song, dance, and so forth, he then rejoices in that delightful state composed of bliss by virtue of His grace. (50)

Having performed [the ritual] and recited [the mantra] always for the Goddess at the boundary-land of the world of the Nāgas, in forests, or in mountain caves, one shall bring all the Nāgas under one's control. || 51 ||

Together with them—[the reading "together with them" (taiḥ saha) is supported by the principal manuscript]—that wise person rejoices both in that world and here, enjoying manifold pleasures established in the realm of the Nāgas. (52)
When a man, while beholding another's property, maintains pure vision and, having performed [the rite] and recited [the mantra], attains through Dharma the imperishable world. || 53 ||
Having brought those very beings under his control, that hero rejoices perpetually both in that world and here, amidst the activities of gods and asuras. || 54 ||

In whatever great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) one may be, by performing [the rite] and reciting [the mantra] while gazing at the sun during the solar transit, one becomes possessed of great splendor and destroys the darkness of the disease of worldly existence. || 55 ||
The sun, the progenitor, rises both in the solar world and here on earth;
likewise, having brought all under his control in the forest, the self-controlled one shall lead the world into subjection.
One who constantly bathes in the waters of the Puṇyanadī (the "Merit River"), or at its edge, or even within it, who always drinks from it and dwells by it; || 57 ||

Having performed [the rite] and recited [the mantra], the wise man, by the grace of those [sages] both there in the world known as that of the Brahman-sages and here [on earth], rejoices with the Brahman-sages. (58)
He enjoys enjoyments preceded by the resonance of Brahman, accompanied by Brahmin-sages; endowed with great and exceedingly pure prosperity that is truly brahmic. (59)
The king, who dwells in the royal palace of horses, shines constantly in the holy temple of the deity and likewise in the house of perpetual worship.
The deities accept [offerings] made in a temple of the deities, in a garden situated near one's own home, and in an exceedingly beautiful house. (61)
One should constantly invoke [the deities] there and worship them with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other offerings;
one should recognize the gods to be present there through the power of their proximity.
In a place equal to the abodes of the gods, adorned with divine splendor, secluded, exceedingly pure, and auspicious with masses of perfumes and incense; (63)
On a highly meritorious pedestal for the deity, adorned with lamps, mirrors, bells, and heaps of flowers, and likewise in a very lofty house. (64)
Having performed [the ritual] and recited [the mantra], O Goddess, a man shall always bring others under his control;
and a man endowed with the power of meditative visualization (bhāvanā) becomes divine in this world. 65.
He plays like a god; he is a god possessing divine enjoyments and divine pastimes.
He has divine vision, a divine form, and dwells in divine enjoyments. (66)
Honored by the gods, that proud man shall roam upon the earth like a god,
traveling in celestial vehicles preceded by elephants and horses.

Having performed [the rite] and chanted [the mantra] in a temple of Śiva, in a sacred field of Śiva, or in the vicinity of a Śivaliṅga, one who delights in Śiva will likewise abide in the world of Śiva and in this world as well. (68)
The yogi, ever disciplined, rejoices constantly with the servants of Śiva in the highly meritorious field of Viṣṇu, in the abode of Viṣṇu, and in its vicinity. (69)

Having resorted to the Vaiṣṇava state, performed [the rite], and recited [the mantra], the practitioner brings the Vaiṣṇavas under his control, both in the world of Viṣṇu and likewise here on earth. (70)
He rejoices constantly, pure like another Viṣṇu himself;
on the seat of Viṣṇu, supreme perfection is attained, which immediately bestows divinity. (71)

[Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Practice and the Majesty of the Worship of the Virgin (Kumārī)," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 24 ||
[Chapter Twenty-five] Īśvara said:
The holy fields shall now be described; listen to me regarding them according to their primary importance.
A field of merit, the bank of a river, a cave, or a mountain peak. || 1 ||
Sacred sites, the confluence of rivers, purifying forests, secluded gardens, the foot of a bilva tree, and the slope of a mountain. (2)
A grove of Tulasī, a cow-pen, a temple of Śiva devoid of a bull, the roots of an Aśvattha or Āmalakī tree, a cow-shed, and the midst of water—[these are auspicious]. || 3 ||
A temple, the shore of the ocean, one’s own home,
the presence of spiritual teachers, and likewise a place where the mind is one-pointed.
A secluded place devoid of animals is declared to be the best of all;
indeed, whatever man performs worship in such a secluded spot, [attains the highest merit].
O Goddess, when one offers to her an auspicious leaf, flower, fruit, or water,
due to the abundance of faith and devotion and the profusion of ritual materials for worship, [the merit is great].
Likewise, by worshipping here in this secluded place, there shall be the presence of the Goddess;
worship performed in Vārāṇasī always bestows the full fruit.
Twice that [merit] is said to be obtained in the presence of Puruṣottama;
and twice even more than that is said to be obtained specifically in Dvāravatī.
In all fields and sacred seats (pīṭhas), worship is equal to that at Dvāravatī;
it is said to be a hundredfold on the Vindhya mountains, and equal to that on the Gaṅgā as well.
In Āryāvarta, in Madhyadeśa, and likewise in Brahmāvarta [the reading "Hmadesha" appears in manuscript *ka*],
worship yields fruit just as it does at Prayāga and Puṣkara, even on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains.
Beyond that, it is said that the water of the Karatoyā river yields four times the merit;
and from that, O Pārvatī, the Nandikuṇḍa yields four times the fruit again.
Then, four times that [number] is said to be [the merit] in the presence of Jalpeśvara;
there, at the Yoni of Siddheśvarī, it is considered twice even that.
Thereafter, it is said that [the merit] is fourfold on the waters of the Lauhitya River;
it is equal to that at Kāmarūpa, and everywhere, both in water and on land.
Just as Viṣṇu is the most excellent of all, and just as Lakṣmī is the highest of all,
so too is the worship of the Goddess praised in Kāmarūpa, the abode of the gods.
The sacred field of the Goddess Kāmarūpa exists; there is nothing else equal to it.
Elsewhere the Goddess is rare, but in Kāmarūpa she is in every house. (15)
Then, it is said that [the merit] on the summit of Nīlakūṭa is a hundredfold;
even greater than that, it is said to be twofold at the Śivaliṅga of Hāraka.
Twice that [merit] is said to be obtained by one’s own kin;
and a hundred times that is said to be obtained within the maṇḍala of the womb of Kāmākhyā.
Whoever has performed the worship of the Great Goddess even once at Kāmākhyā— || 17 ||
He obtains his desires in this world and the nature of auspiciousness in the next;
there is no other equal to him, and no enemy exists for him. (18)
He attains his desired object and is born with a long life;
his movement shall be unimpeded by others, like that of the wind. (19)
He indeed becomes invincible in battle and in philosophical debate;
for she is proclaimed to be the root-form of the Great Goddess, in the form of the womb. (20)
Having worshipped that Goddess there, one is not subject to rebirth;
it is declared to be a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) and must never be disclosed.
The Goddess said:
"In battle, during childbirth, in fear of disease, and likewise in times of calamity—what should be done then, O Mahādeva? Tell me that here."
Īśvara said: For the foremost of practitioners, there is no impurity, nor is there any fear of disease;
for those who are pure and devoted to the practice of dharma, whence could the arising of calamities come? (23)
O Goddess, if an obstacle should arise due to the binding force of past karma, then at that very moment, O Supreme Sovereign, the wise practitioner should perform this rite. (24)
Incense, flowers, incense smoke, lamps, and food offerings—worship that is devoid of these does not bestow auspiciousness. (25)
Then, having performed the offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), one should worship the deities of the cakras;
one should fully worship the eight-cornered, the three-cornered, or the bindu-shaped [mandalas]. (26)
Having done thus, one should recite the vidyā, offer it, and then dismiss it;
by giving food to a young maiden, one shall become a partaker of the complete fruit. || 27 ||
Alternatively, one should contemplate oneself as being composed of that [reality] through the state of non-duality;
endowed with the state of non-duality, one’s body is made into the triple-city (tripurīkṛta). (This is the reading in manuscript Kha. || 28 ||
One should worship the Goddess within one's very self with the ritual offerings according to the prescribed rule;
for the machine known as one's own body is the most auspicious of all machines.
Having made Ānanda his heart through the placement (nyāsa) of the syllables, and having praised the gurus according to the rule, the person should recite the vidyā with undistracted mind. (30)
With garlands of fragrant flowers and ornaments of golden jewelry,
he was smooth, very sweet, capable of assuming any form at will, and captivating.
Having established great auspiciousness within his body through gentle speech and a smile,
he took recourse in the practice of non-violence and remained devoted to the welfare of all living beings.
One should always abide in one's own true nature and move about on earth like a god;
with a mind undisturbed by sorrows and free from longing for pleasures. (33)
Free from passion, fear, and anger, and devoid of mind and ego,
one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) in front of a woman at night, and not otherwise.
When mental satisfaction has arisen, even when surrounded by lions and tigers or when facing the arrival of an enemy army, one should perform the mental worship.
Or even when bound in prison, one who is devoid of materials for worship [is saved];
this is the supreme secret, this is the great means of securing well-being.
One should carefully guard this divine, unsurpassed sequence of worship, which consists of mantra and Veda, is pure, and bestows all spiritual accomplishments. (37)
It bestows knowledge, grants desires, is most excellent, and produces immediate conviction;
it must never be given to just anyone, nor ever to an atheist.
"By knowing this, the knower immediately becomes supreme at that very moment.
The Goddess said: "How can there be a vision of the worlds for people in the world of mortals? (39)
"Therefore, O Mahādeva, tell me [of them] according to the distinctions of regions and countries.
Īśvara said:
"Among humans, Bhārata is the most excellent; and therein lies the meritorious land. (40)
The worlds devoted to merit are superior; among them, the man of knowledge is distinguished.
But those devoid of both knowledge and merit, who are intent only on enjoyment, are like Piśācas.

Barbarians, who are like beasts and dwell in the realm of the departed, know by means of valid cognition that "that exists," yet they do not strive for it. (The reading *jānanti* is found in the Kha manuscript.)
He enjoys various kinds of pleasures, equal in extent to the world of mortals;
he knows not what is fit or unfit to be eaten, nor what ought or ought not to be done. (43)
They perform sacrifices according to improper rites, preceded by enjoyments consisting of honey;
yet again, O Goddess of Gods, in this world they are measured by the standards of night-stalkers (demons).
In this world, life itself is merely wealth; one who is intent on the acquisition of wealth and accumulates it, yet remains excluded from both giving and enjoyment, [lives in vain]. (45)
But the person who dwells solely upon the genitals and the belly, regarding the world of Yakṣas as his standard, is honored in the world of Yakṣas. (46)

In a region consisting of righteous conduct, one who dwells in righteous conduct is honored in the world of the ancestors, being free from disease, possessed of beauty, and enjoying worldly pleasures. (47)
In the highly meritorious Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), which is graced by the celestial river,
he was an expert in various sacrifices through the relationship of the worshipped and the worshipper.
One whose inner organ is pure, who is wise, and who indicates the world of men—[this applies] to the pure movement of the black antelope, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (49)
The enjoyer, devoted solely to giving and sensual enjoyment, constantly performs all those duties consisting of the Śruti and Smṛti that ought to be done. (50)
One should wander in the world like a god, possessing the measure of the divine realm;
then, upon the seat of her who consists of the three qualities, she is the remover of the three qualities (an alternative reading says: "the giver of freedom from the three qualities"). || 51 ||
In the presence of the Great Goddess, whether in a place of great merit, in secret, or even in public,
[one should worship] with those who are either devoid of joy or full of joy, appearing in the forms of the South and the North.

Whether the yogi is not of that nature or is of that nature, or is even joined with worldly enjoyment, he shall become free from the three qualities (niṣtraiguṇya), O Goddess, by the grace of Mahādevī. (53)

[Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Worship during Times of Adversity at the Auspicious Seats," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 25 ||
[The Twenty-sixth Chapter] The Goddess said:
"What kind of person should a disciple be, and what kind of person should a guru be?"
Of what nature might initiation be, and how should one perform it? Tell me, O Lord.
Īśvara said:
Now, out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, I shall explain initiation (dīkṣā),
since without it there can be no fruit from any mantra whatsoever.
Because it bestows divine knowledge and because it effects the destruction of sin, it is called *dīkṣā*; I shall now describe to you the teacher and the disciple.
In the beginning, this imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
the Blessed One, having become the Guru, indeed bestows the Great Vidyā.
Then that divine guru, the Ṛṣi, having revealed the divine Vidyā, made his disciples the Divine Currents (Divyaugha). Listen now, O Pārvatī, as I describe them:
Prakāśa, then Vimarśa, and another, Ānanda. (5)
Due to the difference in names, I manifested in the world with a divine form;
from those [three] three were born, and they are indeed the three Siddhas.
"Knowledge, truth, and fullness"—thus they were addressed by the illustrious mouth [of the Lord].
They are divine and eternally present near me, both here on earth and elsewhere as well.
They dwelt there, and from them three were likewise born, known by the names Svabhāva, Pratibha, and Subhaga (according to the reading *svaka* in the manuscript).
Those who are identical with my own self dwell perpetually upon this very earth;
they all possess serene countenances and are endowed with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
These [deities] have two eyes and two arms, endowed with graceful forms;
likewise, those headed by Ānandanātha are designated as Māyā, Lakṣmī, and so forth.
The nine [names] have nine distinct names consisting of nine syllables each;
through their conjunction with the seven-syllable [mantra], each becomes sixteen syllables long.
Those sixteen eternal forms should be known in their proper sequence;
O fair-faced one, Vimalā and Jayinī are to be worshipped in the center in this manner.
The two [names] obtained through synonyms are "attained" (prāpta) and "obtained in time" (kālāvāpta);
another is well-known externally as "the one from outside" (bāhyataḥ). These are the three names for the practitioner (sādhaka). // 13 //
Having assumed a human form and knowing the reality of the meaning of all tantras, I myself wander about for the sake of introducing [beings] to the mantras and tantras. 14.
A Guru who is a Śākta leads to supernatural powers (ṛddhi), while one other than that bestows the opposite;
such a Guru is endowed with all virtues and possesses a mind untouched by defects.
Free from disease, not too old, eloquent, and speaking clearly;
handsome, with a pleasant countenance, pure, free from greed, and well-versed in many mantras. (16)
Free from doubt, he is the master in severing doubts and in exercising restraint and favor;
he is beyond dualities, devoid of ego, truthful in speech, and firm in his vows.
One who knows the duties of each stage of life, is free from envy, pure, not given to excessive counsel, eloquent, and devoted to recitation and worship; || 18 ||
He is a knower of the meaning of all tantras, compassionate, and non-violent;
he is content with whatever comes by chance, peaceful, observant of vows, and upright. (19)
Speaking preceded by a smile, clarity, acting without delusion, contentment, absence of pride, lack of greed, and blamelessness. (20)

Impartiality (or independence, according to another reading), lack of greed, desire for [the pupil's] welfare, gravity, and speaking what is beneficial—one who possesses such qualities should be known as a teacher; any other brings suffering to the disciple. (21)
Endowed with his former qualities as was fitting, he was exceedingly sweet-spoken;
with a pure body and face, wearing clean garments, he was pure.
He was averse to censuring others and to visiting the sight of deities; he was free from longing for the food of others, for women, or for the oppression of the earth.
Endowed with compassion for all people, acting with discernment, having conquered the senses, a believer, devoted to the guru, pure, and of very firm resolve. (24)
Free from greed, possessing steady friendliness, taking the words of the guru as authoritative, and always maintaining firm devotion toward the guru, the mantra, and the deity; 25.
A disciple should be of such a nature; otherwise, he causes suffering to the guru.
Having determined the time for initiation during an auspicious moment free from defects, [the guru should proceed]. (26)
The disciple, being composed, should take refuge in the Guru for the sake of grace;
showing reverence, he should say, "Be gracious, O Lord, O God," and likewise, "So be it. (27)

Having prostrated, he should sit at the side; likewise, he should move about with permission. He should attend upon [the teacher] while looking toward his face and perform whatever is commanded with reverence. (28)
One should not speak untruth before him, nor should one engage in excessive chatter;
likewise, one should avoid lust, anger, greed, pride, laughter, and flattery. (29)
Fleeting actions, matters concerning Brahmins, lamentation, the giving of debts, as well as the taking [of debts], and the buying and selling of goods. || 30 ||
A disciple should never act [in opposition] toward the guru;
for the guru is Śiva himself in person—therefore, one should praise, bow down to, and serve him. (31)
As it is with the deity, so it is with the mantra; as it is with the mantra, so it is with the guru;
as it is with the guru, so it is with one's own self—such is the sequence of devotion, O Dear One.
But he who, disregarding the word of his guru, acts according to his own intellect, shall never attain success through mantras or the worship of deities. (33)
One should certainly perform his worship with the mantra as prescribed, [offering] a seat, a bed, clothing, ornaments, and likewise sandals. (34)
One should honor the teacher’s shadow, his wife, and whatever else belongs to him; as well as the teacher’s bed, seat, throne, sandals, umbrella, and shoes. (35)
One should never step over bath-water or a shadow;
upon seeing one's guru, one should become joyful, overflowing with supreme bliss. (36)
Extremely terrified, with eyes trembling, he beheld the lotus feet;
having joyfully offered all his possessions, he then carried out what was commanded.
One should perform [this] with every effort so that he may be pleased;
having prostrated once like a staff before the guru, regarding him as one's chosen deity. (38)
With all his limbs bristling with horripilation, he shall obtain the fruit of ten million acts of worship;
whatever object is most dear to him, he should offer that to Him with devotion. (39)
He who, on this earth, makes anything whatsoever his own without having first given it to his guru, shall become a master of the Yoginīs. (40)
Whatever object is obtained through begging or by other means, one should respectfully eat it oneself only after offering it and receiving his instruction. 41.
For this alone is what must be done by true disciples as repayment to the guru:
that, with a pure disposition, they surrender themselves entirely to the guru. (42)
The state of being a teacher and that of being a disciple [are determined] by the duration of one year;
she should cause him to incur the fault committed by herself, and a wife [should transfer] her own sin to her husband.
Likewise, the sin acquired by the disciple certainly reaches the guru;
indeed, a true guru should examine the disciple within his own hermitage for one year.
Then the wise man, being well-composed, should contemplate the time for initiation;
initiation during the autumn season or in Vaiśākha bestows the most excellent fruit. (45)
Initiation in the months of Phālguna, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Jyeṣṭha is considered middling;
those in Āṣāḍha and the month of Māgha are esteemed as the lowest by the virtuous.
Śrāvaṇa, Caitra, Pauṣa, and Bhādrapada are censured;
yet, even during these censured months, initiation is declared auspicious if it occurs during an eclipse.
On the equinoxes and solstices, during the month of Āṣāḍha, on the festival of Madana (the spring festival),
and during an eclipse of either the sun or the moon— that day shall be fruitful.
A wise person should begin the recitation of mantras during the bright fortnight on an auspicious day;
it should be performed on a Sunday, a Thursday, a Friday, a Monday, or a Wednesday. (49)
The full moon day, the fifth, the second, the seventh, as well as the thirteenth and the tenth, are praised and grant all desires. (50)
On a day pure in its five limbs, during the rising of one's own [natal] sign and star, when Jupiter and Venus are rising, the ascendant is pure, and it is adorned by the twelve [planets]. || 51 ||
O beloved, when the moon and stars are favorable and the zodiacal sign is stable, initiation is auspicious;
that initiation is of three kinds: Māntrī, Śāktī, and Śāmbhavī.

Initiation through mantra (māntrī-dīkṣā) is said to be that which is performed by means of mantras, worship, the seat, the locus, meditation, yoga, and so forth, according to the form prescribed in the scriptures.
When the Siddhas, having perceived their own power, perform initiation for a disciple by means of that power alone and without external means, this is proclaimed as the Śākta initiation.
Even without any ulterior intention on the part of both teacher and disciple,
it brings about the manifestation of Śiva-nature solely through the grace of the Guru.

But the remaining Śāmbhavī initiation causes the immersion into Śiva; through it, universal knowledge arises from ignorance, and there is protection from the bondage of saṃsāra. (Note: *śeṣā* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
Since a mantra is said to be that which brings about complete accomplishment,
then one should perform the ritual acquisition of the ground as previously described by me to you.

One should perform the extraction of the arrow-head and other [foreign objects] according to the sacrificial injunctions, preceded by auspicious rites and the chanting of the Vedas by the Brahmins. (Note: The reading "yājñe" is supported by the variant "yājñīka.")
One should offer an oblation to Vāstu and likewise construct a mandala;
for the attainment of all auspiciousness, one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Having determined the time at least seven days in advance, the Guru should worship the Supreme Deity with a mantra favorable to the disciple. (60)

At night, the preceptor should indeed offer the prescribed oblations to them according to the ritual procedure, using names beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*, [specifically] the names of the Lords of Night (*rātrīśa*).
One should perform worship at night and also worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas),
each presiding over their respective banner and resplendent with their respective colors.
Having offered an oblation of milk-rice to them, the preceptor should pray to them,
holding a vessel of water joined with a continuous stream and consecrated by those respective mantras.
O Goddess of gods, having placed [the image] upon his head, he should follow it in circumambulation;
at the outset, the Guru, with undivided mind, should protect the divine sacrifice.
May the gods, together with Śakra and the others, who have been thus honored and gratified, protect the sky (or the monastery);
may the world-protectors be well-pleased; homage be to you! 65.
On the evening prior to the taking of the bride, he should dwell with his teacher and others for the night, observing the prescribed rules. (66)
According to the prescribed rites, he constructed a beautiful pavilion, adorned with a lovely altar in its center,
crowded with banners and flags, and decorated with canopies and other ornaments.
It was adorned with rows of lamps of the smokeless, peaceful, perfectly awakened Buddha;
it was honored with flowers, unbroken grains, fruits, jars, parched grain, and rays of light. (The reading "arci" is found in the Ravi manuscript.)
It was adorned on all sides with garlands of tree sprouts,
enclosed by plantain trunks, and decorated with betel-nut trees.
O lady of excellent countenance, one should purify that house, the wheel-king, and likewise the child with the five products of the cow, using the root mantra consecrated [with it]. (70)
Having made equal portions of the five products of the cow, one should purify them;
having consecrated them with the root mantra, one should purify them with the tips of *kuśa* grass.
By that, there shall be complete purification and the eradication of all sins;
even having committed the various great transgressions (mahāpātaka), if one drinks the products of the cow (gavya), [one is cleansed]. 72.
The knowers of the Vedas say that [it] destroys [all sins] by the mere drinking [of it].
[One should initiate] the disciple who has bathed well, is dressed in clean garments, and possesses a steady mind. (73)
Having established [the disciple] at a distance according to the rule, the Guru should perform sacrifice daily;
he should offer oblations in the consecrated fire with milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in sweet substances. || 74 ||

The preceptor, having duly worshipped the Supreme Deity in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and having tied his topknot with the root mantra alone, [should then approach] the child who has gone to the bed.
Relying upon the Dream-Man, one should cause the head to sleep first. The mantra is stated as: *Tāra* (Oṃ), *hili* twice, followed by *śūlapāṇaye* and *dviṭha*. (76)
This mantra for the Dream-Man is proclaimed for recitation at bedtime:
"Obeisance to the unborn, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul. (77)
Salutations to Rāma, who possesses the universal form and is the lord of dreams;
tell me the truth regarding all matters in their entirety within my dream.
"O Maheśvara, by your grace I shall accomplish the success of my rite;
having prayed to the Lord at the time of sleep with the mantra, one should then go to sleep. (Note: "svapi" is an alternative reading found in manuscript *kha*.)

In the morning, the preceptor should ask the child about whatever auspicious or inauspicious things were seen in the dream; or, having performed worship to the preceptor, the child, fasting and with senses subdued, [should report them]. (80)
Having gone to a bed of darbha grass at night, one should report whatever dream is seen:
a maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, a lamp, a palace, a lotus, or a river.
Saffron, a bull, a garland, gold, a fruit-bearing tree, a mountain, a sacrificial horse, raw meat, and spirituous liquor. 82.
Having seen all such things as these, one may attain accomplishment;
[but one should avoid seeing] a caṇḍāla, a donkey, a crow, a pit, an empty place, or anything inauspicious. (83)
If a man sees a naked person smeared with oil, a dry thorny tree, or the roof-terrace of a palace, he shall contract a disease. (84)
Upon seeing a bad dream, one shall attain success through the fire-oblation (homa).
One should declare it auspicious if it is auspicious; if it is inauspicious, one should perform a hundred oblations.
This is the procedure taught in sequence for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the disciple’s bed, performed with the Astra-mantra. 85.

[Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Initiation and the Characteristics of the Guru and Others," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 26 ||
[The Twenty-seventh Chapter] Īśvara said:
Now, having completed the daily morning rites according to the previous [instructions],...
Having worshipped the gods and the ancestors with garments, ornaments, and decorations. || 1 ||
The disciple, well-adorned, observing silence, and decorated with flowers and sandalwood paste, should choose the preceptor with devotion and also honor the Brahmins. (2)
Accompanied by various auspicious musical instruments and preceded by the chanting of the Vedas,
as well as by the auspicious blessings of women and likewise those of the Brahmins.
Satisfied by hymns accompanied by shouts of victory, his mind purified,
[he beheld the temple] beautiful with rows of garlands of lamps and perfumed with various incenses.
O Goddess, the Guru should enter the pavilion according to the prescribed rite as before;
having performed the other [preliminary] rites as before, he should sit down upon his seat.
Likewise, O fair-faced one, having prepared another [image] with saffron,
O lady of noble hips, [place it] upon the altar, or else with the powder of vermilion.

When the Cakrarāja [or *Cakrarāja*, as the reading in manuscript Ka] has been drawn, and upon it, in its center, a layer of *darbha* grass has been spread, one should place a well-characterized vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or clay. (7)
O Goddess of the Suras, having thoroughly washed the pitcher— which measures thirty-two finger-breadths in both width and height— with the Astra mantra, [one should proceed].
It was filled with divine substances such as sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, gorocana, and saffron, and was wrapped in a pair of garments.
Having placed within it nine gems, [he should offer] a new [seat] pleasing to the eye, adorned with flower garlands and the like, smeared with curd and sandalwood paste.
Madayantī, sahadevī, dūrvā, and likewise ashes,
as well as the seven types of earth, should be placed together with five sprouts.
The Guru, having strewn barley and flowers with the thought that they are celestial trees, [should place it] surrounded on all sides by most enchanting red threads.
Having established [the fire] with the root mantra, one should worship it beginning with the support (ādhāra);
one should worship that [fire], which is the form of the fire-maṇḍala, together with its constituent parts (kalās). || 13 ||
In that manner, one should worship a pitcher consisting of the sun with its digits there;
likewise, one should worship water consisting of the moon with its digits.
These three fires are proclaimed; they are traditionally held to be of the nature of that [flame].
Having filled one's joined palms with flowers, one should offer them into those very [fires]. 15.

If the flower falls in the directions of the West, North-West, North, or East, it is auspicious; if it falls in an inauspicious direction, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the Astra-mantra for the sake of pacification.

Then, having performed the unsurpassed [rite] in due order according to the previously stated procedure, and having worshipped and offered oblations according to the rules with the thought that the preceptor is a deity; || 17 ||
Having worshipped the Aṅgāvṛtis and then cooked the sacrificial porridge (caru),
one should offer one portion to Mahādevī and subsequently sacrifice the remainder into the fire.

Having properly meditated upon the Great Goddess as the primary object of focus, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter mixed with the three sweets into a well-kindled fire.
That person who offers oblations into a fire that lacks flames or one that is not well-kindled becomes weak of digestion, afflicted by disease, or short-lived. || 20 ||
Therefore, one who desires health, long life, and ultimate prosperity should offer oblations only when the fire is well-kindled, and never when it is not kindled. (21)
Likewise, the ignorant person who offers oblations into a fire that is accompanied by smoke becomes blind,
and the sacrificer, along with his sons, perishes.
One should not offer oblations into a fire that is merely kindled, nor into one that is not yet well-fueled;
rather, for the successful completion of the rite, oblations should be offered into a fire that is blazing and licking upward with its flames.

Having offered oblations to Maheśānī, who is the embodiment of consciousness, and having immediately thereafter completed the previously mentioned ritual, the Guru, filled with youthful exuberance, should perform the rite.
Having summoned the disciple with effort and covered his face with a cloth, he should sprinkle him with special arghya water according to the prescribed rite.
O Goddess, ocean of compassion in the Vinaya, refuge of all prosperity;
O Mother, protector of your child, show mercy toward this infant. (26)
O Goddess of the gods, O support of compassion, O Sovereign, show mercy to this wretched man who has been bound by nooses headed by Aśiṣāṇa. 27.
Let him be bound by worldly and otherworldly enjoyments;
let all his devotion be offered to him, the refuge of the partless.
Having thus petitioned the Great Goddess within the lotus of his heart, he should cause the disciple to hear [the mantra], contemplating, "I am the divine Śiva. (29)
The Guru should cause [the disciple] to hear the divine Siddhānta, which dispels internal darkness,
wherein the entire universe— both stationary and moving— is composed of the thirty-six principles.
And the body also arises from that [consciousness]; therein Śiva exists in two ways:
Śiva when enveloped by the sheaths is the individual soul (jīva), while the one free from sheaths is the Supreme Śiva. || 31 ||
The knowledge of the Self has been proclaimed as the supreme human goal by those who know the Self;
O Great Goddess, the letters of the alphabet are celebrated as eternal sounds. (32)
The power of mantras is declared here to be indeed inconceivable;
thorough knowledge of the tradition from the gurus is what bestows accomplishment. (33)
It is said that through faith in the words of the Guru, all accomplishment is attained;
and in this regard, the authority is established within oneself—this is what is proclaimed as faith. (34)
O Pārvatī, by contemplating the oneness of the gurus, the mantras, and even the deities, as well as of the mind and the vital breath; || 35 ||
Know this, O Pārvatī, as the thorough knowledge of the inner self;
one should contemplate that bliss, which is the form of Brahman, within the body. (Note: *dehe* is the reading in the Ka-pāṭha.)
Its five manifestors, beginning with the letter *ma*, have been proclaimed;
through them alone is its worship performed, and success comes through secrecy, not otherwise. (37)
And because of manifestation (the reading *prakṭā* for *prākaṭyācca*), one should conceal [the teaching] from fear, as one would [conceal] a mother’s lover;
through the firmness of the cultivation of non-duality, the attainment of the Command (*ājñāsiddhi*) is proclaimed. (38)
One should not revile the right [hand] nor the left; one should not revile various philosophical views. One should never even count those who commit acts of reviling, malice, and the like. (39)
O Goddess, the disclosure of the secret is for a true disciple (or female disciple, as per the Kha reading) alone, and not for others;
one should always be intent upon the pursuit of knowledge with a disposition of Śiva. 40.
Lust, anger, as well as greed, pride, and delusion, likewise violence, theft, and envy—whatever is censured in the worlds. (41)
A wise person should always avoid hatred toward women and the like;
the teacher alone is his god, and he should always worship him alone.
Without doubt, freedom from possessiveness is considered the ideal state in all circumstances;
one should abandon action that is devoid of fruit, for it is indeed impermanent. (43)

But when even these five are not obtained, there should always be constant reflection on the sequence; and freedom from fear toward everything should be known [to exist] in one who is dear to all the Viṣṇus. 44.
For here, the Hotṛ priest is the Self itself, and the object to be purified is the Self;
O lady of excellent vows, there is no fruit anywhere that surpasses the attainment of the Self. (45)
O Pārvatī, this supreme command of Śiva has been declared to you;
all the sciences, beginning with the Vedas, have been revealed by it as if by a courtesan.
Indeed, this knowledge is concealed within all philosophical systems;
the wise man should be initiated therein in every way for the sake of the manifestation of his own self. (47)

Then, having visualized his own red and white feet upon the region of the disciple’s head, one should imagine his body as being washed and augmented. (Note: *mā* is the reading in the manuscript; *māṃ* is a variant. 48.
Then the noble-minded Guru should cause [the energy] to flow with those nectars from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), blazing with the brilliance of fire. 49.
The supreme [goddess], who possesses the brilliance of ten million suns, the radiance of ten million moons, pure, and the burner of the fuel of ignorance. (50)
With those very rays, he should burn away the bonds of his sins;
having resolved "I am Śiva," he should gaze with a compassionate eye (the reading *karuṇadravā* is found in manuscript *kha*).
Completely liberated from all sins and devoid of all defects,
the Guru himself becomes Śiva, his mind free from doubt.
With the hand of Śiva, the yogi should touch the disciple’s head while reciting the mantra according to the prescribed sequence; having entered the body of the disciple, he [should perform the rite].
Having grasped his own self, the Guru should unite it with [the disciple's] self;
having himself become the embodiment of the mantra, he should transfer [it] with devotion through the mind.
On the golden pericarp [is] the syllable *hauḥ*; on the eight filaments are the pairs of vowels;
on the eight petals situated in the directions are the eight groups of consonants joined with the *vaṃ* syllables. (55)

O Goddess, having respectfully seated [the deity] upon a pure square seat consisting of the king of yantras of the Mātṛkās, [one should bathe it] with the stream of nectar from the jar. (The reading "kā kapāṭhaḥ" is noted. 56.

The supreme preceptor should cause [the disciple] to bathe with the root-mantras and the three [limbs], and having clothed him in silk garments, he should anoint him with sandalwood paste and other unguents. (57)
Having adorned his disciple or son as was available, and having seated him by his side—being serene and tranquil in mind—the teacher [proceeds]. (58)

Having performed the placement of the *mātṛkās* upon his limbs, the preceptor himself should then perform the placement of the limbs of the *vidyā* upon the hand of the disciple who has removed the cloth from his face. (59)
Having considered the respective qualifications [of the recipients], one should reveal the various substances;
otherwise, there would be a total loss [of merit] due to revealing them to those who are unfit. (60)
One should cause the food to be offered with the mantras of reality and the *grāsamudrā*.
Then the Guru, with a serene mind, [should recite] his own supreme [mantra] as previously described. (61)
Having first fashioned the sandals together with Bālā, one should offer them;
one should impart Bālā into the right ear, and afterwards, one should announce the desired object.
O Pārvatī, having placed one's own foot upon the head of the child,
[one should impart] all the mantras either once or in their proper sequence according to the rule.

Having performed [the rites] according to one's authority, and having touched the child's hand upon his own limbs, he should touch some part of the child's body, such as the *mātṛkā* [mantras] and so forth.
The father-guru should give a name consisting of two, three, or even four syllables, ending with the word "Ānandanātha."

Then, having instructed him in the rules of conduct (*ācāra*), the Guru himself should touch the consciousness within his heart with the three *kūṭas*, and having wiped that limb three times, [he should do so] with the three [syllables], O Brahmin. (Note: *anvaśiṣyat* is the reading in manuscript *ka*; *parāmṛśet* is the reading in manuscript *ka*. 66.

Having embraced him thus and respectfully smelled his head, one should then transform the disciple into one's own form and contemplate him as complete. (The reading "pūrṇī" is found in manuscript Pā.)
Then the teacher, being of noble intellect and serene mind, should recite the vidyā one thousand and eight times so as not to suffer a loss of his own power. (68)
Having achieved his purpose and fulfilled his duty, he should, according to the extent of his wealth,
abandon stinginess regarding his resources as well as pride and delusion.
One should satisfy one's own guru with elephants, horses, chariots, and other vehicles, as well as male and female servants, cattle, land, gold, clothing, and so forth. (70)
Whatever substance is in the ear of Kumbhakarṇa, as well as in the entire pavilion,
having offered wealth, life-breaths, and the body— all of it— to him.
Falling at his feet like a staff upon the ground, the man said:
"Salutations to you, O Blessed Lord, the Auspicious One in the form of the Guru."
Be gracious, O Abode of Compassion, toward me who am tormented by my own wretchedness; for in body, mind, and speech, I have no other refuge but you. (73)
May the supreme Goddess, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, be pleased with you. O son, fix your mind on her and remember her alone at all times.
"May there be no sense of duality for you; become composed of perfect bliss.
Having spoken thus, he greeted him with words of nectar, saying, "Arise! (75).
Raising him up with both hands, I said, "O beloved (variant reading:
O virtuous one), being pleased, may all perfections quickly be yours through my grace. (76)
Likewise, a disciple whose mind is serene, who has understood everything that is to be known,
and who is endowed with devotion and faith, should indeed feed the Kumārīs.
Then, having satisfied the Brahmins as well as the poor, the blind,
and the wretched with very sweet cooked foods, he should also feed his kinsmen.

One should satisfy them with various kinds of perfumes, flowers, and garlands; then, having received blessings from them, one should offer those which bring victory. (Note: *samarthīyāt* is the reading in manuscript *ka*; *jayāvahāḥ* is the reading in manuscript *ha*.)
Having received initiation from a true guru, he becomes a great upholder of the Great Vidyā;
he shall possess authority over all mantras and is born on earth as omniscient. (80)
[Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Procedure for Initiation," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 27 ||
[The Twenty-eighth Chapter] The Goddess said:
"Tell me the procedure for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) so that the perfection of the mantra may be attained."
Īśvara said:
Now I shall describe the procedures for the rite of *puraścaraṇa*.
Without which a mantra would not be perfected even in hundreds of years;
having received initiation from a guru according to the prescribed rule, the best of practitioners [should proceed]. (2)
In that very manner, one should daily worship the Goddess at dawn with undistracted mind,
remembering oneself as being composed of her, endowed with devotion and faith.
Having recited the mantra either one thousand and eight times, or up to fifty thousand times, one should then perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).

For the pacification of defects that are deficient or excessive, a person with a purified inner self, having received the command of the Guru, should recite [the mantra] eight times more than the prescribed number.
One should perform worship with effort out of a desire for the accomplishment of one's own mantra-vidyā,
O Pārvatī, for all mantras and vidyās whatsoever.
The command of the Guru alone shall be the root, since accomplishment comes through his command;
likewise, lack of faith and atheism are due to merit performed in a previous birth. (Variant reading in manuscript *kha*: "performed in a previous birth.")
O Goddess, three obstacles are said to exist regarding the accomplishment of mantras;
therefore, the practitioner of mantra should diligently perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for the destruction of those obstacles.
Out of the intoxication of wealth, he disregarded the mantra as well as the preliminary rites.
He should be known as a debtor to the mantra; for the sake of his peace, [the mantra] should be given to the people.
Just as a body devoid of life is incapable of any activity, so too is he. (10)
Even if a mantra is devoid of the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), it is proclaimed as such;
therefore, the wise practitioner of mantra should perform it by all means, or have it performed by his guru. 11.

In the absence of the Guru, a Brahmin who is devoted to the welfare of all living beings, whose inner heart is pure, and who is affectionate—especially through his garments—[should act as his representative]. (12)
One who knows the lineage and is learned in the family scriptures, having again performed the honoring of the preceptor and having received the vidyā once more, should then employ it. || 13 ||
At the outset, one should resort to a field of merit in order to perform the preliminary service,
on the fourteenth day, or the eighth, or at the moment of the new moon.
The commencement of the Goddess’s worship must be performed by the most excellent practitioners.
First, having fasted, then having performed his daily rites and being pure— || 15 ||

O Supreme Goddess, having worshipped the twice-born, the gods, and the gurus with devotion, one should likewise worship Gaṇeśa, the Mothers, and the ancestors. (Note: *mātṛkā* and *mātṛkāḥ* are both acceptable readings. 16.
Whether in a village, a city, a country, a town, or a port,
one should determine the location for the lamp in the name of the presiding deity of the field.
One should contemplate the place for the lamp in the field of Śakti and the field of Śiva;
O Goddess of beautiful eyes, one should fashion it as circular, in the shape of a tortoise.
Having divided that space into nine compartments, one should inscribe the letters;
the vowels in pairs, both in the cardinal directions and on the eight petals.
The 'a' group has been described, O Goddess; then the seven groups beginning with 'ka' should be written, O Goddess, in order starting from the east and ending with Kubera.
O Pārvatī, one should write the hundred-thousand-syllable [mantra] in the northeast corner of the grid known as the Kūrma;
know that the square in which the name of the field appears is its mouth.
O beautiful one, know that the pair of hands is located on the sides of the limbs;
then, O Goddess, the region of the two sides is called the location of the belly.
Then, O Goddess, two feet are proclaimed at the end, and the tail;
by means of the mouth, hundreds of desires are accomplished. (23)
O Maheśānī, [if it is] in the region of the throat, it causes the destruction of all undertakings;
in the belly, it brings suffering and poverty; and in the feet, it is said to cause loss.
If it is in the tail, there will be loss of wealth; thus have I spoken.
Taking recourse to a place for a lamp, one should perform recitation and worship. (25)
Having bowed to the Guru according to the prescribed rite as previously described,
one should take recourse to the rosary, which is the Mātṛkā in the form of phonemes.
The Praṇava, the Goddess Mātṛkā, and Māyā are the triad of nectars that bestow the perfection of mantras, are pure, and destroy the flood of all sins. (27)
Through the conjunction with the three nectars, even a corrupt mantra becomes effective;
furthermore, one made of pearls bestows the fruit of liberation of speech. (28)
It constantly bestows all accomplishments and brings all the worlds under one's control;
it may be made of pearls or likewise of crystal. (29)
A rosary of rudrākṣa beads bestows the infinite fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
a coral rosary, however, brings subjugation and accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings.
A garland fashioned from pure rubies bestows the fruit of sovereignty;
a garland produced from *putrajīva* seeds grants sons and grandsons. || 31 ||
Through a rosary of lotus seeds, great fortune and fame arise;
a garland of red sandalwood, moreover, grants subjugation and all prosperity.
A rosary made of large conch shells is recommended for heroes in rites such as killing and driving away; however, it does not bestow auspicious results for the other two [classes of practitioners].
One should construct [the maṇḍala] with five thousand or twenty-eight hundred [squares];
it should not be made with fewer or more, nor with seeds and so forth, for the sake of prosperity.
Among them, one Meru made of gross material should be given to all;
it is the first and the grossest, and from that, each subsequent one is successively smaller and more minute. (Note: *tataḥ* is the reading in the Kha manuscript.)
Therefore, one should place [the thread] in sequence, extending it in the form of a serpent;
likewise, for each seed-syllable situated therein, one should fashion a Brahma-knot.
Otherwise, a consecrated garland used for the rite of recitation becomes fruitless, even if it were made of rudrākṣa beads, indrākṣa beads, or likewise crystal beads. (37)
Nothing else should be inserted in the middle, such as putrajīva or similar seeds;
if one were to insert anything else in the rosary during the rite of recitation, [the mantra becomes ineffective]. (38)
He who always makes a rosary from seeds of a single species then falls into association with outcasts of evil deeds. (39)
In another birth, he is born as one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
having taken up the divine garland according to the previously described procedure.
Thereafter, endowed with the aforementioned yoga, one should begin the recitation;
remaining there, always pure, one should recite the vidyā exactly one hundred thousand times.
Curd, milk, cow's ghee, sugarcane products excluding jaggery, sesame seeds, white mung beans, and tubers excluding the kemuka; || 42 ||
The coconut fruit, as well as the plantain, the *lavaṅgī*, the mango, the *āmalaka*, the jackfruit, and the *harītakī*. (43)
The wise consider sacrificial food (haviṣya) to be highly recommended for other vows;
however, that which is not dedicated to Viṣṇu is unobtainable and is deemed inauspicious during those other vows.
Indeed, all that must be abandoned if one desires one's own success:
alkaline substances, salt, meat, garlic, and eating from bell-metal vessels. (45)
One should avoid black gram, adzukis, lentils, kodrava, and chickpeas;
likewise, betel nut, eating twice a day, quarreling, and negligence. (46)
One should avoid muttering prayers at night that contradict the Śruti and Smṛti; one should also observe sleeping on the ground, celibacy, silence, and freedom from envy. (47)
Daily bathing at the three periods of the day, avoidance of trivial activities, constant worship, constant giving, and the chanting of praises and hymns to the deities. (48)
Worship according to the specific signs, faith in the Guru and the Deity, and devotion to the recitation of mantras—these twelve are the duties that bestow success in mantra. (49)

One should avoid speaking with women, Śūdras, outcasts (patita), those who have fallen from their caste through neglect of initiation (vrātya), atheists, or those who have consumed the leavings of others; one should also avoid speaking untruths and speaking harsh words. 50.
One should not speak even with those who are truthful during recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth;
otherwise, everything performed becomes entirely fruitless.
One should always remain constantly free from desire through the actions of speech, mind, and body;
one should avoid hearing songs, dances, instrumental music, and the like, as well as watching dances.
One should completely avoid garlands, fragrant ointments, and the wearing of flowers; one should also avoid sexual intercourse, conversation about it, and social gatherings concerning it. (53)
A man performing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) should not engage in crookedness, shaving, oil massage, eating food that has not been offered, or harming living beings.
One should not touch women who have not bathed, nor likewise Śūdras or twice-born men who have not bathed;
one should also avoid massaging and other such acts that were not previously intended.

One should abandon bathing in warm water, as well as the use of fragrant substances such as *āmalaka* and the like; one should cleanse the body of Śiva, both externally and internally, with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
One should bathe with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) or with pure *āmalaka* alone;
provided one’s hands are not unpurified, nor is one naked, nor is one covered on the head. (Note: *apavitrakaraḥ* or *apavitrakalagnaḥ* is an alternative reading.)
Neither while seated, nor lying down, nor walking, nor standing up, nor on a street, nor in an inauspicious place, nor in a place of darkness, should one perform the recitation (japa). 58.
If one mutters while talking, it is said to be fruitless for that duration;
when a sound is uttered incorrectly, one should utter the *praṇava*. (59)
But when the word "pāmara" has been uttered, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) once;
and in the case of much idle chatter, having sipped water (ācamana) and performed the ritual placement of the limbs (nyāsa), one should then recite the mantra.
Upon seeing, speaking with, or hearing those who have fallen from their caste or those born of the lowest castes,
or upon sneezing, passing wind, or yawning, one should suspend the recitation of prayers.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should recite the remainder of the prayer, or else gaze upon the sun and other luminaries;
wearing always clean garments, he should lie down upon a bed of kuśa grass.
One should wash the bed every day and sleep alone without fear;
one performing the *puraścaraṇa* should observe such rules as these.
Having spoken thus, one should perform the recitation according to the stated number, neither too slowly nor too quickly, for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*.
Contemplating with his intellect the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra,
he should recite it with one-pointed mind from the morning until midday.
One should perform that which has been undertaken according to its prescribed number day by day;
if one performs it either less or more than that, the person becomes fallen from his vow.
The rule of uninterrupted continuity has been proclaimed; one must not let even a single day pass by.
From the transgression of a day, the loss of accomplishment arises for that person. (67)
Having recited the mantra over water, one should provide [the deity] Sulocana with drink;
then, according to the prescribed rule, one should worship the God at the three junctions of the day.
One should not recite the mantra alone at only one twilight or at both twilights;
staying in a single village, one should go and pay homage to the guru alone.

In this context, prostration with the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga) is indeed the worship of the deity; one should perform both the daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites, as well as maintain association with the virtuous.
If one is capable, one should perform the bath at the three periods of the day; otherwise, one may do it twice or even once.
Furthermore, one should first perform the bath in water belonging to another.

Upon completing the count, one should offer oblations into the consecrated fire in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) prepared according to the prescribed rules, using one's own substances in an amount equal to one-tenth of the total number of recitations.
Alternatively, having recited [the mantra] every day, one should perform oblations amounting to a tenth part of that;
likewise, having worshipped the deity in water, one should perform [oblations] amounting to a tenth part of the homa.
At the end of the mantra "tarpayāmi," one should perform the libation upon the head with water as prescribed.
Recitation, fire-offering, libation, purification, and the feeding of Brahmins [constitute the ritual]. 74.
One should perform each [rite] with a tenth part of the preceding one, consisting of five limbs:
one's own consecration (abhiṣeka), the rite for expiating sins (aghamarṣaṇa), the offering of water to the Sun (sūryārghya), and the drinking of water. 75.
Thereafter, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) ten times for each preceding [rite];
worship with devotion through these ten limbs is called *puraścaraṇa*.
That which is called *puraścaraṇa* is for the sake of one’s own accomplishment of the mantra;
indeed, it consists of performing the recitation as prescribed in one’s own ritual manual (*kalpa*), having observed the rules as stated. (77)
That procedure ending with Vijayā has been proclaimed by the best of teachers;
at its conclusion, one should perform a great worship and feed the Brāhmaṇas. (78)
In this way, one should indeed satisfy the Guru; thus the mantras of the practitioner (mantrin) become effective.
For Brahmins engaged in the rite of fire-oblation (homa), the recitation (japa) shall be double.
