For the other castes, however, the three-fold [set] and so forth have been prescribed;
one limb should be omitted from that, for otherwise one would not obtain the desired result. (80)
Whatever may be deficient in its constituent parts, that cannot accomplish the desired purpose;
therefore, one should by all means feed the Brahmins for the sake of ensuring the completion of the ritual's components. (81)
Since even a defective rite becomes complete through the mere propitiation of the Brahmins, rites that are deficient or excessive do not fulfill one's desires. (82)
If all these [elements] reach such perfection and become complete, then a wise man should, with effort, feed them in all ritual acts. (83)
Even those actions that are otherwise certain to bear fruit become useless if they involve feeding low-born persons; they are like seeds sown in barren soil. (84)
Alternatively, another method for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described:
during an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, one who is pure and has previously fasted [should perform it]. || 85 ||
Standing in a river flowing toward the ocean with water reaching up to his navel, he should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantra from the moment of its commencement until its conclusion. 86.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites in sequence, each being one-tenth of the preceding;
and with one-tenth of the oblation, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa). || 87 ||
One should provide a meal for Brahmins equal to one-tenth of the number of consecrations;
at the conclusion of that, the best of practitioners should perform a grand worship.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru and satisfy the Brahmins with devotion;
thereby the mantra will attain perfection and the deity will be pleased. 89.
Then, for the sake of attaining success in the mantra, one should worship and satisfy the guru;
or else, one should satisfy the guru, who is the very form of the deity, with devotion. (90)
"Even one who is devoid of *puraścaraṇa* achieves success in mantra without doubt.
[Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for *Puraścaraṇa*," in the *Śrīgandharvatantra*, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 28 ||
[The Twenty-ninth Chapter] Īśvara said:
O Goddess, one should likewise recite [the mantra] fifty thousand times according to the previously stated procedure.
At night, his mouth should likewise be filled with betel leaf according to the prescribed injunctions. || 1 ||
Having assumed a body capable of taking any form at will, like a passionate woman (or "like a beautiful woman," according to the Kha-pāṭha reading),
one who is joined with the Kula should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times during the middle portion of the night.
Whatever action is performed here yields infinite fruit.
O Great Goddess, in the Mūlādhāra is the self-manifested Liṅga. || 3 ||
One should mentally recite the mantra right there upon that form of light situated in the source;
O Goddess, one should meditate on Kuṇḍalinī, who has the form of the syllables of that Vidyā.
In the heart, in the center of the triangle, in the *bāṇaliṅga*, and in the radiant light—
having meditated there with the mind, one should perform a hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) with concentrated focus.
In the center of the triangle at the crown of the head, one should place the other [mantra] facing west;
staying there with concentrated mind, one should recite it one hundred thousand times, wherever one may be.
When three hundred thousand [recitations] have been accomplished in this manner, whatever state arises, by resorting to that with one's being, one becomes just like the deity. (7)
One should recite this vidyā one hundred thousand times here for the sake of the abundance of enjoyments;
there is no need for meditation, nor ritual placement, nor worship, nor preliminary rites.
For those desiring perfection, accomplishments are attained through mere recitation;
however, when ten million recitations are completed, the mind becomes identical with the mantra.
Indeed, one should recite [the mantra] with the mind alone and not otherwise, as long as the mind has not attained perfection in the very nature of the mantra itself, O Pārvatī. (10)
Making the mind focused solely on meditation, one should offer that meditation to Brahman;
when the field of Brahman is known, the Lord who knows all is known.
Nine locations are described; listen attentively, O beloved.
That form of light is in its support at the location of the penis, shining like a crest of flame.
Situated at the navel, it has the luster of the solar disc and the brilliance of the rising sun;
in the heart, it takes the form of a flame of light, and at the throat, it possesses the radiance of a lamp’s flame.
Between the eyebrows it resembles a jewel; above that, it has the radiance of the sun;
at the uvula, it is like the orb of the moon; and beyond that, it is similar to lapis lazuli.
In the ninth [kalpa], O Goddess, I indeed exist in the form of a linga, possessing universal splendor and resembling a bell of lapis lazuli; for there are nine lingas which I am.
Having sequentially pierced the nine locations with the mantra, one should cause Kuṇḍalī—
who was unconscious— to drink the nectar and then lead her back to the foundation (ādhāra).
One should thus remember the mantra residing in the root-place in its proper sequence;
having recited it nine hundred thousand times for Tripurasundarī— (17)
O Goddess, he was born according to the prescribed rites like another form of Rudra;
having performed nine hundred thousand recitations of mantras, he indeed fashioned nine lingas.
One should then recite it nine times; thus one obtains the fruit of nine hundred thousand recitations.
First there is the birth-impurity (jātasūtaka), and when it has passed, there is the death-impurity (mṛtasūtaka).
A mantra that is joined with two *sūtaka* (impurities) does not succeed;
having personally rendered it free from those, one should indeed recite the mantra with focused intelligence.
That mantra, free from the two types of birth-impurity (sūtaka), bestows all accomplishments upon those born of noble lineages,
places, and castes, who are pure, illustrious, and virtuous.
It is certain that among these twice-born ones who maintain the sacred fire and subsist on alms,
whoever there may be— whether a teacher or even a disciple— (22)

If one does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the *yonimudrā*, it is said that for such a person there is "birth" (*sūtaka*); no accomplishment arises from their recitation. (23)
And those mantras whose seeds (or noble ones) are concealed, O Dear One, will not yield fruit;
yet mantras endowed with consciousness are traditionally held to grant all accomplishments.
Mantras are said to be devoid of consciousness; they are merely phonemes.
They do not yield any fruit at all, even from a million or ten million recitations.
Whatever nature first arises when the mantra is uttered,
that fruit is not obtained by a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, or even ten million recitations.

O Goddess, the meaning of the mantra—which effects the breaking of the knot in the heart and the growth of all its limbs—is now being told; listen first to that, O beloved. (Note: *mantrārtha* is the reading in manuscript Kha. 27.

The meaning of the essential nature, the meaning of the tradition, that which is called the secret, and the Kaulika; likewise, the meaning of all secrets and the meaning of the Great Reality itself. (28)
O Supreme Goddess, the meaning of the syllables is indeed the meaning of existence alone;
the King of Mantras is born from the union of Śiva and Śakti. (29)
Having realized her as being composed of that [reality], gladdened by supreme bliss, embodied as mantra, and a beautiful woman beyond creation, the goddesses worship her at their own will.
She whose nature consists of the friction between Śiva and Śakti is of the nature of Brahman;
she resides on the ground of the embrace resulting from the expansion of that manifestation, characterized by Indra.
Because she brings about for the knower a form consisting of knowledge, she is mantra by nature;
she resides within the central point (the visarga), established in the supreme state which consists of the locus of space.

Furthermore, she resides within the space of vibration, which is the manifestation of the expansion of the vital breath in the midst [of the body], and which is the counterpart (bimba)— the reading "pratirūpa" is also found— of that curved form (kuṭilārūpaka) in the portion of the sky.
Furthermore, in the middle mantra-cluster, within the third cluster, [it belongs] to that which is situated in the state of the quivering radiance of the two peaks of Rāhu. || 34 ||
She is celebrated as the one whose form is the universe, joined with the syllables that express both dharma and adharma, as well as poison and nectar. || 35 ||
The Supreme Power, however, is Mātṛkā in her collective form;

she is the Goddess consisting of the three peaks (kūṭas), possessing both the nature of the totality and the individual parts. (Note: *devī* is the reading in the manuscript; *ka* is the marginal correction. *ṇīm* is the reading in the manuscript; *ka* is the marginal correction. || 36 ||
In the three peaks, however, is the syllable *hrīṃ*, the auspicious third eye of the Goddess;
the letter *ha*, because it has fire as its nature, destroys the succession of dualistic distinctions.
The letter *ra* (repha), because it is mounted upon the form of the fire of time (*kālāgni*), causes the destruction of the flood of sins.
The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of those two is the letter *ī*, together with the *bindu* which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇātman*).
The Moon bestows immortality, and Desire fulfills all longings without exception;
the Tradition, whose nature is Great Awakening, resides in the mouth of the Guru. (39)
O Supreme Goddess, the greatness of the manifestation of all forms has its support in the Root-Vidyā consisting of Śiva, Śakti, and so forth. (Note: *ātmanā* is the reading in manuscript *ka*. 40.
The entire world is pervaded by her; listen attentively, O beloved!
The universe consists of the five elements, and she is its eternal essence. (41)
The root-vidyā consists of those [syllables], yet I shall explain it to you:
from the letter *ha* the ether (*vyoma*) is produced, and from the letter *ka* the wind (*prabhañjana*).
From the letter *ra* arises fire, and from the letter *sa* the origin of the water-element;
from the letter *la* the earth was born, and therefore she consists of the entire universe.
Fifteen qualities have been declared; auspicious Prakṛti consists of them.
Whatever specific power is said to belong to whichever particular object, [that is its nature]. (44)
She alone is the Goddess who is the sovereign of all, and He is the Great Lord who is everything;
through pervasion by the fifteen syllables, She consists of the qualities of the five elements. (Note: *pañcabhūtātmikā* is the reading in the Kāmarūpa recension.)

Furthermore, by means of five, six, and four syllables, distinguished by vowels and consonants, there are thirty-seven divisions. (In the first seed-syllable, there are the four *a*-sounds and the *ī*-sound, making five vowels; with six consonants, there are thus eleven. In the second seed-syllable, there are the five *a*-sounds and the *ī*-sound, making six vowels; with seven consonants, there are thus thirteen. In the third seed-syllable, there are the three *a*-sounds and the *ī*-sound, making four vowels; with five consonants, there are thus nine. When divided in this manner, there are thirty-three.)

At the end of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) are the three points (*bindu*), making thirty-six; their collective totality is one. Thus, Vidyā is that which possesses thirty-seven divisions. || 46 ||
Through its thirty-seven divisions, this Vidyā, which consists of the nature of the thirty-six principles and whose own-being transcends the principles, is always to be meditated upon.
Among the elements beginning with earth, each subsequent element is pervasive;
the preceding element is pervaded by it, and its qualities reside within that which pervades them. (48)
O Goddess, she resides pervading all things through the distinction of gross and subtle;
therefore, sound, which is the quality of space, remains established by pervading air and the other elements. (49)
By means of the seed-syllables of space situated within the Vidyā, one should perceive the fivefold sound;
that which exists as their causal form is the supreme, consisting of space (or, according to the Kha manuscript, consisting of resonance). 50.
It is the seed for those possessing the nine qualities of existence, and it is also the designator of the qualities themselves;
this is because of their relationship as cause and effect, and with the intention of expressing their identity. (51)
By means of the triad of Mahāmāyās and also by the *bindu*, there is the tetrad of the elements—wind, fire, water, and earth—and of the [four] tangibles. 52.
O Goddess, one should meditate upon that which has arisen through the distinction between the gross and the subtle;
that triad of forms is manifested by the three *repha* sounds. (53)
The primary form of fire is produced by its seed-syllable;
however, the gross and subtle essence is said to be produced by the moon-seed-syllables residing in the Vidyā. (54)
In the world, a connection between nectar and its flavor is well known;
fragrance is the quality of the earth, and writing is the expresser of that fragrance. (55)
O Maheśvarī, the state of being threefold arises from the binding of the three worlds through [limited] cognition; it is the supreme body of the subjects who are impure, pure, or mixed. (56)

Then, by means of the triad of Krodhīśas situated within the Vidyā-tattva, the ten [deities] beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha are manifested; likewise, they are indeed the designators of the Unmanifest (avyakta). || 57 ||
O Goddess, abiding in the form of the vital breath, he is the twelfth, yet again the eleventh;
for though the Puruṣa is truly one, he indeed manifests in many ways.
The deities known as Rudreśvara and Sadeśa possess measured forms; those [deities] described by the triad of bindus possess immeasurable and infinite forms. (59)
Śānti, Śakti, and Śambhu are the awakeners of the triad of Nādas;
in the root-circumference of the womb, the threads and other elements are swallowed up. (60)
Likewise, all the mantras are established here within this Vidyā;
the meaning of the tradition (saṃpradāya), received through the lineage of gurus, has thus been declared. (61)
Moreover, O Goddess of the Gods, even a Nigarbha is within the range of Śiva, the Guru, and the Self (the variant reading *gaurava* is also found).
And as for its nature, O Goddess of the Gods, I shall describe it to you by way of illustration.

Through the contemplation of the identity of Śiva, the Guru, and the Self, one realizes that they are of that same nature; having understood the partless state (niṣkalatva) in Śiva, and likewise the identical form of the Guru, and through the power of that vision, [one realizes] the self-nature of the Self as Śiva.
One who is bowed with devotion and untainted by the emergence of doubt should meditate;
I shall now describe the Kaulika [practice] regarding the two deities of the Cakra as well. 46.
The identity of the knowledge, the guru, and the self is demonstrated, as well as its method [the reading *dṛśyate* is found in manuscript *ka*].
Likewise, the wheel consisting of mantra is the supreme body of the deity. (65)
It exists as the nature of one hundred and eleven deities;
with the letter *la*, it consists of four squares joined with three circles.
O Dear One, the pair of lotuses consists of the nature of fire and moon through the nine syllables produced from the three *hṛllekhās*. (67)
O Dear One, joined with three *bindus*, it is born as the nature of the nine *yonis*;
conjoined with the three mandalas, the wheel consists of the nature of power (*śakti*) and fire (*anala*).
By means of the three seed-syllables of space, it consists of the triad of subjects,
takes the form of will, knowledge, and action, and is joined with the three absorptions (ādanas).
The Bindu-cakra, which consists of all the phonemes (varṇas), is immediately of the nature of Śiva;
it constitutes the state of Gaṇeśa for the Great Goddess through [the conjunction of] the Moon, Sun, and Fire.
Furthermore, the supreme goddess, in the form of the planets, is endowed with will, knowledge, and action, as well as the three qualities, and even with the organs of cognition and action.
O Goddess of the gods, by means of those very internal instruments [of action], as well as by nature, by the qualities (guṇas), and by the self through its bondage to masculinity; || 72 ||
The formation of the constellations is now described;
this [formation] also occurs through the Ḍākinīs and others, who are the mistresses of the bodily constituents such as the skin. (73)
Joined by the Yoginīs established in the eight groups,
she who possesses universal forms assumes the form of a Yoginī and sports.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna; furthermore, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. || 75 ||

The individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) are, by those very [letters], of the nature of a heap (rāśi); she [the Goddess] exists as the three rows beginning with 'a', 'ka', and so forth, according to the sequence of the third and subsequent [syllables]. (76)
She became Gaṇeśa, the Great Knowledge, consisting of the supreme speech and all forms of verbal expression;
she is the essence of the planets within the three peaks of the seed-syllables, points, and sounds.
This [Vidyā], which has the form of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra), consists of fifteen syllables produced from the three Hṛllekhās, along with twelve other manifest letters. (78)

The state of being a Yoginī belongs to the Vidyā through the six syllables beginning with Śakra (Ś), which are included within the Vidyā; and the state of being a Rāśi belongs to it through those [syllables] excluding the last one. || 79 ||
Thus, the Great Goddess (Maheśvarī) is the form of the wheel whose nature is the expansion of the universe;
O Goddess, as is the body of the Goddess, so too is the body of the Guru. (80)
And by His grace, even the disciple shines forth in that very form.
One should then contemplate a triangle in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus. (81)
Right there, one should kindle the seed-syllable of Mādana by relying upon the Bindu;
it resembles ten million moons, consisting of consciousness and bliss, and is supreme. (82)
The secret supreme state is situated above the forehead;
the bhaga is established in the foundation, resting upon the city of the triangle. 83.
Indeed, she whose form is like a lotus fiber is the cause of the universe's emergence;
her fourth form, consisting of will, knowledge, and action, resides in the heart. (84)
One should contemplate Śakra in the middle of the forehead, shining like a lamp;
and the fifth [deity] at the eyes and the nose, resembling ten million flashes of lightning. 85.
Śiva, conjoined with that which is called Nāda, is established within the three voids;
resembling ten million suns, he is situated upon the Great Lotus (Mahāpadma). || 86 ||

O Goddess, one should contemplate the supreme syllable *sakāra*, resembling the rising sun, in the middle of the mouth; and one should contemplate the syllable *mādana*, which bestows boons, in the belly. (87)
One should contemplate the syllable *ha* within the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) as the *haṃsa*;
and upon the sixteen-petaled [lotus], one should contemplate Indra in the form of the syllable *oṃ*.
The syllable *hrīṃ* is in the lotus of the heart, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
the two dots (*bindu*) are in the pair of breasts, and the half-moon is in the shape of the barley-grain (*yava*).
At its tip, however, are the Nāda and Bindu, joined with Śiva and Śakti;
O Great Goddess, there is the Kāmarāja, which is supremely capable of attraction.
In the navel-lotus and in the triangle is the letter *sa*, with the luster of a pomegranate;
O Great Goddess, on the two feet is the letter *ma*, resembling a lamp.
O Goddess, one should contemplate Indra, whose nature is splendor, situated upon the back [of the central deity], as the fourth [deity] within the center of the womb, radiant like a lamp. (92)
O Goddess, one should contemplate the three seed-syllables of Vidyā as being in the state of the Yoni, together with Śiva in the form of the Liṅga and that pair of Bindus. 93.
The *liṅga*, the *yoni*, and the *sattva*—the fourth has been described by me.
Now, O sinless one, I shall explain for you the meaning of all the secrets. 94.
In the Mūlādhāra, having assumed the form of Vāgbhava within that blazing nature,
she possesses a body composed of fifty phonemes endowed with thirty-eight Kalās.
Vidyā is in the form of Kuṇḍalinī, the piercer of the three mandalas;
she resembles the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes and has a form like a spider's thread. || 96 ||
Attached to the lunar orb in the sky, she is the very nature of a stream of nectar;
she eternally pervades the entire universe and is the embodiment of eternal bliss. || 97 ||
O Supreme Goddess, the realization that "this is one's own self" is the secret meaning; O Goddess, I shall explain to you what is known as the meaning of the Great Principle (mahātattva). (98)
In the partless, supreme, subtle, untainted (in the Kha recension: "beyond characteristics"), and devoid of objective states;
in the supreme reality that transcends space, whose very form is light and bliss. || 99 ||
One should unite [the self] with one's own nature, the reality that transcends the universe yet consists of the universe;
for at that time, both lights and even darknesses are manifest. 100.

Therefore, the nature of universal inseparability shines forth everywhere as the Great Reality, radiant with the power of the essence of divine play. (The reading "sodbale" is found in manuscript *kha*.)
Preceded by a state in which all conceptual constructions and mental fluctuations have been cast aside, this secret meaning has been proclaimed by me; it produces immediate realization. 102.
[Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, the Determination of the Means for Attaining Vidyā, in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 29 ||
[The Thirtieth Chapter] | The Lord said:
O Goddess of gods, out of affection for you, I shall speak even that which ought not to be told.
At the end of the three peaks is the seed-syllable of Haṃsa, adorned with the bindu and nāda.
Or else, O Goddess, it is difficult for those of sinful mind to attain through the contrary method.
The letter *ha* is the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), while the letter *sa* is said to be the individual soul (*jīva*). (2)
Both are renowned throughout the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
The letter *Ha* is enriched with a white color and possesses a radiance equal to ten million moons. (3)
The letter *sa* is rich in red color and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns;
for this mantra, there is no need for mere recitation, as its very contemplation is the practice.
Therefore, it is renowned as Ajapā, endowed with Śiva and Śakti;
the letter *ha* is said to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the mantra of the Nyāsa-vidyā.
The letter *sa* is declared to be the living soul (*jīva*), adorned with desire (*kāma*). Delight (*mādana*) is the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), while *vi[kāsa]* is said to be Śiva. (6)
That which follows [the letter 'sa'] and resides within the 'sa' should be known as contraction (saṃkoca), whose nature is Śakti.
Contraction is the supreme Śakti, while expansion (vikāsa) is supreme Śiva. || 7 ||
Contraction and expansion constitute the two syllables "ha" and "sa";
within these, in the form of a vowel, she who wears a garland of dots resides in the letter *ha*.
"O fair-faced one, because of their constant association, the vital breath (prāṇa) is said to be the drop (bindu).
The previously mentioned mantra expresses the unity of Śambhu and Śakti. (9)

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, O lady of excellent hips, this mantra has been declared for the purpose of achieving the unification with the power of the individual soul (jīvaśakti) by means of the path that culminates in time and karma.
He who practices with a disciplined mind can accomplish even the impossible;
and you [should practice] this Lord of Mantras which has been proclaimed for the sake of achieving the identity of the individual soul with the Supreme. (11)
"O Goddess, know this to be the truth from my words: abandon the desire for fruit or lack of fruit.
O highly fortunate one, I declare that when this mantra is recited equally [without such desire], [the goal is attained]. (12)
All mantras succeed, they give life and purify;
they cause one to breathe, O highly fortunate lady—I speak the truth, the absolute truth. (13)
The cultivation of existence by means of the state of "I am that" (so'ham-bhāva) is considered true cultivation;
however, existence by means of the state of "I am that" is what has been characterized [as the goal]. 14.
Having formed the sense of "I" and then abandoned it, he should become firm in that very state of "I-ness.
When the state of Śambhu has become firm, one should contemplate the Bindu within Śambhu.
Since Śambhu, who consists of truth, consciousness, and bliss, and possesses three forms,
is always proclaimed in every ritual action, therefore everything is composed of that.
Śambhu alone shines forth within those known as the assembly of the virtuous;
desire desires [the object], and the mind attains that very nature through the sense of duality. (Note: *kāmaḥ kāmayate yato bhedam iti tadrūpatāmatiḥ* is an alternative reading. || 17 ||

Where there is the pervasion of consciousness and existence, there bliss arises; where bliss exists in an entity, there is the abiding of consciousness and existence. (Note: "citsattvayoḥ" is the reading in some versions. 18.

That which is consciousness (cit) is said to be existence (sattā), and that which is existence is called consciousness (cit). O fair-faced one, when the identity of consciousness and existence has thus been firmly established, || 19 ||
Through bliss, immersion arises very quickly;
then the universe, consisting of bliss, shines forth as non-different from one’s own self. || 20 ||
Thus, when all existence consists of Śambhu, when everything originates from the auspicious Śiva,
and when there is the enjoyment of all powers, one who is liberated while living may dwell upon the earth.
The vowels are declared to be the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of that which is the reality of existence; and consciousness is the union with the *bindu*. (22)
O Supreme Goddess, the constituent parts (avayavas) may be different;
therefore, by that method, the mantras become propitious, and not otherwise.
The *bindu*, the emission (*sarga*), the two *hasa*s, and the fourth vowel as the fifth—know these, O Lady, to be the unfolding of consciousness within the body of the *mātṛkā*. (34)
Therefore, those mantras and other vidyās that are deficient in form are considered to be like lifeless bodies, incapable of performing their functions.
One should join Ramā, Māyā, and the Haṃsa-seed (Haṃ), preceded by Vāgbhavī;
O Supreme Goddess, [one should place] "So'ham" at the end of Śakti, as well as Māyā and Ramā.
O Goddess, [worship] Krodhīśa conjoined with Śakra in the place called Kāmārāja;
it is joined with Māyā and the Bindu, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns. (27)
O highly fortunate one, this vital breath (prāṇa), situated in the center of the throbbing triangle and enveloped by many rays, is hidden; it has been revealed here in this knot.
One should awaken the Vidyā by means of Bodhinī and illuminate it by means of Sandīpanī; the conjunction of Tāra, Māyā, and Ramā is called the illuminator of the mantra. (29)
One should cause the living to live by means of this knowledge and practice immortality through the nectars;
O Pārvatī, hear now of its various methods of accomplishment as well.
Having the form of the seed-syllable *vāgbhava*, shining like a lamp and having the nature of a thread,
she proceeds by way of the path of Brahman through the sequence of piercing the *liṅgas*.
Having drunk the divine nectar of consciousness (*viśada*), which flows like a stream of milk, O Goddess, one should enter the *kula* once again after having drunk the nectar of the *akula*. 32.
Once again, O fair-faced one, one should go to the Ākula at the dvādaśānta,
[located] in the great thousand-petaled lotus, where the Vāgbhava [bīja] is like the full moon.

Then, having pierced the *brahmagranthi*—that is, having pierced the support called *śākta* which lies between the two supports of fire (*vahni*) and poison (*viṣa*)—one should cause [the breath] to enter the root of the self through the path of the nostril by means of the support known as the sixty-seventh. (34)

O Goddess, having filled the tongue—which is of the nature of the letters of the Mātṛkā—with speech that has gone outside, [one should contemplate it] on the tip of the tongue in the form of a lamp. || 35 ||

O Dear One, one should contemplate that flame of the lamp, which has the form of the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, extending from the base up to the aperture of Brahmā, and from there down to the tip of the tongue.
Having recited this one hundred thousand times, one becomes a destroyer of all sins;
with unimpeded intellect regarding the scriptures, one shall be victorious even over Bṛhaspati.
In debate, in the assembly, he was one who paralyzed the speech of his opponent; a conqueror of the pride of the host of true scholars, possessing unimpeded power. (37)
O Śivā, by means of his poetic compositions, he becomes a creator of great epics;
thus, O Goddess, I have described to you the practice of Vāgbhava as well. (38)
Then one should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess, whose nature is the seed-syllable of Kāmakalā—resembling the rising sun and like the flickering flame of a lamp. (39)
O beloved, as it proceeds through the path of Brahman up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
it flows with streams of falling drops resembling pure lac-dye.
[She is] one who has swallowed up the entire expanse of the worlds as her very life, and whose ground of egoism has been destroyed by the treading upon [her] own great majesty. 41.
Having meditated thus, O Great Goddess, one may bring this entire world under control;
one should visualize [the syllable] within the womb of women as resembling a flickering flame or the moon.

Whether she be a human woman, a goddess, or even an asura, once she has surrendered her entire being and fallen under the power of that vision, O Goddess, she becomes subject to his will. (Note: *ka* is an alternative reading for *vaśagā*). 43.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the practice of the Śaktikūṭa:
from the foundation to the aperture of Brahmā, it possesses a radiance equal to lightning and fire. (45)

O Goddess, one should contemplate the Peak of Power (śaktikūṭa) as consisting of flowing nectar, comparable to the essence of a downpour of rain that showers the bliss of immortality upon embodied beings. 46.

Merely by the sight of serpents, he renders them motionless; he is the destroyer of the poison known as *sthirajaṅgama* (poison from stationary and moving creatures), and the eradicator of poisons and secondary toxins. || 47 ||
[The reading "mahāroga-raudra" appears. For those afflicted by great disease, [he is] like the rays of the autumn moon.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, why has the art of desire (kāmakalā) been indicated but not revealed? (48)
"By the mere remembrance of whom a man attains union (sāyujya), the Lord said:
O wise one, hear that threefold nature which is hidden in all the Tantras. (49)
She is named the gross, the even, and likewise the subtle, whose body is the mantra;
she has the great bindu of the sky as her face and the moon and sun as her two breasts.
When the earth, shining with half a digit of Mount Sumeru, was placed at the bottom of the netherworld, this triple-world became composed of [only] a single digit. 51.

The meaning of manifestation (prakāśa) which is expressed by the three seed-syllables of Lalitā is [the letter] *i*; its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is the vowel *ī*, and that [manifestation] has proceeded in a threefold manner through the bindu.
That syllable, which is the essence of the fourth state, is said to possess three points (bindus):
the point situated above the letter *ī* is the face, while the two below it are the sun.
The two breasts are the burning fire and the cooling moon; the womb would be the half-moon digit (ardhakalā).
Since you are of that very nature, O Unborn One, may that [state] belong to the practitioner as well. (Note: *tadātmakatvād* is the reading in the Kha manuscript.)
O wise one, hear now of that which arises from it, which brings about the supreme great awakening:
its upper face consists of the upper bindu, and its [other] faces consist of the two lower bindus. (55)
One should visualize the two breasts with the remaining [parts] and the rest of the limbs with what is left over.
Thus has the external meditation on the Kāmakalā been described to you. (56)

I shall speak again of that very same [deity], whose nature consists of the intermediate stages of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), flashing like a streak of lightning from the base of the body up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). (57)
O Goddess, one should meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī, who is the very embodiment of that Vidyā, the supreme goddess who pierces the six cakras and consists of the three points (bindus). 58.
And one should meditate upon her, who has the form of the half-moon digit, as residing in the center of the lotus;
thus she, whose form is the Kāmakalā, remains awake within the moving and the unmoving.
And she is said to consist of the three Vedas; there is nothing whatsoever without her.
The Sāman is declared to be her face, and the Ṛk and Yajus to be her two breasts.
O Supreme Goddess, the supreme digit (kalā) known as Atharvaṇa is the very form of the Heart;
it is the fourth state (turīya), which is indeed Brahman itself, absolute and alone.
This meditation on the form of Kāmakalā is the supreme and most secret [teaching];
it must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who is not a devotee.
This very disclosure is traditionally held to cause the exhaustion of one's lifespan;
it leads to the destruction of the practitioner, therefore one should not disclose this. (63)
If one should disclose [this] out of greed, delusion, pride, or hatred, he shall soon meet death by means of weapons, poison, and the like. (64)
[Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Practice of the Three Vidyā-Kūṭas," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 30 ||
[The Thirty-First Chapter] The Goddess said:
O Īśāna, tell me the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) that was previously indicated.
Īśvara said:
An oblation for the Goddess may be made with Kiṃśuka flowers or even with Kusumbha blossoms.
Or with *nāgakesara* flowers, *madhūka*, red lotuses (*raktapadmaka*), *karavīra*, or *arjuna* flowers, mixed with the three sweets (*madhuratrika*). || 2 ||

O fair-faced one, having prepared a quadrangular sacrificial pit that bestows all accomplishments and is endowed with excellent characteristics, one should perform the fire-oblation in the consecrated fire.
Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess, the wise one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
he should perform the daily and occasional rites, but he should not perform optional rites on a sacrificial mound.
A square measuring one cubit, smeared with cow dung,
and likewise a sand mandala one finger-joint high.
There too, having performed the smearing, the fire-oblation (homa) performed therein bestows fruit.
Likewise, with barley or rice grains, a finger-breadth (aṅgula) shall consist of eight [such units].
With hands that are not too long and measure twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
one should perform the construction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and other rites using hands of this measurement.
The oblation that pleases Tripurā is performed in a fire-pit known as the triangle.
From west to east, there are three lines with their tips pointing eastward, each measuring one span (prādeśa). [Note: Some readings include *mātrakaḥ* at the end.]
Having drawn the forms of Mukunda, Indu, and Purandara,
one should then draw three lines toward the south.
The lines should have the nature of Vaivasvata, Brahmā, and Ananta;
O Goddess, having first drawn a triangle in the center, one should then proceed with the exterior.
One should fashion a most beautiful hexagon according to the prescribed rule;
outside of that, an eight-petalled lotus with an auspicious pericarp should be drawn within a circle.

Having constructed a square mandala with four gates, one should place a handful of flowers in the center and arrange the sacrificial implements, such as the *sruva* ladle; [specifically] the *sruva*, clarified butter, curd, *dūrvā* grass, and fuel sticks.

Having arranged the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) and the *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī* vessels to his left, having filled the *prokṣaṇī* with water and purified it three times by pouring it back, having placed them facing toward the *prokṣaṇī*, and having consecrated them with the *bālā* mantra, he should wipe them three times with *dūrvā* grass—once from the root to the tip, again from the tip to the root, and once more from the tip to the root—using that same *bālā* mantra. Then, spreading the *dūrvā* grass with its tips pointing eastward and northward, while reciting the Root Vidya, he should worship the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) with the words, "Salutation to the sacrificial ground. Finally, having worshipped Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara in the center of the triangle:

Having meditated upon the union of those two and having worshipped them, one should cause the fire of consciousness (*saṃvidagni*)—which has arisen from the root, emerged through the door of the eye on the forehead, and is joined with the external fire—to descend into her womb with the mantra: *vaiśvānara jātaveda ihāvaha lohitākṣa sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya svāhā*.

Then, having raised the fire with the mantra: *oṃ uttiṣṭha puruṣa haripiṅgala lohitākṣa sarvakarmāṇi dehi me dāpaya svāhā*, [one should offer it] held within the womb of Kāmeśvarī with the mantra: *oṃ citpiṅgala hanahana dahadaha pacapaca sarvajñājñāpaya svāhā*.

Having meditated and reciting the root mantra followed by *vauṣaṭ*, one should gaze at the fire, protect it with the Astra-mantra, and taking the blazing fire, circumambulate the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) three times clockwise. Then, with the mantra *hūṃ phaṭ*, one should cast a single burning fuel-stick toward the southwest as the "flesh-eating fire" (*kravyādāgni*). Touching the ground with both knees, one should establish the fire in the center and worship the Goddess with the mantra *klīṃ mahātripurasundaryai vahnimūrtaye namaḥ* (or *namo*). Having unified that fire with the external fire through the nostrils from the navel-center, one should perform the sacrifice.

Having meditated upon the Fire within the womb of Kāmeśvarī with the root mantra *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ āṃ so’haṃ*—[with the variant reading *vahnicaitanyāyai*] followed by *namaḥ*—and having worshipped the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon its body with: *sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *svastipūrṇāya śirase svāhā*, *uttiṣṭhapuruṣāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *dhūmavyāpine kavacāya huṃ*, *saptajihvāya netrebhyo vauṣaṭ*, and *dhanurdharāyāstrāya phaṭ*, [one should contemplate the Fire] possessing the luster of molten gold.

Having meditated upon [the deity] who holds a *śakti* and a *svastika*, whose lotus-hands are graced by the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), whose body and hands are adorned with divine ornaments, who stands upon a lotus, wears white garments, possesses three eyes, and has his hair bound in a topknot; and having recited the mantras for the seven tongues of fire—*yūṃ* for the red one in the northeast, *rūṃ* for the red one in the east, *nūṃ* for the blue one in the southeast, *vūṃ* for the black one in the southwest, *śūṃ* for the white one in the west, *karālī* in the south, and *bahurūpā* in the north—one should offer salutations to the fire born from the womb of Kāmeśī with the mantra: *sarvabhāvebhyo namaḥ*.

Having thus completed the rites of *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarman*, *nāmakaraṇa*, *annaprāśana*, *cūḍākaraṇa*, and *upanayana* with the respective mantras; having performed the injunction "I perform such-and-such a rite for such-and-such a fire," having sprinkled water around it, strewn grass, and encircled it with fuel-sticks; having meditated again and worshipped the fire within a triangle using the fire-mantra; having offered seven oblations into the seven tongues of flame (this is the reading in manuscript *ka*); and having performed threefold oblations with the mantras *vaiśvānara*, *uttiṣṭha*, and *citpiṅgala*; [one should worship] the six limbs in the six corners.

On the eight petals, one should offer salutations with: "Obeisance to Agni Jātavedas, Saptajihva, Havyavāhana, Aśvodaraja, Vaiśvānara, Kaumāratejas, Viśvamukha, and Devamukha. Then, having worshipped Brahmā to the south of the fire within the enclosure of the earth-element, and having placed the vessel of clarified butter (ājyasthālī) in front, one should visualize the King of Śrīcakras upon the Bahurūpā tongue, and within that, the Citkalā adorned with a complete circle of rays; having thus contemplated, performed the sacrifice, and offered the daily oblations, one should fill the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the smoke from the pavilion.

Having kindled the lamps and offered fuel-sticks (*samidh*), one should offer whatever is desired. Having presented the ritual offerings (*bali*), one should perform the *vyāhṛti-homa* with these four mantras: "Oṃ bhūr, svāhā to Agni, to the Earth, and to the Great One"; "Oṃ bhuvaḥ, svāhā to Vāyu, to the Atmosphere, and to the Great One"; "Oṃ svar, svāhā to Āditya, to the Sky, and to the Great One"; and "Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar, svāhā to the Moon and to the Stars. After performing this *vyāhṛti-homa*, one should then offer the fuel-stick as an offering to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa*), worship the Goddess, and finally dismiss her.
The daily fire-offering has been declared by me; now hear concerning the optional fire-offering:
with jasmine, *mālatī*, and *jātī* flowers mixed with honey. (12)
Or by offering *kuṣmāṇḍa* fruits filled with ghee, mastery of speech (*vāgīśatva*) arises; likewise, by offering *yavāsa* flowers or *karavīra* flowers combined with clarified butter. (13)
By performing oblations, the practitioner of mantras may delude the inhabitants of the three worlds;
by offering *campaka* and *pāṭala* flowers into the fire, he attains unsurpassed prosperity.
An oblation with lotuses as red as the dawn bestows perfect prosperity;
with red water-lilies, the world is brought under control; and with blue ones, one may bring even the wicked into subjection. (15)
O beloved, by offering white lotuses in the fire, one obtains prosperity and sovereignty; by offerings of white water-lilies, one gains fortune as well as all good fortune.
By performing a fire-oblation with Bandhūka flowers, one may bring all sentient beings under one's control.

O fair-faced one, having offered milk, curd, honey, and clarified butter separately, [the same result is achieved]. (Note: *hunet* is the reading in manuscript Kā; *māt* is the reading in manuscript Kha. 17.
Longevity, strength, health, and prosperity arise for men through a nocturnal fire-oblation performed with goat meat smeared with blood. (18)
By employing the three sweets according to the procedure taught by the Guru, a man shall bring another kingdom under his control and become an enjoyer of all desires. || 19 ||
Indeed, through a hundred thousand oblations of grapes, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained;
likewise by oblations of plantain fruits and coconut fruits.
Kings come under one's control, as does incomparable prosperity; likewise, all women certainly become submissive by means of *jambū* fruits. (21)
Through bilva fruits one attains incomparable prosperity, and through its leaves it shall be the same;
through pieces of sugarcane there is the attainment of happiness, and by its juices kings become submissive.
O Goddess, one shall accomplish all undertakings by means of an oblation of sesame seeds and clarified butter;
likewise, by an oblation of ghee, milk-rice, sugar, and honey. (23)
The three worlds come under one's control and one obtains wealth and grain;
with vaṭakas served with their accompaniments, one shall destroy all calamities.
Through the oblation of camphor, the power of speech arises for men;
O Goddess, through the oblation of saffron, one destroys all sufferings. (25)
Through the oblation of musk, the gods come under one's control; of this there is no doubt.
By means of an oblation of sandalwood and agallochum, one may bring all the worlds under one's sway.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the measure for the successful accomplishment of the oblation:
one should offer a full hundred flowers, and likewise a hundred sesame seeds (this is the reading in manuscript *ka*). || 27 ||
The parched grain (lāja) should be the measure of a handful; the clarified butter (ghṛta) should be the measure of one karṣa;
the honey and milk should be half a mouthful (culluka-ardha); and the cooked food (anna) should be the size of a single morsel (grāsa). || 28 ||
And with whole and broken fruits according to one's desire;
the plantain fruit should be cut into four pieces, unless it is already small and has not been cut. (29)
One should prepare a large piece of coconut that is pleasing to the mind;
and at the place of the joints, one should provide a sugarcane stalk that brings satisfaction to the mind. (30)
The grape fruit should be whole; from that, it should be the size of a *guñjā* seed.
[In the case of] camphor, musk, and so forth—[where "so forth" includes saffron (*ghusṛṇa*)—it should be taken] as that which brings satisfaction to the mind. (31)
This measure of oblations has been declared, which brings about all accomplishments;
or else, O Dear One, with *kiṃśuka* flowers that destroy the multitude of sins. (Note: *pāpasaṃghātanāśakaiḥ* is the reading; *pāpasaṃghātanaiḥ* is an alternative reading. 32.
O fair-faced one, a wise person should perform the homa with various distinct substances gathered together according to his capacity;
he shall destroy the entire multitude of obstacles—of this there is no doubt. (33)

[Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for the Fire Offering and its Substances," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 31 ||
[The Thirty-second Chapter] The Goddess said:
"How does the mudrā consisting of fire, moon, and sun come to be established?"
Īśvara said:
The castes are of the nature of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire, as are the three worlds.
The sixteen vowels are lunar; the others, beginning with 'ka', are solar.
Those are declared to be fiery, as are the ten others beginning with 'ya'. (2)
Silver is the moon, gold is the sun, and copper is fire;
these are declared to be the metallic components according to the numerical value of the vowels and consonants.
One should have a seal (mudrā) fashioned from those metals, free from any admixture of other materials;
having washed it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) on an auspicious day.
On Sunday, at an auspicious lagna, one should place the previously mentioned lotuses dedicated to the Mothers;
furthermore, one should place water-pots upon their petals, starting from the center.
O Goddess, they should be pure, wrapped with threads, smeared with sandalwood paste on the outside,
perfumed with excellent incense, and provided with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
O Goddess, one should fill it with a decoction prepared according to rule from the medicinal ingredients,
combined with *rocanā*, *candana*, *kuṅkuma*, and light *kastūrī*.
Having filled them with fragrant water, one should wrap them in auspicious cloths,
[adorned] with pearls, rubies, lapis lazuli, gomedas, diamonds, and corals.
One should place, in those jars respectively, topaz, emerald, and sapphire, as well as fruits marked with gems.
One should place tender mango sprouts upon the mouths of the jars;
and having placed that mudrā upon the central jar amidst many auspicious rites, [one should proceed].
Having divided the three seed-syllables into three parts, and likewise the Mātṛkā into three parts,
one should worship the Moon, Sun, and Fire by distributing them, O Goddess.
There, having invoked the supreme goddess Sammohanī, one should then worship her;
thereafter, having performed breath control according to the rules, one should install the Mātṛkā as before.
She has three eyes, the luster of the young moon, and is as red as the rays of the rising sun;
she holds a rosary, a goad, arrows, a noose, and likewise two lotuses. (Note: *akṣamālāṅkuśaśarā* is the reading.)

One should worship the eternal Goddess, who consists of the letters, beginning with the seed-syllables of Māyā, Śrī, and Kāma, and who carries in her lotus-hands the Puṇḍra, the sugarcane bow, and the book. (Note: *puṣtakān* is an alternative reading for *pustakam*). 14.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with various kinds of flowers, fragrant incenses, enchanting lamps, and diverse offerings.
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with sugar and ghee,
and worship Vyāpinī and the others in order within the water-pots (kumbhas) placed in the cardinal directions.
Vyāpinī, Pālinī, and thereafter Plāvinī, Kledinī;
Dhariṇī, Mālinī, Harṣiṇī, and likewise Śāntinī. || 17 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, these eight [mantras] are indeed all-pervading;
having recited them more than a thousand times, one should then touch that ring.
O Goddess, one should likewise offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter into the consecrated fire,
and according to the prescribed rite, one should pour the remnants of those oblations into that [liṅga].
Having taken clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle while aiming at the *samohana* [mantra],
O Goddess, one should recite the *mātṛkā* joined with the three seed-syllables and the nasal bindu.
Then, having placed the wife of the fire-god [the sacrificial ladle] behind him, he should indeed perform the oblation;
having respectfully seated the disciple within the mandala of the goddess Mātṛkā.
Having consecrated the disciplined disciple with the nine auspicious jars while reciting the mantras beginning with "surāstvām," the Guru should bestow that ring upon him.
This is the protective mudrā, which destroys poisons and diseases;
it especially provides protection against wild beasts, thieves, predatory animals, and the like. (23)
It brings all things under control, is pure, bestows purity, and removes impurity;
a lord of men should wear this on his forefinger according to the prescribed rite. (24)
One attains victory in battle, endowed with supreme prosperity;
O Goddess, one should divide the Mātṛkā as it has been declared into nine groups.
The planets born from the nine divisions are the lords of the nine gems: the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu. (26)
O Great Goddess, one should fashion a mudrā with the nine gems according to one's desire;
having worshipped all the planets within those gems according to the prescribed rite. (Note: There is a variant reading "teṣu ratneṣu" for "tadratneṣu".)
Having invoked the goddess Sammohanī, who is likewise supreme,
one should worship her and perform all rites such as recitation (japa) and fire-offerings (homa) according to the path previously described.
For whoever wears this mudrā, the planetary spirits (grahas) shall come under his control;
his good fortune increases, and his prosperity shall be unimpeded. (29)
(Nyā-ka-pāṭha:
For one who is hostile to him, all calamities perish;
Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, and the like cannot look upon him, being overcome with fear. || 30 ||
Wealth, jewels, and prosperity increase higher and higher;
yet, without the seal of established authority, one falls downward even while wearing the insignia.
Therefore, O beloved, one should wear it according to the prescribed rite so as to obtain its fruit.
[Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Wearing Mudrās," in the illustrious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 32 ||
[The Thirty-third Chapter] The Goddess said:
"The King of Wheels has been described by you, but its consecration has not been revealed."
The Lord said: The consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is said to be threefold: in the image, in the [liṅga] disc, and likewise in the disciple. || 1 ||

O Pārvatī, once the disciple has been established through initiation, he should, O beloved, fashion an image made of jewels, or of gold, or of silver. (Note: *arcā* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)

Having installed [the deity] in an auspicious house according to the prescribed rules, one should perform the consecration rite (pratiṣṭhā) duly and conduct a festival every month with great magnificence and elaboration.
One should perform worship day after day with the sixty-four types of offerings;
first, one should carry out the preliminary rites such as the consecration (adhivāsa) according to the procedure prescribed for initiation.

The preceptor, who knows the true meaning of the ritual procedure, being a master of the sciences, should first perform the preliminary rites according to the prescribed rule, providing [the disciple] with garments, ornaments, perfumes, and other such items. (This is the reading from the Kha manuscript.)
One should wash the King of Mandalas with the five nectars and the five products of the cow;
having worshipped it according to the ritual rules upon an altar in such a house.
Then, one should place the cakra upon a couch that is exceedingly enchanting and perfumed with the fragrance of various flowers, by way of the suṣumnā path.
Then, having anointed [the image] with saffron, agallochum, musk, camphor, and various types of sandalwood, one should further apply it with diverse fragrances and saffrons.
Having covered it with a divine garment, one should perfume it with camphor;
having thoroughly incensed it with incense and illuminated it with lamps, O Pārvatī.
O Śivā, one should place eighty-one jars, wrapped in cloth and filled with water scented with camphor, upon that [mandala] consisting of eighty-one squares.
The square mandala should be filled with pure golden vessels, adorned with flower garlands and other ornaments, and provided with eighty-one squares.
The preceptor, along with his disciple, should remain there as celibate students;
then, having performed all those rites according to the rules at the very dawn, they should depart.
The Guru should enter the pavilion according to the previously described procedure;
having prepared another seat as before, he should sit down upon it.
Having likewise prepared the seat, one should then raise the wheel;
having washed it according to the prescribed rule with the five nectars and the five products of the cow.
Having placed [the image] upon a blessed throne (bhadrapīṭha), one should meditate upon the Goddess there;
first with honey, clarified butter, and milk, and then with coconut water.
Having consecrated [the image] with sugarcane juice and water accompanied by mantras,
one should duly perform the full ablution (abhiṣeka) with those very same jars according to the prescribed rite.
Having indeed consecrated [the deity] with a golden pitcher filled with water from all the sacred fords,
and having lifted that discus with both hands, one should place it upon a golden pedestal.
Then, having meditated upon the Goddess in his heart according to the yoga of meditation as described, he,
with a one-pointed mind, likewise invoked her into the center of the wheel.
O Goddess, having prepared the wheel according to the prescribed rite and having touched it with the hand,
one should [anoint it] with saffron, agallochum, musk, yellow pigment, sandalwood, and camphor.
Then, having again smeared the wheel with a golden rod and having performed the delineation of the lines, one should worship it, beginning with the base (ādhāra).

One should establish the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) therein with the *Prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra: [The extraction of the seed-syllable is as follows: "Kṣīrodadhi" [the ocean of milk] adorned with the nasal resonance (*sanāda*) and the bindu; Nakulīśa [the letter *ha*] mounted upon the letter *ra*; marked with the seed-syllable *iṃ* preceded by *māyā* [the letter *ī*]; Kāmadeva [the letter *ka*], Agni [the letter *ra*], and Sadyojāta [the letter *o*]—by these, [it becomes] *kroṃ*. The seed-syllable of Śiva [the letter *sa*] together with the moon [the bindu] is *hasa*. Then, with the words beginning with "possessing emission" (*sargavān*), the extraction of the seed-syllable *so'ham* is formed. Kṣīrodadhi is completely adorned with the nasal resonance and the bindu. (21)
Nakulīśa is mounted upon fire and marked by the crescent moon of Māyā;
Kāmadeva is mounted upon fire and adorned with Sadyojāta. || 22 ||
Endowed with the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, this triad of seed-syllables (*bījatraya*), O Goddess, accompanied by the moon, is the seed of Śiva that bestows all life-force. (23)
At the end of that, O Supreme Goddess, is the imperishable Bhṛgu, the possessor of creation;
thereafter comes Mahātripurasundarī, ending with the sixteenth vowel (Ū).

In due order, O Pārvatī, the vital breaths here are the vital breaths, and likewise the individual soul (jīva) is situated here; furthermore, all the senses of this [one] and of that [one] are present here.
Speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and likewise the vital breaths—
having returned here from that place, may they dwell happily for a long time, O beloved of Agni.

This is the *prāṇamantra*: (Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Hasa Soha Mahātripurasundaryāḥ, prāṇā iha prāṇāḥ [15] jīva iha sthitaḥ [15] sarvendriyāṇi [15] vāṅ-manas-nayana-śrotra-ghrāṇa-prāṇā ihāgatya sukhaṃ ciraṃ tiṣṭhantu svāhā). This is clearly declared as the bestower of life to all beings. Having established the life-breaths (*prāṇa*) of the Goddess there by means of this mantra, [one should proceed]. (27)

Touching it with the tips of his fingers, he should recite the mantra; thereafter, he should worship the Śrīcakra with the aforementioned ritual offerings (upacāras) at the three junctions of the day for three days.
In each of those instances, O Goddess, one should likewise perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the Great Goddess according to the rite,
with one hundred and eight offerings of milk-rice (pāyasa) saturated with sweet substances.
O Goddess, filled with joy, he celebrated a great festival accompanied by various kinds of musical instruments, preceded by dance and song, and joined with shouts of victory and hymns of praise.
Then, having performed [the rite], one should give the teacher the previously mentioned sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
thereafter, one should satisfy the women and also gratify the Brāhmaṇas.
Thus, O Goddess, one who brings about the presence of the Goddess in the consecration, as well as in the yantra, the mantra, the Kula, and likewise in the ornament of the Kula; || 32 ||
One should worship [the deity] in the Traipura, or according to the scripture (śāstra), or likewise within oneself; or in an image, or in the fire, or in a Śiva-liṅga, or in the Guru. (33)
O Goddess, O sinless one, the supports for worship have been described by me;
one should not worship the Goddess elsewhere if one desires one's own welfare. (Note: *yadi* is the reading in manuscript *ka*).
[Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Consecration of the King of Mandalas," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 33 ||
[The Thirty-Fourth Chapter] Īśvara said:
Listen, O wise one, to the Kula conduct; it is being described by me in its various details.
Having nourished [the fire] with clarified butter on the new moon day, one should sacrifice to the Supreme. || 1 ||
One should not commit violence against living beings, nor should one cause pain to oneself;
without tasting the causal substance, O Śivā, one should not remember Sundarī.
Without liquor, meat, or dalliance with another's wife,
the worship of the Great Goddess is like a meal consisting of non-bovine products.
Food that is not made from sugarcane and not derived from cows is considered the food of the dead;
one should never, under any circumstances in this world, observe a vow of fasting while consuming such food.
Whether his mouth has a foul odor or even a colorless appearance; whether he lacks Kaula ornaments or is devoid of red flowers. || 5 ||
Endowed with a heart free from doubt, the bearer of Śiva’s leaf should likewise worship Sundarī with an undistracted mind.
Therefore, one should not worship the Supreme Goddess with *tulasī* flowers or its leaves;
one should not look upon a virgin’s womb, nor should one gaze at anything loathsome.
O Śivā, one should not look at a naked woman, nor another's wife with exposed breasts; for there is no salutation due to seeing young girls occupied in play. (8)
One should not practice that by which the mind becomes corrupted; for by doing what is displeasing to women, even a perfected one (*siddha*) will surely perish. (2 ca ka pāṭhaḥ |????)
One should not eat food that has been brought [to him] more than once, nor that which possesses a foul odor;
rather, one should eat what is personally pleasing, stable, savory, praiseworthy, and likewise sweet. (10)
For the supreme lords who accomplish the noble [aim], the auspicious food should be very little or even less;
moreover, pungent, sour, and salty [flavors] should not be particularly dear to them. (Note: *ro* is the reading in manuscript Pāṭha. 11.
One should eat that which is digested quickly and not in excess;
one should eat before one's desire to eat arises, leaving the meal unfinished.
When the fire is once covered, it does not increase at all;
therefore, a wise man who possesses the skill of digestion should carefully nourish the fire with food. (Note: *kha-pāṭha* reads *bandhayet*; *bhuktayuktimān* is the variant reading. || 13 ||
When the internal fire remains balanced, the body shall be free from disease;
and when the body is free from disease, one may accomplish all ritual actions.
When the fire is situated in a state of imbalance, the body becomes useless;
yet for human beings, the body is the sole means for achieving the goals of human endeavor (puruṣārtha). 15.
Therefore, with every effort, one should purify that which is free from disease. Even the gods are victorious here by virtue of this; how much more so, then, humans and others? 16.
The boat is said to be both the means for crossing the ocean of existence and its physical form;
by means of this body, one easily crosses that which is otherwise difficult to traverse.
O Goddess Śivā, life is as fruitless as being afflicted by a disease;
O Śivā, worship performed in a smoky house, in darkness, or in an unknown place is likewise [fruitless]. (Note: *ajñāte* is an alternative reading for *ajñāne*. 18.
O Pārvatī, know that the worship of Mahādevī leads to hell;
for in the Satya Yuga, the vital breaths are considered to reside in the bones, while in the Tretā Yuga, they are held to reside in the flesh.
In the Dvāpara age, the vital breaths are considered to reside in the skin; in the Kali age, they are held to reside in food. Therefore, O Goddess, the vow of fasting is abandoned in the Kali age.
In this Kali age, one should never perform a sacrifice involving violence without the offering of a *bali*;
O Goddess, the most excellent of practitioners should not cut the *bali* himself. (21)
Without the offering of a sacrifice (balidāna), the Goddess’s pleasure cannot be attained through other means;
indeed, this very mantra is proclaimed as the supreme one for the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa). || 22 ||
Awake, O beast! For you are not another; you are indeed Śiva.
Since this body is dependent upon Śiva, therefore attain the state of Śiva.
Many should never be slain if one desires one's own welfare;
for where many are killed, a destructive ruin is wrought there.
O Śivā, the uprooting of bondage indeed occurs very quickly;
O Goddess, the same applies even to others who are as dear to one as one's own life. (25)
Unrighteousness, which arises from harming others, will gradually seize everything;
O Goddess, it belongs to him who lives here by oppressing others for his own sake. (Note: *niṣpīḍya* is the reading in some manuscripts.)
He who, disregarding the prescribed rite, performs a sacrifice to Śiva after killing living beings, shall never attain success either in this world or in the next.
Great portents indeed arise there for him, O Maheśānī, without a doubt, due to violence and cruel commands during sacrifices and the like. (28)
Unrighteousness arises from harming others and yields extreme suffering in its ultimate consequence;
likewise, I declare this [truth], for what is not seen through delusion? (Variant reading: "I declare this, for what is not seen through delusion?")

O Śivā, for those who desire the attainment of happiness for only a limited time, this supreme delusion—the most dreadful *paramoha*—destroys them here in this world. (Note: *kiyatkālasukhāvāpti* is the reading found in manuscript *ka*.)
O Pārvatī, the sense of "mine-ness" (mamatā) regarding the body and the beloved—which are exceedingly difficult to attain—is the cause of great suffering; indeed, it is not found elsewhere.
Because at the time of casting off the body, there arises for both Indra and Candra—as well as for us two and for the lustful man—a joy that grants all desires, just as it does for the dog. (32)
The act of killing is not praised for one who has attained Brahman or for one seeking to realize Brahman, when he perceives all beings as his very own self. (33)
Then, having realized the Self as being like all beings, one attains Brahman;
Śakti, Maheśvara, and Brahman—these three are synonyms for the same reality. || 34 ||
The distinction between female, male, and neuter exists only in terms of the word, not in terms of the ultimate reality;
in the end, for men, she becomes subservient and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In this world, even for women, that which has the form of a male is subject to control and bestows all accomplishments;
however, that which consists of the neuter nature shines forth by itself.
From the union of either of these two, there arises the single thought of "I" (mataikabhāvanā).
[The reading *niṣṭhīvana* is preferred over *vala vara śūkā*. There is the sound of spitting, sneezing, and the emission of downward wind. (37)
He who performs [this] during the midst of worship becomes a beast for the Yoginīs;
therefore, the wise man should always understand the customs and practices of various regions. (38)
The practice of the fifth [alternative] and so forth would not be independent anywhere;
for in whatever region there is a particular custom, the Dharma is of that same nature. (39)
There is no conflict with those who have sought refuge, nor even with the Supreme Person, as if with a god. (40)
One should rely upon the teacher’s sons, wife, and so forth, exactly as one would the teacher himself;
and on the festival days (parvan), one should especially worship the family tree with the sprouts of its fruit.
One who lacks desire for false speech, for the wives or wealth of others, for self-praise, or for reviling others, shall not even touch bliss. (42)
One should never go anywhere without having spoken to a Śakti who is facing him;
upon seeing a group of women, one should bow down, intent on devotion. (43)
One should never eat products derived from the *puṇḍra* sugarcane;
rather, a wise person should always perform worship that bestows all prosperity.
Having observed the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, one should abandon defects during the fifth [rite];
one should bathe with fragrant waters so that the body becomes pure. (45)
He should always wear stainless garments, remaining himself stainless and pure;
with body and face well-anointed, he should never be coarse.
Having made his body auspicious and being intent on speaking softly, the hero should not speak excessively, nor ever speak harshly. (47)
Having assumed the form of a Gandharva, he was intent on playing the lute;
his eyes were rolling from wine, and he was accompanied by a woman with intoxicating eyes. || 48 ||
One who always possesses the nature of a deity and has mastered the essence of music—whether he be an ascetic or even a king—is praised as the best of practitioners. (49)
The king [attains his goal] through scattered requisites, while the ascetic does so through the restraint of the senses;
indeed, among the four stages of life, the stage of the Avadhūta is the greatest.
Eating meat and drinking wine, indulging in the objects of the senses, he took delight in women, adorned by those who were themselves adorned. || 51 ||
He whose inner self is gladdened by the abundance of various blisses,
and whose senses are motionless— he is the great ascetic, the Avadhūta.
Garlands, sandalwood, clothing and the like, ornaments, whatever unguents there may be— whatever is obtained by chance, even if offered by others. (53)
One should enjoy things without greed and should not be possessed by attachment;
one should always practice yoga in a solitary, secluded, and pleasant place. (54)
When the senses of a great-souled monk are restless, then he should diligently undertake wandering to sacred fords and other such places. (55)
Adorned with his own supernatural powers, he should wander for alms and not dwell long in any one place.
"O Mother, give me alms; I am adorned with earrings; I shall satisfy [the gods]! 56.
Having attained incomparable power, he was neither intoxicated nor envious;
even in prosperity, he was free from pride and endowed with equanimity and virtue.
With a heart full of joy at all times, devoted to giving and enjoyment,
he dwelt in a supreme and beautiful palace, radiant with a glow like red lac.
Upon a beautiful and auspicious lion-throne made of jewels, provided with divine furnishings, adorned with gems and gold, and covered with a most excellent and lovely carpet.
The quarters of the sky were made fragrant by the scents of various flowers,
and the interior was filled with delight by the incense of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and frankincense.
In a place radiant with lamps burning with camphor and blazing with jewels,
there was a parasol resembling the autumnal moon, adorned with pearls and rubies.
Having placed [the image] above, adorned with white chowries hanging from golden staffs at its crest, one should enter there after taking possession of a seat.
Anointed with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and musk,
he was richly adorned in all the finery of love and decorated with jewel ornaments.
Adorned with garlands and various ornaments, he was exceedingly captivating;
his mouth was filled with betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor.
With all mental fluctuations stilled and his eyes rolling like those of one intoxicated by wine,
he placed before him [or, according to another reading, around him] a Śakti who was well-attired and most enchanting.

[He meditates on] the Self, which consists of Tripura, as stainless, devoid of qualities, and pure, adorned with various jewels and garments of *dukūla*, *kṣauma*, and *kauśeya*. (Note: *kauśeya* is the reading in manuscript P. 66.
By contemplating [the deity] as non-different from one's own self, a person attains identity with it;
through such enjoyment, he himself becomes Tripurabhairava and attains liberation. 67.
From that very source Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara have arisen;
they are indeed that, there is no doubt, therefore one should not conceive of them as separate from it. 68.
O fair-faced one, the deluded who perceive duality surely fall;
one should always satisfy and adorn all women, for they are the givers of everything.
Filled with joy by means of garments, ornaments, perfumes, and the like, as well as drinks and foods, one becomes *rājasa* in the first [watch] and *tāmasa* in the second. (70)
In the third [chapter], the subject matter is sattvic; in the fourth (the reading "caturthe" appears in manuscript *ka*), it concerns the five ultimate goals.
At the conclusion of worship, fire-offerings, and recitation, there are oblations for the suppression of enemies.

In the third [watch] he was intoxicated by the enjoyment of gifts, and in the fourth, being self-conceited, his mind was fixed on that [object], his life-breath absorbed therein, and he was reeling from the intoxication of wine. || 72 ||
The sattvic divine state arises again for one who is steadfast;
however, the tamasic state indeed leads to destruction in the human realm.
O Śivā, from the opposite of this, untimely death may occur,
O fair-faced one, caused by poison, weapons, people, thieves, or robbers.
O Pārvatī, know that the total destruction, root and branch, of that evil-minded one follows;
his sons, friends, wife, and others, as well as his companions and servants, likewise perish. (75)
O Śivā, he whose Brahmins, brothers, and other kinsmen languish in great misery, and whose women in the inner apartments behave with wicked conduct; 76.
For one who delights in hunting and is fond of gambling, portents arise accompanied by the cries of "Alas! Alas! among the subjects. (77)
Oppressed and overwhelmed by afflictions, he encounters misfortune at every step—he for whom these [senses] are excessively satisfied, well-disposed, and proclaiming his good fortune. (78)
His lifespan increases constantly, and great prosperity remains stable in his home, O Goddess of the Gods, even if quarrels should arise without cause. (79)
Women who utter inauspicious words should predict his ruin (the reading "ni" is found in the Kāśmīra manuscript).
These and other such defects [are to be considered] during a planetary crisis.
For the increase of longevity and likewise for pacification, the king should perform the Koṭihoma;
there is no rite superior to the Koṭihoma for the destruction of misfortune.
There is nothing equal to that for the destruction of great calamities in the kingdoms of kings;
one should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) during the twilights, intent upon the recitation of mantras.
Indeed, within one year, that which destroys all obstacles shall be accomplished;
for one who loses their knowledge through the drinking of liquor, O beautiful-eyed one, [this practice is necessary]. (83)
Or if he should produce a transformation [of the deity], he will again go to a downward state;
[there may be] delirium (or the reading "pralāpa"), falling away, laughter, anger, madness, and terror. (84)
Laziness, excessive anxiety, engaging in what is undesirable for others, violence, envy, jealousy, hypocrisy, delusion, and negligence; 85.
Possession, death, and fainting are declared to be the transformations [of the self].
Equanimity toward all beings and equality regarding honor and dishonor [are its characteristics]. (86)
He is impartial toward enemy and friend alike, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal;
his external mind has ceased its activity through the bliss arising from the contemplation of Brahman. 87.
At all times and in all places, there is equanimity and changelessness;
his eyes do not blink, and his speech is accompanied by a sweet smile. || 88 ||
These qualities of the nectar have been described; they are difficult to find on earth:
dispassion, the desire for liberation, renunciation, and mastery over all things. (89)
The practice of the eightfold yoga, the complete renunciation of desire for enjoyments, compassion toward all living beings, and the arising of qualities such as omniscience. || 90 ||
The attainment of such qualities as these is said to be the characteristic of success (siddhi):
renown, the acquisition of vehicles, ornaments, and the like, and long life. (91)
Sovereignty over kings and women, mastery over the world, great power, wealth, and the abundance of sons, wives, and other such riches; || 92 ||
The inferior accomplishments (siddhis) have been described here for practitioners;
however, the superior accomplishments are undoubtedly manifest for human beings. 93.
O Supreme Goddess, it is for his sake that noble women, being deeply afflicted, sigh with tears falling, without [even] five [words], and with voices faltering. 94.
All his actions, though performed everywhere with diligence, will be fruitless;
for the fire born of the torment of separation from his beloved consumes him and his lineage down to the seventh generation.
Therefore, one should please one's beloved and not touch even the slightest thing unpleasant to her;
for the beloved is the cause of success and the root upon the paths of worldly existence.
A wife is declared to be the most important [relative], she who at the beginning is joined by the grasping of the hand;
since she is born from him of her own accord, she is therefore called "jāyā" (the one who is born). 97.
O Great Goddess, if one has a single devoted wife who is virtuous and a companion, what need is there for others? Just as I am your lord, so [is he yours]. 98.
Viṣṇu with Śrī, Brahmā with Sarasvatī, and Purandara with Śacī—each having accomplished their desired purpose by attracting a man to their minds with a single [glance]. (99)
Having obtained her alone, he should not even mentally recall another woman; for if his wife is unchaste in the home, he himself becomes a defiler of the family lineage. (100)
O Goddess, his treasury, which was thus described as being ravaged by mice, desired [to be restored] of its own accord without any effort. 101.
But whenever she is his, she is not called "another's woman," even if he has drawn her away by force or by enticing her with wealth and other such means. (102)
O Maheśānī, he who goes to another's wife attains the lowest state;
O Śivā, whether it be one's own wife or another's, she is [the same] when devoid of passion.
Having attained that lack of desire, longing, and faith which she previously lacked, she should become so;
however, when a woman becomes ill-behaved, he should abandon her but never strike her. (104)
O Goddess, one should abandon an extremely wicked woman who goes to base men; having cast her out naked at the king's gate, one should never take her back.

If one reveals the Kula scripture, the Kula practices, and the unsurpassed Kāma-yāga to those who are unworthy, even a perfected one will certainly perish. (Note: *kula* is the reading in the Ka manuscript. 106.
(2 *nya kha pāṭhaḥ |?????
