[Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kula Conduct," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 34 ||
[The Thirty-fifth Chapter] The Goddess said:
How can there be an accomplishment for those practitioners who maintain a secret form?
And what kind of goal is to be accomplished, O Lord, or what kind might be desired? (1)
"And what kind of worship should be performed? Tell me that in great detail.
Īśvara said:
"A man, having performed the rite for his desired object in an extremely secret manner, should perform the worship."
Then, by worshipping Śakti, he attains his desire and partakes in bliss;
through the fruit of that worship, [he casts off] misfortune, which is filled with suffering and poverty. (3)
Everything becomes pacified and one is born as a lord upon the earth;
because it is most highly secret, it is therefore prescribed for the night.
If [the practice] is made public, there will be failure in the task; the beautiful lady becomes angry.
O beloved, for one devoid of devotion to the Guru, the spiritual practice is fruitless.
"By the grace of my Guru, I am the all-pervading, all-knowing Lord;
therefore, the worship of Śakti must always be performed so that she may remain well-pleased. (6)
O Daughter of the Mountain, worship that is devoid of power is fruitless and spreads only outwardly;
likewise, meditation devoid of bliss is as useless as that which bears no fruit.
Even when capable, one should avoid pride, cruelty, and shame, as well as anger and envy;
one should never strike even with a flower, even if that flower takes the form of pride.
One should not feel wonder at her power, for she is of that very nature;
those bound souls who are deluded by the scriptures perish when they are struck with wonder.
He who bows with devotion to Śakti with a one-pointed mind shall achieve success in all his aims and, in the end, attain liberation. (This is the reading of Sva-ka.)
One attains certain liberation through the worship of Śakti; one who is averse to the worship of Śakti is a vulgar man, the lowest of persons. (The reading *sahasra* is found in manuscript *kha*. 11.
How can that shameless one say, "I worship the Great Goddess," when here there is no entitlement whatsoever without worship and fire-offerings?
O Great Goddess, without the fire-oblation (homa), the sacrifice to Śakti is ineffective;
without the sacrifice to Śakti, the fire-oblation is fruitless—of this there is no doubt. (13)
Therefore, a practitioner whose self is purified of worldly existence, who is skilled in the meaning of all tantras,
and who knows reality, should always rely upon Śakti.
Or, if one lacks the capacity for wine, one should examine the conduct of the various castes;
having encountered that which exists among the diverse castes, one should follow it and not abandon it. (15)
Completely freed from all doubt, the omniscient and supreme practitioner,
having performed the rite of the sacrifice of power (śaktiyāga), shall become Indra upon the earth.
One should perform worship at midnight in a secluded place free from animals, being adorned with all ornaments and beautified with fragrant sandalwood paste. || 17 ||
Having drawn forth the pure power, the beautiful woman with lovely eyes, adorned with necklaces and ornaments, and devoid of aversion or shame; (18)
One should place [the image] upon a beautiful, costly spread over a cotton mattress; one should place a well-scented jar filled with wine on the left. (Dāphala, Ka-kha reading). 19.
Having made his heart one with bliss, with a mind immediately serene,
he should bow to the Guru according to the prescribed rite and contemplate that nectar.
Having placed meat, fish, and likewise mūdrā before Śivā,
one should then contemplate the vessel of arghya as the nectar of fire, sun, and moon.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having made a tilaka on her forehead with vermilion,
one should write there the object to be accomplished, interwoven with the root mantra.
Having adorned her again with perfumes, flowers, and garlands, and having rendered her fragrant with incense, O Pārvatī, one should light lamps. (The reading "saghora" is found in manuscript K. 23.
One should place the supreme Vāgbhava-kūṭa from the navel down to the feet,
and the Kāmabīja from the heart down to the navel.
One should contemplate his body from the head down to the region of the heart as consisting of all the gods, a form composed of all mantras.
The practitioner should visualize Śakti, Kāmeśvarī herself, directly before him;
placing his hand upon his heart, he should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
One should contemplate oneself as Kāma and Śakti as the supreme Kāmeśvarī; one should repeatedly drink wine stirred by the tongue of Śakti. (27)
One should drink liquor purified by mantra, silently and without laughter.
At the end of a meal, drink is poison; at the end of drinking, food is poison. (28)

One should know that food which is accompanied by liquor to be nectar (amṛta), for it was drunk in ancient times first by Viṣṇu and thereafter by Śaṅkara. (Note: *pītā* is the reading in manuscript *ka*, while *pīta* is the reading in manuscript *pā*).
It was indeed drunk by Śakra and likewise by Puṣpadanta;
it was drunk by Śukra in ancient times and practiced by Dattātreya.
Then, having been brought to the earth by the illustrious Balarāma, I therefore drink this meritorious liquor with devotion. || 31 ||
For the destruction of the bonds of the individual soul and for the attainment of divine knowledge,
I drink this purifying nectar, the medicine for worldly existence.
Having offered liquor, meat, and whatever else may be a decoration of the family to Śakti, one should then apply the remainder to oneself alone. (33)
Having made [the disciple] drink the beverage again, one should drink the nectar from his mouth;
then one should purify the lamp, for it becomes a lamp and not otherwise.
And the practitioner should drink the honey until the arising of bliss, his mouth filled with betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor. (35)
O Supreme Goddess, the bestower of perfection, he whose eyes are rolling with wine, who is naked, yet the ornament of his lineage, should speak these words with humility.
"The fourfold aims have been entrusted to you; therefore, grant me success.
Having thus obtained her favor, he should cause her to be naked (or "sky-clad," as per the reading in manuscript *ka*). || 37 ||

Having understood the bhaga to be like a triangle, which bestows all accomplishments, and having recollected it as consisting of the three peaks (kūṭas), one should meditate upon it as composed of universal bliss. 38.
Contemplating oneself as the non-dual form of the deity, one should worship with kisses upon the face—which resembles the full moon—and upon the Full-Moon Mountain (Pūrṇādri). 39.
The great sacred seat Jālandhara is said to be the two breasts;
beyond that, the Apāna is the pair of thighs, and [the seat] Kāmarūpa follows after that.

That sacred seat which is the mouth of Brahmā, secret and bestowing all happiness, from which the gods, goddesses, sages, and even human beings [have arisen]. (Note: "bhāvajāḥ" is the reading in manuscript *kha*.)
All these manifest themselves because of that [power] hidden on the surface of the earth;
and that pīṭha, O Maheśvarī, is of two kinds: hidden and manifest.
O Dear One, that which is secret is of great merit compared to that which is manifest, and it is difficult for beasts to attain;
yet, O Goddess of the Gods, that which is secret is obtained everywhere by those who worship the Kula.
One should worship the Goddess here and there with such ritual offerings;
one should attract the vulva by means of the *liṅga* and drink the nectar from the mouth [or tongue, according to the variant reading]. 44.
In this [practice], nail-marks and tooth-wounds are fashioned as flowers;
the embrace, moreover, is musk, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood. (45)
O Goddess, there is kissing, praising, churning, and seizing, O Śivā;
with three peaks there is a triple blow, and from those triple blows, the recitation is performed as one.
Having done this, O Great Goddess, he shall become that very Kāmeśvara;
O Goddess, how else could one perform the Kula worship without wine and meat? (47)
The merit of thousands of other births perishes for him;
yet at the time of cessation, his own [nature] is filled once more with the nectar of existence. 48.
The mouth has the form of a drop (bindu), and below that is a pair of [cups] (kula);
it is filled with the nectar of all vidyās and bestows the power of all speech. (49)
O Goddess, it accomplishes all aims and is the cause of enchanting all;
beneath that, O Supreme Sovereign, one should contemplate one's own body.
O Goddess, by meditating upon or worshipping Him who is perfectly endowed with all knowledge and who bestows mastery over all things, one becomes possessed of the arts of love.
Having understood the various forms of the lineage and having reflected upon them, since one is born into a noble family, how could one reveal that [secret]? 52.
In this way, through the yoga of practice, one becomes perfected; it is not otherwise.
Within a month, the accomplishment of attraction is achieved; within three months, one becomes a lord of speech.
Thus, in the fourth month, one becomes the domain of the Guardians of the Quarters (Dikpālas);
in the fifth, one becomes the five arrows of love (Pañcakāma); and in the sixth, one becomes Rudra—of this there is no doubt. (Note: *pañcakāma* is the reading from manuscript *kha*).
Meditation together with the woman and worship indeed with her alone;
deprived of her, the practitioner of mantra never attains success. (55)
One should perform meditative cultivation together with a woman and likewise offer oblations with her;
for a practitioner of mantra separated from her never attains success.
Women are gods; women are life-breaths; indeed, women alone are the ornament.
One should always remain attached to women; otherwise, one would even [be estranged] from one's own wife. (Note: *ama* is a variant reading for *api*).
One should perform the night-walk at night, and the worship of Śakti at night;
one should engage in conversation regarding the Kula at night, and complete all other [rites] at night. || 58 ||

Then, O Goddess, having performed the morning bath and having offered libations to the gods, the ancestors, and the sages, one should worship the Goddess with ritual services according to the prescribed rule.
The Supreme Deity accepts the worship performed in the forenoon;
O Goddess, the hosts of Yoginīs accept that which is performed at midday.
The worship performed in the afternoon is carried off by yakṣas and rākṣasas;
that which is offered in the forenoon is declared to be nectar (amṛta). (Note: *yat* is the reading in some manuscripts.)
O Goddess of gods, at midday that [blood] is considered supreme;
therefore, O Maheśvarī, with every effort, a householder together with his wife should always perform the external worship only in the morning.

[Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rituals for Optional Worship and Other Practices," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 35 ||
[The Thirty-Sixth Chapter] Īśvara said:
O beautiful one, I shall now explain the further power of the one possessed of conceptual thought.
Just as the practitioner brings about the power of another by means of his own power. || 1 ||
O Śivā, through association with an uninitiated woman, there shall be a loss of spiritual attainment;
therefore, with every effort, one should initiate one's own Kaula consort.
Just as success comes to men through the sole practice of service to the Guru, so too does one become a lord of accomplishments through meditation upon the Mahāpadma grove. (3)
Just as one becomes liberated while living merely by meditating upon Tripura, so too does one become free from sin merely by remembering the Gaṅgā. || 4 ||
By the mere remembrance of this woman, she likewise grants boons;
there is no need for ritual bathing, nor worship, nor meditation, nor even the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa).
Merely by the recollection of the mantra, she grants boons to women;
having brought her own beloved wife, who was virtuous and of great renown.
Having found a preceptor devoted to his own lineage, one should initiate him with the Kula-vidyā;
having initiated him, the preceptor should treat him like his own daughter.
"From this day forward, my daughter, be devoted to the worship of the family deity;
according to the prescribed rite, bring your husband under your control. (Note: *samānaya* is the reading for *vaśyamānaya*.)
"Remember no one other than your husband, who is the very form of Śiva, even in your mind. Having received this command from her guru, she should prostrate herself on the ground like a staff.
O you whose wealth is fame, place the shadow of your lotus feet upon my head;
for if a woman were not initiated [into this], how could there be worship of the lineage? (10)

O Queen, if the family worship is not performed because the family tradition has been neglected, then having reached a day of the Bhūtas in a secluded place devoid of animals [one should perform it]. 11.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights,
having carefully brought pure and beautiful vermilion (sindūra), one should place it upon [the image].
Having drawn a wheel with beautiful lines and supreme brilliance—six-cornered and situated within the interior of a lotus—upon a fireproof earthen dish; || 13 ||
In the center of that, O Goddess, one should draw an image with vermilion;
having written the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) on the cheek, it should be interwoven with the root mantra.
Then, O Goddess, one should write the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) upon all the joints of the limbs;
having placed the floral liquor (puṣpāsava) in the mouth, one should recite the Vasantasundarī mantra. 15.

(Kāma, Indra, the fourth [vowel], joined with Bindu and Nāda—*Īṃ*; Bhuvaneśī—*Hrīṃ*; likewise *Klīṃ Hrīṃ Ai*; O Nīlasubhage, hili hili, Vicce Svāhā—this is Vasantasundarī. Kāma, Indra, and the fourth [vowel], accompanied by Bindu and Nāda;
that seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśānī, together with the twelfth vowel and the Bindu. (16)
Then, O beautiful Nīlā, after "hili hili," one should utter the word "vicce svāhā"; this is the Vasantasundarī-vidyā. (17)

Having performed meditation upon Sundarī, the practitioner, whose heart is filled with the bliss of consciousness and whose mind is steady, should perform the ritual placement of the vital breaths (jīvanyāsa).
Between consciousness and the liquor of wine, consciousness alone is more important;
O Goddess, one should unite with that consciousness both within oneself and within the Kula lineages.
With his mouth filled with betel, adorned with red ornaments,
and seated upon a red throne, he [placed] his family upon a couch.
Seated on the left side, adorned with red garments, enriched with all the ornaments of amorous attire, and with eyes sparkling and trembling. || 21 ||
[She] whose pair of breasts has conquered the broad frontal globes of a mighty elephant;
resting her arm upon his shoulder, she artfully grasped the hem of his garment as it hung over her breast. || 22 ||
Then, O Goddess, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the image as before;
O you who are worshipped by heroes, the worship should be performed according to the previously stated rule. (23)
With his mouth filled with betel, that family [of practitioners] is thus designated;
then, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with a mind focused through the yoga of meditation.
Extending for a hundred yojanas, situated between rivers and mountains,
she was confined within thousands of other islands by means of fetters and other restraints.
Her gait was agitated by the weight of her breasts; she possessed dark eyes and adorned her heavy hips with the ornament of her rounded buttocks. (26)

Her heart captivated by the practitioner, she crept into the interior of the cave, within the space of the enclosure wall secured with iron door-panels. (Note: *vividhāntare* is the reading in manuscript *kha*.)
Having performed the recitation of the *kulākula*, the practitioner brings [the deity] under control;
I shall now describe the intermediate fire-oblation (*homa*) by which one becomes composed of Brahman. (28)
Know that this world, both conscious and unconscious, consists of Śiva and Śakti;
I shall tell you what has been seen through the power of my knowledge. (29)
O Śivā, in a solitary and pure place, with the collection of channels purified,
one should sit comfortably on an even seat with the body held straight.
Seated in the lotus posture, the practitioner of purified consciousness should cleanse the path of the vital breath through inhalation, retention, and exhalation.
Having covered the hands, they rest upon the staff in the *ādhāra-yoga* posture;
the eyes are fixed on the tip of the nose, free from blinking or opening. || 32 ||
The self is situated between the eyebrows; one should touch the teeth with the teeth, the lower lip with the upper lip, and the palate with the tongue.
This, however, is the Sundarīmudrā, which bestows the joy of Sundarī;
[it is formed] by the wind arising from the support (ādhāra) within the supreme thousand-petaled lotus.
Having agitated the circle of nectar, which has the form of the flame of the lamp of the family,
one should again visualize a stream of nectar falling into the root lotus.
And thus one should divide [the offering] into seven parts for the sake of the Goddess's presence,
having recollected the supreme [Goddess], who consists of Brahman, through the root mantra and the yoga of meditation.
In the heart, within the center of the lotus, in the Bāṇaliṅga, and in the radiant light—
there one should worship the primordial Goddess, who takes forms at will, in the heart.
Having invited [the deity] through *pūraka* (inhalation) and established [him] through *kumbhaka* (retention),
and having fully realized the wheel of the body, one should joyfully offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings.
With the water of supreme nectar contained within the vessel of the Kuṇḍalinī,
one should offer water for the feet at the two feet, and then again cause the arghya offering to be presented.

The bees from the thousand-petaled lotus, whether agitated or unagitated, should offer the supreme nectar-water as an *ācamana* (sipping water) for the mouth. (Note: Regarding the word *lulitālulita*, there is a variant reading *cyutim ka pāṭhaḥ*.)
The wise one should offer fragrance consisting of the thirty-six principles;
non-violence is the supreme flower, and non-stealing is indeed a flower. (41)
Compassion is a flower, forbearance is a flower, and the restraint of the senses is a flower; likewise, freedom from delusion, absence of envy, and absence of hatred are flowers as well. (42)
The wise know that non-attachment and truth are likewise flowers;
one should always offer these flowers of inner disposition. (43)
One should offer wind with incense, present light with a lamp,
likewise offer the ocean of wine, and offer a mountain of meat.
One should give the sun and a mirror, the moon and an excellent umbrella;
likewise, one should give the ornament of bliss, a garment, and a fly-whisk.
One should offer this bell, which consists of the sound of the unstruck resonance (anāhata).
Then, the best of practitioners [should worship] with those arising from the aesthetic sentiments (rasa), such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and others. 46.
One should gratify the Supreme Goddess with dance, song, and instrumental music;
[with] sound, through the differentiation of phonemes, amidst the mass of light and space.
In the center of the thousand-petaled lotus, one should contemplate the supreme Sundarī;
and in its center, the liṅga of Bhairavānanda, joined with the yoni.
Having brought about the unification of those two, one should then cause the nectar to flow;
then, through the union with the tongue and the throat, one should drink that nectar. 49.
That which is drunk by yogis is not wine made from molasses or flour;
O Daughter of the Mountain, it is the water contained within the earth, and within that, the void.
O Īśvarī, the wind resides within the void; within the wind is sound;
within that is resonance (nāda); and within resonance is the Bindu, the Lord.
In the midst of that, however, is the supreme light, a subtle crest of flame higher than the highest,
resembling the flash of lightning and radiant as a thousand suns.
Extremely subtle due to her beautiful vision, formless, without abode, consisting of supreme bliss, and full—she is the supreme Sundarī. 53.

The dissolution of the earthly elements and of those belonging to the earth should be performed through meditative absorption; likewise, the dissolution of the waters into water, and of the void into the void, should be performed. 54.
One should dissolve the winds into the wind, and the sound into the resonance;
there, one should dissolve the lights into that [resonance], and thus the mind is dissolved into Brahman. (55)
The mind commits evil deeds; the mind is stained by evils.
But when the mind has become mindless (*unmanībhūta*), there is neither dharma nor sin. (Note: *syunma* is an alternative reading for *manasi*.)

Thus, through meditation, O Śivā, the steadfast one, filled with supreme bliss, turns the ocean of saṃsāra into a mere puddle in a cow’s hoofprint. (Note: *hṛṣṭaḥ* is the reading in the Kha manuscript.)
He who holds liberation from worldly existence in his hand would be my equal on earth;
such worship is said to consist of knowledge, for no fire-sacrifice (homa) is like it. (58)
Know that the form of the *kuṇḍa* consists of a dot (*bindu*) and three circles;
it is delightful with the girdle of bliss and adorned by the womb of the measures (*mātrā*). (59)

O Goddess, having meditated upon that supreme Brahman within the blazing fire manifested by the expansion of all-encompassing knowledge, one should offer the supreme oblation of phenomenal existence (prapañca-havis).
The syllable known as Mātṛkā is the form of sound, yet it is resplendent as the imperishable (akṣara).
When that imperishable is offered as an oblation here, the soundless Brahman arises.

O Goddess, merit and demerit are the oblation; O Auspicious One, what is done and what is not done is the oblation; likewise, intention and hesitation, as well as dharma and adharma, are the oblation.

With the ladle of the mind, I constantly offer the functions of the senses as oblations into the blazing fire of the self, which is the sacrificial offering, by way of the path of the *suṣumṇā*. (Note: *dharmādharmau* is the reading in some manuscripts. 63.
With my two hands [the *prakāśa* and *vimarśa*], I grasp the *unmanā* ladle;
I offer into the fire that which is filled with the oil of the portions (*kalā*) of merit and demerit. 64.

O Śivā, when the knower of mantras has become free from the phenomenal world (niṣprapañca), he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the two mantras at the end, joined with the wife of Vahni (the svāhā-utterance).
Then that practitioner, consisting of consciousness, is manifest as Brahman alone.

[Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Reality of the Invocation and Worship of Śakti," in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara within the illustrious Gandharva Tantra. || 36 ||
[The thirty-seventh chapter] | The Goddess said:
From embracing the wives of others, as well as from associating with the base...
And from attachment to those born in the inverse order, a man becomes an outcast. || 1 ||
O Lord, O Supreme Ishvara, how can one attached to power be liberated?
That very attachment is the obstacle to liberation according to the Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas. (Note: "Parameśvara" is the reading in manuscript ka.)
For Śakti is indeed the root of the world; she alone is the very form of the world.
By abandoning woman, the world is abandoned; by abandoning the world, one becomes happy. (3)
"O Lord of Gods, [the use of] all [women] is censured in all rites everywhere; how then could they be suitable for that? Such is the established position of those who know the Vedas. (4)
Īśvara said:
O Maheśānī, this has already been explained before;
the course of dharma is subtle, and it is not understood by the deluded.
For through knowledge the universe is stainless, O beloved, while through ignorance it is stained;
this Fire, O Great Goddess, is all-pervading and the consumer of all.
How was he instructed by those learned in the Vedas regarding the sacrifice to the deities?
And likewise, O daughter of the mountain, how is it that water is said to be pure?
Honey is that which has been enjoyed by bees from flowers; it is the residue of what was left by flies. How can the drinking of wine, which is defiling, be prescribed for use in a sacrifice?
O Pārvatī, how is it that cow's milk— the essence of cows— and oil produced from seeds are prescribed for use in rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors?
Know, O lady of virtuous vows, that through the destruction of the seed comes the destruction of many;
likewise, among all wives, one who has been born will continue to be born. (Note: *janiṣyate* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
Purified once by Vedic mantras, it becomes a purifier;
likewise, when cleansed by both Vedic and Tantric rites, this liquor becomes pure.
O Goddess of gods, there is no fault in the accomplishment of the Mahāvidyās;
whatever the custom is in a particular place, such indeed is the dharma there. (12)
In this matter, delusion is a great defect; therefore, O beloved, abandon delusion.
One who is devoid of the state of non-duality has a dualistic mind and is thus a seeker of sensual pleasure.
If one devoid of the state of divinity, or again through a state of lust, should unite with the power of another, he becomes a violator of the Guru’s bed. || 14 ||
O Śivā, she who by the prescribed method brings one to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra,
by an improper method casts one into the ocean of hell.
Without the *śakti*, without wine, and without the contemplation of non-duality (*advaitabhāvanā*),
the practice of the *Mahāvidyā* is like a sacrifice devoid of clarified butter.
O Great Goddess, when duality exists, there is the conceptualization of castes and classes;
but when the mind has dissolved into Brahman, it attains the state of non-duality.
Who is Kāma? Who might be Indra? Who is Brahmā? Who is Janārdana?
Who is the god? Who is the asura, the yakṣa, or the piśāca? Who is the immortal, O Śivā? (18)
O Śivā, who is a twice-born, or who is a Śūdra; who is a Mleccha, and who is the lowest? What is beautiful form, and what is deformed? Who is diseased, and who is free from ailment? (19)
Furthermore, what is pure and what is impure? What is a real entity and what is a non-entity?
Who is a friend and who is an enemy? And who is one to be slain, or indeed one who is not to be slain at all? (20)
Furthermore, what is edible and what is inedible, or what belongs to you and what belongs to me—this is all constructed by ignorance; cut through this doubt with knowledge.
Know her, O Pārvatī, to be my supreme knowledge;
she performs many functions for that which is one, and assumes many forms for that which is one.
It is certain that the many forms and bodies belong to this very one alone;
the mass of non-dual bliss is revealed by knowledge alone. (23)
The meat that is in the limbs [of sacrificial animals] is meat comparable to nectar;
however, the slaughter of the animal is for that purpose alone, for without it, one would become a slayer of a Brahmin. (24)
One should recognize that those who perceive duality are like cattle, while those who know non-duality are the true Brahmins;
therefore, the ignorant man incurs great sin through the crime of theft. (Note: *tantra* is omitted from the manuscript reading. 25.
However, the drinking of liquor in sacrifices is not [a sin]; otherwise, one becomes a sinner.
O auspicious lady, everything is pure if one's underlying disposition (vāsanā) is not contemptible.

O Śivā, whatever body is seen in this world— from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, including all things moving and stationary— that is composed of primordial matter (prakṛti) and is the result of past karma.
Action is performed by nature (prakṛti), yet the person (puruṣa) is called its witness;
deluded by her māyā, he then thinks, "I am the doer. (28)
The Puruṣa is not the agent, O Goddess; Prakṛti is said to be the agent.
The Puruṣa possesses no instrument of action, O Beloved, because he is eternally devoid of qualities.
Likewise, O Goddess, the agency of action is established in the qualified [nature]; this which is perceived as agency in the Puruṣa is [actually] grounded there. (30)
O Goddess, O sinless one, just as the redness of the *japā* flower appears in a pure crystal, so am I—the imperishable one who pervades all things externally and internally—like the sky. (31)
Always equal toward all, pure, unattached, stainless, and immovable;
that which is truth, knowledge, and infinite—that Supreme Brahman, I am indeed that. 32.
Having fixed one's mind upon Brahman, one is not tainted while performing action;
indeed, it is possible for one to cross the ocean of worldly existence by means of both [paths].
Whether by the right path or the wrong, whether through suffering or through happiness,
one may cross the ocean by means of a raft made of jars or by means of an excellent ship.
Therefore, O lady of excellent vows, this Kaula [path] is superior even to the Dakṣiṇa;
O Goddess, without the knowledge of Kula, there is never liberation at any time. (35)
For this Māyā is indeed powerful, consisting of the qualities (guṇas);
she is celebrated as Prakṛti by those proficient in Sāṃkhya and Yoga. (36)
She is called "Knowledge" and "Ignorance" by those who perceive the true meaning of the Vedas; she is called "Great Knowledge" by some, and "Great Illusion" by others. (37)
"She is the power of all beings"—thus she is worshipped by some;
indeed, all worship her, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. (Note: *sarve tāṃ* is the reading in the Ka and Kha manuscripts.)
There is no difference for me between her, Viṣṇu, or Brahmā;
she is one who is delighted by those bowed down by the hardships of yoga, enjoyment, and austerity.
She alone, when propitiated by the practitioner through whatever means according to the prescribed rite, bestows upon men enjoyment, heaven, and liberation.
Bound by the shackles of saṃsāra, a person is liberated by her;
O Goddess, without satisfaction in her, liberation is simply not found. (41)
Therefore, men who desire liberation should with great effort [worship] her, for she is honored by men and [grants the goal] to those whose minds have been restrained.
Through yoga and other means, they take refuge in her whose nature is eternal bliss;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise I, worship her as our own self. (43)
O Goddess, established in the state of a beast, Vidhi propitiated Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, with the hardships of asceticism and through supreme devotion.
Having obtained the power of will and Vāgīśī, he brought about creation;
yet Brahmā, though noble-minded, out of delusion accepted [her] as his daughter, becoming like a bound beast. 45.
That loathsome and unrighteous act has not ceased even to this day;
therefore, a bound soul (paśu) should not even mentally recall the power of another. 46.
The Brahmins, relying on that very state, worship her alone;
for them, wine, ghee, and milk are the friends of all living beings.
They may take cakes, flour-pastries, and meat provided by their power;
or else, being intent on their agreements, they may remain dependent upon that power.

Established in his divine state, Viṣṇu gratified her who is the embodiment of bliss and whose form is the protection of the world, by means of the enjoyment of honey-wine, maireya-wine, and other offerings. || 49 ||
Having obtained Lakṣmī, who consists of the power of knowledge and whose form is the support of the universe,
he became the protector of the world, free from all agitation.
The kings, relying upon that very state, likewise worship her;
so too do the gods, the Daityas, the sages, and other humans. (51)
For they constantly worship Viṣṇu alone for the sake of attaining their spiritual state;
and he, whose self is purified by that devotion, indeed protected that very disposition of theirs.
Those who rejoice in that state and always protect it are indeed all most beloved to the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace.
O Goddess, in order to turn people away from that state of being, Hari, the Lord of the world and Sovereign of the universe,
commanded me as follows.
The Blessed One said: "All shall become divine once my true nature is revealed;
however, he who prioritizes the state of a beast and reviles my true nature [shall not]. (55)
"O God, by means of fabricated scriptures, turn those who are averse to my nature away from it.
Īśvara said:
Having placed that command of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor upon his head... (56)
In that very manner, O Great Goddess, I composed this extensive Tantra,
concealing its divine nature while presenting the perspective of the bound soul (paśu).
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, in the Vaiṣṇava system indeed,
the state of being a bound soul (paśubhāva) is honored, and the censure of Śakti is disregarded.
That power which belongs to all beings becomes twofold once again;
O Pārvatī, that Goddess exists both in a gross form and in a subtle form.
In her gross form, that Goddess, desiring happiness, deluded all people and this entire triple world with her many forms. (Note: *bahurūpā* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
O Supreme Goddess, she remains established with a form fashioned by her divine play;
people, deluded by her māyā, do not recognize her due to their own nature. 61.
But some very foolish people, destined for hell, strike her with blows and the like, as well as with harsh words and insults. (Note: *mūḍhā* is the reading; *ca sumūḍhā* is a variant. 62.
Indeed, some wise men, who accomplish the four aims of human life, honor her with ornaments, garments, enjoyments, and even service. (63)
Those who act against their wishes will certainly fall;
know her to be of subtle form, residing within the end of all things.
Having united the Goddess, the mother of the three worlds, who is the embodiment of supreme bliss, with the highest bliss by means of the primary path of Brahman; (variant reading: *parānande*).

From the union of those two, the nectar arises; with that, the wise one, O Goddess, whose mind is fixed on the purified channels, should satisfy the Yoginī by means of breath-retention. (Note: *sudhīḥ* is the reading, not *manaḥ* as found in manuscript *ka*).
One should cause the vital breaths to enter through the channel and offer them into its mouth;
when that mouth is pierced by the wind, the Supreme Goddess ascends upward.
Therefore, having drawn in that wind and retained it by means of kumbhaka, one should accumulate it;
and with those accumulated winds, [one should direct] that [power] which moves along the path of the *kula*.

Having raised [the breath] into the supreme *haṃsa* within the thousand-petaled great lotus and the orb of white light, one should contemplate the unity of those two with the intellect. (Note: *aikya* is the reading in the Ka-pāṭha.)
The oblation and other rites prescribed therein consist of the moon and the sun; taking up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles for those two, one should offer the imperishable oblation (*havis*).
In the supreme wheel at the root-support (mūlādhāra), there is the auspicious power Kuṇḍalinī;
by her whirling motion, this [breath] goes outward day after day.
According to the measurement of Dineśa’s fingers, that [penance] is half when performed as a fast;
it should be double at the time of sexual intercourse, and triple outside of a meal.
O Goddess, if from this point upward the vital wind (māruta) flows for three days, or if it is deficient, the life-force (prāṇa) abandons the body below that [point]. || 73 ||
As long as this wind, the lord of the universe, flows within it, so long does this body move; without it, it is known to be motionless.
Having made the breath motionless, the yogi becomes a perfected practitioner;
for by the breath, the mind of living beings is led outward, O Śivā. (Note: *prāṇinām* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
When the breath has become perfectly steady, the mind too shall attain steadiness.

When the state of non-duality between these two is realized, both attain immobility. (Note: *ka* refers to the reading "bhāvena" and *tvagaiteyoḥ* refers to the reading "tvagaterdvayoḥ" in the respective verses.)
Know the body to be free from disease, and having abandoned the physical frame, [attain liberation].
Having attained the state of non-duality, he shall not return here again.
O Goddess, this unsurpassed perfection of the body has been described as a secondary consequence. 78.
By that very procedure, Maheśvarī was thoroughly pleased; by her, a man bound by the fetters of saṃsāra is liberated. (The reading *anenaiva* is found in the Kha manuscript.)

O Goddess, for a person whose mind has not been captured, O Maheśvarī, there is no liberation at all without satisfaction regarding that [practice]. (Note: *ani-* is the reading in the *ka* manuscript; *tanni-* is the reading in other manuscripts. 80.

[Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Śakti and the Attainment of the Body," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 37 ||
[The Thirty-eighth Chapter] Īśvara said:
Worshipped for a long time, she who possesses a subtle form becomes pleased.
But he is not so pleased by enjoyments and by the practice of austerities as [he is by this]. || 1 ||
Therefore, by pleasing her with enjoyments, one shall be liberated by her and become happy;
for even I, O Goddess, formerly served her by way of yoga. (2)
The goddess, remaining within my subtle form, was not fully satisfied, seeing me devoid of power and likewise bowed down with face averted. (3)
With a dejected face and a heart burning with grief,
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, fell under the sway of anxiety.
Having approached me and likewise Viṣṇu, he went to the Ocean of Milk,
to the beautifully adorned Ratnadvīpa on the northern shore of the Kṣīroda.
Standing there between us two, Brahmā became absorbed in meditation upon the lotus-like feet of the Goddess situated within the center of his heart-lotus.
Fixing his mind [on her], the one whose soul was absorbed in yoga recited the supreme Devīsūkta.
Then, after a long time had passed, the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds, [appeared].
The goddess, bearing a trident and a noose, adorned with a crown and other ornaments, four-armed and three-eyed, is as ruddy as the rays of the rising sun. (8)
Then Śivā, being pleased, revealed her own form to him;
and beholding her gracious, the Creator, the teacher of the entire world, [was filled with joy].
With his face bowed in devotion, he praised her and prostrated before her.
Brahmā said:
"You are Sāvitrī, the goddess of speech; you are Śrī, the mother of the entire world. (10)
Svāhā, you are in the sacrifices to the gods; Svadhā, you are in the sacrifices to the ancestors; and indeed, you are the oblation in the worlds of the gods and among humans.
You are indeed the sciences and the mantras; you are the Vedas, for you are the essence of the vowels.
You are truly the essence of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), which is especially that which cannot be uttered.
You alone are the supreme power, whose form is the cause of the universe;
you are to be contemplated again and again through the eightfold yoga by means of its characteristics and other attributes.
O Goddess, that which is made firm is Your eternal form—
that which is unmanifest, indefinable, and partless of the Supreme Self.
That subtle form of yours alone is the entire world; that which is our power of creation is likewise the power of Hari for maintenance. (Note: *jaganmayi* is the reading in manuscript *kha*.)
Likewise, you are that eternal power of the Lord residing within;
you are the fierce power inherent in fire,
and you are the burning power of the sun's rays.
You are more delightful than abundant moonlight;
I praise you, O Ambikā, and I bow down to you. || 16 ||
You are the woman for those who love women; you are the sacred knowledge (vidyā) of those whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas);
you are the desire of all the worlds, and likewise, you are the illusory power (māyā) of Hari.
You, by whom Brahman is revealed, are eternal; be gracious to me!
You are the beginning of the universe, you are without beginning, the source of the universe, and yet unborn.
From the infinite entire world, you alone are of a singular form;
though one, you become threefold, performing the acts of creation, maintenance, and destruction.
You are the boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, the bestower of happiness and liberation;
you are eternal and you are transient, and you are the enchantress of all that moves and is immobile.
Salutations to you, O Mother of the worlds, eternal one in the form of creation;
salutations to you in the form of maintenance, and salutations to you in the form of dissolution.
Being thus praised by Viriñci, that Yoganidrā appeared visibly before Brahmā, the Supreme Self.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the World, O All-pervading One, I am well-pleased by this hymn of yours.
Choose a boon—may it be auspicious for me—that dwells in your heart. (23)
Īśvara said:
"Beholding me, the cause of the dissolution of the universe,
you should grant me the power of creation, and you [should grant] that power of preservation which resides in Viṣṇu."
O Mother, grant me the power of withdrawal within Īśāna; salutations be unto you!
The Lord of Beings moves alone; he does not seek a second.
"Likewise, O Lord of All, delude him so that he himself desires to seize [your] wife.
The Goddess said:
"O Brahman, that which has been spoken by you is true and not otherwise. (26)
Having deluded Śaṅkara, the Lord, by means of my form as Satī, O Lord of the World, I shall destroy this entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile. (27)
"Even there, O Pārvatī, having cast off that body, I shall come into being," thus the Supreme Goddess addressed Brahmā.
Being gazed upon by the Creator of the World, she vanished right there;
and when she had disappeared, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the Worlds, [remained].
With palms joined in reverence, Prajāpati said to Viṣṇu:
"Grant me that heroic state which is fit for the act of universal destruction. (30)
"Therefore, O Great God Viṣṇu, point out that which is difficult to obtain in the worlds.
Having heard those words, the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign, [spoke].
"O blessed lady, he commanded me to attain the state of a hero, which is very difficult to obtain.
Abiding in that heroic state, O mother, I attend upon you. (Note: *tvāṃ* or *tiṣṭha* is an alternative reading. 32.
Even now, O Supreme Goddess, O Mother, salutations again and again to you!
You are the primordial nature of all beings, for you are the progenitor of the entire universe. (The variant reading "prakṛtis tva" is noted. 33.
O Goddess of gods, that form of mine which is proclaimed to be the nature of the earth is you alone; it is not "me," nor am I it, O Mother—truly, salutations, salutations! (34)
That second form of mine which is said to consist of water—you are indeed that; I am not other than you, nor do I exist apart from you, O Mother. This is the truth; salutations, salutations! (35)

O Mother, that third power of mine which belongs to Agni and causes the agitation of the universe is you alone; there is no "I" for me, nor am I separate from you—this is the truth. Salutations, salutations!
The fourth form is that of Vāyu, the agent of creation and destruction; you alone are she. O Mother, it is not "mine," nor am I; this is the truth—salutations, salutations! (37)
And you alone are that fifth [state] which consists of the transformation of all things; O Mother, you are not "mine," nor am I yours—this is the truth. Salutations, salutations!
She who is celebrated as the nourisher of all the gods—that you alone are; O Mother, it is not "me," nor am I [other than you]; this is the truth. Salutations, salutations! (39)
O Mother, that seventh form of mine which brings delight to the world is you alone; it is not mine, nor am I it—this is the truth. Salutations, salutations!
That eighth form of mine which effects both preservation and destruction is you alone;
I am not other than you, nor do I exist apart from you, O Mother—this is the truth. Salutations, salutations!
And yet, I do not exist, nor does anything whatsoever belong to me on this surface of the earth;
for this entire world is pervaded by you alone, and indeed, you are the whole universe.
The Goddess said:
"O child, you speak the truth; the entire world is pervaded by me.
These incarnations of mine, such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others, are indeed my own. (43)
You alone am I, and you are not another; I am Brahmā, and I am Viṣṇu as well.
I alone am the entire universe; nothing exists apart from me.
"O child, whatever you see upon the surface of the earth, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, that is none other than myself; of this there is no doubt. (45)
"Behold today the entire universe, with all its moving and non-moving beings, gathered here in one place.
Having spoken thus, the Sovereign of the World showed [herself] to Śambhu.

Having seen the entire universe entered into his own body in manifold ways, Śambhu—deluded by Māyā and seeing [himself] as consisting of the universe—said: "O Mother of the Universe, deliver me from the midst of this ocean of delusion. (Note: *jaganmayīm* is the reading; *tato dṛṣṭvā* is an alternative reading. 47.
[Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Śiva’s Attainment of Power," in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara within the glorious Gandharva Tantra. || 38 ||
[The Forty-Ninth Chapter] Jaganmāyā said:
"Do not despair, O Mahādeva; remain steadfast in every way."
How indeed are you a knower of the Kula, and furthermore, how are you a knower of existence?
Thus have you been questioned by me; do not forget yourself—that abode consisting of bliss, which is conjoined with the distinctions of one's own knowledge.
Both the Puruṣa and Prakṛti are eternal and exist together;
the Goddess possesses qualities and supreme power, while the Puruṣa is devoid of qualities and powerless.
That [Māyā], whose nature is beginningless ignorance, a portion of Me, and appearing in the form of duality,
approached His presence, desiring to create, yet remaining lowly.
Formerly, indeed, the Supreme Being was entreated by me with the desire to create;
having been addressed thus, "Delight me with joy," the Lord was approached with boldness.
As soon as he was overcome by me, that omnipresent Lord became possessed of attributes;
then, through the abundance of those various blisses, I too became joyful again and again.
O Lord, because both were insentient, they entered a state of void;
then, from the two whose nature is bliss, the primordial and eternal Śakti was born.
She consists of the three qualities (guṇatraya) and has the nature of the three points (bindu);
having placed the Puruṣa below, she has the nature of the half-syllable *ha*.
She, whose nature is that of fire, moon, and sun, delights in the reverse order;
she is established in the form of all things without head, ending with the letter *ha*, and devoid of the final [letter]. 9.
We worship that very Self which moves incessantly within;
O Mahādeva, this entire creation is established upon the three *bindus*.

Know that the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, including all things moving and stationary, consists of the five elements; it is unreal, yet it appears as real through delusion. (11)
O Mahādeva, this earth is an artificial creation and not real;
it is neither a Brāhmaṇī, nor a Caṇḍālī, nor a goddess, nor a human woman. || 12 ||
Know that water is merely taste—neither a twice-born nor a Pukkasa (or as another reading has it, neither a Pukkasa nor a Śvapāka).
But fire is merely form; how can there be any conception of caste therein?
The wind is indeed merely touch, being neither superior nor inferior;
and space is merely sound, belonging to that pervasive Great Self. (14)
O Goddess, a fool, deluded by the manifestation of ignorance, imagines inferiority; yet this body, whether stationary or moving, is composed of these five elements. (15)

That which is the conjunction of the five, which is neither a Brāhmaṇa nor a Pukkasa (the latter being the reading in the Kāśmīra recension), one should know that to be unreal; the Truth is Brahman, and that [conjunction] is not it.
Śiva, the embodied soul, is distinct from the body and possesses the nature of supreme bliss;
he who knows that "He is Brahman" is alone considered a true Brāhmaṇa. || 17 ||
That which is observed, O Lord, in this body composed of the five elements, when the group of sense-faculties is impelled by the five winds, is auspicious. (18)
O Lord, the notion that the self is the agent is a great delusion born of ignorance;
for while the senses are active, the self appears to be the actor to those who lack discernment. (Note: *avivekī* is an alternative reading for *vivekī*.)
Just as the moon appears to be running when the clouds are rushing along,
so too do the body, senses, mind, and intellect appear to move by relying upon the consciousness of the Self.

Just as people rely upon the light of the sun for their own purposes, so too do they depend upon the body, the senses, the qualities, and actions upon the stainless Self, which is existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda). 21.

Just as the sky appears blue through the error of non-discrimination, so too do agency and other qualities falsely attributed to the Self arise from ignorance regarding the mental adjunct (mānasopādhi). (Verse 22)

Just as movement and other qualities are imagined in the moon reflected in water according to the nature of the water, so too do passion, desire, pleasure, pain, and the like proceed when the intellect exists. (The reading "satyā" is found in the Kha manuscript. 23.
In deep sleep that [cognition] does not exist; therefore, its destruction belongs to the intellect and not to the Self, just as light belongs to the sun, coolness to water, and heat to fire.

The nature of the Self—consisting of existence, consciousness, bliss, eternity, and purity—is twofold: the aspect of existence and consciousness belonging to the Self, and the modification of the intellect. (Verse 25)
Through non-discrimination, having joined [the two], one proceeds with the thought "I know";
yet there is no modification of the Self, nor does the awakening of the intellect ever cease. (26)
The individual soul (jīva), having known everything as consisting of the Self, yet perceiving itself as the doer and the seer, becomes deluded.
Having perceived the Self as being like a snake in a rope, the individual soul carries fear.
If it is known that "I am not the individual soul, but the Supreme Self," one becomes fearless;
for the One alone illumines the self as well as the senses, such as the intellect and the rest. 28.

A lamp, like a jar or other objects, is not illuminated by those things produced from its own self; likewise, for the Self, which is of the nature of consciousness, there is no desire for another consciousness nor a need for it in its own awakening. (Note: *bodhe* and *bodharūpasya* are alternative readings found in manuscript *ka*.)

Just as a lamp has no desire for a lamp in its own self-illumination, so too, by means of the scriptural statement "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), [the Self] negates all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). (Verse 30)
One should realize the identity of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) through the great sayings (mahāvākya);
the visible world, such as the body and so forth, is born of ignorance and is momentary like a bubble.
One should know that which is distinct from this [body] to be the stainless "I am Brahman.

Because I am distinct from the body, there are for me no birth, old age, emaciation, dissolution, and so forth; because I am separate from the body, there are for me no birth, old age, and the like. (Variant reading: *dehātyatvāt*.)
There is no attachment to objects such as sound because I am devoid of sense organs; and due to the absence of a mind, I have no suffering, passion, hatred, fear, or the like.

For according to the teaching of such scriptural injunctions as, "He is indeed without breath, without mind, pure," [it is established that] He is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), actionless (niṣkriya), eternal (nitya), free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), and untainted (nirañjana). 34.
I am changeless, formless, eternally liberated, and stainless;
I am the eternal, pure, free, one, indivisible, blissful, and non-dual. || 35 ||
"That which is Truth and consists of Knowledge—that Supreme Brahman, I am indeed that.
Having cultivated this latent impression (*vāsanā*) "I am Brahman" through constant practice, [one attains liberation].
It removes the distractions of ignorance, just as an elixir removes diseases. || 36 ||
Śambhu said:
"O Mother of the World, tell me how the Self is distinct from the body, what it is like, where it resides, and how that Brahman is known."
Jaganmāyā said:
Due to ignorance, the Self appears as if limited; when that ignorance is destroyed, the Self shines forth by itself alone, like the sun when the clouds have cleared.
Having made the soul turbid with ignorance stainless through the practice of knowledge, ignorance itself perishes, just as water [purifies] by means of the *kataka* nut. (39)
For cyclic existence, joined with passion, hatred, and the like, is indeed like a dream; when awakening is absent, it appears as real, but when awakening is present, it becomes as if unreal. (40)
The world appears as real only so long as Brahman—the non-dual substratum of all—is not known, just like the silver [seen] in a mother-of-pearl shell. (41)
All various manifestations are conceived within the eternal Viṣṇu, who is the essence of Truth-Consciousness, just as bracelets and other ornaments are fashioned from gold. 42.

Just as the all-pervading Hṛṣīkeśa, like space, appears as if divided due to various limiting adjuncts (upādhi), yet becomes one [as pure space] when those [adjuncts] are destroyed; so too [is the Self]. (The reading "ekavat" is supported by manuscript *kha*.)

It is solely due to various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that caste, color, stage of life, and so forth are superimposed upon the Self, just as distinctions of taste, color, and so on are [superimposed] upon water. (Variant reading in manuscript *kha*: "rasavarṇādi") 44.
The body, born from the fivefold great elements and accumulated through karma, is said to be the locus for the experience of pleasure and pain. (45)

The subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra), which is the instrument of experience, arises from the unevolved elements (apañcīkṛta-bhūta) and is endowed with the five vital breaths, the mind, the intellect, and the ten sense organs. (46)
The indefinable beginningless ignorance is called the causal limiting adjunct (*upādhi*);
one should realize the Self as distinct from these three adjuncts. (Variant readings: *ātmānam avadhārayet* / *ātmā kham pāṭhaḥ*) 47.
Having contemplated the Self as abiding in all beings, and likewise all beings within the Self, contemplate indeed upon the One alone. 48.
Observe that this world is neither real by way of its arising nor by way of its dissolution.
The mind commits sins; the mind is defiled by sin.
When the mind has become *unmana* (transcended), there is neither dharma nor transgression. 49.

[Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction on Knowledge Given by the Goddess to Śiva," in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara within the glorious Gandharva Tantra. || 39 ||
[Fortieth Chapter] Śambhu said:
O Goddess of the lords of gods, tell me how both have become manifest.
And how does knowledge consisting of Śiva and Śakti likewise arise? || 1 ||
Jaganmāyā said: They say that the male state is Śiva and the female state is the supreme Prakṛti;
Śiva is composed of knowledge within the body, while the supreme Śakti is composed of intellect.
Śukra is Śiva and mahāmedas is Śakti; likewise, Kuṇḍalinī is Śakti and the liṅga is Śiva.
Thus, in the world, the yoni is seen as Śakti and the liṅga as Śiva. (Note: *śiva* is the reading in the Ka-pāṭha.)
Thus is the Śakti Tripurā, and thus is Śiva Tripura;
no distinction exists between these two, for that which is Śakti is certainly Śiva.
There is no Śakti without Śiva, nor is there Śiva devoid of Śakti; there is no distinction between them as they have become one, just like the moon and its moonlight.
Thus, those two exist in all beings in a twofold manner;
therefore, this entire world of moving and non-moving things is not distinct from them.
Father, mother, and son—this manifold state of being is false;
yet, through the very firm practice of ignorance, it has become solidified and remains established in the heart. (7)
Through the word of the guru and through firm practice, a person should know that [reality];
he indeed certainly becomes liberated while living and composed of all beings.
My body, with its various limbs, is being described; listen with respect.
I am indeed Brahman and none other; this very thing is the body.
The consciousness of all beings has the nature of the Śabdabrahman;
it is manifested in the form of phonemes through the various divisions of mantras, vidyās, and so forth.
Having illuminated [the seat] with saffron, agallochum, musk, gorocanā, sandalwood,
and camphor upon your pedestal, it should be so arranged that the [deity] remains situated within the Śakti.
In that regard, worship should always be performed according to the specific prescriptions for each respective path;
for the mantra is the primordial body of all the gods.

The mantra-practitioner should worship that [Guru] as being identical in nature with the deity of the mantra and one's own self. O God, what is further described as the second [form] is that which falls within the scope of meditative visualization.
Having fashioned an image made of jewels, constructed from pure gold,
one should worship the God there every day and also month by month.

Or else, one should perform the unsurpassed great festival lasting for the rainy season; provided that one is not turned away by resorting to hypocrisy or due to the loss of wealth. (Note: *doṣo nāśya* appears to be a variant reading for *dravyanāśa*.)

May the ancestors and the hosts of gods turn their faces away from that evil-minded one who has frustrated my desire in the performance of this great festival. (Note: *samarā* is an alternative reading for *sāmarā*.)

Therefore, when the next day has arrived, having awakened [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, one should worship daily with devotion until the completion of its great festival. (The reading *pūrṇāntam* is found in manuscript *ka*; *pūrṇam* is in manuscript *ma*. 17.
The third [type] is said to be a yantra or a jewel fashioned from gold;
having understood it as being merely my own form, the wise one [should do so] through a true guru. (18)
One whose self is absorbed in me should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, through the non-duality of me;
[using] sandalwood, agallochum, musk, yellow pigment, camphor, and saffron. (19)
Having drawn [the mandala] with noble flowers, one should worship according to the procedure taught by you;
one should apply an ointment made from darbha grass grown on the shoulders of a boar.
One should perform the rubbing away of impurities with darbha grass grown from the body of Varāha;
therein my pleasure becomes complete for twelve years.
One should always keep the empty space free from obstacles and other hindrances by means of red flowers that provide fragrance and pleasant touch. || 22 ||
Having clothed him within the interior of the palace with garments that grant ultimate happiness—extremely pure, white, and captivating to the mind—with your own emblem; || 23 ||
One should install and worship [the deity] together, for I do not exist without you, nor, O God, are you the Lord without me. (24)
Therefore, one who desires success should always install us here;
or whoever should recite this supreme mantra with coral and pearls [as beads]. (25)
O Śaṅkara, whoever performs worship daily with devotion and faith, according to the very method of the conduct of the observance (samayācāra) spoken by you, [attains the goal]. || 26 ||
Embracing that Śiva with four hands in the form of Time,
and joined with Māmakī as his creative power (kalā), I make him the Lord of the City.
My fourth form is supreme and hidden upon the surface of the earth;
there, worship must always be performed according to the ritual of the Kula sacrifice.

In all states of woe and everywhere, the Kaula Dharma is the supreme and great one; while all the Sūtras and Nigamas are accessible, the Kaula Dharma is indeed difficult to attain. (The reading *svā* is found in manuscript *ka*.)

This Kaula tradition, though naturally difficult to traverse, appears as if easy to follow, wherein the origin of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others is proclaimed. (Note: *prabhavaḥ* is the reading in manuscript *ka*; *prabhavaḥ* is the reading in manuscript *tam*.)

That supreme abode of mine, the form of Brahman whose birth is manifest, has been attained through the grace of the true Guru; therein lies worship of great exaltation. (Note: *labdhvā* is the reading in manuscript *ka*).
That which reveals Brahman and is established in it is called Brahman;
through the vision of which the auspicious Brahman shines forth by itself.
By the mere touch of this [mantra], one merges into Brahman itself;
having merged as it were into the ocean of bliss, one no longer perceives the ocean of worldly existence.
"The Kaula dharma has been proclaimed by you; having attained that, one should worship the Kula.
My form is the Supreme Śakti, and you, O Lord, are the Linga. (34)
"O Śaṅkara, know that semen is Śiva and the menstrual flow is Śakti;
O Maheśvara, this entire world is completely filled by you and me. (35)
I alone am the Supreme Brahman; through the distinction of Śiva and Śakti, this world has become differentiated. Herein, delusion alone is the cause.
That which is spoken of as "you" and "I" is the great delusion of ignorance; "That thou art"—that alone am I, for neither you nor I exist, but only That.
"There is indeed no difference between us; understand this through reasoning, O Śaṅkara! When you are dissolved within me, I am indeed you, the Lord. (38)
O Śiva, when we two have met in the form of straight lines, O Maheśvara, one attains great liberation through that very experience of enjoyment. 49.
Even through thousands of millions of eons and hundreds of millions of eons, there would be no joy for me from worship performed here in any other manner. (40)
O Śiva, I derive no pleasure from loads of meat, nor likewise from oceans of wine,
as much as the joy that arises for me from the nectars of the bhaga and liṅga.
"I alone am all women here in the worlds, O Mahādeva"—thinking thus, the wise, endowed with devotion, worship me. (This is the reading in the Ta-Ka manuscript. || 42 ||
Those gods whose life-breaths are centered in me, who wear my garments and my ornaments, who do not abandon their own duties, and who have come to me alone for refuge; || 43 ||
Furthermore, those wealthy ones, even while living on this earth, are liberated;
you should know yourself by the mere touch of my body. 44.
Enter into me, O Lord of All; accept me, the eternal one.
Cast away your doubt, O Mahādeva; do not forget your own self.
"Viṣṇu drinks from my left breast and Brahmā from my right;
you, O Mahādeva, drink the nectar flowing from my lower lip."
Approaching, touching, or looking at women, and sporting with them, the best of practitioners should nevertheless perform meditation, worship, and recitation for me. (47)
The practitioner of mantra should always be endowed with power; he must not be devoid of it. O God, one who is separated from that power is incapable of performing any ritual action.
Just as a woman deprived of her husband is excluded from all ritual duties, so too is a mantra-practitioner devoid of power; therefore, be endowed with power. 49.
If a single wife is virtuous and submissive, her conduct leads to prosperity;
but a wicked wife is a destroyer of the family and leads only to ruin. 50.
O Śiva, just as a treasury on the bank of a river is divided by clans, so too does bliss arise from the union of the bhaga and the liṅga. (51)
One should know that very Brahman, which is infinite and the means to liberation;
it consists of worshiping the Guru, the drawing in of the hands [of the senses], and the performance of rites for the removal of obstacles. (52)

Whispering secrets into the ear is indeed the āsana; kissing the cheeks is the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi); embracing is contentment; and restraint of the senses is self-control. || 53 ||

Breath control (prāṇāyāma), drawing [the deity] toward the breasts, and ritual placement (nyāsa) are prescribed here; likewise, nail-marks, tooth-bites, and the like, as well as the offering of incense and lamps.
Flatteries at the end of lovemaking, the union of limbs like beautiful flowers, the sight and touch of the vulva, and the rubbing of the penis against its transformations; || 55 ||
The drinking of the nectar from the lower [mouth], as well as self-entrance, the casting out and lifting up, and likewise falling and rising; || 56 ||
The ritual services such as libations, churning, and likewise the oblation;
the sound of "sītkāra," the muttering of mantras, and the state of single-minded devotion to the offering to Brahman. (57)
Moaning, singing, hymning (the reading *stutya* is found in manuscript *kha*), and the emission of semen— O Mahādeva, it is precisely in this manner that my worship is proclaimed.

Whoever performs this daily practice of the one [goddess] who possesses many forms (bahurūpiṇī), being himself liberated while living and a god, shall accomplish even that which is impossible to achieve. 59.

One should worship while remaining in the state of the Vāmā, using enjoyments such as the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other offerings; or else, by abandoning the actions prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, or by fully resorting to them.
By abandoning those respective actions, one is born into inferior births;
yet, having experienced much happiness there—[a state] very difficult for others to attain—[61]
By the grace of the practice of knowledge and through enjoyment, one may attain liberation;
thus, the enjoyer indeed experiences many kinds of most enchanting pleasures.
And having encountered various such [conditions], one should enter into detachment;
likewise regarding things that are essence-less, those that possess essence, and those that are utterly devoid of substance. (63)
Having thus distinguished [the Self] through various means such as discernment (viveka),
the practitioner who knows yoga, fixing his mind upon the supreme reality which is the essence, [proceeds].
This entire world of moving and non-moving beings is essence-less, unreal, and devoid of beginning or end;
therein alone exists some Reality that is truly imperishable.

Then, having realized that Brahman which consists of bliss within himself, the practitioner [should sit] on a soft seat in a solitary, secluded, and beautiful place. (Note: "mṛḍa" is read as "duḥkha" in some versions. || 66 ||

Seated, one should contemplate Brahman, overflowing with supreme bliss, delighting in the contemplation of Brahman, and free from longing for worldly enjoyments. (Note: *parāmodī* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
Taking a single wife, a yoginī who accompanies him,
the yogin shall accomplish that which is otherwise unachievable, with the yoginī alone as his companion.
O Lord, O Supreme Ishvara, just as you have been deluded by me along with Parvati, so too did the goddess Parvati speak again to Shankara. (69)

[Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kulayāga and the Knowledge Consisting of Śiva and Śakti," in the glorious Gandharvatantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 40 ||

[The Forty-first Chapter] Having bowed to the auspicious one, the abode of liberation, whose bliss is incomparable and of a single flavor, the supreme Śivā, full of joy like a disciple, spoke to him: 1.
Pārvatī said:
Be gracious, O you who consist of supreme bliss, whose form is perfectly tranquil (or, according to another reading, whose form is accompanied by Śakti).
Whatever supreme reality has been known by me in its true essence— [2]
O Lord, you have fully explained all the mantras, the supreme rites, the yogas, the meditative absorptions, the knowledge, and likewise other things desired by me. (3)
O Lord, you ought to explain in truth that reality which is the cause of them— supreme beyond the supreme— the Śāmbhava state, which is unsurpassed.
I wish to know in truth the nature of the pervasion of the expressed form;
for it is true, O Lord, that manifestation is dependent upon reflective awareness. (5)
"You alone shall be under my control; speak as you have been told, O Śaṅkara.
Śambhu said:
"It is most secret, subtle, and beyond the reach of speech and mind."
"That which was guarded by me with effort is not told to anyone;
indeed, it is my conviction that you are none other than I. (Note: *pyasya* is an alternative reading for *pyasi*.)
"You too remember this; it is known by you as well, O beloved:
that the perfection of the union of Being and Consciousness results in my being under your control, since she [the Goddess] is under your control and I am hers. (Note: *mama vaśyā* is the reading.)
And they declare that very thing to be the answer; what I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth.
For when that [reality] alone exists as a state of non-duality, being beginningless, endless, and consciousness itself—then [it is the truth].
Then the sages, the best among the knowers of reality, call it Śāmbhava;
it is that very state when one becomes full of bliss through the realization "I am this. (10)
At that very moment, the state of Śambhu arises; this has been stated in these three words:
"Śakra (or Śakti), Triśūlī, Sarga. If one is adorned by these very [words], then that is the end.

For she alone is proclaimed as the supreme Śrī by the sages, the abode of the great "I" which is the absolute oneness consisting of the mass of light and bliss. (Note: *mahamā* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
Because she is devoted to Me for the sake of the great accomplishment, she is called "Parā" (the Supreme).
O Parameśānī, those mantras which are joined with her at the very beginning [attain success]. (13)
It is my conviction that they sustain one another through mantras;
these sixty-seven phonemes of Prakṛti are the agents of the creation and other processes of the world. (14)
Because these constitute the very life-force of this world, it is unsurpassed.
Pārvatī said:
"They are both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala), and they are the awakeners of the path to liberation. (15)
"There are indeed many mantras; tell me the unsurpassed among them.
Śambhu said:
"Even these [mantras] spoken by us are oceans of misfortune for some."
O Goddess of the lords of gods, you are the cause of the Manūs for us two;
O Maheśvarī, having obtained you, we have attained all mantras indeed. (17)
That which is to be attained by us two is also known as the unsurpassed;
it exists as both accessible and inaccessible due to the repetition of these syllables. (18)
And because [the Self] is the cause that cannot be approached, O beloved, [we two] are the ones to be approached;
for it exists within the inner self of all, either as "this-ness" (idantā) or as "I-ness" (ahantā). || 19 ||
But that meaning which is being realized is itself the definitive realization of Śiva,
by virtue of its nature as full subjectivity (pūrṇāhantā), and not through artificial subjectivity (kṛtrimāhantā).
He who sees this entire universe as both external and internal truly sees; O Great Goddess, within the state of non-duality, you alone are beloved by all living beings.
Even those who are ignorant of You are all beloved of the Unsurpassed One.
Pārvatī said:
"That supreme reality, the glorious Parā, which was previously taught by You—"
That very state has been declared by me as Nirvāṇa;
now, among the most secret things, that alone is the unsurpassed [teaching]. (23)

O Lord, whose form is permeated by the awareness of supreme bliss, I do not desire attachment of the mind even to this very state of absolute liberation (kaivalya), which you praise. (Note: The reading "cetaḥśleṣa" is supported by manuscript *ka*.)
Śambhu said:
"O beautiful one, both things you have described are indeed true;
however, that unsurpassed state previously mentioned is to be attained through the supreme [path]. (25)
Even though this is thus agreed upon by both of them, there is nevertheless a great difference between them;
for the latter [the Śaivas] possess twenty-seven internal and external qualities of action. (26)
O Maheśvarī, because she is devoid of the limiting adjuncts of pride, form, and action, some hold the view of the Yoginīs that she is worthy of worship as a portion of our own creative power (kalā).
Even for others, that unsurpassed state previously described is attainable.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, you have described its majesty to me in many ways. (28)
By this means, one should never see anything as ill-spoken;
for everything that is desired has been explained, and even that which was spoken is unsurpassed. (19)
"I am not able to determine this in its true essence; please tell it to me.
Śambhu said: "In ultimate reality, there is no difference between us two because of our absolute non-duality. (30)
"This is such-and-such," as was said before, I have accepted [it]. The goddess of the voice has been attained; no further deliberation is required. || 31 ||

If that which is to be attained through the stability of other states arises from the effects of the qualities (guṇas), then I shall once again declare the definitive determination of the meaning already spoken by me. (32)
That which was previously described as the unsurpassed, transcending the sphere of mind and speech, undergoes a threefold division from the seed-syllables known as Bindu and Nāda. (33)
Those very [energies] become [the three goddesses] through the division of Sat, Cit, and Ānanda; for from that *bindu* which is my own essential nature, *nāda* indeed arises, O Radiant One.

O Goddess, because of the state of the equality (samarasībhāva) of the two, that which is called the Seed (bīja) has been declared for us both; and on the path of the knowledge of unity, O Goddess, this [seed] is the designator of Śambhu.
Having honored [the deities] according to the sequence of their colors, one should perform the meditation on union (mithunabhāvanā).
O Great Goddess, by proceeding in this manner, one shall attain that which is beyond the unsurpassed (anuttaratā).
Like fire within wood, when fully aroused, one should cross over the earth;
but that [power] which consists of the state of *śakti* arises from the friction of the consonant (*vyañjana*, variant: *vārjana*). || 67 ||

Having honored [the deity] with the vow-offering (*vrata-homa*), one should personally practice one's own true nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, that which is of such a nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*) ending in reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). || 38 ||
I lead each one higher and higher through that sequence and its reverse;
contraction and expansion are the two natures associated with the sun.

Those two, however, should be as sacrifices, being temples of light and bliss, consisting of existence and consciousness, the essence of action, and devoted to the practice of the liberated self. (40)

That which is the unsurpassed cause for us two is the fruit hanging from the hollow of Śiva’s staff, ending with the wife [of the fire] within the heart. (Note: *hṛdayānala* is the reading in manuscript *ka*; *śivadaṇḍīvilaṃ* is the reading in manuscript *kha*. 41.
Manifest within, it is immeasurable and facing in all directions;
it is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, resembling a waveless ocean.
It is pure existence and pure consciousness, enveloped in the essence of their unity;
devoid of darkness and light, it is the supreme reality, far greater than the subtle atom.
And because it is the greatness of the great, that which is designated as Brahman is unsurpassed;
therefore, contemplate that very thing with a concentrated mind. (44)
By this practice, the mantra quickly becomes possessed of being and attains identity with it;
when, through the perfection of that identity, one perceives the entire universe as abiding within oneself.
Through that state of rest, by virtue of its oneness with that [reality], it will attain bliss—just as when the clear sky is suddenly filled with dense clouds. (46)
Just as [a bird] flies up and dissolves [into the sky], so too does the world dissolve into the unsurpassed Self;
in this way, O lady of noble vows, the realization of recognition (pratyabhijñā) shall be achieved for you.
"Afterwards, I am no longer able to experience that self-evident bliss;
for you are the Supreme and possess supreme power, whereas such [bliss] was not ordained for me. (48)
"Beyond this, I know nothing; I swear this to you many times.
Having heard this, the Great Goddess indeed perceived this deliberation regarding the matter. (Note: *vimarṣaṇa* is an alternative reading for *darśana*. 49.
That very thing was immediately revealed by him, whose mind was filled with wonder:
"This is a great marvel to me, that he remains here complete. (50)
Having reflected thus, Sundarī embraced the foot of the God;
then, through their mutual friction, she was greeted by intense bliss.

That every reality which is essentially luminous has attained its state of absolute isolation (kevalatā), yet has reached [the state of] reflective awareness (vimarśa)—this is the ultimate ontological condition. (52)
The intellect of those whose being consists solely of one-pointed attention is itself the nature of the witness.
What need is there for those wretched means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), by which [the self] would otherwise be unproven? (Note: *kaistaiścidevāpramāṇakaḥ* is an alternative reading. 53.
The light of the sun does not depend on the illumination of a lamp;
for everything is revealed within the mirror of vast, stainless expanse. || 54 ||
Thus, the universe consists of consciousness and is divided into thirty-six principles (*tattvas*).
At the beginning is the pure principle, which is fivefold and beyond darkness (*tamas*).
When Śiva was fashioned from the letters beginning with *ha* and ending with *kṣa*, he became differentiated as Śiva, Śakti, Sādākhya, Īśa, and Vidya. (56)
