Kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, and niyati are said to be the armor (or bondage).
Preceded by Māyā, they consist of the letters beginning with *va* and ending with *ya*. || 57 ||

Pradhāna, [and] the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the five [subtle elements] beginning with *mātra*; the five beginning with hearing (*śrotra*), the five beginning with *tva* (touch), and the five beginning with speech (*vāk*). || 58 ||

The five subtle elements (tanmātras), beginning with [the letter] *ma* (or *mā*, or *yā*, according to the various readings), and the five [gross elements] beginning with earth (*bhūmi*) and [the letter] *ka*; these are remembered as the Śiva-tattva, the first vibration of the Lord who desires to create. (59)
His very will is the elephant-goad of the principle of power (śakti-tattva), which has withered away;
having manifested the universe by his own will, he remains veiling it through the principle of I-consciousness (ahantā). || 60 ||
That very [consciousness] is the *tattva* called Sādākhya, intent upon bestowing grace upon all;
that same [consciousness], perceiving the universe through the sense of "this-ness," becomes the *tattva* of Īśvara. (61)
The identity between "I" and "this" is declared to be that which is called *vidyā*.

The principle of *māyā* is the cognition of differentiation regarding those entities that constitute one's own limbs [of being]. (Variant readings: *aikyam* for *aikyaṃ*; *tvavibhedinī* for *vibhedadhīḥ*) || 62 ||
Śiva, having assumed contraction through Māyā, is called the principle of the individual soul (puṃstattva).
Indeed, this very one is perceived as the transmigrating being, the living soul, and the enjoyer. (63)
The powers of knowledge, agency, perfection, eternity, and so forth, having become contracted through that [primordial] contraction, exist in the form of *kalā*, *vidyā*, and the rest. (64)
From Māyā arises that which is called Kalā, characterized by limited agency;
Vidyā is the cause of limited knowledge; and Rāga is the cause of attachment (or, according to another reading, exertion). || 65 ||
Whether it be Time as the delimiting factor or Necessity (niyati), this very restriction— namely, "this alone must be done by me and nothing else"— is the form of constraint.
Prakṛti is the equilibrium of the guṇas; it is the birthplace of the ego (ahaṃkāra) and the rest.
Ahaṃkṛti is the cause of the cognition "I," "mine," and "this. (Note: There is a variant reading *ahiṃsā* for *ahaṃ*. || 67 ||

The intellect (buddhi) is the cause of determination (adhyavasāya), which is of the nature of certainty (or, according to the *ka* manuscript, of necessity). The mind (manas) is declared to be the seed of conceptualization (saṃkalpa) and discursive thought (vikalpa). 68.
From speech and so forth, that is, from sound and so forth, there arise speech and so forth, as well as hearing and so forth;
the instruments for hearing and the other senses are to be understood as the five subtle elements (tanmātras). (69)
The five elements, beginning with space and ending with the earth, constitute the cause of the [five] directions.
Within the pure [reality] consisting of the supreme and inferior powers, there is the pentad beginning with Vidyā.
That which is other than that is declared to be the principle of Vidyā, the Aparā-śakti (according to the reading in manuscript Kha).

Now, this goddess Parā-śakti is of the nature of the womb (*garbhiṇī*), carrying within her the half of the pure and impure paths (*śuddhāśuddhādhva*). (According to the reading in manuscript Ka: "the remover of the half-path"). || 71 ||
When the principles (tattvas), beginning with earth, are dissolved into their cause,
then the causes alone emit their powers (śaktis) outwardly.

In the supreme will, there is the opening [of the eyes], the state of being complete in bliss, and the root-nature of the vowels consisting of the powers of action, will, and knowledge—these are the six. (73)
From that, the power of will (*icchaiśanā*) arises, consisting of the manifest and unmanifest universe;
then there are four neuter phonemes (*ṣaṇḍavarṇāḥ*), which are pure selves impelled [by the preceding powers]. (Regarding "ṣaṇḍā" after "varṇāḥ," the reading "kha" is neuter. || 74 ||
When the powers of supreme bliss (anuttarānanda) and will (icchā) are joined within the power of will,
the triangle and the hexagon then become established within that will.
Through the union of the two triangles, the powers of supreme bliss [are formed]; likewise, through the union of unmeṣa, the manifest form of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) arises. (76)
From the aforementioned conjunction of the three powers arises the trident, which devours duality;
it flourishes in all activities through mutual non-opposition. (77)

In no way can this form belong to them as something produced; rather, it is the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of the object of experience, which is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and this is what constitutes creation. (Note: *vimarśaḥ* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
The Supreme Śakti, whose form consists of the sixteen digits (kalās), gives birth to the seed-syllables,
just as the lunar days (tithis) begin with the first (pratipad) and end with the fifteenth.

Just as the sun and moon move within one's own heart for the sake of maintaining existence, so too are the primordial digits of emanation known to have the nature of reflective awareness (vimarśa). 80.
This Goddess Mātṛkā exists in two ways, by way of being both the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the womb (*yoni*).

With her body eternally manifest and blazing, she is the birthplace of the universe, having the form of a triangle (*śṛṅgāṭa*) from which the universe arises. (Note: *ka* in the text appears to be a scribal error for *ca*.)
The heart of this consciousness is that supreme light;
just as a tree exists within a banyan seed, so too is the universe present therein. (Note: *veda* is the reading in manuscript *ka*.)
When investigated, that which is not distinct from its cause—such as the reality of jars and the like being nothing other than clay—is not found to be anything else upon analysis. (83)

Thus speak the final words of the Śrutis, which declare the truth, based on the definitive conclusion: "In the beginning, this entire world, including the gods, did not exist; what else could have existed? (The variant reading *kha* is: "What else was there?"). 84.

Within this seed-syllable which denotes pure existence, the entire universe—from the earth element up to Māyā—remains with its objective forms and conceptualizations dissolved; thus, only that [pure existence] remains. (85)

Then the Vidyeśvaras and Sadāśivas, whose essence consists of knowledge and action, dissolve into the trident— which is the power (Śakti), the wielder of the trident (Triśūlinī), and Kālī— whose nature comprises fourteen kalās.

Above and below, within the body of emanation, everything is dissolved; beyond that, in this manner, within supreme consciousness, that consciousness of emission [gradually unfolds]. (The variant reading *sā sarvasaṃkucitā* is noted. 87.

Or rather, [it exists] in that which is beyond speech and mind, in whatever place it may be, stainless, and within the range that transcends the surging waves (or: the waves of the fruit) of the thirty-six principles.
She dissolves into the Great Mantra, which is the Self of all, into that very nature;
when the abode has been stirred from some cause by someone, it becomes radiant. (89)
Offering all this as an oblation, one is not afflicted by poverty;
O Goddess, it consists of five times five and is the manifestation of the fivefold vibration.

Contracting [the senses], discerning, and consisting solely of the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspandaka*), bringing about the dissolution of the "I" (*aham*)— which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the "this" (*idam*)—
one who is intent on valor enjoys his own nature, which removes all inauspiciousness. (91)
[Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the System of Unsurpassed Knowledge," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 41 ||
[The Forty-second Chapter]
Śrī Pārvatī said:
How is speech produced, and how does it dissolve?
Tell me the definitive determination of speech, and afterwards, declare its true nature.
Īśvara said:
From the Unmanifest (avyakta) the vital breath (prāṇa) is produced; from the vital breath the mind (manas) is produced;
from the mind speech (vāk) is produced; speech dissolves into the mind. (2)

The Goddess said: "Who is it that desires food? And who eats [or drinks, according to the reading 'pibati īśa']? Who is it that drinks? Who is it that stays awake? Who is it that sleeps? And who, once asleep, awakens? (3)
Īśvara said: Prāṇa desires food, and Hutāśana indeed eats it;
Vāyu remains awake while one sleeps, and Tejas awakens one when asleep. || 4 ||
The Goddess said:
Who indeed commits sins? Or who is stained by sin?
Who is bound and who is liberated? And who is released from sins? (5)
Īśvara said:
The mind commits sins; the mind is stained by sin.
When the mind has become free from mentation, there is neither dharma nor transgression.
The Goddess said:
"This power (Śakti), which is the ether residing within the body yet devoid of the body—how can that which is situated in the body be simultaneously devoid of both the embodied one and the body? (7)
How does the individual soul (jīva) abide in the body, or what is proclaimed to be the individual soul?
By what does this soul see, and by which path does it move about? (8)
How can the *jīva* be with parts (*sakala*), and how can it be without parts (*niṣkala*)?
By what does this *jīva* live, and what is the food of the *jīva*? (Note: *Sakala* is an alternative reading for *saphala*.)
From where does the individual soul (jīva) dissolve, and from where indeed is it born?
What is the soul, how is the vital breath (prāṇa), and by what is the soul proclaimed? || 10 ||
O Śaṅkara, tell me this entire truth according to its true nature, by which, O Lord, I, submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, may be liberated. (11)
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, for I shall explain that which you have requested.
I shall tell it to you without doubt—the auspicious essence of essences.
Wind, fire, and space as the third—these are designated as the living soul (jīva).
That jīva is called the vital breath (prāṇa), conceived as being as subtle as the hundredth part of the tip of a hair.
The individual soul (jīva) and the vital seed (śukra) are to be understood as existing as long as they are established with the quality of sattva;
when joined with the quality of rajas, the wind is proclaimed to be the individual soul.
When joined with *tamas*, he would certainly be delighted;
and when joined with *sattva*, he becomes a promoter of dharma and knowledge. || 15 ||
When joined with rajas, the lord enjoys sense objects;
and when joined with tamas, he is then defiled by sin.
The tip of the nose, the navel, and the heart as the third—
these places have been ordained for the individual soul by Śiva.
"The heart-lotus and the head remain as long as [the principle of] *sattva* is established;
this is called 'abiding in the body' by Śiva, the Supreme Self. (18)
As long as the individual soul does not move, it attains immobility;
situated in the navel, having realized the partless [Brahman], one is liberated from the bondage of birth. || 19 ||
Abiding in the navel at all times, the omnipresent Lord dwells in the heart;
situated within the mouth and the nostrils, He experiences the objects of the senses.
The individual soul (jīva), residing within the body, perceives both [the world] and Maheśvara;
established in the body, the embodied soul (dehin) experiences auspicious enjoyment.
When the living being, having abandoned the body, has resorted to the external space, then that living being becomes one whose object is the Self; of this there is no doubt. || 22 ||
One should meditate upon this partless Brahman as Sadāśiva;
having meditated upon Śiva as the innate reality, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
Pervading all, residing in every body, and established at the tip of the nose,
he is perceptible to all beings, yet he is not perceived.
The individual soul (jīva), which is the pure principle (śuddhatattva) and stainless, resides in the center of the navel;
it is radiant like the sun, blazing with rays, and auspicious. || 25 ||
The individual soul (jīva) resembles half of the letter *ha*; that soul is situated within the body.
It is known to reside in the cavity of the navel, remaining there as it encounters the objects of the senses. (Note: *nābhirandhracita* is an alternative reading.)
By that [Self], this entire universe is pervaded, just as milk is pervaded by ghee;
and it is not the cause of itself through the five vital breaths, prāṇa and apāna.
Through the application of inhalation and exhalation, it moves upward, just as a dry leaf is carried into the sky by the wind. (28)
In this manner, that which is called the *jīva* wanders by means of the five vital breaths, *prāṇa* and *apāna*;
joined with the four *kalās*, it revolves while stationed within the heart. (29)
But just as, O Goddess, a ball struck by its own stick leaps up and falls down again and again, swiftly and without rest; (the reading *tatastu patane* is also found). 30.
Pārvatī said:
"This entire Brahman is beyond the ether, stainless, partless, pure, peaceful, devoid of phenomenal expansion, and without defining characteristics. (31)
It is imperceptible, unknowable, and devoid of both destruction and origination;
it is absolute, solitary, peaceful, and resembles pure crystal. (32)
O Śaṅkara, tell me that knowledge by which one is liberated in that very instant— [a knowledge] free from the yoga of the instruments of action and devoid of causes and means of proof.
Īśvara said:

O highly fortunate lady, it was this very Kumāra, the son of Brahmā, who, having approached Viṣṇu—the Lord of Yoga and the sole cause of the universe—[spoke]. (Note: *yogīśam* is the reading in some manuscripts.)
With supreme devotion, he said: "O Lord, speak the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) by which the wise man, having quickly cast off all sin, attains the Person who is higher than the highest. (35)
To him he said: "Learn [the truth] from me, the Lord of the Universe, through the yoga of faith, devotion, and meditation;
not by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth."
By means of renunciation alone, they attained immortality. || 36 ||
Beyond the sky, it is placed in a secret cave;
it shines brilliantly,
which the ascetics enter, having ascertained its meaning through the wisdom of the Vedānta.
Through the yoga of renunciation, the self-controlled become purified. (The reading *saṃnyāsayogāt* is found in the Gītā Kaivalya Pāṭha.)
At the time of the ultimate end, they shall all be completely liberated through supreme immortality in the worlds of Brahmā;
and one who dwells in a secluded place, seated upon a comfortable seat—
Pure, with his neck, head, and body held erect. || 38 ||
Staying in his own hermitage, having restrained all the senses and bowed with devotion to his own guru,
[he beheld] the painless, pure [Self] within the lotus of the heart.
Having reflected upon that which is luminous and free from sorrow in the midst [of all things]. || 39 ||
The inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite-formed,
auspicious, peaceful, immortal Brahman, the source [of all],
which is indeed one and devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
The wondrous rite, which is consciousness, bliss, and formless. || 40 ||
Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the Master, who has Umā as his companion, who is three-eyed, blue-throated, and tranquil,
the sage goes to the source of all beings.
The witness of all, beyond darkness. || 41 ||
He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Indra; He is the Imperishable, the Supreme Self-ruler.
He alone is Viṣṇu, He is Prāṇa, He is Time, He is Fire, and He is the Moon. (42)
He alone, having known all that has been and that is yet to be—the eternal—transcends death; there is no other path to liberation. (43)
Perceiving the Self abiding in all beings and all beings within the Self,
one attains the Supreme Brahman through no other means.

Making the self the lower fire-drill and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill, the wise man burns away evil through the practice of the churning of knowledge (*jñāna*). (Note: *jñāna-* is the reading from manuscript *kha*.)
That very self, its nature utterly deluded by māyā,
assumes a body and performs all actions through various enjoyments such as women, food, drink, and the like.
He alone attains complete satisfaction while awake. || 46 ||
And in the dream state, the individual soul (jīva) is the experiencer of pleasure and pain within the world of phenomena imagined by its own māyā;
at the time of deep sleep, when everything has dissolved.
Overcome by darkness, one attains the nature of pleasure. || 47 ||
And again, through the connection with the karma of another birth, that very same living being sleeps and wakes;
he who sports within the three cities is the living being.
From that, however, everything diverse has been born. || 48 ||
That which is the support, bliss, and indivisible consciousness,
wherein the three cities (the body, speech, and mind) dissolve;
from this [consciousness] arise the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs.
Space, wind, fire, water, and the earth which sustains all things. || 49 ||
Furthermore, that which is Brahman—the Self of all, the great abode of all, eternal, and subtler than the subtle—that very reality is you alone. (50)
Having realized that "I am that Brahman," by which the manifold world of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth is illumined, one is liberated from all bonds. (51)

Whatever may be the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoying within the three abodes—I am distinct from all those; I am pure consciousness, the eternally auspicious Śiva. (The reading "the witness" [sākṣī] is found in manuscript K.)
Everything has arisen in me alone; everything is established in me;
everything goes to dissolution in me—that Brahman which is without duality (or, according to another reading, without difference), that am I.
I am indeed subtler than the subtlest; likewise, I am the Great One, I am the manifold universe,
I am the Ancient One, I am the Puruṣa, I am the Lord.
I am golden; I am the form of Śiva. || 54 ||
I am without hands or feet, yet possessed of inconceivable power;
I see without eyes, I hear without ears; I perceive all, being of a distinct and transcendent form.
And there is no knower; I am eternally consciousness and existence.
By many Vedas I alone am to be known; I am the author of the Vedanta and the knower of the Vedas.
For me there is neither merit nor sin, nor is there destruction.
There is no birth, nor body, senses, or intellect. || 56 ||
Earth is not mine, nor are water, fire, air, or space;
having thus understood the nature of the Supreme Self, [one remains established therein].
Dwelling in the cave [of the heart], partless, and without a second. || 57 ||
It attains the state of the pure Supreme Self, the witness of all, which is devoid of both being and non-being. || 58 ||
Whoever thoroughly studies this tantra becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified from the drinking of liquor;
he becomes purified from what should and should not be done; he becomes purified from approaching those who should not be approached.
[Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Knowledge of Reality," in the glorious Gandharva Tantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara. || 42 ||
[This is completed; may it be offered to the illustrious Śiva.]
